| **Additional neutral Higgs bosons** (CP‑even \(H^{0}\), CP‑odd \(A^{0}\) of a 2‑Higgs‑Doublet Model, MSSM) | \(\displaystyle O_{S}= (\bar q\,P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\mu),\qquad O_{P}= (\bar q\,P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu)\)  (and the chirality‑flipped versions with \(P_{L}\) on the quark current) | The leptonic current is **pure scalar or pseudoscalar**: \(\bar u(p_{-})\,\mathbb{1}\,v(p_{+})\) or \(\bar u(p_{-})\gamma_{5}v(p_{+})\).  These bilinears **do not require a chirality flip**; they couple a left‑handed muon to a left‑handed anti‑muon (or right‑handed to right‑handed) and therefore survive in the \(m_\mu\!\to\!0\) limit. |
| **Lepto‑quarks** that generate tree‑level four‑fermion scalar operators (e.g. \(S_{1}\) or \(R_{2}\) scalar lepto‑quarks) | Same \(O_{S},O_{P}\) as above, with Wilson coefficients proportional to the product of the lepto‑quark Yukawa couplings divided by the lepto‑quark mass squared. | Same reason as for Higgs: the leptonic bilinear is scalar/pseudoscalar. |
| **Heavy neutral gauge bosons with mixed vector‑axial couplings** (Z′ that couples to right‑handed quarks and left‑handed leptons) can, after Fierz rearrangement, generate scalar operators at one loop. | (Effective) \(O_{S,P}\) as above, albeit loop‑suppressed. | Same as above. |

### (d) Amplitude and branching‑fraction scaling  

The generic tree‑level contribution of a heavy scalar \(ϕ\) (mass \(M_{ϕ}\)) that couples to quarks and leptons as  

\[
\mathcal L\supset y_{qb}^{ϕ}\,\bar q P_{R} b\,ϕ + y_{\mu}^{ϕ}\,\bar\mu P_{R/L}\mu\,ϕ^{\dagger}+{\rm h.c.}
\]

produces, after integrating out \(ϕ\),

\[
C_{S}^{ϕ}= \frac{y_{qb}^{ϕ}\,y_{\mu}^{ϕ}}{M_{ϕ}^{2}},\qquad  
C_{P}^{ϕ}= \frac{y_{qb}^{ϕ}\,y_{\mu}^{ϕ}}{M_{ϕ}^{2}} \times (\pm 1),
\]

with the sign determined by the CP nature of \(ϕ\).  

The **amplitude** becomes  

\[
\mathcal A_{\rm NP}^{(S,P)} = -\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt2}\,\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\,
   V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}\;
   f_{B_{q}}\,\frac{m_{B_{q}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{q}}\;
   \bigl(C_{S} - C_{P}\bigr)\;
   \bigl[\bar u(p_-)\, \mathbb{1}\;(\text{or }\gamma_{5})\,v(p_+)\bigr].
\tag{1}
\]

Notice **no factor of \(m_{\mu}\)** appears anywhere.  

Squaring and summing spins gives

\[
|\mathcal A|^{2}\;\propto\;
\left|C_{S,P}\right|^{2}\,
\frac{f_{B_{q}}^{2} m_{B_{q}}^{4}}{(m_{b}+m_{q})^{2}}\,,
\qquad
\mathcal B \;\propto\;
\frac{1}{M_{ϕ}^{4}}\,
\bigl|y_{qb}^{ϕ} y_{\mu}^{ϕ}\bigr|^{2}.
\tag{2}
\]

Thus **the branching fraction scales as \(\displaystyle \frac{|y_{qb}^{ϕ}y_{\mu}^{ϕ}|^{2}}{M_{ϕ}^{4}}\)**, *independent* of the muon mass.  Any sizable NP coupling can raise \(\mathcal B\) by orders of magnitude relative to the SM value.

### (e) Typical size  

* In the MSSM at large \(\tan\beta\) the effective scalar coefficient is  

  \[
  C_{S}^{\rm MSSM}\simeq C_{P}^{\rm MSSM}\;\approx\;
   \frac{m_{b} m_{\mu}\tan^{3}\!\beta}{M_{A}^{2}}\,
   \frac{1}{(1+\epsilon_{0}\tan\beta)(1+\epsilon_{\ell}\tan\beta)} ,
  \]

  which **reintroduces a factor \(m_{\mu}\)** but is *enhanced* by \(\tan^{3}\!\beta\).  For \(\tan\beta\sim 60\) and \(M_{A}=300\) GeV the branching fraction can be 2–3 times the SM value.  

* For a **generic scalar lepto‑quark** of mass \(M_{LQ}=1\) TeV with couplings \(y_{qb}^{LQ}\,y_{\mu}^{LQ}\sim 0.3\) one gets  

  \[
  \mathcal B \sim 10^{-8}\;(\text{about }3\times\text{SM}),
  \]

  well within present experimental reach.

---

## 2.  Right‑handed (or mixed‑handed) vector/axial operators  

If the NP introduces **right‑handed quark currents** that couple to the *same* axial leptonic current, the operator basis enlarges to

\[
O_{10}^{\prime}= (\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\mu).
\]

### (c) Why the muon‑mass factor can be avoided  

The leptonic part is unchanged (axial), so the helicity suppression *still* exists **unless** the quark current carries a different phase that interferes with the SM left‑handed contribution **and** a *scalar* density appears via the equations of motion:

\[
\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b = \frac{1}{2m_{b}}\,\partial_{\mu}\bigl(\bar q P_{R}b\bigr) + \mathcal O(p/m_{b}^{2}).
\]

When the heavy‑quark equations of motion are used, the **right‑handed vector operator can be Fierz‑rearranged into a scalar operator suppressed by \(m_{b}\)**.  The net result is that an amplitude proportional to \(C_{10}^{\prime}\) still carries the **muon‑mass factor**, but *if* the NP also supplies a **right‑handed leptonic current** (\(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}P_{R}\mu\) or \(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\mu\)), the product

\[
(\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\mu)
\]

produces **no helicity suppression** because the lepton bilinear \(\bar u\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}v\) couples a left‑handed muon to a right‑handed anti‑muon – the same chirality configuration that a scalar does after a Fierz transformation.  In practice this shows up as the **operator**

\[
O_{VLL}^{\prime}= (\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\mu),
\qquad
O_{VRR}= (\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}P_{R}\mu).
\]

These are **not present in the SM** and would be generated by, for example, a **heavy \(Z'\) with right‑handed quark couplings and left‑handed lepton couplings**.

### (d) Parametric dependence  

Assume a heavy neutral gauge boson \(Z'\) of mass \(M_{Z'}\) with couplings  

\[
\mathcal L\supset g_{qb}^{R}\,\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b\, Z'^{\mu}
          + g_{\mu}^{L}\,\bar\mu\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}\mu\, Z'^{\mu}
          + g_{\mu}^{R}\,\bar\mu\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}\mu\, Z'^{\mu}.
\]

Integrating out the \(Z'\) gives

\[
C_{V}^{(R\!L)} = \frac{g_{qb}^{R}\,g_{\mu}^{L}}{M_{Z'}^{2}},\qquad
C_{V}^{(R\!R)} = \frac{g_{qb}^{R}\,g_{\mu}^{R}}{M_{Z'}^{2}} .
\]

The amplitude (after using the meson matrix element \(\langle0|\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b|B_{q}\rangle=i f_{B_{q}}p_{\mu}\)) reads

\[
\mathcal A_{Z'} = i\,\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt2}\,
   \frac{\alpha}{\pi}\,
   V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}\,
   f_{B_{q}}\,p_{\mu}\;
   \bigl[C_{V}^{(R\!L)}\,\bar u\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}v
        +C_{V}^{(R\!R)}\,\bar u\gamma^{\mu}P_{R}v\bigr].
\tag{3}
\]

Because the lepton bilinear now contains a **projection operator**, the spinor product does **not vanish** in the chiral limit; explicitly

\[
\bar u(p_-)\gamma^{\mu}P_{L,R}v(p_+)\;p_{\mu} = 
\bar u(p_-)\slashed{p}\,P_{L,R}v(p_+) = 0\;{\rm (if\;both\;states\;massless)} ?
\]

In fact, for a *pure vector* current the contraction with the meson momentum gives zero for on‑shell massless leptons (current conservation).  The **non‑vanishing piece comes from the axial component of the lepton current** (i.e. the difference of left‑ and right‑handed couplings).  Therefore the **only way to fully remove the \(m_{\mu}\) suppression** with a vector boson is to have **different chiralities for the two muons**, i.e. a *mixed* operator of the form  

\[
O_{VRL}= (\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\mu) - (\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}P_{R}\mu)
\]

which is equivalent to a **axial lepton current** with *right‑handed* quarks.  After Fierz rearrangement one obtains an **effective scalar** piece proportional to \(C_{VRL}\) times \(m_{\mu}\) **only if** the lepton current is *purely axial*.  Hence, **vector‑type mediators can only evade helicity suppression if they generate scalar/pseudoscalar four‑fermion operators at tree level** (as in a heavy Higgs) or if they produce a *tensor* operator (see below).

The **practical up‑shot**: a simple right‑handed Z' alone does **not** lift the muon‑mass factor; it merely adds a *second* term proportional to the same factor.  **Lifting the suppression requires a scalar‑type coupling**.

---

## 3.  Tensor operators  

A tensor bilinear couples the two muon spins in a way that does not enforce opposite helicities:

\[
O_{T}= (\bar q\sigma_{\mu\nu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\sigma^{\mu\nu}\mu), \qquad
O_{T5}= (\bar q\sigma_{\mu\nu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\sigma^{\mu\nu}\gamma_{5}\mu).
\]

### (c) Helicity‑suppression removal  

The leptonic part \(\bar u\sigma^{\mu\nu}v\) connects **same‑helicity** spinors; the matrix element survives in the massless limit.  Tensor operators can therefore give an amplitude **independent of \(m_{\mu}\)**.

### (d) Parametric scaling  

A heavy coloured scalar that couples as \(\lambda_{qb}\, \bar q P_{R} b\,\phi\) and \(\lambda_{\mu}\,\bar\mu\sigma^{\mu\nu} \mu\,\phi\) after integrating out \(\phi\) yields

\[
C_{T}\sim\frac{\lambda_{qb}\,\lambda_{\mu}}{M_{\phi}^{2}},\qquad
\mathcal A_{T}\sim \frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt2}\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\,
               f_{B_{q}}\frac{m_{B_{q}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{q}}\,
               C_{T}\;\bigl[\bar u\sigma^{\mu\nu}v\bigr].
\]

Squaring gives  

\[
\mathcal B\;\propto\;\frac{| \lambda_{qb}\lambda_{\mu}|^{2}}{M_{\phi}^{4}}.
\]

Tensor operators are **strongly constrained** by radiative decays \(b\to s\gamma\) and by limits on electric‑dipole moments, but in specific lepto‑quark models (e.g. vector lepto‑quark \(U_{1}\)) they can appear at tree level with modest couplings.

---

## 4.  Summary table of the *helicity‑suppression‑lifting* possibilities  

| NP source | Generated operator(s) | Helicity‑suppression status | Amplitude scaling (schematic) | Branching‑fraction scaling | Typical mass/coupling range that gives \(\mathcal B\sim \mathcal O(10^{-8})\) |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------------------|------------------------------|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Heavy neutral CP‑even/odd Higgs** (2HDM‑II, MSSM) | \(O_{S},O_{P}\) (scalar/pseudoscalar) | **No** \(m_\mu\) factor (leptonic scalar bilinear) | \(\displaystyle \mathcal A\sim \frac{y_{qb}\,y_{\mu}}{M_{H}^{2}}\,f_{B}m_{B}^{2}\) | \(\displaystyle \mathcal B\sim \frac{|y_{qb}y_{\mu}|^{2}}{M_{H}^{4}}\) | \(\tan\beta\sim 50\), \(M_{A}\simeq 300\!-\!500\) GeV → \(\mathcal B\) up to 3–5×SM |
| **Scalar lepto‑quark \(S_{1}\) or \(R_{2}\)** | \(O_{S}, O_{P}\) at tree level | **No** \(m_\mu\) factor | \(\displaystyle \mathcal A\sim \frac{g_{b\ell}\,g_{q\ell}}{M_{LQ}^{2}}\,f_{B}m_{B}^{2}\) | \(\displaystyle \mathcal B\sim \frac{|g_{b\ell}g_{q\ell}|^{2}}{M_{LQ}^{4}}\) | \(g\sim0.3\), \(M_{LQ}=1\) TeV → \(\mathcal B\approx 1\times10^{-8}\) |
| **Heavy pseudoscalar \(A^{0}\) with large \(\tan\beta\) (MSSM)** | \(O_{S,P}\) (enhanced by \(\tan^{3}\!\beta\)) | **Effective** removal of \(m_\mu\) *via* \(\tan^{3}\!\beta\) enhancement | \(\displaystyle \mathcal A\sim \frac{m_{b}m_{\mu}\tan^{3}\beta}{M_{A}^{2}} f_{B}\) (still contains \(m_{\mu}\) but multiplied by huge \(\tan^{3}\!\beta\)) | \(\displaystyle \mathcal B\sim \frac{m_{b}^{2}m_{\mu}^{2}\tan^{6}\beta}{M_{A}^{4}}\) | \(\tan\beta\sim 60\), \(M_{A}=300\) GeV → \(\mathcal B\approx 2\times\)SM |
| **Vector lepto‑quark \(U_{1}\) (3,1,2/3)** | After Fierz: \(O_{S},O_{P},O_{T}\) | **No** \(m_\mu\) factor (scalar & tensor pieces) | \(\displaystyle \mathcal A\sim \frac{g_{L}^{2}}{M_{U}^{2}}\,f_{B}m_{B}^{2}\) | \(\displaystyle \mathcal B\sim \frac{g_{L}^{4}}{M_{U}^{4}}\) | \(g_{L}\sim1\), \(M_{U}=2\) TeV → \(\mathcal B\) a few ×10⁻⁹ |
| **Right‑handed Z′ with mixed lepton chirality** | \(O_{VRL}= (\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}P_{L}\mu) - (L\leftrightarrow R)\) → via Fierz → scalar | **No** \(m_\mu\) factor (scalar piece after Fierz) | \(\displaystyle \mathcal A\sim \frac{g_{qb}^{R}g_{\mu}^{L}}{M_{Z'}^{2}}\,f_{B}m_{B}^{2}\) | \(\displaystyle \mathcal B\sim \frac{|g_{qb}^{R}g_{\mu}^{L}|^{2}}{M_{Z'}^{4}}\) | \(g\sim0.1\), \(M_{Z'}=3\) TeV → \(\mathcal B\sim1.5\times10^{-9}\) |
| **Tensor exchange** (e.g. colour‑octet scalar) | \(O_{T},O_{T5}\) | **No** \(m_\mu\) factor | \(\displaystyle \mathcal A\sim \frac{\lambda_{qb}\lambda_{\mu}}{M^{2}}\,f_{B}\frac{m_{B}^{2}}{m_{b}}\) | \(\displaystyle \mathcal B\sim \frac{|\lambda_{qb}\lambda_{\mu}|^{2}}{M^{4}}\) | \(\lambda\sim0.2\), \(M=2\) TeV → \(\mathcal B\sim5\times10^{-10}\) |

> **Key point:** whenever the **leptonic bilinear is scalar, pseudoscalar or tensor**, the matrix element \(\bar u\,\Gamma\,v\) does **not** vanish for massless muons, so the **helicity suppression disappears**.  The resulting branching fraction scales as the **square of the NP coupling divided by the fourth power of the heavy mediator mass**; no factor of \(m_{\mu}\) appears.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Practical consequences for phenomenology

1. **If experimental measurements converge on the SM value with ≤ 5 % precision**, any NP that contributes a scalar/pseudoscalar operator with \(|C_{S,P}|\gtrsim 0.1\) (i.e. \(|y_{qb}y_{\mu}|/M^{2}\gtrsim 10^{-9}\,\text{GeV}^{-2}\)) is ruled out.  This corresponds roughly to:
   * \(M_{H}\lesssim 1\) TeV with \(\mathcal O(1)\) Yukawas,  
   * \(M_{LQ}\lesssim 2\) TeV with couplings \(\gtrsim 0.3\),  
   * \(\tan\beta\lesssim 30\) for \(M_{A}\lesssim 500\) GeV in the MSSM.

2. **A measured branching fraction significantly above the SM prediction** (e.g. a factor 2–3 excess) would immediately point to **scalar/pseudoscalar or tensor contributions**; vector‑type Z′ explanations would still need an accompanying scalar piece to fit the size of the excess.

3. **The effective lifetime** \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) is an additional discriminator: scalar operators flip the sign of the interference with the heavy‑mass eigenstate, moving the measured \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) away from the SM prediction of ≈ 1.6 ps.  A deviation of ≳ 10 % in \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) together with a rate consistent with SM would signal a *large scalar* contribution that somehow cancels in the total rate—another clean NP hallmark.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Bottom line

*The SM amplitude is helicity‑suppressed because it contains only the axial‑vector operator \(O_{10}\).  New‑physics that introduces **scalar (\(O_{S}\)), pseudoscalar (\(O_{P}\)) or tensor (\(O_{T},O_{T5}\)) four‑fermion operators** eliminates the muon‑mass factor.  The amplitude then scales simply as \(\displaystyle \frac{g_{\rm quark}\,g_{\rm lepton}}{M_{\rm NP}^{2}}\) (or its square for the branching fraction) and can be orders of magnitude larger than the SM prediction if the couplings are \(\mathcal O(1)\) and the mediators are at the TeV scale.*

user_message: Given that studying muonic atoms in vacuum eliminates collisional broadening and Stark quenching from dense media, leaving residual background gas (~10^−9 mbar) as the only perturbation — what specific diagnostic measurements and calibration procedures would you implement during an experiment to empirically verify that residual‑gas effects (pressure shifts, collision rates, and gas‑composition dependent perturbations) are below the 1% systematic threshold for spectral line positions, state‑preparation fidelity, and molecular formation‑rate determinations?
assistant_response:
Below is a **step‑by‑step “quality‑assurance” plan** that can be inserted into any muonic‑hydrogen‑in‑vacuum experiment (e.g. a high‑precision Lamb‑shift or μCF‑rate measurement).  
It is organized around the three observables that ultimately enter the physics analysis  

| Observable | What we have to know | 1 % systematic budget |
|------------|---------------------|-----------------------|
| **Spectral line position** (e.g. μp 2p→1s Lyman‑α) | Pressure‑induced line shift Δν(p) ≤ 0.01 × Δν\_stat  | ≤ 10 kHz for a 1‑GHz natural linewidth (≈ 0.001 %). |
| **State‑preparation fidelity** (population P\_{1s} after de‑excitation) | Collision‑induced loss P\_{loss} ≤ 0.01 × P\_{1s} | ≤ 1 % loss. |
| **Molecular formation rate** (e.g. dμt → (dμt) → α + n + μ) | Collision‑induced suppression ΔR/R ≤ 0.01 | ≤ 1 % rate change. |

The plan contains **(i) diagnostics that directly measure the residual‑gas environment**, **(ii) in‑situ calibration measurements that translate that environment into an empirical bound on the three observables**, and **(iii) cross‑checks that validate the whole chain**.  

---

## 1. Real‑time Residual‑Gas Characterisation  

| Diagnostic | How it works | Typical performance (10⁻⁹ mbar regime) | How the output is used |
|------------|--------------|----------------------------------------|------------------------|
| **Ion‑gauge with Bayard‑Alpert geometry** (calibrated against a Spinning‑Rotor Gauge) | Measures total pressure p\_{tot}. | Accuracy ± 15 % at 10⁻⁹ mbar; resolution ≈ 5 × 10⁻¹¹ mbar. | Provides the *absolute* number density n = p/k\_B T for rate calculations. |
| **Residual‑Gas Analyzer (RGA) with a cold‑trap** | Quadrupole mass spectrometer (mass range 1–100 amu) equipped with a cryogenic (4 K) charcoal trap to suppress the intense jet‑gas load while letting the background through. | Detection limit ≈ 10⁻¹² mbar for H₂, D₂, He, N₂; compositional accuracy ± 10 % for each species. | Supplies the *partial pressures* p\_i → species‑specific cross‑sections σ\_{i}. |
| **White‑light interferometric thickness monitor on the supersonic jet** | Optical interferometer measures the column density of the jet (N\_{jet}) in real time. | Relative precision ≤ 0.2 % for a 100 µm thick jet. | Allows subtraction of the jet’s contribution to the total pressure measured by the ion gauge (p\_{bg}=p\_{tot}−p\_{jet}). |
| **Fast pressure burst monitor** (piezo‑electric diaphragm) | Detects micro‑pressure spikes when the pulsed jet opens. | Time resolution ≤ 5 µs, sensitivity ≈ 10⁻⁹ mbar. | Verifies that the background does not rise above the nominal level during the data‑taking window (see timing strategy below). |
| **Cryopump temperature sensor & NEG current monitor** | Monitors NEG pump activation (adsorption capacity) and cryopump temperature (to detect accidental desorption). | 0.1 K temperature stability; NEG current noise < 5 µA. | Guarantees the pumping speed stays constant; any drift would be reflected as a pressure change flagged by the gauge. |

All of these diagnostics are **logged synchronously** with the muon‑arrival trigger (time stamp < 100 ps) so that each physics event can be associated with a calibrated pressure snapshot.

---

## 2. Calibration Measurements that Convert Pressure ↔ Observable Shifts  

### 2.1. Pressure‑Shift Calibration for Spectral Lines  

1. **Reference transition:** Use a *well‑known* muonic‑hydrogen transition that is **insensitive to external fields** (e.g. the 2s→1s two‑photon transition in μp, natural width ~ 0.1 kHz).  
2. **Controlled pressure scan:** Introduce a calibrated amount of *pure* hydrogen gas (or helium, whichever is *not* part of the main reaction) into the chamber in steps from 10⁻⁹ mbar up to 10⁻⁶ mbar using a *precision leak* (Capacitance Manometer‑controlled).  
3. **Measure line centre** with a frequency‑comb‑referenced UV laser (absolute accuracy ≤ 10 kHz).  
4. **Fit Δν(p) = β · p** (linear regime holds up to ≈ 10⁻⁵ mbar). The slope β (Hz mbar⁻¹) is the *pressure‑shift coefficient*.  
5. **Result:** In μp, β ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁶ Hz mbar⁻¹ (literature). Our measured β must agree within 10 % (systematic error on β) → **maximum shift at 10⁻⁹ mbar** is 3 × 10⁻⁶ Hz, i.e. **≪ 1 %** of any realistic line width.  

*If the measured β deviates significantly,* repeat with different background gases (He, N₂) to isolate a possible **chemical‑shift component** (different polarizability). The worst‑case shift is then taken as the systematic error.

### 2.2. Collision‑Rate Calibration for State‑Preparation Fidelity  

1. **Prepare a pure 1s population** using the standard Stark‑mixing + laser de‑excitation sequence.  
2. **Probe the 1s population** immediately after preparation by **stimulated Raman probing**: apply a narrow‑band 2p↔1s laser pulse and detect the emitted Lyman‑α photons with a photon‑counting VUV PMT. The *count rate* ∝ P\_{1s}.  
3. **Repeat** the measurement **with and without** a deliberate increase of background pressure (e.g. raise to 5 × 10⁻⁸ mbar using a calibrated leak).  
4. **Extract the loss fraction**  
   \[
   \frac{P_{\rm loss}}{P_{1s}} = 1-\frac{N_{\rm high\,p}}{N_{\rm low\,p}} .
   \]  
   For a pure hard‑sphere cross‑section σ ≈ 10⁻¹⁹ m² the expected loss at 5 × 10⁻⁸ mbar over a 0.5 µs preparation window is < 10⁻⁴.  
5. **Linearity check:** Plot loss vs. pressure; the slope gives an *empirical* σ\_{eff}. Compare σ\_{eff} to the theoretical value; any excess indicates **unaccounted processes** (e.g. charge‑exchange with ionised background).  
6. **Result:** At the nominal 10⁻⁹ mbar the predicted loss from the fitted slope is < 2 × 10⁻⁶ → **well below the 1 % target**.

### 2.3. Molecular‑Formation‑Rate Calibration  

The formation rate R is extracted from the time distribution of fusion products (neutrons α‑particles) after the muon stop. To verify that background gas does not bias R:

1. **Baseline run** at 10⁻⁹ mbar (usual operating pressure). Record the time‑histogram H\_0(t).  
2. **Pressure‑enhancement run**: raise the background to 5 × 10⁻⁸ mbar (same gas composition) while keeping the jet unchanged. Record H\_1(t).  
3. **Fit both histograms** with the standard kinetic model (capture → molecular formation → fusion → muon decay). Extract the formation‐rate parameters λ\_f^{(0)} and λ\_f^{(1)}.  
4. **Define the pressure‑sensitivity coefficient**  
   \[
   \kappa = \frac{\lambda_f^{(1)}-\lambda_f^{(0)}}{p_{1}-p_{0}} .
   \]  
   In published data κ ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ mbar⁻¹ (i.e. a 1 % change in λ\_f needs ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁶ mbar).  
5. **Apply the coefficient** to the *measured* background pressure p\_{\rm bg} (including the jet’s contribution subtracted via the interferometer). The **systematic correction** is Δλ\_f = κ·p\_{\rm bg}. With p\_{\rm bg}=10⁻⁹ mbar, Δλ\_f/λ\_f ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁴ % – far below 1 %.  

*Cross‑check:* Perform the same procedure with a different tracer gas (e.g. He) that has a larger elastic cross‑section. The resulting κ(He) should be consistent with the prediction from σ\_{He} (≈ 5 × 10⁻²⁰ m²). Any discrepancy > 10 % flags unseen contamination.

---

## 3. Timing Strategies to Isolate the Vacuum Window  

| Timing element | Implementation | Why it matters for background‑gas control |
|----------------|----------------|-------------------------------------------|
| **Muon‑arrival trigger** | Fast CVD diamond detector (rise < 50 ps) placed 5 cm upstream of the interaction zone. | Provides a precise *t = 0* for all subsequent gates. |
| **Gate‑open window** | Open the data‑acquisition (DAQ) gate only for **Δt = 5 µs** after the muon stop (or for the expected molecular‑formation time window, typically 0.2‑4 µs). | Since the mean free time τ\_{\rm coll} ≈ 2 × 10⁴ s, the probability of a collision inside Δt is P≈ Γ\_{\rm coll}Δt < 10⁻⁹. |
| **Jet‑pulse synchronization** | Use a fast valve (rise time ≈ 30 µs) driven by the same RF reference as the muon bunch; the jet is on only for a 200 µs window that starts **100 µs before** the muon arrival and ends **100 µs after**. | Guarantees that the jet’s dense core never overlaps with the DAQ gate. The background pressure measured by the ion gauge is taken *during* the jet‑off interval. |
| **Laser‑pulse timing** | De‑excitation laser(s) fired at **t = 0.5 µs** (well after capture, well before fusion). The laser pulse length is ≤ 5 ns. | Any collisional quenching would appear as a change in the Lyman‑α yield *after* the laser; the absence of a time‑dependent tail confirms negligible collisions. |
| **Delayed‑background acquisition** | Record a “background” dataset with the same timing but **no muon beam** (by blocking the proton driver). This measures any spurious counts from residual gas fluorescence or detector dark counts. | Subtracts any pressure‑related background that would otherwise bias the line shape or rate. |

---

## 4. Cross‑Validation Procedures  

1. **Gas‑swap test** – Replace the supersonic jet gas (e.g. D₂) with a **non‑reactive calibrant** (pure He) while keeping all other parameters identical. The μ‑atom spectrum should not move; any observed shift must be due to background‑gas effects and is taken as a systematic bound.  

2. **Pressure‑extrapolation** – Perform the full physics measurement at three background pressures (10⁻⁹, 5 × 10⁻⁹, 2 × 10⁻⁸ mbar). Fit the observable (line centre, P\_{1s}, λ\_f) versus p. The extrapolated intercept at p = 0 must agree with the p = 10⁻⁹ mbar result within the statistical error; the slope provides a *direct* empirical limit on pressure‑induced bias.  

3. **Monte‑Carlo sensitivity study** – Build a Geant4/ROOT simulation that includes the measured partial pressures, known elastic/elastic cross‑sections, and the exact timing gates. Propagate a large number of pseudo‑events to compute the expected shift in each observable; compare the simulated shift with the experimentally derived bound.  

4. **Independent pressure sensor cross‑check** – Install a **cold‑cathode gauge** in addition to the Bayard‑Alpert gauge. Their readings at 10⁻⁹ mbar differ by < 5 %; the larger value is used as a conservative estimate of n.  

5. **Long‑term drift monitor** – Record the pressure and RGA spectra continuously over the whole data‑taking campaign (typically weeks). Plot Δp vs. time; if any drift exceeds 20 % of the nominal value, the corresponding data blocks are flagged and re‑analysed with an updated systematic correction.

---

## 5. Summary of the Empirical Verification Chain  

1. **Measure** total pressure p\_{tot} (ion gauge) and gas composition {p\_i} (RGA) **in real time**.  
2. **Subtract** the jet contribution (interferometer) → obtain **background pressure** p\_{\rm bg}.  
3. **Apply** the *pressure‑shift coefficient* β (from an in‑situ calibration scan) to compute a **maximum frequency shift** Δν = β·p\_{\rm bg}.  Verify Δν < 0.01 × σ\_{\rm stat}.  
4. **Use** the *collision‑loss coefficient* σ\_{eff} (from the Raman‑probe loss scan) to compute a **population loss** P\_{\rm loss}=nσ\_{eff}\bar v · t\_{\rm prep}.  Verify P\_{\rm loss} < 0.01 · P\_{1s}.  
5. **Apply** the *formation‑rate pressure coefficient* κ (from the pressure‑scan of the molecular‑formation histogram) to compute Δλ\_f = κ·p\_{\rm bg}.  Verify Δλ\_f/λ\_f < 0.01.  
6. **Cross‑check** all three corrections with the *pressure‑extrapolation* data sets and the *Monte‑Carlo* simulation.  
7. **Document** the full error budget: each systematic contribution (pressure shift, collision loss, formation suppression) is listed with its *experimental* (measured) value and the *assigned* uncertainty (typically the larger of statistical error of the calibration scan or 10 % of the correction). The total summed in quadrature must be ≤ 1 %.  

When all the above steps are completed and the quantified corrections are **below 10⁻⁴ – 10⁻³** (i.e. at least two orders of magnitude smaller than the 1 % target), the experiment can confidently claim that *residual‑gas effects are negligible* and that the remaining systematic budget is dominated by other sources (laser frequency reference, magnetic fields, detector efficiency).  

--- 

### Quick Checklist for the Run‑Leader  

| Item | Done? (✓/✗) | Comments |
|------|-------------|----------|
| Calibrated ion gauge vs. spinning‑rotor gauge at 10⁻⁹ mbar. |  |  |
| RGA tuned with cryo‑trap, partial pressures logged each spill. |  |  |
| Interferometric jet‑column measurement synchronized to valve trigger. |  |  |
| Pressure‑shift scan (H₂, He, N₂) completed, β extracted. |  |  |
| Raman loss scan (1s population vs. pressure) completed, σ\_{eff} extracted. |  |  |
| Molecular‑formation pressure scan (λ\_f vs. p) completed, κ extracted. |  |  |
| Timing gates (Δt = 5 µs) verified with fast oscilloscope. |  |  |
| Background‑only runs (no muon beam) recorded for detector baseline. |  |  |
| Monte‑Carlo model updated with measured n, σ\_i, gate windows. |  |  |
| All systematic contributions summed < 1 %. |  |  |

Crossing every line on this list constitutes **experimental proof** that the residual‑gas environment in the vacuum chamber does not introduce a > 1 % systematic error in any of the key observables needed for high‑precision muon‑catalyzed‑fusion studies.

Each item includes * **what is measured**, * **how it is measured**, * **the required statistical/ systematic precision**, and * **the calibration/validation procedure** that proves the number is trustworthy at the sub‑percent level. --- ## 1. Laser‑Driven State‑Preparation Diagnostics | # | Diagnostic | Principle & Observable | Required precision for ≤ 1 % fidelity | Typical implementation (µH‑vac) | Calibration / Cross‑check | |---|------------|------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------------------|---------------------------| | **1.1** | **Laser‑induced fluorescence (LIF) on the 2p → 1s (Lyman‑α) line** | A narrow‑band UV laser (λ≈ 0.2 µm) excites the μ‑atom from 1s → 2p; the subsequent spontaneous 2p→1s photon is detected. The **inverse** process (probing leftover 2p population) is used after the preparation step: fire a weak probe laser tuned to 2p→3d (or 2p→4s) and record the fluorescence. | ≤ 0.5 % uncertainty on the residual 2p (or higher‑n) population. | • UV‑enhanced MCP or VUV‑photomultiplier placed 90° to the beam.
• Photon‑counting with a fast (≤ ns) discriminator.
• Accumulate over 10⁴ muon‑stop events per laser setting. | – **Absolute efficiency calibration** using a known weakly‑bound hydrogen‑like ion (e.g., He⁺ produced in a separate source) whose 2p population can be set to 100 % by laser pumping.
– **Background subtraction** by running the probe laser off resonance. | | **1.2** | **Stark‑mixing‐induced depopulation measurement** | Apply a calibrated electric field E (10–30 kV cm⁻¹) between parallel plates. The mixing rate Γₛₜₐᵣₖ ∝ E² gives a known depopulation of the ℓ‑sublevels. – **Numerical simulation** (Schrödinger–Stark solver) to convert measured fluorescence change into ℓ‑population. | | **1.3** | **Microwave quench spectroscopy** (n = 2 → 1) | A resonant microwave pulse (≈ 0.5 GHz for μp 2s→2p) drives the remaining 2s population to 2p, which then decays to 1s and emits a photon. The probe will only interact if the atom is still in the *target* state (e.g., 1s). The **absence** of a response indicates successful preparation; any residual signal quantifies the failure probability. | ≤ 0.2 % on the failure probability. | • Optical delay line (fiber or free‑space) with sub‑ps timing; trigger on the muon detector.
• Same photon‑counting setup as 1.1. | – **Delay‑line calibration** using a fast photodiode (≤ 5 ps jitter).
– **Probe‑laser power sweep** to verify linear response (no power‑broadening). | | **1.5** | **Electron‑decay tagging** (muon‑decay as “clock”) | The muon decay electron (e⁻) is detected with a scintillator placed around the interaction volume. A change of the decay rate (e.g., due to altered capture probability) indicates residual unprepared atoms. | ≤ 1 % relative change in decay rate. | • Plastic scintillator + SiPM, time resolution ≈ 150 ps.
• Continuous acquisition of muon‑stop → electron‑arrival timestamps. | – **Decay‑law fit**: compare to the known 2.2 µs exponential; any deviation beyond statistical error → residual population.
– **Monte‑Carlo validation** of the correlation model. | **Combining the diagnostics**: By performing each of the above measurements on the same data set and solving the linear system that relates the observed signals to the populations of 1s, 2s, 2p, and higher‑n states, you obtain a **redundant, over‑constrained estimate** of the preparation fidelity. The known neutron TOF (≈ 65 ns m⁻¹) provides an *external* timing reference for the neutron scintillator array. | ≤ 1 ns absolute timing (sufficient because neutron TOF dominates; used to verify detector chain). | Liquid‑scintillator + fast PMT (rise time 0.5 ns). | – **Benchmark** against a calibrated picosecond laser‑triggered photo‑electron source. | | **2.7** | **Cross‑correlation of independent channels** | Compute the cross‑correlation function between the M‑det timestamps and the L‑det timestamps over 10⁶ events. The peak position yields the **systematic offset**; the width yields the combined jitter. | Combined jitter ≤ 50 ps → each individual ≤ 30 ps. | Offline software (ROOT/NumPy); use maximum‑likelihood fit of a Gaussian peak. | – **Bootstrap resampling** to estimate statistical error; verify that systematic drift over a run < 10 ps. | **Validation Procedure** 1. **Run a “zero‑delay” test** – set the laser trigger to fire simultaneously (within the programmable delay module) with the muon‑detector trigger. The measured μ‑laser time difference should be exactly the programmed delay; any residual offset indicates cable or module errors. 2. **Cycle through a set of known programmable delays** (0 ps, 100 ps, 200 ps … up to 5 ns). For each step perform a fast Fourier transform (FFT) of the coincidence histogram; the peak must shift linearly with the programmed value. Linear regression residuals must be **< 2 ps**. 3. **Temperature‑stability test** – vary the laboratory temperature by ± 5 °C (or turn on a heater) and repeat the calibration. The timing offset should change by less than **1 ps °C⁻¹**; if not, add additional thermal shielding or use temperature‑compensated cables. 4. **Long‑term drift monitoring** – record the muon‑laser offset every 5 min during a typical 8‑hour run. Fit to a linear trend; drift must be < 10 ps h⁻¹. Apply a software correction to the timestamps if necessary. When all the above checks satisfy the numerical criteria, the **overall systematic uncertainty on the relative timing** between muon stop and laser‑pulse preparation is **≤ 30 ps (rms)**, which corresponds to a **≤ 0.001 %** error on any process that occurs on the µs time scale (fusion, molecular formation). For reactions that are sensitive to sub‑ns timing (e.g., interference of two sequential laser pulses that drive a Raman transition), the ≤ 50 ps budget guarantees a **≤ 0.5 %** uncertainty on the transition probability. --- ## 3. Combined “Fidelity‑+‑Timing” Validation Campaign | Phase | Action | Data set size | Expected statistical error | Systematic cross‑checks | |-------|--------|---------------|---------------------------|------------------------| | **A. BB photon density at the corresponding microwave frequencies (≈ 10‑30 GHz) at 300 K is approx 10⁴ photons cm⁻³ Hz⁻¹ → rate < 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. | Insignificant. | | **2.9** | **Scattered pump‑laser light / stray UV photons from the de‑excitation laser** – could photo‑ionise residual H₂ creating additional ions** | A typical de‑excitation laser (5 mJ, 5 ns, 0.2 µm) yields a photon fluence of ≈ 10²⁰ ph m⁻². At a distance of 10 cm the photon density drops to ~10¹⁶ ph m⁻³, giving a photo‑ionisation rate of ≈ 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ for the residual H₂ (σ≈10⁻¹⁸ cm²). The produced ion density stays ≲ 10³ m⁻³, far below the values in 2.3. | No measurable shift. | | **2.10** | **Electrostatic charging of dielectric surfaces (e.g., quartz viewports)** – slowly builds up static field** | Measured charge accumulation on a quartz window in a 10⁻⁹ mbar chamber under μ‑beam illumination is ≤ 0.1 pC mm⁻² → surface potential ≈ 0.1 V. Field at 5 mm ≈ 2 V m⁻¹. | Same as 2.4 → Δν ≈ 10⁻⁴ Hz (<< 1 %). | **Conclusion of the table:** *Every listed long‑range mechanism produces a fractional perturbation **≤ 10⁻¹⁰**, i.e. at least **8 orders of magnitude** below the 1 % systematic budget.* The only plausible route to a 1 % effect would be a **gross failure** of the vacuum or shielding (e.g. pressure rising to 10⁻⁴ mbar, or a massive, uncontrolled DC field of order kV cm⁻¹). Both situations are easily detectable and can be prevented with standard UHV practice. --- ## 3. Quantitative “what‑if” scenarios that would reach the 1 % line | Failure mode | Required magnitude to cause Δν/ν ≈ 10⁻² | Is it realistic? | |--------------|-------------------------------------|-----------------| | **Static electric field** (Stark shift) | Δν = ½ α E² ⇒ E_required = √(2 Δν/α) ≈ √(2 · 2 × 10¹² Hz / 5 × 10⁻⁴⁰ C m² V⁻¹) ≈ **3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹** (≈ 3 kV mm⁻¹). | This is a kilovolt‑per‑millimeter field – impossible to arise from the few‑volt bias on skimmers or patch potentials. To get Δν ≈ 2 × 10¹² Hz, need n ≈ 10³ × 10⁹ m⁻³ → p ≈ 0.4 Pa (≈ 3 mbar). | 3 mbar is ***far*** above our operating pressure; would be seen as a huge pressure rise, and the muon beam would stop. | | **Background ion density** (Coulomb Stark) | Same formula as static field – need ion density ≈ 10¹⁸ m⁻³ → p ≈ 0.4 Pa. | Same argument. | Thus, **any realistic departure** from the intended UHV conditions remains **orders of magnitude** below the 1 % limit. --- ## 4. Mitigation checklist (what to do to keep the residual‑background contribution safely under 10⁻⁴, i.e. a safety factor of 100 × the 1 % budget) | Aspect | Recommended hardware / procedure | Measured performance target | |-------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------| | **Base pressure** | - 3‑stage pumping: (i) scroll pump → rough, (ii) 350 L s⁻¹ turbomolecular pump, (iii) NEG‑pump + cryogenic sorption (4 K charcoal).
- Bake‑out at 200 °C for ≥ 48 h. | **p ≤ 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar** (ion‑gauge reading, calibrated against a spinning‑rotor gauge). | | **Local jet pressure** | - Differential pumping with two or three skimmers (0.5 mm aperture, 30 mm spacing).
- Pulsed valve duty cycle ≤ 0.5 % (typical 200 µs open, 200 ms cycle). | **Peak density in interaction zone** ≈ 10¹⁴ cm⁻³, **average background** ≤ 10⁻⁹ mbar. | | **Electric‑field shielding** | - Grounded copper mesh (mesh size ≈ 0.5 mm) placed 2 mm downstream of each skimmer to suppress stray potentials.
- Active bias cancellation: a pair of “compensation electrodes” driven by a feedback loop (voltage sensor + PID) keeping the field at the interaction centre < 1 V m⁻¹. | **Measured static field** (by Stark spectroscopy of a reference species, e.g. Rb) ≤ 5 V m⁻¹ → Δν ≤ 10⁻⁴ Hz. | | **Magnetic‑field control** | - μ‑metal shields (2 mm thick, triple‑layer) around the interaction chamber.
- Three‑axis Helmholtz coils for active cancellation; field measured by a fluxgate sensor (resolution 10 nT). | **Residual field** ≤ 20 nT (rms), **gradient** ≤ 5 nT mm⁻¹. | | **Surface charge monitoring** | - UV‑LED “bleaching” of dielectric windows between cycles (to neutralize any photo‑charging).
- Periodic Kelvin‑probe scans of critical surfaces (skimmers, viewports). | **Patch‑potential amplitude** ≤ 0.5 V over 1 mm → field at centre ≤ 0.2 V m⁻¹. | | **Ion‑background suppression** | - Inline **electron‑suppressor** (biased ring) to repel secondary electrons from pumps.
- Use of **low‑outgassing** materials (316 L stainless steel, OFHC copper) and **bake‑cleaned** NEG cartridges. | **Ion density** ≤ 10⁶ m⁻³ (verified by residual‑ion mass spectrometer). | | **Laser‑induced stray photons** | - Beam dumps with > 99.9 % absorption at 0.2 µm, surrounded by blackened baffles.

- **In‑situ spectroscopy** of a well‑known atomic line (e.g., Na D‑line) as a Stark/Zeeman probe before each data run. | **Real‑time pressure drift** < 1 % of setpoint; **field drift** < 0.1 % of setpoint. | --- ## 5. Bottom‑line numbers | Perturbation | Maximal realistic shift (worst‑case numbers) | Fraction of 1 % budget | |--------------|---------------------------------------------|------------------------| | **BB‑induced AC Stark** | 10⁻³ Hz | 5 × 10⁻¹³ % | | **Residual static E‑field (10 V m⁻¹)** | 10⁻⁴ Hz | 5 × 10⁻¹¹ % | | **Residual B‑field (10 nT)** | 0.14 Hz (Zeeman of 2p) → Δν/ν ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹⁴ | 7 × 10⁻⁹ % | | **Ion density at 10⁻⁶ mbar** | 10⁻⁶ Hz | 5 × 10⁻⁹ % | | **Patch potentials (0.5 V mm⁻¹)** | 10⁻⁴ Hz | 5 × 10⁻¹¹ % | | **Cumulative sum (root‑sum‑square)** | ≈ 0.15 Hz | ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹⁴ % | All numbers are **far below the 1 % (≈ 2 × 10¹² Hz) target**. Even adding a generous safety factor of 100 (to account for unknown systematic cross‑talk) still leaves us at **≤ 10⁻⁹ %** of the allowable budget. --- ## 6. Practical verification protocol (short checklist for each run) 1. **Pressure log** – record base pressure (ion gauge) and peak jet pressure (QMS) every 10 s. 2. **Field map** – before data taking, scan the interaction volume with a small (≈ 1 mm) electrostatic probe; verify E ≤ 5 V m⁻¹ everywhere. 3. **BB reference measurement** – run a “dark” (no muon) control for 30 min, acquire the same spectroscopic channel; any line‑shift beyond 0.1 kHz triggers a vacuum‑leak check. 4. **Stark calibration** – deliberately apply a known DC field (e.g., 50 V m⁻¹) and record the induced shift; confirm the measured polarizability matches the theory to within 5 %. This validates that the instrument is sensitive enough to detect any larger stray field. 5. **Ion monitor** – enable the residual‑ion detector (micro‑channel plate) for the last 5 µs of each muon cycle; a count rate > 10 Hz signals unexpected plasma formation and aborts the run. Following this protocol guarantees that **any hidden long‑range effect is detected** long before it could contaminate the final μCF fusion‑rate or spectroscopic result at the 1 % level. --- ### TL;DR * In a 10⁻⁹ mbar UHV chamber the **collision probability**, **black‑body photon density**, **static or fluctuating electric/magnetic fields**, and **ion density** are all so tiny that the induced **fractional shifts** on muonic‑hydrogen transition frequencies or on dμt formation rates are **≤ 10⁻⁹ %**, i.e. **≥ 8 orders of magnitude** smaller than the 1 % systematic ceiling. * The only way to breach the 1 % limit would be a **catastrophic pressure rise (> 10⁻³ mbar)**, a **kilovolt‑per‑millimeter stray electric field**, or a **Tesla‑scale magnetic field**—conditions that are trivially detectable and easily avoided with standard UHV engineering. * Implementing a **three‑stage pumping system**, **differential pumping with skimmers**, **grounded shielding meshes**, **magnetic µ‑metal shielding**, and **real‑time pressure/field monitoring** gives a comfortable safety factor (≥ 10⁴) and guarantees that vacuum‑related perturbations remain far below the 1 % systematic uncertainty required for next‑generation muon‑catalyzed‑fusion experiments.

user_message: What calibration procedures and control measurements would you perform to validate the timing, energy, and angular response of the neutron and alpha detectors used to identify resonant muonic molecular formation?
assistant_response:
Below is a **complete calibration‑and‑control‑measurement plan** that turns the neutron‑TOF array and the forward α‑telescope system from “raw sensors” into **quantitatively trusted observables** for the resonant‑formation study.  
The plan is divided into three functional blocks (timing, energy, angular response) and is followed by a set of **control measurements** that verify that the calibrated response holds under the exact experimental conditions (beam‑related backgrounds, magnetic field, vacuum, jet flow, etc.).

---

## 1.  General Calibration Philosophy  

| Principle | Implementation |
|-----------|----------------|
| **Traceability to primary standards** | Use **NIST‑certified** α sources (⁴⁰K, ²⁴¹Am) and **well‑characterised neutron standards** (⁹⁰Sr‑⁹⁰Y, ²⁵²Cf, D‑D/D‑T generators). |
| **In‑situ cross‑checks** | Perform calibrations **with the full detector geometry, shielding, and data‑acquisition chain** in place, not on a bench stand‑alone. |
| **Redundancy** | At least two independent methods for each quantity (e.g., timing from a laser‑triggered γ and from a prompt neutron source). |
| **Stability monitoring** | Continuous “monitor runs” interleaved with physics data (e.g. a low‑rate LED pulser for the neutron PMTs, a weak α source for the SiC telescopes). |
| **Environmental logging** | Record temperature, pressure, magnetic field, high‑voltage supply drift for each run; apply small corrections offline if needed. |

---

## 2.  Timing Calibration  

### 2.1  Neutron‑TOF Array  

| Step | Action | Rationale | Expected precision |
|------|--------|-----------|--------------------|
| **2.1.1** | **Prompt γ‑flash** from a thin **C‑13(p,γ)N‑14** reaction. Use a 0.5 MeV proton beam (or a pulsed deuteron beam on a thin LiF target) to generate a sub‑ns‑wide γ burst that travels to the neutron detectors (≈ 1 m) simultaneously with the muon‑beam RF reference. | Provides an absolute **t = 0** reference that is independent of the muon beam; any systematic offset in electronics or cable lengths appears as a common shift. | ≤ 0.2 ns (limited by γ‑detector jitter). |
| **2.1.2** | **Fast neutron reference** from a **DD generator** (2.45 MeV neutrons) triggered by the same RF. Place the generator at the interaction point (or at a known offset) and record the TOF distribution; the flight distance is known to ± 1 mm, so the expected TOF ≈ 45 ns. | Verifies the **overall slope** (conversion from channel number to time). | ≤ 0.5 ns systematic on the TOF scale. |
| **2.1.3** | **Laser‑derived “optical timing”**: deliver a picosecond UV laser pulse (≤ 100 ps) via an optical fiber to a **fast UV‑sensitive photodiode** mounted next to each neutron detector. The same laser pulse is used to trigger the data‑acquisition system (common start). | Checks the **detector‑to‑digitiser latency** for each channel individually; useful for correcting channel‑by‑channel time walk. | ≤ 0.1 ns per channel. |
| **2.1.4** | **Electronic time‑walk correction**: inject a set of calibrated charge pulses (different amplitudes) into the pre‑amplifier input of each detector while recording the measured time. Build a time‑walk curve and apply a software correction. | Ensures that the measured TOF does not depend on neutron pulse height (important because neutron PSD pulses have a spread of amplitudes). | Residual walk < 0.2 ns over the full dynamic range. |
| **2.1.5** | **Bunch‑structure verification**: run the muon beam at low intensity, record the RF‑phase of each muon and the associated neutron hits. The phase distribution should be flat for background neutrons and sharply peaked for resonant events. | Confirms that the **global clock** is correctly phase‑locked to the accelerator, and that any drift is caught early. | Phase jitter < 0.5 ns. |

### 2.2  α‑Detector (SiC ΔE‑E Telescope)

| Step | Action | Rationale | Expected precision |
|------|--------|-----------|--------------------|
| **2.2.1** | **Fast pulsed LED** (UV‑visible) coupled to the detector front‑end (via a thin transparent window). The LED pulse is synchronized to the same RF as the neutron calibration. The silicon response is essentially instantaneous (< 1 ns). | Provides a **t₀** reference for the α channel; useful for checking relative timing between neutron and α systems. | ≤ 0.3 ns. |
| **2.2.2** | **Direct α‑source coincidence**: place a thin ²⁴¹Am sheet (≈ 5 kBq) in front of the telescope and record the α pulse together with a **fast plastic scintillator** positioned directly behind the source (serves as a timing start). The known α energy (~5.48 MeV) gives a well‑defined pulse shape. | Checks the **overall delay** from detector to digitiser, and the **time‑walk** for large ionising pulses. | ≤ 0.5 ns. |
| **2.2.3** | **Cross‑calibration with neutron TOF**: fire the DD generator; some neutrons will scatter off a thin polyethylene foil placed just in front of the α telescope, producing recoil protons that are detected as a fast signal in the ΔE layer. The recoil‑proton TOF can be compared with the neutron TOF to verify relative timing between the two subsystems. | Guarantees that the **neutron‑α relative timing** used in the physics analysis is correct. | ≤ 1 ns. |

---

## 3.  Energy Calibration  

### 3.1  Neutron Energy (via TOF)

| Step | Action | Reason |
|------|--------|--------|
| **3.1.1** | **DD/D‑T generators** placed at known distances (e.g., 0.5 m, 1 m, 1.5 m). The emitted neutrons have precise energies (2.45 MeV for DD, 14.1 MeV for DT). Record TOF spectra; the peak positions give the conversion factor *channel → time → velocity → energy*. | Provides three calibration points spanning the energy range of interest; any non‑linearities in the TOF‐to‑energy conversion are revealed. |
| **3.1.2** | **Neutron scatter calibration**: insert thin carbon or polyethylene scatter foils at a known angle (θ) relative to the detector line. The scattered neutron energy is given by kinematics: \[E' = E \frac{(A\cos\theta)^2 + \sin^2\theta}{(A+1)^2}\] (A = target mass). Measure the TOF of the scattered neutrons and compare with the prediction. | Checks the **energy‑dependent resolution** and validates the TOF reconstruction algorithm (including the effect of detector rise time). |
| **3.1.3** | **Monte‑Carlo validation** (GEANT4/MCNP). Simulate the exact geometry, including detector thresholds, to generate a synthetic TOF spectrum for the calibration sources. Match data and MC to fine‑tune the detector response functions. | Provides a systematic‑uncertainty budget (e.g., multiple scattering, detector dead‑layers). |

**Resolution Goal:** ≤ 5 % (σ) for 2.45 MeV neutrons → translates to ≤ 2 ns timing resolution after correcting for walk.

### 3.2  α‑Detector Energy Calibration

| Step | Action | Reason |
|------|--------|--------|
| **3.2.1** | **Standard α sources**: ²⁴¹Am (5.48 MeV), ²⁴⁰Pu (5.30 MeV), ²³⁸U (4.20 MeV). Place each source at the detector entrance, acquire ΔE‑E spectra, and fit the loci in the 2‑D histogram. | Establishes the **ΔE vs. E relationship** and the absolute energy scale (ΔE thickness known from manufacturer). |
| **3.2.2** | **Silicon‑detector pulser**: inject calibrated charge pulses (via a test capacitor) into the pre‑amp. Convert injected charge to equivalent energy (1 MeV ≈ 0.16 pC in silicon). This cross‑checks linearity across the full ADC range (0–10 MeV). | Guarantees linearity, especially important because the α energy shifts we are looking for are of order 0.1 % (≈ 5 keV). |
| **3.2.3** | **Energy‑loss verification**: mount a thin Mylar or Al foil (known areal density) in front of the telescope, measure the resulting shift in the α peak, and compare with SRIM calculations. | Confirms that the detector **dead‑layer thickness** and any additional material (e.g., jet gas window) are correctly accounted for. |
| **3.2.4** | **Temperature‑dependence mapping**: vary the detector temperature (e.g., from 20 °C to –30 °C) using a Peltier cooler and record the α peak position. Derive a correction function ΔE(T). | Silicon gain drifts ~0.1 %/°C; this step removes that systematic. |
| **3.2.5** | **In‑situ γ‑calibration**: place a ⁵⁹Co (122 keV) source near the detector and record the low‑energy tail in the ΔE channel; use it to confirm the **electronic noise floor** and baseline stability. | Guarantees that the low‑energy cutoff does not bias the α peak fit. |

**Resolution Goal:** ≤ 1 % (σ) on the α kinetic energy (≈ 50 keV FWHM for 5 MeV alphas), sufficient to resolve a 0.1 % shift (≈ 5 keV).

---

## 4.  Angular Response Calibration  

### 4.1  Neutron Array

| Step | Action | Reason |
|------|--------|--------|
| **4.1.1** | **Isotropic neutron source**: use a weak, encapsulated ²⁵²Cf source (≈ 10⁴ n s⁻¹) placed at the centre of the interaction volume. Record the count rate in each detector element. The distribution should be flat within statistical errors after correcting for solid‑angle differences. | Provides the **relative efficiency** vs. polar angle (θ) for each bar. |
| **4.1.2** | **Collimated beam test**: mount a thin polyethylene collimator (hole 5 mm) on a motorised rotation stage, place the DD generator behind it, and rotate the stage to fire neutrons at known angles (0°, 30°, 60°, 90°). Measure the response of each detector element as a function of angle. | Determines the **angular resolution function** (point‑spread) and any systematic mis‑pointing of bars. |
| **4.1.3** | **Monte‑Carlo mapping**: simulate the full array geometry (including housing, shielding, and the jet nozzle) to compute the detection efficiency ε(θ,φ). Compare simulated yields with the collimated‑beam data to validate the MC model. | Provides a correction matrix that can be applied during physics analysis (e.g., to unfold the true angular distribution of the neutron emission). |
| **4.1.4** | **Stability check**: during physics runs, inject a tiny amount of **Boron‑10** (via BF₃ gas) into the jet for a few seconds; the (n,α) reaction yields a characteristic 0.48 MeV γ that can be detected by a small HPGe placed near the array. The angular distribution of those γ’s is known; any deviation flags a change in detector alignment. | Ensures that any mechanical shift (e.g., due to thermal expansion) is caught. |

### 4.2  α‑Telescopes

| Step | Action | Reason |
|------|--------|--------|
| **4.2.1** | **Mask‑scan**: fabricate a precision steel mask with a grid of 1 mm holes. Place it in front of the telescope and move a collimated α source (⁴⁰K) behind the mask on an XY‑stage. Record the hit map to verify the **active area** and any dead zones. | Validates the geometric acceptance and any edge effects that would bias the forward‑angle measurement. |
| **4.2.2** | **Angular calibration with a rotating source**: mount a thin ²⁴¹Am disk on a motorised goniometer that can be tilted from –30° to +30° relative to the detector normal. Measure the α energy loss in the ΔE layer as a function of angle; the measured angular dependence must match the known path‑length increase (≈ 1/cosθ). | Checks the **angular dependence of detector response** (e.g., pulse‑height defect for grazing incidence). |
| **4.2.3** | **Monte‑Carlo validation**: simulate α particles entering the telescope at various angles (including multiple scattering in the jet gas) with GEANT4; compare simulated pulse‑height spectra with the data from the rotating source. | Provides the transformation matrix from measured ΔE‑E space to true laboratory angle. |
| **4.2.4** | **Alignment survey**: use a laser tracker or a theodolite to record the absolute positions (x,y,z, θ, φ) of each telescope relative to the beam axis with < 0.1 mm and < 0.1° uncertainty. | Supplies the geometry needed for the angular‑efficiency correction used in the physics analysis. |

---

## 5.  Control Measurements (Physics‑Level Checks)  

These runs are taken **with the same detector configuration** but under conditions where **no resonant µ‑molecular formation** should occur, or where the signal is known a priori.  They serve to verify that the calibrated response correctly predicts what is observed.

| Control | How it is performed | What it tests |
|---------|---------------------|----------------|
| **C1 – Empty‑target run** | Close the jet nozzle; the interaction chamber is evacuated to ≤ 10⁻⁹ mbar. | Verifies that any prompt neutron/α signal is *zero* (or at the level of cosmic‑ray background). Confirms that background subtraction works. |
| **C2 – Off‑resonance kinetic energy** | Set the electrostatic decelerator to a kinetic energy far from any known molecular resonance (e.g., 50 eV when the dµt resonance is at 0.5 eV). | The fast component (τ ≈ 10‑50 ns) should disappear, leaving only the slow µ‑decay background. Demonstrates that the TOF‑cut truly isolates resonant formation. |
| **C3 – Different isotope mix** | Replace the D₂ jet by pure H₂ (or by a D₂+He mixture). No dµt formation is possible; only µ‑transfer to He and µ‑capture occur. | Checks that the angular distribution becomes isotropic and that the neutron yield drops to the expected µ‑capture level. |
| **C4 – “Laser‑off” vs. “laser‑on”** | Run the Lyman‑α de‑excitation laser at full power for one set of spills and block it for the next set (same beam conditions). | The fast neutron/α yield should increase when the laser is on (more µ‑atoms reach 1s fast) – a direct cross‑check of the **state‑preparation efficiency** that was calibrated by the photon detector. |
| **C5 – Magnetic‑field reversal** | Reverse the direction of the µSR field (B → –B) while keeping everything else identical. | The resonant formation rate (which is spin‑independent) must stay unchanged; any observed change would indicate a residual spin‑dependent detector effect (e.g., asymmetric acceptance). |
| **C6 – Known nuclear reaction benchmark** | Inject a thin foil of LiF into the jet and fire the DD generator. The (n,α) reaction in Li produces a well‑known α line at 2.05 MeV. Record it with the α telescopes. | Provides an **independent cross‑check** of the α energy calibration under exactly the same electronic and HV conditions as the physics data. |
| **C7 – Cosmic‑ray tagging** | Operate the detector with the muon beam off for a few hours, record coincidences with external plastic scintillator panels (cosmic‑ray veto). | Supplies a pure background spectrum for neutrons and alphas; used to validate the background model in the physics fits. |
| **C8 – High‑rate stress test** | Increase the muon beam intensity by a factor of ~3 (still within detector limits) to verify that **pulse‑pile‑up** does not bias timing or energy extraction. | Guarantees that the calibration holds at the maximum physics‑run rate. |

Each control run is analysed **exactly** as a physics run (same reconstruction, same cuts).  The comparison of the extracted parameters (fast‑component amplitude, angular asymmetry, energy shift) with the *a priori* expectation provides a quantitative **systematic uncertainty** for each observable.

---

## 6.  Data‑Quality Monitoring (Online)  

| Monitor | Implementation |
|---------|----------------|
| **T0‑stability** | Plot the prompt γ‑flash time (from step 2.1.1) vs. run number; any drift > 0.2 ns triggers a recalibration. |
| **Neutron‑PSD ratio** | Real‑time histogram of the PSD figure‑of‑merit; deviations > 5 % flag a change in scintillator gain or temperature. |
| **α‑peak position** | Fit the ⁴⁰K α line in a 1‑minute window; log the centroid. Drift > 2 keV → adjust HV or apply correction. |
| **Angular count map** | Every 5 min, produce a 2‑D histogram of neutron hits per bar; monitor for sudden non‑uniformities (possible mechanical shift). |
| **Muon‑decay electron rate** | Verify that the electron veto rate stays within ± 5 % of the expected value; large excursions may indicate beam‑loss or detector dead time. |

All online monitors are fed into an **alarm system** that pauses data‑taking automatically if any parameter exceeds its tolerance band.

---

## 7.  Summary of Calibration & Validation Workflow  

1. **Pre‑run (offline)**  
   - Calibrate each neutron bar and each α telescope using the sources and procedures in Sections 2–4.  
   - Build the **efficiency, timing, and energy response matrices** (lookup tables) and store them in the analysis framework.  

2. **Start‑of‑run (online)**  
   - Run the **prompt γ‑flash** and **laser‑LED** timing checks; verify that the global clock is locked.  
   - Record a short (≈ 1 min) **Cf‑252** run to confirm angular uniformity.  

3. **Physics data acquisition**  
   - Interleave **control blocks** (C1‑C8) every 30 min (or after each 10⁶ muon pulses) to monitor stability.  
   - Continuously log environmental variables and detector‐HV readings.  

4. **Post‑run analysis**  
   - Apply **time‑walk corrections**, **energy linearity corrections**, and **angular efficiency corrections** using the pre‑built matrices.  
   - Fit the **fast‑component TOF** and **angular asymmetry** for each energy‑scan point.  
   - Compare the extracted resonant parameters against the **control‑run expectations**; assign systematic uncertainties based on the spread observed in the control measurements.  

Following this comprehensive scheme, the neutron‑TOF and α‑telescope subsystems will deliver **sub‑nanosecond timing**, **≤ 5 % neutron‑energy resolution**, **≤ 1 % α‑energy precision**, and **angular efficiencies known to better than 2 %**, all of which are sufficient to separate the resonant muonic‑molecular formation signal from the non‑resonant background with high confidence.

user_message: Studying muonic atoms in vacuum eliminates collisional broadening and Stark quenching from dense media, leaving residual background gas (~10^−9 mbar) as the only perturbation. Given that premise, what are the quantitative limits that this residual background gas imposes on achievable spectral linewidths, reaction‑rate measurements, and coherence times for muonic hydrogen (μp/μd/μt) experiments, and what vacuum, pumping, and diagnostics specifications (e.g., base pressure, gas composition limits, differential‑pumping geometry, residual‑gas analyzers, cryo‑trapping capacity, acceptable leak rates) are required to ensure those limits are not the dominant systematic uncertainties?
assistant_response:
## 1.  What “residual‑gas” actually does to a muonic atom in vacuum  

When a μ⁻ is captured by a hydrogen isotope it forms a muonic atom (μp, μd, μt) that immediately begins a radiative cascade down to the 1s ground state.  After the cascade the atom drifts freely until one of three things happens  

| Process | Typical rate (s⁻¹) | Dependence on the residual gas |
|----------|-------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Muonic‑atom spontaneous decay** (μ⁻ → e⁻ ν ν̄) | λ\_μ = 1/τ\_μ ≈ 4.55 × 10⁵ s⁻¹ (τ\_μ = 2.197 µs) | independent of background |
| **Resonant molecular formation** (e.g. dμt + D₂ → (dμt)⋆) | λ\_res ≈ 10⁶–10⁸ s⁻¹ when the relative kinetic energy is tuned to a resonance (the rate is set by the target density, not by the background) | depends on the *intended* target density (jet, gas cell…) |
| **Collisional perturbation by residual gas** (elastic scattering, Stark mixing, pressure shift, quenching) | λ\_bg = n\_bg · σ\_el · v\_rel  | **directly proportional to the residual‑gas number density n\_bg** |

Because the muon lifetime is only a few micro‑seconds, any additional process that adds a **fractional rate larger than ≈10⁻³ λ\_μ** (≈ 5 × 10² s⁻¹) will start to compete with the intrinsic physics you want to measure.  In practice we demand that *all background‑gas‑induced rates* be **≤ 10⁻³ × λ\_μ** (i.e. ≤ 0.5 kHz) so that they contribute **≤ 0.1 %** to the systematic error budget on linewidths, reaction rates, or coherence times.

Below we translate that requirement into concrete quantitative limits for three key observables:

| Observable | How the residual gas enters | Target quantitative limit |
|------------|-----------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Spectral linewidth (pressure broadening)** | Collisional de‑phasing gives a Lorentzian width Δν\_col = λ\_bg/(2π). | Δν\_col ≤ 1 Hz (≪ the natural linewidth of the 2p–1s Lyman‑α transition, Γ≈ 1.3 GHz). |
| **Reaction‑rate measurement (e.g. resonant dμt formation)** | Background collisions can either (i) *remove* the µ‑atom from the beam (elastic scattering) or (ii) *induce* non‑resonant transfer (e.g. μd → μHe).  The systematic error in the extracted rate is roughly λ\_bg / λ\_res. | λ\_bg / λ\_res ≤ 10⁻³ ⇒ λ\_bg ≤ 10⁴ s⁻¹ (for a typical resonant formation rate λ\_res≈10⁷ s⁻¹). |
| **Coherence time (µ‑spin rotation, hyper‑fine coherence)** | Each elastic collision randomises the phase; the decoherence rate Γ\_φ ≈ λ\_bg. | Desired T₂ ≥ 10 µs ⇒ Γ\_φ ≤ 10⁵ s⁻¹ ⇒ λ\_bg ≤ 10⁴ s⁻¹ (same order as the reaction‑rate requirement). |

Thus **the same upper bound on λ\_bg (≈ 10⁴ s⁻¹)** satisfies all three performance goals.

---

## 2.  From λ\_bg to a pressure specification  

The elastic scattering cross‑section for a slow muonic atom on a neutral atom (H₂, D₂, He, N₂…) is dominated by the *polarisation* interaction and is of order

\[
\sigma_{\rm el}\;\approx\;(0.5\!-\!2)\times10^{-15}\;{\rm cm^{2}}
\]

(precise values: σ(μp–H₂) ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ cm² at 300 K; σ(μp–He) ≈ 0.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ cm²).  

The relative thermal speed at room temperature (300 K) is

\[
v_{\rm rel}\;\approx\;\sqrt{\frac{8k_{\rm B}T}{\pi m_{\rm red}}}
   \;\approx\;1.0\times10^{5}\;{\rm cm\,s^{-1}}
\]

for reduced masses in the 1–4 amu range.  

Hence

\[
\lambda_{\rm bg}\;=\;n_{\rm bg}\,\sigma_{\rm el}\,v_{\rm rel}
\]

with the number density related to pressure by the ideal‑gas law

\[
n_{\rm bg}\;=\;\frac{p_{\rm bg}}{k_{\rm B}T}
\;\approx\;2.5\times10^{13}\; \frac{p_{\rm bg}}{1\;{\rm Pa}}\;{\rm cm^{-3}}.
\]

Setting λ\_bg = 10⁴ s⁻¹ and σ\_el = 1 × 10⁻¹⁵ cm² gives

\[
n_{\rm bg}\;=\;\frac{10^{4}}{(1\times10^{-15})\,(1\times10^{5})}
          \;\approx\;1.0\times10^{14}\;{\rm cm^{-3}}.
\]

Corresponding pressure at 300 K:

\[
p_{\rm bg}\;=\;n_{\rm bg}k_{\rm B}T\;\approx\;4\times10^{-11}\;{\rm Pa}
            \;\approx\;3\times10^{-9}\;{\rm mbar}.
\]

**Result:**  
*To keep collisional broadening below 1 Hz, the total residual pressure must be **≤ 3 × 10⁻⁹ mbar** (≈ 3 × 10⁻¹² atm) at room temperature.*  

If the experiment is operated at a lower temperature (e.g. 77 K), the same pressure translates into a *four‑fold higher* number density because \(n\propto p/T\).  Consequently the **pressure requirement tightens to ≈ 1 × 10⁻⁹ mbar** at 77 K.

---

## 3.  Composition limits – which gases are most dangerous?  

Because λ\_bg scales linearly with n\_bg · σ\_el, the most problematic species are those with the **largest elastic cross‑section** and/or those that can induce **inelastic processes** (e.g. muon transfer).  Typical cross‑sections at thermal energies:

| Species | σ\_el (10⁻¹⁵ cm²) | μ‑transfer threshold (eV) | Comments |
|---------|-------------------|----------------------------|----------|
| **H₂, D₂, T₂** | 0.8 – 1.2 | none (elastic only) | Main target gas; must be *deliberately* introduced, not part of background. |
| **He** | 0.6 | μ‑transfer from μd, μt at ~0.02 eV | Even a few 10⁻⁹ mbar of He can give a noticeable μ‑transfer loss. |
| **N₂, O₂, CO, CO₂** | 1.5 – 2.5 | can cause muon‑transfer to heavier nuclei (Z ≥ 7) – large loss | Must be suppressed well below the total pressure budget. |
| **H₂O (vapor)** | ≈ 2.0 | same as above | Highly adsorbed; watch out for out‑gassing. |
| **Ar** | ≈ 1.0 | μ‑transfer threshold ≈ 0.04 eV | Not as dangerous as N₂, but still contributes to λ\_bg. |

**Practical composition rule of thumb:**  

*The partial pressure of any “heavy‑transfer” species (He, N₂, O₂, CO, CO₂, H₂O) must be **≤ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar** (≈ 10 % of the total allowed pressure).  Hydrogen isotopes (the intended target) may occupy up to the full 3 × 10⁻⁹ mbar budget, but only if they are *purposefully* introduced via a differential‑pumped jet (see §4).*

---

## 4.  Vacuum system architecture that meets the specification  

### 4.1  Overall layout

```
                +--------------------+    +--------------------+
   μ⁻ beam --> |  Zeeman‑steerer   |    |  Low‑β  (electro)   |
                +--------------------+    +--------------------+
                              |                     |
                              v                     v
                +------------------------------  Interaction  ------------------------------+
                |  Differential‑pumping stages (3–4)  chamber (base ≈ 5×10⁻¹⁰ mbar)   |
                |  ---------------------------------------------------------------   |
                |  • Stage‑1: turbomolecular (150 l s⁻¹)  → 10⁻⁶ mbar                     |
                |  • Stage‑2: cryogenic (4 K) sorption pump → 10⁻⁸ mbar                 |
                |  • Stage‑3: Non‑evaporable getter (NEG) → ≤ 3×10⁻⁹ mbar (target)   |
                |  • Stage‑4 (optional): ion pump for leak‑tolerant isolation       |
                +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    |   Supersonic jet inlet (≈ 1 mm Ø)
                                    v
                +------------------------------+   +---------------------------+
                |  Cryogenic jet (D₂ / T₂)    |   |  Cold‑trap (4 K)  (cryosorb)|
                +------------------------------+   +---------------------------+
```

### 4.2  Pressure budget and component contributions  

| Stage | Pump type | Nominal speed (l s⁻¹) | Expected pressure contribution (worst case) | Remarks |
|-------|-----------|----------------------|---------------------------------------------|---------|
| **1** | Turbo‑pump (oil‑free) | 150 | **≤ 1 × 10⁻⁶ mbar** (dominates when jet is OFF) | Isolated by a gate valve when the jet is ON. |
| **2** | Cryopump (4 K, activated charcoal) | 200 (effective) | **≤ 5 × 10⁻⁸ mbar** | Captures all H₂, D₂, T₂ that leak past stage‑1. |
| **3** | NEG cartridge (TiZrV) | 50 (pump‑speed for H₂) | **≤ 2 × 10⁻⁹ mbar** (dominant) | Must be **re‑activated** (≥ 400 °C) after each run‑cycle; residual‑gas analyzer (RGA) monitors composition. |
| **4** (optional) | Ion pump (100 l s⁻¹) | – | **≤ 1 × 10⁻⁹ mbar** | Provides a leak‑tolerant “safety net” for occasional helium leaks. |

The **total base pressure** reached in the interaction chamber after a 12‑h pump‑down (jet OFF) is typically **5 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar**.  When the supersonic jet is *on*, the local density inside the jet is ≈ 10¹⁴ cm⁻³ (≈ 10⁻⁴ mbar), but the **background** outside the jet remains at the 10⁻⁹ mbar level thanks to the differential‑pumping apertures (skimmers of 0.5 mm and 0.2 mm) and the cryogenic cold‑trap directly downstream of the jet.

### 4.3  Acceptable leak rate  

The ultimate pressure stability is limited by the **total leak rate** Q (Pa·m³ s⁻¹).  To keep p ≤ 3 × 10⁻⁹ mbar with an effective pumping speed S ≈ 200 l s⁻¹ (stage‑3+4):

\[
Q_{\max} = p \times S 
          \approx (3\times10^{-9}\;{\rm Pa}) \times (0.2\;{\rm m^{3}\,s^{-1}})
          \approx 6\times10^{-10}\;{\rm Pa\,m^{3}\,s^{-1}}.
\]

This corresponds to a **helium‑equivalent leak rate** of **≈ 6 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar·L s⁻¹** (≈ 2 × 10⁻¹⁴ mbar·L s⁻¹·Hz⁻¹).  In practice we aim for **≤ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar·L s⁻¹** (one order of magnitude safety margin).  Leak‑testing with a helium mass‑spectrometer should reach a detection limit of **≤ 5 × 10⁻¹² mbar·L s⁻¹** before bake‑out.

### 4.4  Gas‑analysis & diagnostics  

| Instrument | Placement | Sensitivity | Role |
|-----------|-----------|------------|------|
| **Full‑range RGA** (quadrupole, 1–200 amu) | Port on stage‑3 (NEG) | 10⁻¹⁰ mbar (partial pressure) | Continuous monitoring of heavy‑transfer species (He, N₂, O₂, H₂O). |
| **Cold‑trap residual‑gas monitor** (mass‑spectrometer behind the 4 K charcoal) | After cryopump | 10⁻¹¹ mbar | Checks that the cryopump is effectively freezing out H₂, D₂, T₂; alerts when pump is saturated. |
| **Ion‑current gauge (Bayard‑Alpert)** | Near interaction region (cryogenic shielded) | 10⁻¹¹ mbar absolute | Provides real‑time total pressure read‑out (fast response ≤ 1 s). |
| **Capacitance‑manometer** | Upstream of the jet (room‑temperature) | 0.1 % of 10⁻⁶ mbar | Guides the opening of the jet valve to avoid pressure spikes. |
| **Out‑gassing monitor** (temperature‑programmed desorption on chamber walls) | Periodic check | 10⁻¹² mbar | Verifies that water or hydrocarbons do not build up after many beam shots. |

All gauges are **interlocked** to the beam‑dump: if the total pressure exceeds 5 × 10⁻⁹ mbar, the μ⁻ beam is automatically shuttered.

---

## 5.  How the specifications translate into the three performance metrics  

| Metric | Formula (using λ\_bg ≤ 10⁴ s⁻¹) | Numerical result with p = 3 × 10⁻⁹ mbar (300 K) | What the experiment sees |
|--------|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| **Pressure‑broadened linewidth** Δν\_col | Δν\_col = λ\_bg / (2π) | 1.6 Hz | Far below the natural linewidth (∼1.3 GHz) → negligible contribution to the observed line shape. |
| **Systematic shift in reaction rate** (fractional) | δR / R ≈ λ\_bg / λ\_res | λ\_res (typical resonance) ≈ 10⁷ s⁻¹ → δR/R ≤ 10⁻³ | The extracted resonant formation cross‑section will be accurate to the **0.1 %** level (limited by statistics, not background). |
| **Coherence time T₂** (µSR, hyper‑fine) | T₂ ≈ 1/λ\_bg | ≥ 100 µs | Gives a decoherence factor exp(−t/T₂) ≈ 0.98 at 2 µs, i.e. the **µ‑spin precession signal is essentially undistorted** over the whole muon‑lifetime window. |

If the pressure were relaxed to **1 × 10⁻⁸ mbar**, λ\_bg would increase by a factor of ≈ 3, giving Δν\_col ≈ 5 Hz, δR/R ≈ 3 × 10⁻³ and T₂ ≈ 30 µs.  Those values are still acceptable for many spectroscopy goals, but they would **start to dominate the error budget** for the most ambitious λ‑rate measurements (targeting 10⁻⁴ precision) and for precision µSR coherence studies.

---

## 6.  Checklist for a “no‑dominant‑background” vacuum system  

| Item | Spec | Verification method |
|------|------|----------------------|
| **Base pressure (jet OFF)** | ≤ 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar (total) | Ion gauge reading after 12 h pump‑down; confirm with RGA integrated signal. |
| **Background when jet ON** | ≤ 3 × 10⁻⁹ mbar (outside jet core) | Differential‑pump pressure sensor placed 5 cm downstream of the jet; pressure rise < 1 × 10⁻⁹ mbar when jet runs at full flow. |
| **Partial pressure of heavy gases** | He ≤ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar; N₂, O₂, CO, CO₂, H₂O each ≤ 5 × 10⁻¹¹ mbar | RGA spectra; integrate each mass channel over 1 min intervals. |
| **Leak rate** | ≤ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar·L s⁻¹ | Helium leak detector after bake‑out; monitor pressure rise with all pumps isolated. |
| **Cryo‑trap capacity** | ≥ 10⁶ Pa·L (equivalent to 0.01 mbar·L at 4 K) before saturation | Measure pump‑down curve with a calibrated nitrogen leak; observe the “knee” where pump speed drops. |
| **NEG activation** | ≥ 400 °C for 2 h; post‑activation pressure ≤ 2 × 10⁻⁹ mbar | Temperature sensors on cartridge; after each activation perform a short RGA scan. |
| **Vacuum interlocks** | Beam automatically shut if p > 5 × 10⁻⁹ mbar OR He‑partial > 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar | Software logic tied to ion‑gauge alarm; test with simulated pressure spikes. |
| **Out‑gassing budget** | < 1 × 10⁻¹² mbar·L s⁻¹ after 100 beam shots | Temperature‑programmed desorption (TPD) of a representative wall sample; compare to calculated Q. |

---

## 7.  Bottom line  

* **Pressure limit:** ≤ 3 × 10⁻⁹ mbar (total) at 300 K, ≤ 1 × 10⁻⁹ mbar if the experiment is cooled to 77 K.  
* **Composition limit:** heavy‑transfer species (He, N₂, O₂, CO, CO₂, H₂O) each ≤ 10 % of the total pressure budget (≤ 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ mbar).  
* **Pumping architecture:** a cascade of (i) high‑speed turbo, (ii) 4 K cryopump, (iii) NEG cartridge (plus optional ion pump) delivering an effective pumping speed ≥ 200 l s⁻¹ on H₂/D₂/T₂; differential skimmers keep the jet density high while preserving the low background.  
* **Diagnostics:** ion gauge + RGA (continuous), cryo‑trap residual‑gas monitor, periodic helium‑leak test, and a fast interlock system.  

When these specifications are met, the **collision‑induced broadening is < 2 Hz**, the **systematic uncertainty on resonant formation rates is ≤ 10⁻³**, and **muon‑spin coherence times exceed 100 µs**—all comfortably below the intrinsic muon decay limit.  Consequently, the residual background gas **does not dominate** the error budget and the experiment can reach its ultimate physics goals (sub‑kHz spectroscopy, ppm‑level reaction‑rate determination, high‑fidelity µSR coherence).
