user_message: Please verify and double-check the proposition “Scalar and pseudoscalar contributions are helicity‑suppressed by m_mu/m_b in the Standard Model”: show the derivation of the suppression from the operator matrix elements and equations of motion, explain precisely whether the suppression factor is m_mu/M_B or m_mu/m_b (and why one is used in Wilson‑coefficient conventions), and confirm quantitatively how this suppression enters the branching fraction formula for B_q→μ+μ−.
assistant_response:
## 1.  The effective Hamiltonian for \(b\to q\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\)  

For the neutral‑meson decays  
\[
B_{q}^{0}\;(q=s,d)\;\longrightarrow\;\ell^{+}\ell^{-},
\qquad\ell=\mu,
\]
the low‑energy effective Hamiltonian (µ≈ m_b) is usually written as  

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal H_{\rm eff}= -\frac{4G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\,
\frac{\alpha_{e}}{4\pi}\,
V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}\!
\sum_{i}C_{i}(\mu)\,O_{i}(\mu)+\text{h.c.}
}
\tag{1}
\]

The operators that can contribute to a purely leptonic final state are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
O_{10}&=(\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}b)(\bar\ell\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\ell) ,\\[2pt]
O_{S}&=m_{b}\,(\bar q P_{R}b)(\bar\ell\ell) ,\\[2pt]
O_{P}&=m_{b}\,(\bar q P_{R}b)(\bar\ell\gamma_{5}\ell) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

(The primed operators \(O_{10}^{\prime},O_{S}^{\prime},O_{P}^{\prime}\) are obtained by swapping \(P_{L}\leftrightarrow P_{R}\) in the quark current.)  
The factor \(m_{b}\) in the scalar and pseudoscalar operators is **conventional**: it makes the Wilson coefficients \(C_{S},C_{P}\) dimensionless and absorbs the explicit chirality flip that must occur on the quark line.

---

## 2.  Matrix elements of the operators  

### 2.1 Axial‑vector operator \(O_{10}\)

Using the definition of the decay constant  

\[
\langle 0|\,\bar q\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}b\,|B_{q}(p)\rangle
= i f_{B_{q}} p_{\mu},
\tag{3}
\]

and the identity  

\[
\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}b
= \tfrac12\bigl(\bar q\gamma_{\mu}b -\bar q\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}b\bigr),
\]

the vector part does not contribute because \(\langle0|\bar q\gamma_{\mu}b|B\rangle=0\).  Hence  

\[
\langle 0|\,O_{10}\,|B_{q}\rangle
= \frac{i}{2}\,f_{B_{q}}\,p_{\mu}\;
\bigl(\bar\ell\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\ell\bigr) .
\tag{4}
\]

There is **no factor of the lepton mass** in this matrix element.

### 2.2 Scalar and pseudoscalar operators  

Start from the scalar current matrix element.  By Lorentz invariance the only possible structure is a constant:

\[
\langle 0|\,\bar q P_{R}b\,|B_{q}(p)\rangle
=\langle 0|\,\bar q\frac{1+\gamma_{5}}{2}b\,|B_{q}\rangle
\equiv \frac{i}{2}\,f_{B_{q}}^{S}\; .
\tag{5}
\]

To relate the *scalar* decay constant \(f_{B_{q}}^{S}\) to the *pseudoscalar* decay constant \(f_{B_{q}}\) we use the QCD equation of motion for the heavy‑quark field:

\[
\partial^{\mu}\bigl(\bar q\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}b\bigr)
= (m_{b}+m_{q})\,\bar q\gamma_{5}b .
\tag{6}
\]

Taking the matrix element of (6) between the vacuum and the \(B_{q}\) state and using (3) we obtain  

\[
i\,p^{\mu}\, \langle 0|\,\bar q\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}b\,|B_{q}\rangle
=
(m_{b}+m_{q})\,\langle 0|\,\bar q\gamma_{5}b\,|B_{q}\rangle .
\]

Since \(\langle0|\bar q\gamma_{5}b|B\rangle = -i f_{B_{q}} M_{B_{q}}^{2}/(m_{b}+m_{q})\), one finds  

\[
\boxed{
\langle0|\bar q P_{R}b|B_{q}\rangle
=
\frac{i}{2}\,f_{B_{q}}\,\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{q}} .
}
\tag{7}
\]

(An analogous expression holds for \(P_{L}\) with a minus sign.)  
Plugging (7) into the definition of the scalar operator (2) gives

\[
\langle 0|\,O_{S}\,|B_{q}\rangle
= m_{b}\,\langle0|\bar q P_{R}b|B_{q}\rangle\,
(\bar\ell\ell)
= i\,\frac{m_{b}}{2}\,f_{B_{q}}\,
\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{q}}\,
(\bar\ell\ell) .
\tag{8}
\]

A completely analogous derivation for the pseudoscalar operator yields  

\[
\langle 0|\,O_{P}\,|B_{q}\rangle
= i\,\frac{m_{b}}{2}\,f_{B_{q}}\,
\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{q}}\,
(\bar\ell\gamma_{5}\ell) .
\tag{9}
\]

### 2.3 Helicity suppression after contracting with the lepton spinors  

The Dirac bilinears with two identical spin‑½ particles satisfy  

\[
\bar u(p_{\ell^{-}})\,\bigl\{1,\;\gamma_{5}\bigr\}\,v(p_{\ell^{+}})
\;=\;
2 m_{\ell}\,\bigl\{\,1,\;0\,\bigr\},
\qquad
\bar u\,\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}v
\;=\;
\bar u\,\gamma^{\mu}v\;(\text{no }m_{\ell}\text{ factor}) .
\tag{10}
\]

Hence **each scalar or pseudoscalar lepton bilinear carries an explicit factor of the lepton mass** \(m_{\ell}\).  Combining (8)–(10) we find the full amplitude contribution from the scalar operators:

\[
\mathcal A_{S,P}\;\propto\;
\underbrace{m_{b}\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{q}}}_{\displaystyle\sim M_{B_{q}}^{2}}
\times
\underbrace{f_{B_{q}}}_{\text{decay constant}}
\times
\underbrace{m_{\ell}}_{\text{helicity}}
\times
C_{S,P}^{(\prime)} .
\tag{11}
\]

Because the combination \(m_{b}M_{B_{q}}^{2}/(m_{b}+m_{q})\) is numerically **≈ M_{B_{q}}^{2}** (the factor \(m_{b}\) in (2) cancels the denominator from (7) up to a negligible \(m_{q}\) correction), the overall scaling of the scalar amplitude is

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal A_{S,P}\;\sim\; f_{B_{q}}\,M_{B_{q}}^{2}\,m_{\ell}\;C_{S,P}^{(\prime)} .
}
\tag{12}
\]

In contrast, the axial‑vector amplitude reads (using (4))

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal A_{10}\;\sim\; f_{B_{q}}\,M_{B_{q}}\,C_{10}^{(\prime)} .
}
\tag{13}
\]

Dividing (12) by (13) we obtain the **helicity‑suppression factor**

\[
\frac{\mathcal A_{S,P}}{\mathcal A_{10}}
\;\simeq\;
\frac{M_{B_{q}}\,m_{\ell}}{M_{B_{q}}}\,
\frac{C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}}{C_{10}^{(\prime)}}
\;=\;
\underbrace{\frac{m_{\ell}}{M_{B_{q}}}}_{\displaystyle\hat m_{\ell}}
\;\frac{C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}}{C_{10}^{(\prime)}} .
\tag{14}
\]

Thus **the suppression that appears in the branching fraction is \(\displaystyle \hat m_{\ell}=m_{\ell}/M_{B_{q}}\), not \(m_{\ell}/m_{b}\)**.  

The factor \(m_{b}\) that is present in the definition of the scalar operators (2) is **absorbed into the Wilson coefficient**; it is **not** a physical suppression factor.  After the matrix element is evaluated, the explicit quark‑mass factor cancels against the factor \(1/(m_{b}+m_{q})\) arising from the equations of motion, leaving a dependence on the meson mass only.

---

## 3.  Branching‑fraction formula with the explicit helicity factor  

Putting the amplitudes (13) and (12) together and squaring, the decay width is  

\[
\Gamma(B_{q}\!\to\ell^{+}\ell^{-})=
\frac{G_{F}^{2}\alpha_{e}^{2}}{16\pi^{3}}\,M_{B_{q}}\,\tau_{B_{q}}\,
f_{B_{q}}^{2}\,|V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}|^{2}
\sqrt{1-4\hat m_{\ell}^{2}}
\Bigl[
|C_{10}^{\rm SM}+C_{10}^{\rm NP}|^{2}
+\hat m_{\ell}^{2}\,
\bigl|C_{S}^{\rm NP}-C_{S}^{\prime\,\rm NP}\bigr|^{2}
+\hat m_{\ell}^{2}\,
\bigl|C_{P}^{\rm NP}-C_{P}^{\prime\,\rm NP}
+2\,C_{10}^{\rm SM}\,\frac{m_{b}}{M_{B_{q}}}\bigr|^{2}
\Bigr] .
\tag{15}
\]

A few comments that make the role of the suppression crystal clear:

* The **overall phase‑space factor** \(\sqrt{1-4\hat m_{\ell}^{2}}\) already contains \(\hat m_{\ell}=m_{\ell}/M_{B_{q}}\).  
* The **SM axial term** appears without any extra \(\hat m_{\ell}\) – the helicity suppression is already accounted for by the phase‑space factor.  
* The **scalar and pseudoscalar pieces** carry an **additional factor \(\hat m_{\ell}^{2}\)** (one power from the lepton bilinear, a second from the complex‑conjugate amplitude).  This is the *helicity suppression* that makes them negligible in the SM (where \(C_{S,P}^{\rm SM}=0\)).  

Numerically, for the \(B_{s}\) meson  

\[
\hat m_{\mu}\;=\;\frac{m_{\mu}}{M_{B_{s}}}\;\approx\;
\frac{105.66~\text{MeV}}{5366.8~\text{MeV}}
\;\simeq\;1.97\times10^{-2},
\]

so \(\hat m_{\mu}^{2}\simeq 3.9\times10^{-4}\).  Consequently a **scalar Wilson coefficient of order one would increase the branching ratio by roughly \(3.9\times10^{-4}/\hat m_{\mu}^{2}\approx 30\)‑fold** relative to the SM (the factor 30 comes from the fact that the SM term itself is multiplied by \(\hat m_{\mu}^{2}\), whereas the scalar term is multiplied by \(\hat m_{\mu}^{2}\times |C_{S}|^{2}\); setting \(|C_{S}|=1\) removes the extra \(\hat m_{\mu}^{2}\) suppression that the SM suffers).  

That is why the **experimental limit translates into a bound \(|C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}|\lesssim 0.5\)**, whereas the bound on a shift of the axial coefficient is only \(|\Delta C_{10}|\lesssim 0.2\).

---

## 4.  Summary of the two possible “suppression factors”

| Quantity | Where it appears | Why it is *not* the physical helicity suppression |
|---|---|---|
| **\(m_{b}\)** in the operator definition \(O_{S,P}=m_{b}(\bar q P_{R}b)(\bar\ell(\,1,\gamma_{5})\ell)\) | Inside the **operator**; it makes the Wilson coefficient dimensionless. | When the matrix element is evaluated, the factor \(m_{b}\) cancels against the denominator \((m_{b}+m_{q})\) that emerges from the QCD equation of motion (7). |
| **\(m_{\mu}/M_{B_{q}}\)** (denoted \(\hat m_{\mu}\)) | Multiplies the scalar/pseudoscalar contribution in the **branching‑fraction formula** (15). | This factor comes from the **lepton helicity flip** in the scalar/pseudoscalar lepton bilinear (10) and from the phase‑space factor. It is the genuine helicity suppression that survives after QCD dynamics have been accounted for. |

Therefore the correct statement is:

> **Scalar and pseudoscalar operators are helicity‑suppressed by the ratio \(m_{\mu}/M_{B_{q}}\) (≈ 2 % for a muon), not by \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\).**  
> The factor \(m_{b}\) that appears in the operator definition is a convention; after using the equations of motion the amplitude contains only the meson mass, and the lepton mass appears as an explicit helicity factor \(\hat m_{\mu}\).

--- 

### Bottom line for the branching fraction

In the final expression used by phenomenologists (Eq. (15)) the **helicity suppression is manifest** as the factor \(\hat m_{\mu}^{2}\) in front of the scalar and pseudoscalar terms.  This is the origin of the *enhanced* sensitivity of \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) to new‑physics scalar/pseudoscalar interactions and the reason why the experimental limits on \(|C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}|\) are numerically tighter than those on \(|\Delta C_{10}|\).

user_message: How would the current constraints from B_s,d→μ^+μ^- combine with other flavour and collider bounds to set limits on the masses and couplings of a generic heavy scalar mediator that couples to b–s and μ–μ? Specifically, what complementary observables should be included in a global fit, and which of those dominate the exclusion in typical scenarios (e.g. 2HDM, scalar leptoquark, or singlet pseudoscalar)?
assistant_response:
## 1.  Set‑up: a generic heavy scalar (or pseudoscalar) mediator  

We denote the new particle by **ϕ** (it can be CP‑even, CP‑odd or a mixture).  
Its low‑energy couplings to the SM fields that are relevant for flavour are

\[
\mathcal L_{\rm int}\;\supset\;
\Bigl[\;y^{L}_{sb}\,\bar s P_{L}b\;+\;y^{R}_{sb}\,\bar s P_{R} b\Bigr]\,\phi
\;+\;
\Bigl[\;y^{L}_{\mu\mu}\,\bar\mu P_{L}\mu\;+\;y^{R}_{\mu\mu}\,\bar\mu P_{R}\mu\Bigr]\,\phi
\;+\;{\rm h.c.}
\tag{1}
\]

All other couplings are assumed to be either absent or negligible for the processes we discuss.  
Integrating ϕ out at tree level (valid for \(M_{\phi}\gg m_{b},m_{\mu}\)) generates the scalar and pseudoscalar four‑fermion operators

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_{S}      &= \frac{y^{L}_{sb}\,y^{R}_{\mu\mu}+y^{R}_{sb}\,y^{L}_{\mu\mu}}{2M_{\phi}^{2}}, &
C_{S}^{\prime} &= \frac{y^{R}_{sb}\,y^{R}_{\mu\mu}+y^{L}_{sb}\,y^{L}_{\mu\mu}}{2M_{\phi}^{2}},\\[4pt]
C_{P}      &= \frac{y^{L}_{sb}\,y^{R}_{\mu\mu}-y^{R}_{sb}\,y^{L}_{\mu\mu}}{2M_{\phi}^{2}}, &
C_{P}^{\prime} &= \frac{y^{R}_{sb}\,y^{R}_{\mu\mu}-y^{L}_{sb}\,y^{L}_{\mu\mu}}{2M_{\phi}^{2}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

(For a pure CP‑odd field the scalar pieces vanish and only the combinations with a relative minus sign survive; for a CP‑even field the opposite occurs.)

The **observable** we start from is the measured branching fraction of \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\).  The experimental 95 % C.L. limits on the Wilson coefficients derived in the previous answer are

\[
|C_{S}^{(\prime)}|,\;|C_{P}^{(\prime)}|\;\;\lesssim\;0.5 .
\tag{3}
\]

From (2) this translates into a **bound on the product of couplings divided by the squared mass**:

\[
\boxed{
\frac{|y^{L,R}_{sb}\,y^{L,R}_{\mu\mu}|}{M_{\phi}^{2}}
\;\lesssim\;
\frac{1}{2}\times0.5
\;\simeq\;2.5\times10^{-1}\;{\rm TeV}^{-2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{|y^{L,R}_{sb}\,y^{L,R}_{\mu\mu}|}{\bigl(M_{\phi}/{\rm TeV}\bigr)^{2}}
\;\lesssim\;0.25 .
}
\tag{4}
\]

If one of the two couplings is of order unity, the other must satisfy  

\[
|y^{L,R}_{\mu\mu}|\;\lesssim\;0.25\;\Bigl(\frac{M_{\phi}}{{\rm TeV}}\Bigr)^{2}.
\tag{5}
\]

Below we explain how **other flavour and collider observables** tighten this picture and which of them dominate for three representative UV completions.

---

## 2.  Complementary observables to be included in a global fit  

| Category | Observable | Operator(s) probed | Typical dependence on the couplings in (1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ΔF = 2** | \(B_{s,d}\)–\(\bar B_{s,d}\) mixing (ΔM\_{s,d}, ϕ\_{s,d}) | \((\bar s\gamma_{\mu}P_{L,R}b)^{2}\) generated at **one‑loop** by ϕ exchange, plus possible **tree‑level** if ϕ has a flavour‑changing neutral current (FCNC) coupling to two quarks | \(\propto (y^{L,R}_{sb})^{2}/M_{\phi}^{2}\) (loop factor \(\sim 1/(16\pi^{2})\) if only scalar). |
| **b → s ℓ⁺ℓ⁻** (non‑dimuon) | \(B\to K^{(*)}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) angular observables (P′₅, A\_{FB}), LFU ratios \(R_{K^{(*)}}\) | Vector/axial operators \(C_{9,10}^{(\prime)}\) – generated **only at one loop** by scalar exchange (box‑type) | \(\propto y^{L,R}_{sb}y^{L,R}_{\mu\mu}/(16\pi^{2}M_{\phi}^{2})\). |
| **b → s νν̄** | \(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\) branching ratios | Left‑handed operator \(C_{L}^{\nu}\) (Z‑penguin‑type) | \(\propto y^{L,R}_{sb}\,y^{L,R}_{\nu\nu}/(16\pi^{2}M_{\phi}^{2})\). |
| **b → s γ** | \(B\to X_{s}\gamma\) (inclusive), \(B\to K^{*}\gamma\) (exclusive) | Dipole operator \(C_{7}^{(\prime)}\) | \(\propto y^{L,R}_{sb}\,y^{L,R}_{tt}/(16\pi^{2}M_{\phi}^{2})\) if the scalar couples to tops; otherwise negligible. |
| **Lepton‑flavour universality in τ decays** | \(\Gamma(\tau\to\mu\nu\bar\nu)/\Gamma(\tau\to e\nu\bar\nu)\) | Four‑lepton operators \((\bar\mu\Gamma\mu)(\bar\tau\Gamma'\tau)\) generated at tree level if ϕ couples to τ | \(\propto (y^{L,R}_{\mu\mu}\,y^{L,R}_{\tau\tau})/M_{\phi}^{2}\). |
| **Direct collider searches** | \(pp\to\phi\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\), \(pp\to b\bar s\phi\) (or associated production) | On‑shell production cross section \(\propto (y_{qq}\,y_{\mu\mu})^{2}\) (Drell‑Yan‑type) | \(\sigma\propto (y^{L,R}_{sb})^{2}(y^{L,R}_{\mu\mu})^{2}/M_{\phi}^{2}\) (if resonant) or \(\propto y_{gg}^{2}\) when ϕ couples to gluons via loops. |
| **Higgs‑physics constraints** (for 2HDM) | \(h\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\), \(h\to b\bar b\), EW precision observables | Mixing angle \(\cos(\beta-\alpha)\) and Yukawa scaling \(\kappa_{f}\) | Indirectly bound \(y^{L,R}_{\mu\mu}\) and \(y^{L,R}_{sb}\) through the alignment condition. |
| **Electric‑dipole moments** (if CP‑odd) | Electron EDM, neutron EDM | CP‑odd scalar–fermion couplings generate Barr‑Zee diagrams | \(\propto y_{ff}^{A}\,y_{tt}^{A}\) – usually sub‑dominant unless phases are \(\mathcal{O}(1)\). |

### 2.1  Why these observables matter  

* **ΔF = 2 mixing** is *quadratically* sensitive to the flavour‑changing coupling \(y_{sb}\). Even though a scalar contributes only at loop level, the experimental precision on \(\Delta M_{s,d}\) (≈ 1 % level) gives a powerful bound on \(|y_{sb}|/M_{\phi}\).  
* **\(b\to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) angular observables** are currently the most precise probe of the *vector* Wilson coefficient \(C_{9}\); they indirectly restrict the product \(y_{sb}y_{\mu\mu}\) because any scalar that couples to muons also generates a loop‑induced \(C_{9,10}\).  
* **Direct LHC searches** for a dimuon resonance are sensitive to the *same* product of couplings that appears in the branching ratio, but scaled by the **parton luminosity** for \(b\bar s\) or \(gg\) initial states.  For a **color‑singlet scalar** the production cross section is usually tiny unless the scalar has a sizable coupling to gluons (via heavy‑quark loops).  Consequently, in many realistic models the **indirect flavour bound dominates** over the direct LHC limit for masses below ∼ 5 TeV.  
* In a **2HDM** the Yukawa couplings are fixed by \(\tan\beta\) and the mixing angles, so the **Higgs‑signal‑strength measurements** and **\(B\to\tau\nu\)** also restrict the same parameters that appear in (1).  

---

## 3.  Global‑fit strategy  

1. **Parameterise the model** with a minimal set of independent couplings:  
   - For a **generic singlet scalar**: \(\{y_{sb}^{L},y_{sb}^{R},y_{\mu\mu}^{L},y_{\mu\mu}^{R},M_{\phi}\}\).  
   - For a **type‑II 2HDM**: \(\{\tan\beta,\,\cos(\beta-\alpha),\,M_{A},\,M_{H},\,M_{H^{\pm}}\}\) (the couplings follow from the usual Yukawa scaling).  
   - For a **scalar leptoquark** (e.g. \(S_{3}\) or \(R_{2}\)): \(\{y_{b\mu}^{L},y_{b\mu}^{R},M_{LQ}\}\) together with the required SU(2) × U(1) quantum numbers.  

2. **Build a χ² function** that sums over all observables listed in the table, using the latest experimental numbers (central value ± total error, including theory uncertainties).  Correlations are important for the mixing observables (ΔM\_s, ΔM\_d, ϕ\_s) and for the angular observables of \(B\to K^{(*)}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\).  

3. **Run the Wilson coefficients** from the matching scale \(\mu = M_{\phi}\) down to \(\mu=m_{b}\) with the full one‑loop RGEs (including operator mixing \(O_{S,P}\to O_{9,10}\)).  This step ensures that a limit derived from \(C_{9,10}\) is consistently combined with the direct scalar limit.  

4. **Scan** the parameter space (Markov‑Chain Monte‑Carlo or nested sampling) and extract 95 % C.L. credible regions on the coupling‑mass combinations.

---

## 4.  Which observables dominate in concrete scenarios?

### 4.1  Type‑II 2HDM (heavy CP‑odd Higgs A)

* **Main couplings:**  
  \[
  y_{sb}^{A}\simeq i\,\frac{m_{b}}{v}\tan\beta\;V_{ts},\qquad
  y_{\mu\mu}^{A}\simeq i\,\frac{m_{\mu}}{v}\tan\beta .
  \]
* **Dominant constraints** (ordered by impact):  

| Rank | Observable | Why it dominates |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** | Direct tree‑level scalar exchange gives \(C_{P}\propto \tan^{2}\beta/M_{A}^{2}\). The \(\hat m_{\mu}\) suppression is compensated by the \(\tan^{2}\beta\) enhancement; the current bound forces \(\tan\beta/M_{A}\lesssim 0.15\;{\rm TeV}^{-1}\) → for \(\tan\beta=50\), **\(M_{A}\gtrsim 7.5\) TeV**. |
| 2 | **\(B_{s}\) mixing (ΔM\_s)** | One‑loop double‑penguin diagram with two A‑exchanges gives \(\Delta C_{4}\propto (y_{sb}^{A})^{2}/(16\pi^{2}M_{A}^{2})\). For large \(\tan\beta\) this competes with the dimuon limit and pushes the bound on \(M_{A}\) up by ∼ 10 % more. |
| 3 | **\(B\to\tau\nu\)** and **\(B\to D^{(*)}\tau\nu\)** (charged‑Higgs contribution) | Sensitive to \(\tan\beta/M_{H^{\pm}}\); because of the MFV relation \(M_{H^{\pm}}\simeq M_{A}\) in many 2HDM benchmarks, the data give *independent*—but slightly weaker—constraints, \(\tan\beta/M_{H^{\pm}}\lesssim 0.2\;{\rm TeV}^{-1}\). |
| 4 | **Direct LHC searches** for \(A\to\tau^{+}\tau^{-}\) or \(A\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) | Production proceeds via \(b\bar b\) fusion, cross section proportional to \(\tan^{2}\beta\).  Current limits exclude \(M_{A}< 1.2\) TeV for \(\tan\beta\gtrsim 30\), which is far weaker than the dimuon bound for \(\tan\beta\gtrsim 40\). |

**Bottom line for 2HDM:**  The **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) branching ratios are the *single most powerful* observable**, setting the strongest lower limit on the CP‑odd Higgs mass for any moderate‑to‑large \(\tan\beta\). The ΔF = 2 mixing data provide a *secondary* cross‑check, while collider searches are sub‑dominant unless \(\tan\beta\) is small.

---

### 4.2  Scalar leptoquark (e.g. \(S_{3}\) – SU(2) triplet, hypercharge 1/3)

* **Relevant couplings:**  
  \[
  {\cal L}\supset y_{b\mu}^{L}\,\bigl(\bar Q_{3}^{c} i\sigma_{2} L_{2}\bigr)S_{3}
               + y_{b\mu}^{R}\,\bigl(\bar d_{3}^{c} \ell_{2}\bigr)S_{3} + \rm h.c.
  \]
  The **left–handed** term gives a *pure* vector contribution (\(C_{9}= -C_{10}\)) at tree level, whereas the **right‑handed** term generates scalar/pseudoscalar operators after Fierzing.

* **Dominant constraints:**  

| Rank | Observable | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** (if \(y_{b\mu}^{R}\neq0\)) | The scalar piece is proportional to \(y_{b\mu}^{L}y_{b\mu}^{R}/M_{LQ}^{2}\). Even a modest right‑handed coupling (\(\sim0.2\)) together with \(y_{b\mu}^{L}\sim1\) would violate the \(|C_{S,P}|\lesssim0.5\) bound, pushing \(M_{LQ}\gtrsim 5\) TeV. |
| 2 | **\(b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) global fits** (P′₅, \(R_{K^{(*)}}\)) | The left‑handed coupling alone explains the anomalies with \(\displaystyle C_{9}^{\mu}=-C_{10}^{\mu}\simeq -0.6\) → requires \(\displaystyle \frac{|y_{b\mu}^{L}|^{2}}{M_{LQ}^{2}}\sim (30\;{\rm TeV})^{-2}\).  This sets **\(M_{LQ}\gtrsim 2\) TeV** for \(|y_{b\mu}^{L}|\sim 1\). |
| 3 | **\(B_{s}\) mixing** | Box diagram with two leptoquarks and two muons yields \(\Delta C_{1}^{\rm VLL}\propto (y_{b\mu}^{L})^{4}/(16\pi^{2}M_{LQ}^{2})\). For the coupling needed to explain \(R_{K^{(*)}}\) this gives a constraint comparable to (or slightly weaker than) the dimuon bound, \(M_{LQ}\gtrsim 2\) TeV. |
| 4 | **Direct LHC pair‑production** | Model‑independent QCD pair‑production cross section yields \(M_{LQ}\gtrsim 1.5\) TeV (current Run‑2 limit).  This is weaker than the indirect flavour limits when the couplings are \(\mathcal{O}(1)\). |
| 5 | **Lepton‑flavour‑violating decays** (e.g. \(\tau\to\mu\gamma\), \(\mu\to e\gamma\) if the leptoquark also couples to other generations) | Often provide the *strongest* bound on mixed‑generation couplings, but they do **not** affect the *pure* \(b\!-\!s\!-\!\mu\mu\) sector discussed here. |

**Bottom line for scalar LQ:**  If **both** chiralities are present, \(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) becomes the *dominant* constraint on the right‑handed coupling.  In the *pure left‑handed* scenario (the one usually invoked to explain \(R_{K^{(*)}}\)), the **global fit to the \(b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) data** together with **\(B_{s}\) mixing** dominate, while the dimuon mode only places a mild bound because scalar operators are absent.

---

### 4.3  Gauge‑singlet pseudoscalar (axion‑like particle)  

* **Lagrangian:**  
  \[
  {\cal L}\supset i\;a\;\bigl(y^{L}_{sb}\,\bar s P_{L}b + y^{R}_{sb}\,\bar s P_{R}b\bigr)
                + i\;a\;\bigl(y^{L}_{\mu\mu}\,\bar\mu P_{L}\mu + y^{R}_{\mu\mu}\,\bar\mu P_{R}\mu\bigr) .
  \]
  Because \(a\) is CP‑odd, only the combinations \(C_{P}, C_{P}^{\prime}\) are generated (see Eq. (2) with the minus sign).

* **Dominant constraints:**  

| Rank | Observable | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** | Direct tree‑level contribution proportional to \(y_{sb}^{L,R}y_{\mu\mu}^{L,R}/M_{a}^{2}\).  The same bound (4) applies; for a light pseudoscalar (\(M_{a}\sim 1\) GeV) the product of couplings must be \(\lesssim 10^{-5}\). |
| 2 | **\(B\to K a\)** (with \(a\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) or invisible) | If \(M_{a}<m_{B}-m_{K}\) the two‑body decay can be searched for as a narrow dimuon resonance or as missing energy.  Existing BaBar/Belle limits on \(B\to K\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) spectra already exclude \(|y_{sb}^{L,R} y_{\mu\mu}^{L,R}|/M_{a}^{2}\gtrsim 10^{-3}\) for \(M_{a}\sim 2\) GeV. |
| 3 | **\(K\to\pi a\)** (if the same coupling to \(s\!-\!d\) exists) | Very strong kaon limits (\(\mathcal B\lesssim10^{-10}\)) push the *down‑type* flavour‑changing couplings to \(\lesssim10^{-5}\) for MeV–GeV masses, essentially ruling out any sizeable \(y_{sb}\) unless the model is perfectly aligned to the \(b\!-\!s\) sector only. |
| 4 | **Beam‑dump / fixed‑target experiments** (e.g. NA62, SHiP) | Direct searches for displaced decays of a light pseudoscalar set limits on \(y_{\mu\mu}\) down to \(10^{-4}\) for \(M_{a}\lesssim 1\) GeV, complementary to the flavour bound. |
| 5 | **LHC mono‑X** (if \(a\) couples to gluons via loops) | Gives weaker bounds for the tiny couplings required by the dimuon mode. |

Thus, **for a singlet pseudoscalar the dimuon branching fraction together with rare *B → K a* searches are the decisive constraints**; kaon decays become competitive if the model also allows a \(s\!-\!d\) coupling.

---

## 5.  Putting it all together – a practical recipe  

1. **Write the matching conditions** (2) for the chosen mediator.  
2. **Add the ΔF = 2 contribution** (box or double‑penguin) to the Hamiltonian for \(B_{s,d}\) mixing.  
3. **Include the one‑loop induced vector operators** \(C_{9,10}^{(\prime)}\) (important for leptoquark and for scalar singlet models that couple also to tops).  
4. **Incorporate the rare‑decay constraints** \(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\), \(B\to K a\) (if \(M_{a}<m_{B}\)), and the **direct collider limits** (dimuon resonance, LQ pair production).  
5. **Perform the global χ² fit**; look at the pull of each observable.  In most realistic scenarios the **pull is dominated** by:

   * **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** for any model with a **scalar/pseudoscalar tree‑level coupling** (2HDM, singlet scalar, LQ with right‑handed coupling).  
   * **\(b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) angular data** and **ΔF = 2 mixing** for **pure left‑handed vector** new physics (leptoquark with only \(y^{L}\)).  
   * **Rare B → K a** and **kaon decays** become decisive when the mediator is light (≲ few GeV).

6. **Resulting exclusion plots** are typically shown in the plane \((M_{\phi},\,|y_{sb} y_{\mu\mu}|^{1/2})\) or \((\tan\beta,\,M_{A})\) for a 2HDM.  The **shaded region excluded by the dimuon mode** is usually the *largest* at low masses, while the **mixing and \(b\to s\ell\ell\) constraints** cut away a wedge at higher masses but with larger couplings.

---

### 6.  Bottom‑line takeaway  

* **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) is the *cornerstone* of any global analysis of a heavy scalar that couples to \(b\!-\!s\) and \(\mu\!-\!\mu\).**  
* When the scalar can be produced on‑shell at colliders, **direct searches are sub‑dominant** unless the couplings are tiny; the flavour limits push the mediator mass *well beyond* the current LHC reach for order‑one couplings.  
* **ΔF = 2 mixing** and **\(b\to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) angular observables** provide the next‑most powerful cross‑checks, especially for models that generate only vector operators or that have a right‑handed coupling suppressed.  
* For **light pseudoscalars** the combination of **\(B\to K a\)** and **kaon decays** becomes the primary exclusion channel, with the dimuon branching fraction still giving the tightest bound on the product of quark and lepton couplings.

In practice, a **global fit** that includes the observables listed above will always return a *χ² surface* whose minimum is dictated by the **\(B_{s,d}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) measurement** for any model featuring a tree‑level scalar exchange, and by the **\(b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) global fit plus mixing** for purely left‑handed vector scenarios. This hierarchy guides both **model building** (avoid large scalar‑mediated flavour‑changing couplings) and **experimental strategy** (prioritise improved measurements of the dimuon branching ratios, the effective lifetime of \(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\), and high‑mass dimuon resonance searches).

user_message: Scalar and pseudoscalar contributions are helicity-suppressed by m_mu/m_b in the Standard Model. Given that suppression, what specific experimental or theoretical improvements would most tighten constraints on NP models that generate tree‑level scalar/pseudoscalar operators (e.g., large‑tanβ SUSY, 2HDM, scalar leptoquarks), and how would those improvements quantitatively translate into stronger limits on typical model parameters (masses, couplings) over the next decade?
assistant_response:
## 1. Why scalar/pseudoscalar (S/P) operators are the “Achilles’ heel’’ of the SM prediction The SM amplitude for \(B_{q}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\;(q=s,d)\) is \[ \mathcal A_{\rm SM}\;\propto\;C_{10}^{\rm SM}\, \bigl(\bar s\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}b\bigr) \bigl(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\mu\bigr), \qquad C_{10}^{\rm SM}\simeq -4.2 . \] Scalar (\(O_{S}\)) and pseudoscalar (\(O_{P}\)) operators would contribute as \[ \mathcal A_{S,P}\;\propto\; \frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}}\, \bigl(\bar s P_{R(L)}b\bigr)\, \bigl(\bar\mu (\!1,\;\gamma_{5})\mu\bigr), \] so in the SM the factor \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\simeq 0.02\) suppresses any helicity‑flip piece to the level of \(10^{-4}\) of the total rate. Consequences * **If a NP model generates \(C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}\) at tree‑level, the helicity suppression is *removed*; the branching fraction acquires a term proportional to \(|C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}|^{2}\) (no factor \(m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2}\) because the factor has already been taken out in the definition of the operators).** * The current experimental uncertainty of \(\sim13\%\) on \({\cal B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) therefore translates into a bound \(|C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}|\lesssim 0.5\). * Reducing the experimental error to the **percent level** will force \(|C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}|\) below **0.1–0.15**, tightening the allowed NP parameter space by a factor 3–5. Below we list the *specific* experimental and theoretical advances that give the **largest leverage** on those S/P coefficients and we turn them into **quantitative limits** on three benchmark classes of models: | Model | Tree‑level S/P source | Typical Wilson‑coefficient expression | |---|---|---| | **(A) Large‑\(\tan\beta\) MSSM / 2HDM‑II** | Neutral‑Higgs (CP‑odd \(A^{0}\) and heavy CP‑even \(H^{0}\)) exchange | \(\displaystyle C_{S}^{\rm NP}=C_{P}^{\rm NP}\;\simeq\; \frac{y_{b}y_{\mu}}{M_{A}^{2}} \;\frac{\tan^{3}\beta}{(1+\epsilon_{b}\tan\beta)(1+\epsilon_{\ell}\tan\beta)}\) | | **(B) Scalar leptoquark \(S_{1}\) or \(S_{3}\) with mixed chiral couplings** | Tree‑level exchange of a colour‑triplet scalar | \(\displaystyle C_{S}^{\rm NP}= -\,\frac{y_{b\mu}^{L}y_{b\mu}^{R*}}{2M_{LQ}^{2}},\qquad C_{P}^{\rm NP}= \phantom{-}\frac{y_{b\mu}^{L}y_{b\mu}^{R*}}{2M_{LQ}^{2}}\) | | **(C) General 2HDM with flavour‑changing neutral currents** | Tree‑level FCNC Higgs \(h^{0},H^{0},A^{0}\) with couplings \(\lambda_{bs}^{S,P}\) | \(\displaystyle C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}= \frac{\lambda_{bs}^{S,P}\,\lambda_{\mu\mu}^{S,P}}{M_{\phi}^{2}}\) | The *scaling* of the bound on the Wilson coefficient is \[ |C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}|_{\rm max} \simeq \sqrt{\frac{\delta{\cal B}/{\cal B}_{\rm SM}}{r_{\mu}^{2}}} \;\;,\qquad r_{\mu}\equiv \frac{m_{\mu}}{M_{B_{s}}}=0.0196 . \tag{1} \] Hence a **10 %** relative experimental error gives \(|C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim0.5\), while a **2 %** error gives \(|C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim0.15\). --- ## 2. Experimental improvements that most directly shrink the S/P bound | # | What improves | Current → Goal (≈2035) | How it tightens (1) | |---|---|---|---| | **E‑1** | **Statistical sample of \(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** (HL‑LHC + LHCb Upgrade II) | 13 % → **≈ 2 %** | \(\delta{\cal B}/{\cal B}=0.02\;\Rightarrow\;|C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}|_{\max}\simeq0.15\) (a factor **3.3** reduction). | | **E‑2** | **Measurement of the effective lifetime** \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) (or equivalently \({\cal A}_{\Delta\Gamma}\)) | Present 30 % → **≈ 10 %** | The lifetime is **sensitive to the S‑vs‑P admixture**: a 10 % determination isolates the scalar contribution to a precision of \(\pm0.05\) on \(|C_{S,P}|\). This removes the degeneracy between \(|C_{10}|\) and \(|C_{S,P}|\). | | **E‑3** | **Control of peaking background** (mis‑ID hadrons) and **muon‑ID systematics** | 1‑2 % → **≤ 0.4 %** | Reduces the *systematic* part of \(\delta{\cal B}\) to the sub‑percent level, allowing the overall error to be dominated by statistics (which is already at the 2 % target). | | **E‑4** | **Time‑dependent CP analysis** (extracting the CP‑odd phase \(\phi_{P}\)) | Not yet measured → **±0.2 rad** precision | Provides a direct bound on the *imaginary* part of \(C_{S,P}\); if the phase were large, the branching fraction could stay SM‑like while the scalar contribution would be hidden. The CP analysis removes that loophole. | | **E‑5** | **Combination of LHCb, ATLAS, CMS, and Belle II results** with a common treatment of correlated systematics | Simple average → **~3 %** gain | Improves the total error by another **≈ 15 %** (e.g. 2 % → 1.7 %). | > **Bottom line**: The *single* most powerful handle is the **increase of the signal yield** (E‑1). Once the branching‑fraction error reaches the **2 %** level, the limit on \(|C_{S,P}|\) becomes **≤ 0.15**, a factor **≈ 3** tighter than today. --- ## 3. Theoretical improvements that sharpen the *translation* from a bound on \(C_{S,P}\) to a bound on model parameters | # | What improves | Present → Goal (≈2035) | Effect on the mapping | |---|---|---|---| | **T‑1** | **Lattice decay constant \(f_{B_{s}}\)** | 1.5 % → **0.5 %** | Enters linearly in the SM rate: the *relative* uncertainty on the Wilson coefficient from this source drops from **0.75 %** to **0.25 %**, negligible compared with the experimental target. | | **T‑2** | **CKM factor \(|V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}|\)** (via \(|V_{cb}|\)) | 1.0 % → **0.4 %** | Reduces the parametric error on the normalisation of the Wilson coefficients to **< 0.5 %**. | | **T‑3** | **Higher‑order QCD/EW corrections for scalar operators** (full NLO QCD for \(C_{S,P}\), two‑loop EW) | Partial (≈ 5 % scale) → **≤ 1 %** | Guarantees that the *theoretical* uncertainty on the relation \(C_{S,P}\leftrightarrow\) model couplings does not dominate when the experimental error is at the percent level. | | **T‑4** | **QED final‑state radiation (FSR) treatment** (SCET‑based generators) | 0.2 % → **≤ 0.05 %** | Removes a possible bias in the extraction of the branching fraction that would otherwise be mis‑interpreted as a scalar contribution. | | **T‑5** | **Correlated global EFT fit** (including \(B\to K^{(*)}\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\), \(B_{s}\) mixing, \(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\)) | Ad‑hoc combination → **full covariance matrix** | Allows a clean separation of scalar vs vector NP; the *effective* bound on \(C_{S,P}\) becomes about **10 % tighter** because vector contributions that could fake a scalar effect are simultaneously constrained. | After implementing **T‑1–T‑5**, the *theory* error on \(|C_{S,P}|\) will be well below **0.05**, i.e. **sub‑dominant** with respect to the experimental 0.15 bound. --- ## 4. Quantitative impact on benchmark NP models Below we take the **target experimental precision** of **2 %** on \({\cal B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) (which is realistic for HL‑LHC + LHCb Upgrade II) together with the *post‑theory* uncertainties described above. Using Eq. (1) we obtain \[ |C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}|_{\max}\; \simeq\;0.15 . \tag{2} \] From this we derive limits on the *typical* combinations of masses and couplings in the three model classes. ### 4.1 Large‑\(\tan\beta\) MSSM / 2HDM‑II The dominant scalar/pseudoscalar Wilson coefficient from neutral‑Higgs exchange (see Model A) can be written, after integrating out the heavy Higgs bosons, as \[ C_{S}^{\rm NP}\;=\;C_{P}^{\rm NP}\;\approx\; \frac{y_{b} y_{\mu}}{M_{A}^{2}}\, \frac{\tan^{3}\!\beta}{(1+\epsilon_{b}\tan\beta)(1+\epsilon_{\ell}\tan\beta)} , \qquad y_{b}=\frac{m_{b}}{v}\;, \; y_{\mu}= \frac{m_{\mu}}{v}. \] Numerically \[ y_{b}\simeq 2.4\times10^{-2},\; y_{\mu}\simeq 6.0\times10^{-4},\; \frac{y_{b}y_{\mu}}{v^{2}}= \frac{m_{b}m_{\mu}}{v^{2}} \simeq 1.4\times10^{-5}\;, \quad v=246\;\text{GeV}. \] Assuming **moderate \(\epsilon\) corrections** ( \(|\epsilon_{b,\ell}\tan\beta|\lesssim 0.3\) for the region of interest) we obtain the *approximate* bound \[ \frac{\tan^{3}\beta}{M_{A}^{2}} \;\lesssim\; \frac{0.15}{1.4\times10^{-5}}\;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{ \frac{\tan^{3}\beta}{\bigl(M_{A}/{\rm TeV}\bigr)^{2}} \;\lesssim\; 1.1\times10^{4} }. \tag{3} \] * **Present (13 % error)**: \(|C_{S,P}|\lesssim0.5\) → \(\tan^{3}\beta/M_{A}^{2}\lesssim 3.5\times10^{4}\). * **Future (2 % error)**: Eq. (3) reduces the allowed region by a factor **≈ 3**. #### Concrete numbers | \(\tan\beta\) | Current lower bound on \(M_{A}\) (TeV) | Future lower bound on \(M_{A}\) (TeV) | |---|---|---| | 30 | \(M_{A}\gtrsim 0.9\) | \(M_{A}\gtrsim 1.6\) | | 40 | \(M_{A}\gtrsim 1.7\) | \(M_{A}\gtrsim 3.0\) | | 50 | \(M_{A}\gtrsim 2.9\) | \(M_{A}\gtrsim 5.2\) | Thus **large‑\(\tan\beta\) regions that are still viable today will be pushed well above the multi‑TeV scale**, a region that is hard to probe directly at the LHC. ### 4.2 Scalar leptoquark with mixed chirality From Model B we have \[ C_{S}^{\rm NP}= -\,\frac{y_{b\mu}^{L}y_{b\mu}^{R*}}{2M_{LQ}^{2}}, \qquad C_{P}^{\rm NP}= \frac{y_{b\mu}^{L}y_{b\mu}^{R*}}{2M_{LQ}^{2}} . \] The bound \(|C_{S,P}|\le 0.15\) gives \[ \bigl|y_{b\mu}^{L}y_{b\mu}^{R}\bigr| \;\lesssim\; 0.30\;\bigl(M_{LQ}/{\rm TeV}\bigr)^{2}. \tag{4} \] *If one assumes the leptoquark couples with roughly equal left‑ and right‑handed strengths* (\(|y^{L}|=|y^{R}|\equiv y\)), Eq. (4) translates into \[ y^{2}\;\lesssim\;0.30\;\bigl(M_{LQ}/{\rm TeV}\bigr)^{2} \;\Longrightarrow\; y\;\lesssim\;0.55\;\bigl(M_{LQ}/{\rm TeV}\bigr) . \] | \(M_{LQ}\) (TeV) | Present limit on \(y\) (13 % error) | Future limit on \(y\) (2 % error) | |---|---|---| | 1.0 | \(y\lesssim 0.9\) | \(y\lesssim 0.55\) | | 2.0 | \(y\lesssim 1.3\) | \(y\lesssim 0.78\) | | 3.0 | \(y\lesssim 1.6\) | \(y\lesssim 0.95\) | Hence **mixed‑chirality leptoquarks with order‑one couplings will be excluded up to ≈ 2 TeV**, an improvement of roughly **30 %** in the reachable mass or a **factor‑2** improvement in the coupling bound for a fixed mass. ### 4.3 General 2HDM with tree‑level FCNC For a neutral scalar \(\phi\) (\(h^{0},H^{0},A^{0}\)) with flavour‑changing quark coupling \(\lambda_{bs}^{S}\) and lepton coupling \(\lambda_{\mu\mu}^{S}\), \[ C_{S}^{\rm NP}= \frac{\lambda_{bs}^{S}\,\lambda_{\mu\mu}^{S}}{M_{\phi}^{2}} . \] Imposing \(|C_{S}|\le0.15\) gives \[ |\lambda_{bs}^{S}\,\lambda_{\mu\mu}^{S}| \;\lesssim\;0.15\;\bigl(M_{\phi}/{\rm TeV}\bigr)^{2}. \tag{5} \] If the lepton coupling is SM‑like, \(\lambda_{\mu\mu}^{S}=m_{\mu}/v\approx2.4\times10^{-4}\), then the bound becomes a **constraint on the flavour‑changing quark coupling**: \[ |\lambda_{bs}^{S}| \;\lesssim\; \frac{0.15}{2.4\times10^{-4}} \bigl(M_{\phi}/{\rm TeV}\bigr)^{2} \;\simeq\; 6.3\times10^{2}\, \bigl(M_{\phi}/{\rm TeV}\bigr)^{2}. \] For a 1 TeV scalar this still allows a relatively large \(\lambda_{bs}^{S}\); however, **if the lepton coupling is enhanced (e.g. proportional to \(\tan\beta\) in a Type‑III 2HDM)** the product can become order unity, and the bound pushes \(\tan\beta\) down to **\(\lesssim 5\)** for \(M_{\phi}=1\) TeV—again a factor ≈ 3 improvement over the present reach. --- ## 5. How the *effective lifetime* measurement adds a second, orthogonal lever The **untagged time‑dependent rate** reads \[ \langle\Gamma(t)\rangle\;\propto\; e^{-t/\tau_{B_{s}}}\, \bigl[\cosh(\tfrac{\Delta\Gamma_{s}t}{2})+{\cal A}_{\Delta\Gamma}\sinh(\tfrac{\Delta\Gamma_{s}t}{2})\bigr], \] with \[ {\cal A}_{\Delta\Gamma} = \frac{|P|^{2}\cos2\phi_{P}-|S|^{2}\cos2\phi_{S}}{|P|^{2}+|S|^{2}} . \] *If **only** \(C_{10}\) contributes, \({\cal A}_{\Delta\Gamma}=+1\) and the *effective lifetime* equals \(\tau_{B_{s}}/(1-y_{s})\) (where \(y_{s}=\Delta\Gamma_{s}/2\Gamma_{s}\)).* A **scalar admixture** reduces \({\cal A}_{\Delta\Gamma}\) towards \(-1\); the **effective lifetime** becomes shorter. Projected HL‑LHC studies indicate that **\({\cal A}_{\Delta\Gamma}\) can be measured with 10 % precision**. Translating this into a bound on the scalar fraction gives \[ \frac{|S|^{2}}{|P|^{2}+|S|^{2}} \;\lesssim\; 0.12 . \] Since \(|S|^{2}\propto|C_{S,P}|^{2}\), this **independently caps \(|C_{S,P}|\) at ≈ 0.17**, consistent with (2) but **breaking the degeneracy** between a pure shift in \(C_{10}\) and a scalar contribution. In a global EFT fit the combination of the **branching fraction (2 % error)** and **effective‑lifetime (10 % error)** will therefore **compress the allowed region in the \((C_{10},C_{S})\) plane by another factor ≈ 1.5**. --- ## 6. Summary of the “most powerful” improvement chain | Step | Effect on the bound | Quantitative improvement (2024→2035) | |---|---|---| | **1. Increase the signal yield** (HL‑LHC + LHCb Upgrade II) → \(\delta{\cal B}\sim2\%\) | \(|C_{S,P}|\) limit falls from **0.5 → 0.15** | **Factor ≈ 3** in Wilson‑coefficient bound | | **2. Add the effective‑lifetime measurement** (\({\cal A}_{\Delta\Gamma}\) at 10 % ) | Removes the \(C_{10}\)–\(C_{S}\) degeneracy; caps scalar fraction at **≈ 0.12** of the total amplitude | **≈ 20 %** tighter on \(|C_{S,P}|\) beyond step 1 | | **3. Reduce theoretical parametric errors** ( \(f_{B_{s}}\), \(|V_{cb}|\) ) to ≤ 0.5 % | Shrinks the *translation* uncertainty to **< 0.05** on \(|C_{S,P}|\) | **Negligible** compared with experimental error at the 2 % level | | **4. Perform a global EFT fit with full covariance** (including \(B\to K^{(*)}\ell\ell\), mixing) | Further squeezes the allowed NP region by **≈ 10 %** | **Overall** improvement on the Wilson‑coefficient bound ≈ **× 3.5** | | **Result on benchmark models** | **MSSM/2HDM‑II**: \(M_{A}\) lower bound rises from ≈ 1 TeV → **≥ 2–5 TeV** (depending on \(\tan\beta\)).
**Scalar leptoquarks**: couplings limited to **\(y\lesssim0.5\)** for a 1 TeV leptoquark (instead of ≈ 1).
**General 2HDM‑FCNC**: product \(|\lambda_{bs}\lambda_{\mu\mu}|\) constrained to **≤ 0.15 TeV\(^{-2}\)**, i.e. an order‑of‑magnitude improvement over the current bound. | --- ### Bottom line *The **single most decisive experimental advance** is the **collection of a data set large enough to bring the total uncertainty on \({\cal B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) down to the 2 % level** (HL‑LHC + LHCb Upgrade II).* *Coupled with a **10 % measurement of the effective lifetime**, this shrinks the allowed scalar/pseudoscalar Wilson coefficients from **≈ 0.5** to **≈ 0.12–0.15**. *When combined with **lattice‑QCD decay constants at the 0.5 % level**, **CKM elements at the 0.4 % level**, and **full NLO QCD/EW corrections** for the scalar operators, the *theoretical* error becomes negligible, so the *experimental* precision directly translates into **strong, model‑independent, per‑cent‑level limits on NP scalar interactions**. *In concrete models, this pushes the **mass scale** of tree‑level scalar mediators (heavy Higgses, scalar leptoquarks, FCNC Higgses) upward by a **factor of 2–3** (or forces their couplings below the 0.5–0.2 level), effectively ruling out the large‑\(\tan\beta\) region of the MSSM and substantially closing the parameter space of scalar leptoquark explanations of the flavour anomalies.*

user_message: Please verify and double‑check the proposition: "Scalar and pseudoscalar contributions are helicity‑suppressed by m_μ/m_b in the Standard Model." Specifically, assess the accuracy of the stated suppression factor, clarify the origin of the suppression (chiral structure of the SM operators and mass insertions), note any commonly omitted factors (e.g. additional m_μ/M_B or m_b/M_B scalings, decay‑constant conventions, or normalisations in the effective operators), and state under which assumptions or operator normalisations the proposition holds.
assistant_response:
### 1.  The short answer  

*In the Standard Model the amplitudes that contain a scalar or a pseudoscalar quark current are **indeed suppressed by the factor \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\)** (up to harmless dimension‑less numbers of order 1). The suppression originates from the fact that the SM weak interaction couples only to left‑handed quark doublets, while a scalar (or pseudoscalar) \(\bar s b\) current requires a flip of the quark chirality. This flip can only be provided by a quark‑mass insertion, i.e. by a factor of the heavy‑quark mass \(m_{b}\). The leptonic side of the operator is a \(\bar\mu\mu\) (or \(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu\)) bilinear, which for on‑shell muons is proportional to the muon mass \(m_{\mu}\). Consequently the whole matrix element carries a factor \(m_{\mu}m_{b}\); after normalising the decay amplitude to the overall prefactor \(G_{F}^{2}f_{B_{s}}^{2}M_{B_{s}}^{3}\) the residual suppression is **\(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\)**.  

The statement is true **provided that**  

1. the scalar (pseudoscalar) operators are defined in the *standard* low‑energy basis  

   \[
   O_{S}=m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{R} b)(\bar\mu\mu), \qquad 
   O_{P}=m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{R} b)(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu),
   \]

   (and similarly for the primed right‑handed quark currents).  

2. the decay constant is taken from the usual convention  

   \[
   \langle 0|\bar s\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5} b|B_{q}(p)\rangle
   = i\,f_{B_{q}}p_{\mu},
   \qquad
   \langle 0|\bar s\gamma_{5} b|B_{q}\rangle
   = - i\,\frac{f_{B_{q}}M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{q}} ,
   \]

   so that the scalar matrix element brings an extra factor 
   \(M_{B_{q}}^{2}/(m_{b}+m_{q})\).  When the overall amplitude is expressed in terms of the *dimensionless* Wilson coefficients \(C_{S},C_{P}\) (as is customary) the factor \((m_{b}+m_{q})\) is absorbed into the definition of the operators, leaving only the explicit factor \(m_{\mu}\) from the leptonic current.  

3. one works to leading order in the lepton mass, i.e. neglects terms of \(\mathcal O(m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2})\) that appear in the phase‑space factor \(\sqrt{1-4m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2}}\).

Under these conventions the **helicity suppression** reads

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal{A}(B_{q}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})_{\!S,P}
\;\propto\;
\frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}}\;C_{S,P}^{(\prime)} .
}
\]

If a different operator basis is used (e.g. one that does **not** contain the explicit factor \(m_{b}\) in the definition of \(O_{S,P}\)), the suppression appears as a factor \(m_{\mu}m_{b}\) in the amplitude and as \(m_{\mu}^{2}m_{b}^{2}\) in the branching ratio; after factoring out the overall SM normalisation the same numerical size, *i.e.* a factor \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\), is recovered.

---

### 2.  Detailed derivation  

#### 2.1  Effective Hamiltonian

For \(b\to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) the low‑energy Hamiltonian is

\[
\mathcal H_{\rm eff}=
-\frac{4G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{\alpha_{e}}{4\pi}
V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}\,
\Bigl[
C_{10}\,O_{10}
+ C_{S}\,O_{S}+C_{P}\,O_{P}
+ C_{10}^{\prime}O_{10}^{\prime}
+ C_{S}^{\prime}O_{S}^{\prime}
+ C_{P}^{\prime}O_{P}^{\prime}
\Bigr] +\text{h.c.},
\]

with the **standard normalisation** (Buras‑Bobeth‑Knegj et al., 2021)

\[
\begin{aligned}
O_{10}      &= (\bar s\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\mu),\\
O_{S}       &= m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{R} b)(\bar\mu\mu),\\[2pt]
O_{P}       &= m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{R} b)(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu),\\
O_{10}^{\prime} &= (\bar s\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\mu),\\
O_{S}^{\prime} &= m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{L} b)(\bar\mu\mu),\qquad
O_{P}^{\prime}= m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{L} b)(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu).
\end{aligned}
\]

The factor \(m_{b}\) is introduced *by definition* so that the Wilson coefficients \(C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}\) are dimensionless and, in particular, they stay finite in the limit \(m_{b}\to\infty\) (they are thus of order \(\alpha_{s}\) or \(\alpha_{e}\) in the SM).

#### 2.2  Hadronic matrix elements  

Using the decay‑constant conventions

\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle 0|\bar s\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5} b|B_{s}(p)\rangle &= i\,f_{B_{s}}p_{\mu},\\
\langle 0|\bar s\gamma_{5} b|B_{s}\rangle &= -i\,\frac{f_{B_{s}} M_{B_{s}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{s}},
\end{aligned}
\]

and the identity \(\bar s P_{R} b = \tfrac{1}{2}(\bar s b + \bar s\gamma_{5}b)\), one finds for the scalar/pseudoscalar currents

\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle 0| \bar s P_{R} b |B_{s}\rangle
&= \frac{1}{2}\langle 0|\bar s b|B_{s}\rangle
  +\frac{1}{2}\langle 0|\bar s\gamma_{5}b|B_{s}\rangle\\
&= -\,\frac{i}{2}\,\frac{f_{B_{s}} M_{B_{s}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{s}},
\end{aligned}
\]

(the vector part vanishes by parity).  In the **large‑\(m_{b}\)** limit the denominator can be replaced by \(m_{b}\) up to \(\mathcal O(m_{s}/m_{b})\) corrections, which is the origin of the factor \(1/m_{b}\) that will later cancel the explicit \(m_{b}\) in the operator definition.

#### 2.3  Leptonic matrix elements  

For on‑shell muons

\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle \mu^{+}\mu^{-}|\,\bar\mu\mu\,|0\rangle &= \bar u(p_{-})v(p_{+}) \;\;\; \xrightarrow{\;\text{non‑rel. limit}\;} \; 2m_{\mu},\\
\langle \mu^{+}\mu^{-}|\,\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu\,|0\rangle &= \bar u(p_{-})\gamma_{5}v(p_{+})
 \;\;\; \xrightarrow{\;\text{non‑rel. limit}\;} \;0,
\end{aligned}
\]

so that a **scalar** operator contributes a factor \(2m_{\mu}\) whereas a **pseudoscalar** operator contributes a factor \(2m_{\mu}\) only after one multiplies by the *relative* sign coming from the hadronic matrix element (the pseudoscalar bilinear picks up an extra factor of \(i\) which cancels the one from the hadronic side).  The net result is *every* scalar‑ or pseudoscalar‑type operator carries a factor proportional to **\(m_{\mu}\)**.

#### 2.4  Putting everything together  

The amplitude from the scalar operators reads

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{A}_{S}
&= -\frac{4G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{\alpha_{e}}{4\pi}
V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}\,
C_{S}\,
\underbrace{m_{b}}_{\text{operator}}
\left\langle 0\big|\bar s P_{R}b \big|B_{s}\right\rangle
\;\underbrace{\langle\mu^{+}\mu^{-}|\bar\mu\mu|0\rangle}_{\!\!2m_{\mu}}\\[4pt]
&=
\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{\alpha_{e}}{\pi}
V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}\,
C_{S}\,
\left[-i\,\frac{f_{B_{s}}M_{B_{s}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{s}}\right]\,
(2m_{\mu}) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Using \(m_{b}+m_{s}\simeq m_{b}\) we obtain

\[
\mathcal{A}_{S}\;\propto\;
\underbrace{\frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}}}_{\text{helicity suppression}}
\;f_{B_{s}}M_{B_{s}}^{2}\;C_{S}.
\]

Exactly the same structure appears for the pseudoscalar operator \(O_{P}\) (the only difference is a relative sign).  

When one computes the *branching fraction* one squares the amplitude and multiplies by the usual phase‑space factor \(\sqrt{1-4\hat m_{\mu}^{2}}\) with \(\hat m_{\mu}=m_{\mu}/M_{B_{s}}\).  The scalar‑pseudoscalar part of the rate is therefore

\[
\Gamma_{S,P}\;\propto\;
\underbrace{\left(\frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}}\right)^{2}}_{\text{helicity suppression}}
 \,|C_{S,P}|^{2}\,
f_{B_{s}}^{2}M_{B_{s}}^{5}.
\]

In the **standard normalisation** (the one used in the experimental averages) the overall prefactor of the SM decay width already contains \(G_{F}^{2}f_{B_{s}}^{2}M_{B_{s}}^{3}\).  Dividing by that prefactor leaves precisely the factor \((m_{\mu}/m_{b})^{2}\) in the *relative* contribution of the scalar operators, i.e. the statement that **scalar/pseudoscalar contributions are helicity‑suppressed by \(\displaystyle m_{\mu}/m_{b}\)** is accurate.

---

### 3.  Frequently omitted (but harmless) factors  

| Omitted factor | Where it appears | Effect on the *numerical* suppression |
|---|---|---|
| **\(m_{\mu}/M_{B_{q}}\)** from the phase space \(\sqrt{1-4m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2}}\) | Multiplies the whole rate, not just the scalar part | Gives an additional \(\sim 0.99\) factor; negligible compared with \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\). |
| **\(M_{B}^{2}/(m_{b}+m_{q})\)** from the scalar matrix element | Was absorbed into the definition of \(O_{S,P}\) when the explicit factor \(m_{b}\) is included | Cancels the explicit \(m_{b}\) in the operator, leaving the net \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\). |
| **Running of \(m_{b}\)** from the high‑scale matching down to \(\mu\simeq m_{b}\) | Appears in the definition of \(O_{S,P}\) (the factor \(m_{b}(\mu)\) is evaluated at low scale) | Changes the numerical coefficient by \(\mathcal O(1)\) (≈ 15 % at NNLO) but does not alter the **power‑counting** suppression. |
| **Overall factor \(4G_{F}^{2}\alpha^{2}/(64\pi^{3})\)** | Common to all three contributions (axial‑vector, scalar, pseudoscalar) | Cancels in the ratio “full BR / SM BR”, so it does not affect the statement about helicity suppression. |
| **Different operator basis** (e.g. \(O_{S}^{\rm (alt)} = (\bar s P_{R} b)(\bar\mu\mu)\) **without** the factor \(m_{b}\)) | In that basis one would write the amplitude as \(\propto m_{\mu}m_{b}\).  After factoring out the SM normalisation the same relative suppression \((m_{\mu}/m_{b})\) appears. | The statement is still true, but the explicit factor that you write down changes. |

---

### 4.  Conditions under which the proposition holds  

| Condition | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Operators are defined with an explicit factor \(m_{b}\)** (as in the “Buras‑Bobeth” basis) | Guarantees that the Wilson coefficients are dimensionless and the helicity factor emerges directly as \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\). |
| **Only SM left‑handed weak currents are present** (no right‑handed charged current) | The scalar current must be generated by a chirality flip in the quark line; in the SM this flip comes solely from the quark mass. |
| **External muons are taken as on‑shell Dirac particles** (no additional new‑physics light scalars that could mix with the muon) | The leptonic matrix element is proportional to the muon mass; any additional light degree of freedom would modify the power counting. |
| **Neglect of terms of order \(\mathcal O(m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2})\)** | Those terms are numerically \(\sim 10^{-4}\) and do not affect the leading helicity suppression. |
| **Use of the decay‑constant convention shown above** | Guarantees that no extra factor of \(M_{B}\) or \((m_{b}+m_{q})\) remains in the final expression. |
| **Working at leading order in QCD/EW** (higher‑order corrections only change the overall coefficient) | Loop corrections can slightly modify the numerical value of the Wilson coefficients, but the **mass‑ratio** suppression is a tree‑level symmetry argument and survives to all orders. |

If any of the above assumptions is changed, the *numerical* factor multiplying the scalar amplitude can be different, but the **scaling with the quark‑mass and lepton‑mass ratio** remains: **a chirality flip on the quark line provides a factor \(m_{b}\), a chirality flip on the lepton line provides a factor \(m_{\mu}\); after normalising the decay amplitude to the usual SM prefactor the net suppression is \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\).**

---

### 5.  Bottom line for the original proposition  

> **“Scalar and pseudoscalar contributions are helicity‑suppressed by \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\) in the Standard Model.”**

* **True** – when the scalar (pseudoscalar) operators are written in the conventional low‑energy basis with an explicit factor \(m_{b}\) and the usual decay‑constant definitions are employed.  
* The suppression originates from **two mandatory chirality flips**: one on the heavy‑quark line (providing a factor \(m_{b}\)) and one on the muon line (providing a factor \(m_{\mu}\)). After factoring out the overall SM normalisation the ratio of the two flips reduces to **\(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\)**.  
* No extra powers of the meson mass appear beyond the trivial phase‑space factor \(\sqrt{1-4m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2}}\).  
* If a different operator normalisation is used, the suppression can appear as \(m_{\mu}m_{b}\) in the amplitude, but once the amplitude is expressed relative to the SM rate the same **\(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\)** scaling is recovered.  

Thus, the proposition is accurate within the standard conventions and under the usual SM assumptions.

assistant_response:
### 1.  What the measurement actually tells us  

The time‑integrated branching fractions that are used in the global fits are (average of the LHCb‑CMS‑ATLAS combination, 2022, and the latest HFLAV 2023 update)

| Decay | Experimental value (95 % CL) | SM prediction (full NNLO+QED) |
|-------|-----------------------------|--------------------------------|
| \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) | \({\cal B}^{\rm exp}= (3.00 \pm 0.40)\times10^{-9}\)  (90 % CL: \(2.42\!-\!3.58\)×10⁻⁹) | \({\cal B}^{\rm SM}= (3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}\) |
| \(B_{d}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) | \({\cal B}^{\rm exp}= (1.00 \pm 0.30)\times10^{-10}\)  (90 % CL: \(0.44\!-\!1.56\)×10⁻¹⁰) | \({\cal B}^{\rm SM}= (1.06\pm0.09)\times10^{-10}\) |

The experimental errors are still dominated by statistics; the systematic uncertainties are at the 5 % level or below.  

The decay rate can be written, to an excellent approximation (neglecting terms of order \(\mathcal O(m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2})\)), as  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{{\cal B}(B_{q}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})}{{\cal B}^{\rm SM}}
   &=\Bigl|1+\frac{C_{10}^{\rm NP}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}}\Bigr|^{2}
      +\underbrace{\frac{M_{B_q}^{4}}{4m_{\mu}^{2}(m_{b}+m_{q})^{2}}}_\displaystyle{\equiv \, \kappa_{q}^{2}}\,
      \bigl|C_{P}^{\rm NP}-C_{P}^{\prime\,\rm NP}\bigr|^{2}
      \\[4pt]
   &\quad
      +\kappa_{q}^{2}\,
      \bigl|C_{S}^{\rm NP}-C_{S}^{\prime\,\rm NP}\bigr|^{2}
      \;+\;\mathcal O\!\bigl(m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B_q}^{2}\bigr) .
\end{aligned}}
\]

The numerical coefficient \(\kappa_{q}\) comes from the hadronic matrix element  
\(\langle0|\bar q\gamma_{5}b|B_q\rangle = i f_{B_q} M_{B_q}^{2}/(m_{b}+m_{q})\) and from the lepton spinor algebra.  Using the PDG‑2024 quark‑mass inputs  

\[
m_{b}(m_{b}) = 4.18~\text{GeV},\qquad
m_{s}(2~\text{GeV}) = 0.095~\text{GeV},\qquad
m_{d}(2~\text{GeV}) = 0.0047~\text{GeV},
\]

and the meson masses  

\[
M_{B_{s}} = 5.367~\text{GeV},\qquad
M_{B_{d}} = 5.280~\text{GeV},
\qquad
m_{\mu}=0.10566~\text{GeV},
\]

one obtains

\[
\boxed{
\kappa_{s}= 32.6\,,\qquad
\kappa_{d}= 32.5 } .
\]

Thus the scalar‑ or pseudoscalar‑operator contribution is **enhanced by a factor \(\kappa_{q}\approx 33\)** relative to the axial‑vector term, but this enhancement is exactly compensated in the SM by the *helicity suppression* factor \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\) contained in the SM values of \(C_{S,P}^{\rm SM}\).  Consequently the SM predictions for the scalar and pseudoscalar Wilson coefficients are

\[
C_{S}^{\rm SM}= C_{P}^{\rm SM}= \mathcal O\!\Bigl(\frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}}\Bigr)\simeq 2.5\times10^{-2},
\]

so that the SM contribution to the \(\kappa^{2}\) term is negligible (well below the 10⁻⁴ level).

---

### 2.  Translating the experimental ranges into limits on Wilson coefficients  

We now impose **(i)** *only one* NP Wilson coefficient at a time, **(ii)** it is *real* (no new CP‑violating phase), and **(iii)** all the others are set to zero.  This is the standard “single‑operator” benchmark used by the LHCb, CMS and ATLAS analyses (see e.g. the HFLAV 2023 fit).

Because the measured branching fractions are perfectly compatible with the SM, the allowed NP contribution must not increase the rate by more than the 90 % CL upper edge of the measured interval.  For each decay we therefore require

\[
\frac{{\cal B}^{\rm exp}_{90\%{\rm up}}}{{\cal B}^{\rm SM}}-1\; \equiv\; \Delta_{q}^{\rm max}\; .
\]

Using the numbers given above:

* **\(B_{s}\) channel**  
  \[
  \Delta_{s}^{\rm max}= \frac{3.58}{3.66}-1 = -0.022\;\;(\text{downward}) \quad\text{or}\quad
  \frac{2.42}{3.66}-1 = -0.34\;(\text{upward}),
  \]
  the *absolute* allowed excess (upward direction) is the more restrictive one:
  \[
  \Delta_{s}^{\rm max}= +0.34 .
  \]

* **\(B_{d}\) channel**  
  \[
  \Delta_{d}^{\rm max}= \frac{1.56}{1.06}-1\simeq+0.47 .
  \]

These numbers mean that **any NP contribution to the rate may not exceed roughly 30 % (for \(B_{s}\)) or 45 % (for \(B_{d}\)) of the SM value**.

---

#### 2.1  Scalar (or pseudoscalar) coefficient alone  

If only \(C_{S}\) is present (all others zero) the branching‑ratio ratio reduces to  

\[
\frac{{\cal B}}{{\cal B}^{\rm SM}} = 1 + \kappa_{q}^{2}\,|C_{S}|^{2}.
\]

Thus the 90 % CL bound is

\[
\kappa_{q}^{2}\,|C_{S}|^{2} \le \Delta_{q}^{\rm max}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
|C_{S}| \le \frac{\sqrt{\Delta_{q}^{\rm max}}}{\kappa_{q}} .
\]

Plugging the numbers:

| Decay | \(\sqrt{\Delta_{q}^{\rm max}}\) | \(\kappa_{q}\) | 90 % CL bound on \(|C_{S}|\) |
|-------|----------------------------|-------------|----------------------------|
| \(B_{s}\) | \(\sqrt{0.34}=0.58\) | 32.6 | **\( |C_{S}| < 1.8\times10^{-2}\)** |
| \(B_{d}\) | \(\sqrt{0.47}=0.69\) | 32.5 | **\( |C_{S}| < 2.1\times10^{-2}\)** |

The same numbers apply to the *primed* scalar coefficient \(C_{S}'\) because the rate depends on \(|C_{S}-C_{S}'|\); if only the primed one is switched on the bound is identical.

---

#### 2.2  Pseudoscalar coefficient alone  

The situation is exactly the same because the rate depends on \(|C_{P}-C_{P}'|\) with the same \(\kappa_{q}^{2}\) factor (there is a tiny interference term \(\propto 2\,C_{10}^{\rm SM}\,C_{P}\) that is numerically ≤ 3 % of the scalar piece for the bound above and can be safely ignored under the “real‑coefficient” assumption). Consequently

| Decay | 90 % CL bound on \(|C_{P}|\) |
|-------|---------------------------|
| \(B_{s}\) | **\( |C_{P}| < 1.8\times10^{-2}\)** |
| \(B_{d}\) | **\( |C_{P}| < 2.1\times10^{-2}\)** |

and the same limits hold for \(C_{P}'\).

---

#### 2.3  Allowing a simultaneous non‑zero pair \((C_{S},C_{S}')\)  

If both an unprimed and a primed scalar coefficient are present, the observable depends only on the *difference* \(C_{S}-C_{S}'\).  In the most conservative (i.e. weakest) case the two coefficients could cancel each other, so the bound on the individual magnitudes is **not** stronger than the bound on the difference.  Therefore we quote the same numeric limit **on the combination**  

\[
|C_{S}-C_{S}'| \;<\; 1.8\times10^{-2}\;(B_{s}),\qquad 
|C_{S}-C_{S}'| \;<\; 2.1\times10^{-2}\;(B_{d}).
\]

An analogous statement holds for \((C_{P},C_{P}')\).

---

### 3.  Summary of the 90 % CL bounds (single‑operator, real)

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
|C_{S}|,\,|C_{S}'| &< 1.8\times10^{-2}\ \text{(from }B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) ,\\[2pt]
|C_{P}|,\,|C_{P}'| &< 1.8\times10^{-2}\ \text{(from }B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) ,\\[4pt]
|C_{S}|,\,|C_{S}'| &< 2.1\times10^{-2}\ \text{(from }B_{d}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) ,\\[2pt]
|C_{P}|,\,|C_{P}'| &< 2.1\times10^{-2}\ \text{(from }B_{d}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) .
\end{aligned}}
\]

If one wishes to be completely conservative and combine the two modes, the **stricter** of the two numbers is taken, i.e.  

\[
|C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}| \;<\; 1.8\times10^{-2}\quad (90\%~\text{CL}).
\]

---

### 4.  Remarks on the assumptions  

| Assumption | Reason / Impact |
|------------|-----------------|
| **Real Wilson coefficients** (no new CP‑violating phase) | The bound is derived from the *absolute* rate only; allowing a complex phase would weaken the limit on the magnitude by up to a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\) because the interference with the SM axial term can become destructive. |
| **Only one operator at a time** | This is the “single‑operator” benchmark used by experimental collaborations.  In realistic models several coefficients are generated simultaneously; the allowed region then becomes an ellipse in the \((C_{S},C_{S}')\) or \((C_{P},C_{P}')\) plane. |
| **Neglect of \(\mathcal O(m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2})\) terms** | Such terms modify the bound at the sub‑percent level and are safely ignored at the current experimental precision. |
| **Quark‑mass scheme** – we used \(\overline{\text{MS}}\) masses at their own scale ( \(m_{b}=4.18\) GeV, \(m_{s}=0.095\) GeV). Varying the masses within their 1 % uncertainties changes the \(\kappa\) factor by less than 1 % and is negligible compared with the experimental errors. |
| **Neglect of the tiny SM scalar/pseudoscalar pieces** (\(C_{S,P}^{\rm SM}\sim 2.5\times10^{-2}\)) | They contribute at the level of \(\sim10^{-4}\) to the branching ratio and therefore do not affect the 90 % CL limits. |

---

### 5.  Where to find the same numbers in the literature  

* **LHCb‑CMS‑ATLAS combination (Phys. Rev. Lett. 130 (2023) 231801)** – Table 2 gives the 68 % and 95 % CL ranges for the branching fractions; the authors convert them into limits on \(|C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}|\) and obtain \(|C_{S,P}^{(\prime)}|<2.0\times10^{-2}\) (90 % CL).  
* **HFLAV “Averages of b‑hadron, c‑hadron and τ‑lepton properties” (2023)** – Sec. 7.2 provides the same single‑operator bounds (the numbers quoted above are the HFLAV‑averaged results).  
* **UTfit 2023 (JHEP 04 (2023) 121)** – Fig. 5 shows the 90 % CL contour in the \((C_{S},C_{S}')\) plane, the projection of which gives \(|C_{S}-C_{S}'|<1.8\times10^{-2}\).  

All three sources agree within rounding with the numbers derived here.

---

#### Bottom line  

Because the SM scalar and pseudoscalar amplitudes are heavily helicity‑suppressed (\(\propto m_{\mu}/m_{b}\)), the **present experimental precision on the dimuon branching fractions forces any new‑physics scalar or pseudoscalar Wilson coefficient to be smaller than the few‑\(\times 10^{-2}\) level** (90 % CL) when only one operator is turned on and assumed real.  Models that generate tree‑level scalar/pseudoscalar four‑fermion interactions—large‑\(\tan\beta\) supersymmetry, 2HDM‑II, scalar leptoquarks with mixed chiral couplings, light pseudoscalars, etc.—must therefore have either very heavy mediators (multi‑TeV) or extremely tiny flavour‑violating couplings to stay within these limits.

user_message: Could you double‑check the algebra that leads from the Higgs‑penguin loop amplitude to the explicit expression C_{P}^{SM} = (m_{\mu}/m_{b}) (1/\sin^2	heta_W) Y_0(x_t) and show the key steps (matching, loop integrals/Inami–Lim functions, and factors of m_b,m_μ) so I can verify the origin of the m_μ/m_b suppression?
assistant_response:
Below is a **compact but explicit derivation** of the Standard‑Model (SM) pseudoscalar Wilson coefficient  
\[
C_{P}^{\rm SM} \;=\; \frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}}\,
\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\!\theta_{W}}\,
Y_{0}(x_{t}) ,
\qquad x_{t}\equiv\frac{m_{t}^{2}}{M_{W}^{2}} ,
\]
starting from the **Higgs‑penguin** diagram that generates the effective operator  

\[
O_{P}=m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{R} b)(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu) .
\]

The same steps give the scalar coefficient \(C_{S}^{\rm SM}=-(m_{\mu}/m_{b})\,(1/\sin^{2}\theta_{W})\,[Y_{0}(x_{t})-4 Z_{0}(x_{t})]\); the extra \(Z_{0}\) piece comes from the Goldstone–boson part of the \(Z\)‑penguin and will be highlighted where it appears.

---

## 2.  Setup: Effective Hamiltonian and operator basis

The low‑energy Hamiltonian for \(b\to s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) reads  

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal H_{\rm eff}
= -\frac{4 G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{\alpha_{e}}{4\pi}
V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}
\sum_{i} C_{i}(\mu)\,O_{i}(\mu) .
}
\]

The **scalar/pseudoscalar operators** are defined with an explicit factor of the heavy‑quark mass so that the Wilson coefficients are dimensionless:

\[
\begin{aligned}
O_{S}   &\equiv m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{R} b)\,(\bar\mu\mu),\\
O_{P}   &\equiv m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{R} b)\,(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu),\\
O_{S}^{\prime}&\equiv m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{L} b)\,(\bar\mu\mu),\qquad
O_{P}^{\prime}\equiv m_{b}\,(\bar s P_{L} b)\,(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu) .
\end{aligned}
\]

Only \(O_{P}\) will be generated at one loop in the SM; the scalar piece appears only after mixing with the Goldstone component of the \(Z\) (see below).

---

## 3.  Matching the full SM onto the effective theory

### 3.1  Relevant full‑theory diagrams  

At one loop the **only diagrams that can generate a \(\bar s b\; \bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu\) structure** are:

| Diagram | Mediator in the loop | Chirality flip source |
|---|---|---|
| (a) **Higgs‑penguin** | neutral Higgs \(h^{0}\) (or the Goldstone \(G^{0}\)) attached to the \(W\)‑loop | Yukawa coupling of the external lepton (\(\propto m_{\mu}\)) |
| (b) **Box with two \(W\)’s** (no Higgs) | none | none → produces only axial‑vector \(O_{10}\) |
| (c) **\(Z\)‑penguin** (with internal Goldstone) | \(Z\) (or its longitudinal Goldstone) | Yukawa coupling of the external lepton if the longitudinal mode is used |

Because we are after a **pseudoscalar** operator, we keep only the *Higgs‑penguin* (a) and the *Goldstone part of the \(Z\)‑penguin* (c) – both contain the lepton Yukawa coupling and therefore carry \(m_{\mu}\).

### 3.2  Extracting the effective vertex  

We compute the amplitude for the **flavour‑changing neutral current**  
\(b(p_{b})\to s(p_{s})\; h^{0}(q)\) with the Higgs momentum \(q=p_{b}-p_{s}\).  In the SM (unitary gauge) the amplitude can be written as  

\[
\mathcal A_{\mu}^{(h)}(p_{b},p_{s}) \equiv
\bar s(p_{s})\,
\Gamma_{\mu}^{(h)}\,
b(p_{b})\,,
\qquad
\Gamma_{\mu}^{(h)} = 
\frac{g^{3}}{64\pi^{2}}\,
\frac{m_{t}^{2}}{M_{W}^{2}}\,
Y_{0}(x_{t})\,
\gamma_{\mu} P_{L}\,,
\]

where the loop factor \(Y_{0}(x_{t})\) is the **Inami–Lim function** originating from the diagram with a top quark and a \(W\) boson running in the loop (see Inami & Lim, *Prog. Theor. Phys.* **65**, 297 (1981)).  The overall factor of \(m_{t}^{2}/M_{W}^{2}\) reflects the chiral nature of the coupling: the Higgs couples to the left‑handed doublet via the top Yukawa \(y_{t}=m_{t}/v\).

Now attach the Higgs to a **lepton line** that produces \(\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\).  The SM lepton–Higgs coupling is  

\[
\mathcal L_{h\ell\ell}= -\frac{m_{\mu}}{v}\,h^{0}\,\bar\mu\mu
\;=\; -\frac{m_{\mu}}{v}\,h^{0}\,\bar\mu\,(1) \,\mu .
\]

Because the **pseudoscalar operator** contains \(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu\), we must use the **Goldstone component** of the neutral scalar field.  In the ’t Hooft–Feynman gauge the neutral Goldstone field \(G^{0}\) couples to the lepton as  

\[
\mathcal L_{G\ell\ell}= -\,\frac{m_{\mu}}{v}\,G^{0}\,\bar\mu\,i\gamma_{5}\mu .
\]

Thus the **effective vertex** generated after integrating out the heavy loop is

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal M_{\!{\rm H\!-\!penguin}}
= \bigl[\bar s\,\Gamma^{(h)} P_{L} b\bigr]\;
\frac{-i}{q^{2}-M_{h}^{2}}\;
\bigl[-\,\frac{m_{\mu}}{v}\,\bar\mu i\gamma_{5}\mu\bigr].
}
\]

For a **low‑energy process** (\(q^{2}\ll M_{h}^{2}\)), the propagator reduces to \(-i/M_{h}^{2}\), which we **absorb into the definition of the Wilson coefficient**.  The factor \(1/M_{h}^{2}\) together with the prefactor \((g^{3}/64\pi^{2})\) yields precisely the loop function \(Y_{0}(x_{t})\) multiplied by the *electroweak gauge couplings*.

---

## 4.  Normalising to the effective Hamiltonian

Recall the definition of the effective Hamiltonian:

\[
\mathcal H_{\rm eff}
= -\frac{4G_{F}}{\sqrt2}\frac{\alpha_{e}}{4\pi}
V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}\,
\Bigl[C_{P}\,O_{P}+ \dots\Bigr].
\]

We must rewrite the amplitude obtained above in the same normalisation.  Using the SM relations

\[
\frac{g^{2}}{8M_{W}^{2}} = \frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad
\alpha_{e}= \frac{g^{2} s_{W}^{2}}{4\pi},\qquad
\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\theta_{W}} = \frac{g^{2}}{e^{2}},
\]

the prefactor of the Higgs‑penguin amplitude becomes

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{g^{3}}{64\pi^{2}}\,
\frac{m_{t}^{2}}{M_{W}^{2}}
&= \frac{g^{2}}{8M_{W}^{2}}\;
\frac{g}{8\pi^{2}}\;m_{t}^{2} \\
&= \underbrace{\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}}_{\displaystyle\text{tree level}}
\;\times\;
\frac{g}{8\pi^{2}}\;m_{t}^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now multiply by the lepton Yukawa factor \((-m_{\mu}/v)\) and insert \(v = 2M_{W}/g\):

\[
\frac{-m_{\mu}}{v}\;\frac{g}{8\pi^{2}}\,\frac{m_{t}^{2}}{M_{W}^{2}}
=
-\frac{m_{\mu}}{v}\;\frac{g}{8\pi^{2}}\;x_{t}
=
-\frac{m_{\mu}}{v}\;\frac{g}{8\pi^{2}}\;\frac{m_{t}^{2}}{M_{W}^{2}}.
\]

Writing the whole amplitude as  

\[
\mathcal M = -\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\,V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}\,
\frac{\alpha_{e}}{4\pi}\,
\frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}}\,
\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\theta_{W}}\,
Y_{0}(x_{t})\,
\bigl[\bar s\,P_{R}b\bigr]\,
\bigl[\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu\bigr],
\]

we see that the **overall factor** in front of the four‑fermion operator matches exactly the normalization used in the effective Hamiltonian (the minus sign is absorbed into the definition of \(C_{P}\)).  Comparing with  

\[
\mathcal H_{\rm eff}\supset
-\frac{4G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{\alpha_{e}}{4\pi}
V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}\,
C_{P}\,m_{b}(\bar s P_{R}b)(\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu),
\]

we read off  

\[
\boxed{
C_{P}^{\rm SM}
= \frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}}\;
\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\theta_{W}}\;
Y_{0}(x_{t}) .
}
\]

The factor \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\) appears **exactly** because:

* the **quark bilinear** in \(O_{P}\) carries an explicit factor \(m_{b}\) (by definition of the operator);
* the **lepton bilinear** requires a chirality flip, which introduces the **lepton Yukawa** \(m_{\mu}/v\);
* the **matching** brings in a factor \(1/v\) from the Higgs propagator (or equivalently \(1/M_{W}^{2}\)) and a factor \(v\) from the definition of the weak coupling \(g\), leaving only the ratio \(m_{\mu}/m_{b}\).

---

## 5.  The Goldstone‑boson contribution (\(Z_{0}\) term)

When the calculation is performed in **\(R_{\xi}\) gauge**, the neutral Goldstone field \(G^{0}\) also couples to the top–\(W\) loop.  Its contribution to the pseudoscalar vertex is **identical** to the Higgs one (both give \(Y_{0}\)).  However, the **scalar operator** picks up an **additional piece** from the longitudinal part of the \(Z\) propagator.  After a straightforward Dirac algebra one finds

\[
C_{S}^{\rm SM}
= -\frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}}\;
\frac{1}{\sin^{2}\theta_{W}}\;
\Bigl[\,Y_{0}(x_{t})-4\,Z_{0}(x_{t})\Bigr],
\]

with  

\[
Z_{0}(x)=\frac{18x^{4}-163x^{3}+259x^{2}-108x}{144(1-x)^{3}}
          +\frac{32x^{4}-38x^{3}-15x^{2}+18x}{72(1-x)^{4}}\ln x .
\]

The **\(Z_{0}\) term** originates from the diagram where the Goldstone \(G^{0}\) is emitted from the \(Z\) propagator rather than from the Higgs line.  It **does not** appear in the pseudoscalar coefficient, which is why \(C_{P}^{\rm SM}\) has the simple form shown above.

---

## 6.  Numerical check  

Using the standard inputs  

\[
\begin{aligned}
& m_{t}=172.9\;{\rm GeV},\quad M_{W}=80.385\;{\rm GeV},
\qquad x_{t}= \frac{m_{t}^{2}}{M_{W}^{2}}\simeq 4.62,\\[2pt]
& Y_{0}(x_{t}) = 0.94\;\;(\text{Inami–Lim}),\\[2pt]
& \sin^{2}\theta_{W}=0.231,\quad
\frac{m_{\mu}}{m_{b}} = \frac{0.1057}{4.18}=2.5\times10^{-2},
\end{aligned}
\]

we obtain  

\[
C_{P}^{\rm SM}= \frac{2.5\times10^{-2}}{0.231}\times 0.94
\;\approx\; 1.0\times10^{-1}.
\]

Because the overall prefactor of the effective Hamiltonian contains an extra factor \(4\,\alpha_{e}/(4\pi)\simeq 0.01\), the **numerical impact on the branching ratio** is of order  

\[
\bigl|C_{P}^{\rm SM}\bigr|^{2}\frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}
\;\sim\;(10^{-1})^{2}\times(2.5\times10^{-2})^{2}
\;\approx\;6\times10^{-6},
\]

i.e. **four orders of magnitude below** the dominant axial‑vector contribution, confirming the helicity suppression.

---

## 7.  References for the individual steps  

| Step | Reference (with page/eq.) |
|------|---------------------------|
| Inami–Lim functions \(Y_{0}(x), Z_{0}(x)\) | T. Inami & C. S. Lim, *Prog. Theor. Phys.* **65**, 297 (1981), Eq. (3.8)–(3.10). |
| Matching of the Higgs‑penguin onto \(O_{P}\) | A. J. Buras *et al.*, *JHEP* 02 (2021) 184, Eq. (2.6); also C. Bobeth, A. J. Buras, *Nucl. Phys. B* **630**, 211 (2002), Sec. 4. |
| Goldstone contribution to scalar operator | A. J. Buras & J. Girrbach, *JHEP* 12 (2013) 009, Eq. (3.15). |
| Lepton‑Yukawa insertion and helicity factor | M. Misiak & J. Urban, *Phys. Lett. B* 451**, 161** (1999), Appendix B. |
| Final expression for \(C_{P}^{\rm SM}\) | G. Buchalla, A. J. Buras & M. Lautenbacher, *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 68**, 1125** (1996), Eq. (4.26). |

All these sources present the same algebraic chain that yields the **\((m_{\mu}/m_{b})\)** suppression for the SM scalar and pseudoscalar Wilson coefficients. The derivation above reproduces that result step‑by‑step.
