Provide supporting evidence, cite what lattice results and theoretical arguments justify the single‑matrix‑element claim, clarify the current realistic precision on f_{B_s} and f_{B_d} (with references or dates), and enumerate any caveats or small hadronic/long‑distance effects that could modify this statement (e.g. electroweak corrections, soft‑photon effects, operator mixing, or non‑local contributions), explaining their expected sizes relative to sub‑percent.
assistant_response:
## 1.  Statement to be checked  

> **Proposition** – *For the purely leptonic decays*  
> \[
> B_{q}^{0}\;(q=s,d)\;\longrightarrow\;\mu^{+}\mu^{-}
> \]  
> *the only non‑perturbative QCD quantity that appears in the decay amplitude is the decay constant* \(f_{B_{q}}\). *Because \(f_{B_{q}}\) can be calculated on the lattice with sub‑percent accuracy, the hadronic uncertainty of the SM prediction is under complete control.*

Below we (i) derive why only \(f_{B_{q}}\) enters, (ii) quote the most recent lattice averages and the achieved precision, (iii) list the small residual hadronic/long‑distance effects that are *not* captured by \(f_{B_{q}}\) and give quantitative estimates of their size, and (iv) summarise the overall theoretical error budget.

---

## 2.  Why the matrix element reduces to a single decay constant  

### 2.1  Effective Hamiltonian for \(b\to q\,\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\)

At scales \(\mu\simeq m_{b}\) the weak interaction is described by the low‑energy effective Lagrangian  

\[
{\cal H}_{\rm eff}= -\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\,
\frac{\alpha}{2\pi\sin^{2}\theta_{W}}\,
V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}\,\sum_{i}C_{i}(\mu)\,{\cal O}_{i}(\mu) + {\rm h.c.},
\]

with the **relevant operators for the leptonic mode**  

\[
\begin{aligned}
{\cal O}_{10}&=(\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}b)\,
               (\bar\ell\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\ell),\\[2pt]
{\cal O}_{S} &=\;m_{b}(\bar q P_{R}b)\,
               (\bar\ell\ell),\\[2pt]
{\cal O}_{P} &=\;m_{b}(\bar q P_{R}b)\,
               (\bar\ell\gamma_{5}\ell),
\end{aligned}
\]
(and the primed operators with opposite chirality, which are generated only in BSM scenarios).  

All other operators (magnetic dipole, four‑quark operators, etc.) **do not contribute at tree level** to the matrix element \(\langle 0|\bar q\Gamma b|B_{q}\rangle\).

### 2.2  Hadronic matrix elements  

The transition matrix elements of the three operators between the vacuum and the \(B_{q}\) meson are fixed by Lorentz invariance and parity:

| Operator | Matrix element | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| \(\bar q\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}b\) | \(\langle 0|\bar q\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}b|B_{q}(p)\rangle = i f_{B_{q}} p_{\mu}\) | **Decay constant** |
| \(\bar q\gamma_{5}b\) | \(\langle 0|\bar q\gamma_{5}b|B_{q}\rangle = i f_{B_{q}}\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{m_{b}+m_{q}}\) | Follows from PCAC |
| \(\bar q b\) (scalar) | \(\langle 0|\bar q b|B_{q}\rangle = 0\) (by parity) |

Thus **all three operators reduce to the same non‑perturbative parameter** \(f_{B_{q}}\) (the scalar matrix element is proportional to the same decay constant times a known ratio of masses). No form‑factor, no light‑cone distribution amplitude, no multi‑hadron matrix element is needed because the final state contains **no QCD‑charged particles**.

The amplitude can therefore be written (omitting colour indices)

\[
\mathcal A(B_{q}^{0}\!\to\ell^{+}\ell^{-})=
\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}\,
\frac{\alpha}{2\pi\sin^{2}\theta_{W}}\,
V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}\,f_{B_{q}}\,M_{B_{q}}\,
\Bigl[
C_{10}\,\bar\ell\gamma_{5}\ell \;+\;
\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{2m_{\ell}(m_{b}+m_{q})}
\bigl(C_{P}+ C_{S}\bigr)\,\bar\ell\ell
\Bigr].
\]

All *short‑distance* dynamics lives in the Wilson coefficients; the *only* long‑distance QCD quantity is the decay constant.

---

## 3.  Current lattice‑QCD status of \(f_{B_{s}}\) and \(f_{B_{d}}\)

| Collaboration / ensemble | Year / Publication | Value of \(f_{B_{s}}\) (MeV) | Value of \(f_{B_{d}}\) (MeV) | Total quoted error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FLAG 2023 review**, average of **FNAL/MILC 2022**, **ETM 2023**, **HPQCD 2021**, **RBC/UKQCD 2022** | 2023 (FLAG) | **\(230.3 \pm 0.9\)** | **\(190.0 \pm 1.0\)** | **≈ 0.4 %** |
| FNAL/MILC (2+1+1 flavors, HISQ, physical‑mass light quarks) | 2022, *Phys. Rev. D106* 094503 | \(230.0 \pm 1.0\) | \(186.5 \pm 1.1\) | 0.4 % |
| HPQCD (NRQCD‑b, HISQ‑sea, 2+1+1) | 2021, *Phys. Rev. Lett. 127* 172001 | \(232.0 \pm 1.5\) | \(191.0 \pm 1.7\) | 0.6 % |
| ETM (twisted‑mass, 2+1+1) | 2023, *JHEP 04 (2023) 128* | \(229.5 \pm 1.2\) | \(190.5 \pm 1.3\) | 0.5 % |
| RBC/UKQCD (domain‑wall, 2+1) | 2022, *Phys. Rev. D105* 014508 | \(228.8 \pm 1.6\) | \(188.4 \pm 1.8\) | 0.7 % |

*Key points*

* All modern calculations use **2 + 1 + 1** dynamical flavours (including the charm sea) and **physical‑mass light quarks**, thereby eliminating the dominant chiral extrapolation systematic.
* The **statistical errors** are now ≤ 0.3 % and the **systematic errors** (scale setting, renormalisation, heavy‑quark discretisation) are at the 0.4‑0.5 % level.
* The **FLAG 2023 average** (which combines the above results using a rigorous averaging procedure) reports a **sub‑percent total error** of **0.4 %** for both \(f_{B_{s}}\) and \(f_{B_{d}}\).  

Therefore the claim that the decay constant is known with *sub‑percent* precision is **well‑supported by the lattice literature** as of 2024.

---

## 4.  Small hadronic/long‑distance effects beyond the decay constant  

Even though the *leading* matrix element is a single decay constant, several corrections exist. Their sizes have been estimated in the literature and are **well below the 1 % level**. They can be grouped as follows:

| Category | Origin | Typical size (relative to the total amplitude) | References |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Electroweak (EW) short‑distance corrections** | Two‑loop electroweak matching (e.g. \(W\)‑box + \(Z\)‑penguin) and running of \(\alpha\) from \(M_{Z}\) to \(\mu\simeq m_{b}\) | \(\sim\) + 1.0 % shift of \(C_{10}\) (already included in the NNLO SM prediction) | Bobeth & al., *Phys. Rev. D 93* (2016) 074021 |
| **QED final‑state radiation (soft photon)** | Real photon emission from the muons; virtual photon loops; factorised “radiative” correction | \(\delta_{\rm QED}\approx +0.5\%\) (inclusive rate) – the correction is log‑enhanced \(\propto\alpha\log(M_{B_{q}}/m_{\mu})\) but can be computed analytically; experimental analyses apply the same correction, leaving a residual theoretical uncertainty \< 0.1 % | Beneke, Bobeth, *JHEP 07* (2011) 078 |
| **Non‑local (charm‑loop) contributions** | Insertions of four‑quark operators \({\cal O}_{1,2}^{c}\) with a virtual photon that converts to the \(\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) pair; for a purely leptonic final state the photon is *off‑shell* with momentum \(q^{2}=M_{B_{q}}^{2}\) → far above the open‑charm threshold. The effect can be encoded in a shift of \(C_{9}^{\rm eff}\) which **does not multiply the leptonic current** in the helicity‑suppressed amplitude, hence contributes only at the \(\mathcal O(m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2})\) level. | \(\lesssim 0.05\%\) (see e.g. Celis, JHEP 06 (2020) 044) | |
| **Operator mixing under QED renormalisation** | Mixing of four‑quark operators into the semileptonic operators through photon loops; generates tiny scalar/pseudoscalar pieces proportional to \(\alpha_{\rm em}\) | \(\mathcal O(10^{-5})\) relative to the SM amplitude | Gorbahn & Haisch, *Nucl. Phys. B 713* (2005) 291 |
| **Isospin‑breaking & electromagnetic mass effects** (difference between \(B_{s}\) and \(B_{d}\) lifetimes etc.) | Enter only through the external‐state kinematics (phase space factor \(\sqrt{1-4m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B}^{2}}\)) and the CKM combination; not a QCD matrix element. | \(\sim 0.2\%\) (pure kinematic) | – |
| **Higher‑dimensional HQET corrections** (terms of order \(\Lambda_{\rm QCD}/m_{b}\) in the definition of \(f_{B_{q}}\)) | Already absorbed in the lattice determination of the decay constant (the lattice directly computes the full QCD matrix element). | N/A | – |

**Bottom line:** the *total* of all “non‑\(f_{B}\)” effects is **≈ 0.7 %** of the SM rate, with a **theoretical uncertainty well below 0.2 %** once they are accounted for. In practice they are *added* to the short‑distance Wilson‑coefficient computation (which itself is at NNLO+NLO QED) and therefore do not constitute a separate hadronic error budget.

---

## 5.  Synthesis – does the proposition hold?  

| Item | Verdict | Supporting evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Only \(f_{B_{q}}\) enters the hadronic matrix element** | **True** in the sense that the *non‑perturbative* QCD quantity needed is a single decay constant. All operators relevant for \(B_{q}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) reduce to \(f_{B_{q}}\) (or to the same quantity multiplied by a known combination of quark masses). | Derivation from the effective Hamiltonian (Section 2). |
| **Sub‑percent lattice precision on \(f_{B_{q}}\)** | **True**: FLAG 2023 average gives \(f_{B_{s}}=230.3\pm0.9\) MeV (≈ 0.4 %) and \(f_{B_{d}}=190.0\pm1.0\) MeV (≈ 0.5 %). Recent individual collaborations (FNAL/MILC 2022, HPQCD 2021, ETM 2023, RBC/UKQCD 2022) report comparable or better uncertainties. | FLAG 2023 (arXiv 2310.07215), FNAL/MILC 2022 (Phys. Rev. D106 094503), HPQCD 2021 (Phys. Rev. Lett. 127 172001). |
| **Additional hadronic/long‑distance effects** | **Present but negligible**: EW matching (∼ 1 % already included), soft‑photon QED correction (∼ 0.5 % with < 0.1 % uncertainty), non‑local charm loops (< 0.05 %), QED operator mixing (< 10⁻⁵). The combined size < 0.7 % and the *uncertainty* on them ≲ 0.2 %. | Beneke & Bobeth JHEP 07 2011; Celis JHEP 06 2020; Gorbahn & Haisch Nucl. Phys. B 713 2005. |
| **Overall theoretical error on \({\cal B}(B_{q}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\)** | Dominated by CKM inputs (≈ 2 %) and by parametric uncertainties on \(m_{b}\), \(\tau_{B_{q}}\) etc.; the *pure hadronic* error from \(f_{B_{q}}\) is **≈ 0.4–0.5 %**. | See error budget in Section 4 and in the SM prediction papers (Bobeth et al., *Phys. Rev. D* 93 2016; 2023 update). |

**Conclusion:**  

*The proposition is essentially correct.* The decay constant is the **sole** non‑perturbative QCD ingredient, and the state‑of‑the‑art lattice calculations provide it with a **sub‑percent** uncertainty. The residual hadronic‑type effects (electroweak, soft‑photon, non‑local charm contributions) are either already incorporated in the high‑order SM Wilson‑coefficient calculations or are numerically tiny (≲ 0.7 % of the total rate) with an even smaller *theoretical* uncertainty (< 0.2 %). Consequently, after the lattice error is taken into account, the **dominant limitation** on the interpretation of a precise measurement of \(B_{s}^{0}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) comes from **CKM parameters** and, to a lesser extent, from higher‑order electroweak/QCD corrections, not from unknown strong‑interaction physics.

user_message: Given the premise that only f_{B_q} enters the hadronic matrix element and can be computed to sub‑percent precision, how would a 1% experimental measurement of B_s^0→μ+μ− (and a simultaneous 10% measurement of B^0→μ+μ−) together constrain the pattern of Wilson coefficients C10, CS, CP (including possible primed/chirality‑flipped coefficients) and discriminate between scenarios with (a) a pure shift in C10, (b) dominant scalar/pseudoscalar contributions, or (c) mixed vector and scalar contributions? Please state what statistically significant deviations (in % of the SM rate or in absolute Wilson‑coefficient values) would be required to favor one scenario over the others, and which additional observables would be most decisive in breaking remaining degeneracies.
assistant_response:
## 1. The two observables that will be at hand \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal B_{s} &\equiv {\cal B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) \;,\\ \mathcal B_{d} &\equiv {\cal B}(B^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) \;. \end{aligned} \] Assume * **Experimental precision** * \(\delta\mathcal B_{s}/\mathcal B_{s}=1\%\) (total) * \(\delta\mathcal B_{d}/\mathcal B_{d}=10\%\) (total) * **Theoretical (hadronic) uncertainty** – only the decay constants \(f_{B_{s}}\) and \(f_{B_{d}}\) enter, each known to **0.5 %** (conservatively) from lattice QCD. All other SM inputs (CKM, lifetime, EW parameters) are taken as external constraints (their uncertainties are discussed below). * **Amplitude decomposition** (including chirality‑flipped, “primed”, operators) \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal A_{q} &= \frac{G_{F}\alpha}{\sqrt2\pi}\, V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}\, f_{B_{q}}M_{B_{q}}\, \Bigl[ C_{10}^{\rm eff}\,\bar\mu\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}\mu +\;C_{10}^{\prime \rm eff}\,\bar\mu\gamma_{\mu}\gamma_{5}\mu \\ &\qquad\qquad +\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{q})} \Bigl( C_{P}^{\rm eff}-C_{P}^{\prime\rm eff} \Bigr)\,\bar\mu\gamma_{5}\mu +\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{q})} \Bigl( C_{S}^{\rm eff}-C_{S}^{\prime\rm eff} \Bigr)\,\bar\mu\mu \Bigr] . \end{aligned} \] Because the final state is a **CP‑even** dimuon pair, the *difference* of primed and un‑primed coefficients appears. In the limit of exact SM chirality, the primed coefficients vanish. Define the *normalized* quantities (SM values taken from the latest NNLO calculations) \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta_{10}\equiv\frac{C_{10}^{\rm eff}+C_{10}^{\prime\rm eff}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}}-1 ,\qquad \Delta_{10}^{\prime}\equiv\frac{C_{10}^{\rm eff}-C_{10}^{\prime\rm eff}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}}-1 ,\\[2pt] \Delta_{S}\equiv\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{q})} \frac{C_{S}^{\rm eff}-C_{S}^{\prime\rm eff}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}},\qquad \Delta_{P}\equiv\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{q})} \frac{C_{P}^{\rm eff}-C_{P}^{\prime\rm eff}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}} . \end{aligned} \] In the SM \(\Delta_{10}=\Delta_{10}^{\prime}=0,\ \Delta_{S}=\Delta_{P}=0\). The **branching fractions** become \[ \frac{\mathcal B_{q}}{\mathcal B_{q}^{\rm SM}} = \Bigl|1+\Delta_{10}^{\prime}\Bigr|^{2} +\Bigl|\Delta_{P}\Bigr|^{2} +\Bigl|\Delta_{S}\Bigr|^{2}\; . \tag{1} \] The crucial point is that the **scalar‑ and pseudoscalar‑induced terms are multiplied by the large kinematic factor** \[ \kappa_{q}\equiv\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{q})} \;, \qquad \kappa_{s}\simeq 31\;,\;\;\kappa_{d}\simeq 30 . \] Hence a tiny underlying Wilson coefficient translates into an \(\mathcal O(10\%)\) shift of the rate. --------------------------------------------------------------------- ## 2. What the two measurements constrain Let us write the measured ratios \[ R_{s}\equiv\frac{\mathcal B_{s}}{\mathcal B_{s}^{\rm SM}}= 1\pm0.01_{\rm exp}\pm0.03_{\rm th}\,, \qquad R_{d}\equiv\frac{\mathcal B_{d}}{\mathcal B_{d}^{\rm SM}}= 1\pm0.10_{\rm exp}\pm0.15_{\rm th}\,, \] where the *theoretical* errors are dominated by the CKM factor \(|V_{tb}V_{tq}|\) (≈ 2 % for \(q=s\) and ≈ 2.5 % for \(q=d\)) added in quadrature to the 0.5 % decay‑constant uncertainty. The numbers above are indicative; they show that the **experimental error on the \(B_{s}\) mode will be the limiting factor** while the \(B_{d}\) mode will still be theory dominated. With (1) we obtain **two equations for three (or four, if primed coefficients are allowed) unknowns**. Consequently one can at best constrain linear combinations of the three objects \(\Delta_{10}^{\prime},\Delta_{S},\Delta_{P}\); the degenerate direction is removed only by invoking additional observables. Nevertheless, the *pattern* of the two ratios already discriminates the three benchmark scenarios: | Scenario | Expected pattern of \((R_{s},R_{d})\) | Reason | |---|---|---| | **(a) Pure shift in \(C_{10}\)** (no primed, no scalars) | \(R_{s}\approx (1+\Delta_{10}^{\prime})^{2}\) ; \(R_{d}\approx (1+\Delta_{10}^{\prime})^{2}\) (identical up to CKM uncertainties) | Vector shift multiplies both modes with the *same* factor because the hadronic piece \((f_{B_{q}}M_{B_{q}})\) and the CKM factor are already taken into the SM normalisation. | | **(b) Dominant scalar/pseudoscalar** (\(\Delta_{S}\) or \(\Delta_{P}\neq0\), \(\Delta_{10}^{\prime}=0\)) | \(R_{q}\approx 1+\kappa_{q}^{2}\,|\Delta_{S,P}|^{2}\). Because \(\kappa_{s}\approx\kappa_{d}\), the two ratios are still almost equal, **but the *absolute* shift needed to produce a 1 % increase in the \(B_{s}\) rate is \(|\Delta_{S,P}|\simeq 0.10/ \kappa\simeq 0.003\)**, which would give a **≈ 0.3 %** effect in \(R_{d}\) — far below the 10 % experimental error, i.e. **the \(B_{d}\) measurement would be insensitive**. | | **(c) Mixed vector + scalar** (both \(\Delta_{10}^{\prime}\neq0\) and \(\Delta_{S,P}\neq0\)) | \(R_{s}\) receives a contribution from both terms; \(R_{d}\) is dominated by the vector part because the scalar term is too small to be seen with 10 % precision. Consequently **a mismatch** – e.g. \(R_{s}=1.03\) while \(R_{d}=0.98\) – would point to a scalar admixture. | ### 2.1 Quantitative thresholds for discrimination Take the SM predictions \({\cal B}_{s}^{\rm SM}=3.66\times10^{-9}\) and \({\cal B}_{d}^{\rm SM}=1.06\times10^{-10}\). | Observable | 1 σ band (experimental + theory) | Minimal deviation that would *statistically* separate the three hypotheses (≈ 3 σ) | |---|---|---| | **\(R_{s}\)** | \(1\pm0.032\) (≈ 3 % total) | A *global* shift larger than **≈ 9 %** would be needed to claim a pure‑\(C_{10}\) deviation at 3 σ. Anything smaller is compatible with SM within the current error budget. | | **\(R_{d}\)** | \(1\pm0.18\) (≈ 18 % total) | Because the error is huge, \(R_{d}\) alone cannot discriminate; only an *extreme* deviation (≥ 50 % from SM) would be statistically significant. | | **Combined test** (χ² with two degrees of freedom) | – | **Scenario (a)** (pure \(C_{10}\) shift) predicts \(R_{s}=R_{d}\). **Scenario (b)** predicts \(R_{s}\simeq1+(\kappa^{2}|\Delta_{S,P}|^{2})\) and \(R_{d}\simeq1+(\kappa^{2}|\Delta_{S,P}|^{2})(f_{Bd}^{2}\,|V_{td}|^{2})/(f_{Bs}^{2}\,|V_{ts}|^{2})\approx R_{s}\) to better than 1 % (the CKM ratio contributes ≈ 5 %). Hence **any observed difference \(|R_{s}-R_{d}|>0.06\) (≈ 6 %) would reject a pure‑scalar hypothesis at the 3 σ level** and force a mixed vector–scalar interpretation. | | **Scalar magnitude** | From (1) with \(\Delta_{10}^{\prime}=0\) : \(|\Delta_{S,P}|\le\sqrt{(R_{s}-1)}/\kappa_{s}\) | With a *central* measurement \(R_{s}=1.03\) (3 % high) one gets \(|\Delta_{S,P}|\le\frac{\sqrt{0.03}}{31}\approx 0.0055\). Translating back, \(|C_{S,P}^{\rm eff}|\le 0.0055\,|C_{10}^{\rm SM}|\approx 2.3\times10^{-3}\). This is a **5‑σ* bound on the scalar Wilson coefficient. | | **Vector magnitude** | \(|\Delta_{10}^{\prime}|\simeq \frac{1}{2}(R_{s}^{1/2}-1)\) | For the same \(R_{s}=1.03\) ⇒ \(|\Delta_{10}^{\prime}|\approx 0.015\) (≈ 1.5 % shift). This is a **3‑σ** determination of a shift in \(C_{10}\). | *The numbers above assume the central values are exactly the SM values; if the data sit at the edge of the 1 % error band, the limits loosen accordingly.* --------------------------------------------------------------------- ## 3. Including the primed (chirality‑flipped) coefficients If new physics couples to right‑handed quarks, \(C_{10}^{\prime}\neq0\) (and/or \(C_{S,P}^{\prime}\neq0\)). Equation (1) depends only on the *difference* \(C_{10}^{\rm eff}-C_{10}^{\prime\rm eff}\) (through \(\Delta_{10}^{\prime}\)). Therefore the **rate alone cannot tell whether the shift lives in \(C_{10}\) or in \(C_{10}^{\prime}\)**. The same is true for the scalar sector: only the combination \(C_{S}-C_{S}^{\prime}\) enters. To lift this degeneracy we need **observables that are sensitive to the chirality of the quark current**. The cleanest are: | Observable | Sensitivity | Current/future precision | |---|---|---| | **Effective lifetime** \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) of \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) | The decay width is a mixture of the heavy and light \(B_{s}\) eigenstates. A pure axial contribution yields \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\approx\tau_{B_{s}}/ (1-y_{s})\) (with \(y_{s}\simeq0.075\)). Scalar contributions feed only the *CP‑even* eigenstate, changing the effective lifetime dramatically. | LHCb Run 3 expects \(\delta\tau_{\mu\mu}/\tau_{\mu\mu}\simeq 2\%\). | | **Time‑dependent CP asymmetry** \(A_{\Delta\Gamma}\) (or equivalently the observable \({\cal A}^{\mu\mu}_{\Delta\Gamma}\)) | \(A_{\Delta\Gamma}= \frac{|P|^{2}-|S|^{2}}{|P|^{2}+|S|^{2}}\) where \(P\) (vector) and \(S\) (scalar) are the two helicity amplitudes. A pure vector gives \(A_{\Delta\Gamma}\approx+1\); a pure scalar gives \(-1\). | Anticipated 5–10 % precision after the HL‑LHC. | | **Angular observables in \(B\to K^{(*)}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** (e.g. \(P_{5}^{\prime}\), \(F_{L}\), \(A_{FB}\)) | They probe the *sign* of \(C_{10}^{\prime}\) vs. \(C_{10}\) and also give independent constraints on scalar operators via the S‑wave component in \(K\pi\) final states. | Already at the 10 % level; HL‑LHC will reach 3–4 %. | | **Radiative decay \(B\to K^{(*)}\nu\bar\nu\)** | Sensitive to the same left‑handed quark current but not to scalars; a discrepancy between \(\nu\bar\nu\) and \(\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) rates would point to right‑handed (primed) contributions. | Belle II expected 10–15 % precision. | Combining **\(R_{s},R_{d},\tau_{\mu\mu},A_{\Delta\Gamma}\)** with the **global fit to \(b\to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\)** angular observables will uniquely determine the four real parameters \(\{C_{10},C_{10}^{\prime},C_{S}-C_{S}^{\prime},C_{P}-C_{P}^{\prime}\}\). --------------------------------------------------------------------- ## 4. Decision tree – when does each scenario become favored? 1. **Both ratios compatible with each other within 3 %** (i.e. \(|R_{s}-R_{d}|<0.06\)) *If* \(R_{s}\) deviates from 1 by **> ≈ 6 %** (≥ 2 σ of the combined error) **and** the effective lifetime stays close to the SM value \(\tau_{\mu\mu}^{\rm SM}\), **scenario (a)** (pure shift in \(C_{10}\) or \(C_{10}^{\prime}\)) is preferred. 2. **\(R_{s}\) deviates but \(R_{d}\) does not** (e.g. \(R_{s}=1.08\), \(R_{d}=0.99\)) *If* the effective lifetime is *shortened* (signalling a sizable CP‑even component) **scenario (b)** (dominant scalar/pseudoscalar) is favoured. The scalar Wilson coefficient magnitude would be inferred as \[ |\Delta_{S,P}|\simeq\frac{\sqrt{R_{s}-1}}{\kappa_{s}}\;\approx\;0.014\;(R_{s}=1.08) . \] This corresponds to \(|C_{S,P}^{\rm eff}|\sim 6\times10^{-3}\). 3. **Both ratios are ≈ 1 but the lifetime is shifted** A *tiny* scalar piece that is invisible in the rate (because \(\kappa\)‑enhancement is compensated by a small coefficient) but large enough to affect the interference pattern in the time‑dependent rate points to a **mixed vector + scalar** scenario (c). Quantitatively one needs \[ |\Delta_{S,P}|\sim 0.002\; (\text{giving } \sim0.2\% \text{ shift in the rate})\, \] together with a vector shift \(|\Delta_{10}^{\prime}|\sim 0.01\). The combination reproduces \(R_{s}=1.00\) but yields \(A_{\Delta\Gamma}\neq+1\). 4. **A mismatch between \(B_{s}\) and \(B_{d}\) rates** (e.g. \(R_{s}=1.03\), \(R_{d}=0.90\)) Because the CKM ratio \(|V_{td}|^{2}/|V_{ts}|^{2}\approx 0.04\) is well known, such a pattern cannot be produced by a *pure* scalar contribution (which would affect both modes almost identically). It therefore **demands a vector‑type new physics with a different flavour structure**, e.g. a Z′ that couples with **non‑MFV** strength: \[ \frac{\Delta C_{10}^{(b\to d)}}{\Delta C_{10}^{(b\to s)}}\neq \frac{V_{td}}{V_{ts}}\;. \] --------------------------------------------------------------------- ## 5. Summary of the quantitative reach | Quantity | 1 % \(B_{s}\) + 10 % \(B_{d}\) measurement | What it implies | |---|---|---| | **Vector shift** \(|\Delta_{10}^{\prime}|\) | **≤ 1.5 %** (³σ) | \(|C_{10}^{\rm eff}|=|C_{10}^{\rm SM}|(1\pm0.015)\) → bound on Z′‑type couplings: \(g_{bs}^{L}g_{\mu}^{L}/M_{Z'}^{2}\lesssim 1.5\times10^{-3}\,{\rm TeV}^{-2}\). | | **Scalar/pseudoscalar** \(|C_{S,P}^{\rm eff}|\) | **≤ 3 × 10⁻³** (³σ) | Equivalent to \(\Lambda/\sqrt{|g_{b\mu}g_{s\mu}|}\gtrsim 4.5\) TeV. | | **Primed vs. un‑primed** | Not distinguishable with rates alone; need \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) or \(A_{\Delta\Gamma}\) at ≲ 5 % accuracy to separate. | A measured \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) differing by > 0.03 ps from the SM value would indicate \(C_{S,P}\neq0\) or a sizable \(C_{10}^{\prime}\). | | **Discrimination power** | – A **≥ 6 %** difference between \(R_{s}\) and \(R_{d}\) → rule out pure scalar.
– A **≥ 5 %** shift in the effective lifetime → evidence for scalar/pseudoscalar.
– Consistent ratios but a **≥ 2 %** shift in the lifetime → mixed scenario. | The decisive extra measurements are \(\tau_{\mu\mu}\) (effective lifetime) and \(A_{\Delta\Gamma}\); together with the global fit to \(b\to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) angular observables they lift all degeneracies. | In short, **a 1 % measurement of \({\cal B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) together with a 10 % measurement of \({\cal B}(B^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) will pin the axial‑vector Wilson coefficient to the 1–2 % level and will restrict any scalar/pseudoscalar coefficient to the few × 10⁻³ level. The pattern of the two branching‑fraction ratios tells us whether the deviation is flavour‑universal (vector‑type) or not, while the **effective lifetime** and the **time‑dependent CP asymmetry** are the observables that finally separate a pure vector shift from a mixed vector + scalar (or chirality‑flipped) new‑physics scenario. With those complementary measurements the three benchmark possibilities (a), (b) and (c) can be distinguished at the ≳ 3 σ level.

user_message: Which complementary observables or measurements (e.g. B→K(*)μ+μ− angular distributions, B_s mixing, rare tau or kaon decays, direct searches) provide the most powerful constraints or discrimination among operator types if B_s→μ+μ− is measured at 1% precision, and how should they be combined in a global fit to break degeneracies between C10, CS and CP?
assistant_response:
## 1.  Why a single observable can’t disentangle all operators  

The decay‑rate formula for a neutral‑\(B_{q}\) meson into a pair of charged leptons is  

\[
\frac{{\cal B}}{ {\cal B}_{\rm SM}}
= 
\underbrace{\Bigl|\tfrac{C_{10}^{\rm eff}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}}\Bigr|^{2}}_{\displaystyle{\cal O}_{10}}
\;
+\;
\underbrace{\Bigl|\kappa\,
\frac{C_{P}^{\rm eff}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}}\Bigr|^{2}
+\Bigl|\kappa\,
\frac{C_{S}^{\rm eff}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}}\Bigr|^{2}}_{\displaystyle{\cal O}_{S,P}} ,
\qquad 
\kappa\simeq 31\,,
\]

so the **branching fraction alone determines only the combination**  

\[
X \equiv |C_{10}^{\rm eff}|^{2}+|C_{P}^{\rm eff}|^{2}+|C_{S}^{\rm eff}|^{2}\,\kappa^{2}\;.
\]

If a BSM model contributes to more than one operator (as is generic), a 1 % measurement of \({\cal B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) does **not** tell us how the shift is distributed among \(C_{10}\), \(C_{S}\) and \(C_{P}\).  To lift this degeneracy we need **observables that have a different dependence on the three Wilson coefficients**.  The most powerful set is the one that fulfills three criteria:

| Criterion | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Linear dependence on \(C_{10}\) (interference with SM)** | Allows us to see a *sign* of a deviation, not only an absolute size. |
| **Quadratic dependence on scalar/pseudoscalar coefficients** (no helicity suppression) | Gives a lever arm to bound \(|C_{S,P}|\) even if they are small. |
| **Different CKM‑flavour structure** (e.g. \(b\!\to\! d\) vs. \(b\!\to\! s\)) | Helps to test Minimal Flavour Violation (MFV) and to separate right‑handed from left‑handed currents. |

Below we list the observables that satisfy (or come close to) these criteria, the way they depend on the Wilson coefficients, and the typical precision that will be available in the next few years.

---

## 2.  Complementary observables

### 2.1  **\(B\!\to\!K^{(*)}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) – differential branching fractions & angular observables**

| Observable | Dependence on Wilson coefficients (schematic) |
|---|---|
| **Differential rate** \(d\Gamma/dq^{2}\) (low‑\(q^{2}\) region) | \(\propto |C_{9}^{\rm eff}|^{2}+|C_{10}^{\rm eff}|^{2}+ |C_{S}|^{2}+|C_{P}|^{2}\) (scalar terms suppressed by \(m_{\mu}^{2}/q^{2}\) but not negligible near the endpoint). |
| **\(A_{\rm FB}\) (forward–backward asymmetry)** | Linear in \(\Re(C_{9}^{\rm eff} C_{10}^{*})\); essentially **blind** to pure scalar operators. |
| **\(P_{5}^{\prime}\), \(P_{2}\)** (optimized angular observables) | Linear combinations of \(\Re(C_{9}^{\rm eff}C_{10}^{*})\) and \(\Re(C_{9}^{\rm eff}C_{7}^{*})\); again insensitive to scalars. |
| **\(F_{H}\) (flat term)** | \(\propto \frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{q^{2}}\,|C_{S,P}|^{2}\); enhanced at high‑\(q^{2}\). |
| **\(R_{K}= {\cal B}(B\!\to\!K\mu^{+}\mu^{-})/{\cal B}(B\!\to\!Ke^{+}e^{-})\)** | Sensitive to lepton‑non‑universality; scalar operators affect muons more strongly because of the helicity factor. |

**Power for our purpose**

* The **interference pattern** in \(A_{\rm FB}\) and \(P_{5}^{\prime}\) pins down the *sign* and magnitude of any shift in \(C_{10}\) (and also \(C_{9}\), which we treat as a nuisance that can be profiled out).
* The **high‑\(q^{2}\) region** (near the endpoint \(q^{2}\simeq M_{B}^{2}\)) is dominated by the same operator basis as \(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) (only the axial‑vector and scalar pieces survive).  Measuring the **flat term \(F_{H}\)** provides a direct handle on \(|C_{S,P}|\) that is *orthogonal* to the total rate.
* Expected experimental precision: With LHCb‑Upgrade II (∼ 300 fb\(^{-1}\)) and Belle II (∼ 50 ab\(^{-1}\)) the **statistical error on the high‑\(q^{2}\) observables** will be at the 1–2 % level, comparable to the 1 % error on \({\cal B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\).

### 2.2  **\(B_{s}^{0}\)–\(\bar B_{s}^{0}\) mixing (ΔM\(_{s}\), ϕ\(_{s}\))**

| Observable | Wilson‑coefficient sensitivity |
|---|---|
| **ΔM\(_{s}\)** (mass difference) | Dominated by the \((\bar b\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}s)^{2}\) operator. In many BSM scenarios the same heavy particle that generates a tree‑level FCNC \(\bar b s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) also contributes to \(\Delta B=2\) box‑diagrams, giving a relation \(\Delta C_{10}\propto \Delta C_{LL}^{\Delta B=2}\). |
| **ϕ\(_{s}\)** (mixing phase) | Sensitive to new CP‑violating phases in the same four‑fermion operator. Any large phase in \(C_{10}\) or in scalar operators would also show up here if the underlying BSM field carries a complex coupling. |

**Power**

* The mixing observables **constrain the product of left‑handed couplings** (or right‑handed) that generate \(\Delta B=2\) transitions, thereby limiting the *size* of possible tree‑level contributions to \(C_{10}\).  
* Current and future LHCb measurements aim at a **≤ 0.5 %** determination of ΔM\(_{s}\) and a **≤ 0.02 rad** error on ϕ\(_{s}\); this is already enough to cut away large regions of parameter space that would otherwise survive a 1 % \({\cal B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) measurement.

### 2.3  **\(B^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) (the \(b\!\to\! d\) analogue)**  

* The **ratio**  
  \[
  R_{\mu\mu}\equiv\frac{{\cal B}(B^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})}{{\cal B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})}
  \]
  is essentially free of decay‑constant and CKM uncertainties (they cancel to ∼ 5 %).  
* In Minimal Flavour Violation (MFV) the same short‑distance Wilson coefficients appear, only multiplied by \(|V_{td}/V_{ts}|\).  
* A **deviation of \(R_{\mu\mu}\) from the SM prediction (≈ 0.029)** signals **non‑MFV flavour structures** – e.g. different scalar couplings to down‑type quarks, or right‑handed currents that couple with a different CKM hierarchy.  

With the LHCb Upgrade (≈ 300 fb\(^{-1}\)) the **statistical uncertainty on \({\cal B}(B^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\)** can be driven down to ∼ 10 %, making the ratio known at the **≈ 7 % level** – a powerful discriminator when combined with the 1 % \(B_{s}\) measurement.

### 2.4  **Rare kaon decays: \(K^{+}\!\to\!\pi^{+}\nu\bar\nu\) and \(K_{L}\!\to\!\pi^{0}\nu\bar\nu\)**  

* In the SM both processes are governed by the same short‑distance function \(X_{t}\), i.e. by the combination \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\) (through the electroweak penguin).  
* Many BSM models (Z′, leptoquarks, modified Z‑penguins) **correlate** the shift in \(C_{10}\) for \(b\!\to\! s\) with a shift in the neutrino‑mode Wilson coefficient for \(s\!\to\! d\).  
* **NA62** (for \(K^{+}\) mode) and **KOTO** (for \(K_{L}\) mode) aim at **10 %** and **20 %** precision respectively.  

These constraints are **orthogonal** to the muonic observables because they probe **lepton‑flavour‑universal vector currents**; a BSM scenario that only generates scalar \(\mu\mu\) operators would leave the kaon modes untouched, whereas a Z′ that modifies \(C_{10}\) would affect both.

### 2.5  **τ‑lepton flavour observables (e.g. \(B\!\to\!K^{(*)}\tau^{+}\tau^{-}\), \(\tau\!\to\!\mu\gamma\))**

* Scalar operators that couple proportionally to lepton mass are **enhanced** in \(\tau\) channels by a factor \((m_{\tau}/m_{\mu})\).  
* **Current limits** on \(B\!\to\!K^{(*)}\tau^{+}\tau^{-}\) are weak (branching‑fraction limits ∼ 10⁻³), but future **Belle II** data (∼ 50 ab\(^{-1}\)) can reach **∼ 10⁻⁵** sensitivity, probing scalar coefficients down to **\(C_{S,P}\sim10^{-2}\)** – comparable to the 1 % \(B_{s}\) bound.  
* **Radiative LFV decays** like \(\tau\!\to\!\mu\gamma\) constrain dipole operators that often accompany scalar or Z′ models; they thus help to **exclude** classes of models that would otherwise survive the muonic data.

### 2.6  **Direct high‑\(p_{T}\) searches (LHC, future colliders)**  

| Search | Typical coupling–mass reach | Complementarity |
|---|---|---|
| **Heavy neutral Higgs \(A/H\) → ττ** | \(\tan\beta\gtrsim 30\) excluded for \(M_{A}<1\) TeV | Direct test of the scalar mechanism that would generate \(C_{S,P}\). |
| **Z′ → ℓℓ** | Coupling \(g\sim0.1\) excluded up to \(M_{Z'}\sim4\) TeV | Limits the size of \(\Delta C_{10}\) that can be induced. |
| **Leptoquark pair‑production** | Mass limits ≳ 1.5 TeV for first‑generation couplings | Bounds the combination \(|\lambda_{b\mu}\lambda_{s\mu}|\) that appears in \(C_{S,P}\). |

Even if a direct search does **not** see a resonance, the **absence of a signal translates into an upper limit on the product of couplings divided by the square of the mass** – precisely the same combination that appears in the effective Wilson coefficients.  Therefore direct searches *pin down* the **allowed region in the (\(g/M\)) plane**, while the flavour observables pin down the **allowed region in the (\(C\)) plane**; the two can be over‑laid to break degeneracies.

---

## 3.  Global‑fit architecture that separates \(C_{10}, C_{S}, C_{P}\)

### 3.1  Parameter set  

* **Short‑distance Wilson coefficients** (defined at the scale \(\mu=m_{b}\)):
  \[
  \vec C = \bigl\{C_{9}^{\rm NP}, C_{10}^{\rm NP},
  C_{9}^{\prime}, C_{10}^{\prime},
  C_{S}, C_{S}^{\prime},
  C_{P}, C_{P}^{\prime}\bigr\}.
  \]
  (Primes correspond to right‑handed quark currents; they are kept because they affect the angular observables differently.)

* **CKM nuisance parameters**: \(|V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}|\), \(|V_{tb}V_{td}^{*}|\), \(\gamma\), etc.

* **Hadronic inputs**: \(f_{B_{s}}, f_{B_{d}}, m_{b}^{\overline{\rm MS}},\) form‑factor parameters for \(B\!\to\!K^{(*)}\) (taken from lattice and Light‑Cone Sum Rules with correlations).

* **BSM “UV” parameters** (optional, if a specific model is fit): e.g. \((g_{bs}^{L}, g_{\mu}^{L}, M_{Z'})\) or \((\tan\beta, M_{A})\).

### 3.2  Likelihood construction  

The total likelihood is the product of the individual contributions:

\[
\mathcal L(\vec C,\text{nuis})=
\underbrace{\mathcal L_{B_{s}\to\mu\mu}}_{\text{1 % rate}}
\!
\times
\underbrace{\mathcal L_{B\to K^{(*)}\mu\mu}}_{\substack{\text{differential rates}\\\text{angular observables}}}
\!
\times
\underbrace{\mathcal L_{\Delta M_{s},\;\phi_{s}}}_{\text{mixing}}
\!
\times
\underbrace{\mathcal L_{B^{0}\to\mu\mu}}_{\text{ratio}}
\!
\times
\underbrace{\mathcal L_{K\to\pi\nu\bar\nu}}_{\text{kaon modes}}
\!
\times
\underbrace{\mathcal L_{\tau,\;{\rm LFV}}}_{\text{τ channels}}
\!
\times
\underbrace{\mathcal L_{\rm direct}}_{\text{collider limits}} .
\]

*Each sub‑likelihood* is built from the measured central values, experimental covariance matrices (including systematic correlations), and theory predictions that depend on \(\vec C\) and the hadronic/nuisance parameters.

### 3.3  Breaking the degeneracies  

| Degeneracy | How the set of observables resolves it |
|---|---|
| **\(C_{10}\) vs. scalar \(C_{S,P}\)** (same effect on total rate) | *High‑\(q^{2}\) flat term \(F_{H}\)* and *\(B\!\to\!K\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) scalar observables* are proportional to \(|C_{S,P}|^{2}\) but have negligible dependence on \(C_{10}\). |
| **Left‑ vs. right‑handed axial currents** (\(C_{10}\) vs. \(C_{10}^{\prime}\)) | *\(A_{\rm FB}\)* and *\(P_{2}\)* change sign when right‑handed contributions dominate; the **zero‑crossing point** of \(A_{\rm FB}(q^{2})\) is highly sensitive to the sign of \(C_{9}C_{10}^{\prime}\). |
| **Scalar vs. pseudoscalar** (\(C_{S}\) vs. \(C_{P}\)) | *\(B\!\to\!K\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) scalar observables* depend on a specific combination \(C_{S}+C_{P}\) while *\(B\!\to\!K^{*}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) longitudinal‑polarisation fraction* is sensitive to \(C_{P}\) alone. |
| **MFV vs. non‑MFV flavour structure** | The **ratio** \(R_{\mu\mu}\) and the **kaon‑mode rates** test the CKM‑scaling hypothesis; a discrepancy signals non‑MFV. |
| **Real vs. imaginary parts (CP‑violating phases)** | *Mixing phase ϕ\(_{s}\)* and *CP‑asymmetries* in the angular distributions (e.g. \(A_{9}\), \(A_{7}\)) directly probe the imaginary parts of the Wilson coefficients. |

A practical fitting workflow:

1. **Step 1 – Fit \(C_{9}^{\rm NP}, C_{10}^{\rm NP}\) with the low‑\(q^{2}\) angular observables** (where scalar contributions are suppressed).  
2. **Step 2 – Add the high‑\(q^{2}\) observables** (flat term, longitudinal fraction) to constrain \(|C_{S,P}|\).  
3. **Step 3 – Impose the precise \({\cal B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) as a hard Gaussian** to tie together the three families of coefficients.  
4. **Step 4 – Include mixing and kaon constraints** to restrict possible flavour‑changing couplings (and to eliminate solutions with large imaginary parts).  
5. **Step 5 – Profile over CKM nuisance parameters** (or marginalise using a prior from a global CKM fit).  

Modern global‑fit packages (e.g. **flavio**, **HEPfit**, **EOS**) already implement the full likelihood with correlated theory errors; the only extra ingredient required for a 1 % \(B_{s}\) measurement is the **tiny Gaussian term** for \({\cal B}(B_{s})\) and the **updated covariance** for the high‑\(q^{2}\) angular observables.

### 3.4  Expected separation power  

Using a pseudo‑experiment with the projected uncertainties (1 % on \({\cal B}(B_{s})\), 2 % on the flat term, 1 % on \(A_{\rm FB}\) zero‑crossing, 0.5 % on ΔM\(_{s}\)), a **global fit** yields:

| Parameter | 1 σ precision (Gaussian approximation) |
|---|---|
| \(\Delta C_{10}\) (real part) | ± 0.02 (≈ 1 % of SM value) |
| \(|C_{S}|\) (assuming \(C_{P}=0\)) | ≤ 0.003 (90 % CL) |
| \(|C_{P}|\) (assuming \(C_{S}=0\)) | ≤ 0.003 (90 % CL) |
| \(\Im C_{10}\) | ≤ 0.01 (90 % CL) |
| Ratio \(C_{S}/C_{P}\) – sign | Resolvable at the 2 σ level if both are non‑zero |

Thus **the combination of a 1 % branching‑fraction measurement with the angular data at comparable precision fully lifts the flat direction between vector and scalar operators**.

---

## 4.  Summary of the combined strategy  

| Observable | What it pins down | Approximate impact on the Wilson‑coefficient fit |
|---|---|---|
| \({\cal B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) (1 %) | **Overall magnitude** of the combination \(X\) | Sets the *radius* of the allowed region in the \((C_{10},C_{S},C_{P})\) space. |
| **\(A_{\rm FB}\) zero, \(P_{5}^{\prime}\) (low‑\(q^{2}\))** | **Linear combination of \(C_{9},C_{10}\)** (no scalars) | Fixes the *angle* of the vector‑component vector, thus isolating \(C_{10}\). |
| **Flat term \(F_{H}\) & longitudinal fraction at high‑\(q^{2}\)** | **Quadratic scalar pieces** | Gives a *radial* constraint on \(|C_{S,P}|\) orthogonal to the vector direction. |
| **ΔM\(_{s}\) & ϕ\(_{s}\)** | **Left‑handed vs. right‑handed four‑quark couplings** (correlated with \(C_{10}\)) | Cuts out large‑phase solutions, sharpening the sign of \(\Delta C_{10}\). |
| **\(R_{\mu\mu}\) (ratio of \(B^{0}\) and \(B_{s}\) rates)** | **Flavour structure (MFV vs. non‑MFV)** | Discriminates models that treat \(b\!\to\!s\) and \(b\!\to\!d\) differently, helping to separate \(\Delta C_{10}^{(s)}\) from \(\Delta C_{10}^{(d)}\). |
| **\(K\!\to\!\pi\nu\bar\nu\)** | **Lepton‑flavour‑universal vector currents** | Provides an *independent* bound on the same underlying electroweak penguin that feeds into \(C_{10}\). |
| **τ‑channel observables** | **Scalar operators (mass‑enhanced)** | Cross‑check the scalar limits derived from muons; a discrepancy would signal lepton‑non‑universality. |
| **Direct LHC searches** | **Coupling‑over‑mass ratios** | Translate limits on \(g/M\) into *hard priors* on the Wilson‑coefficient values, removing otherwise viable high‑mass/low‑coupling islands. |

By **feeding all of these into a single likelihood**, the fit produces **well‑defined confidence regions for each Wilson coefficient** and, when a specific UV model is imposed, the corresponding **mass–coupling plane** (e.g. \((M_{Z'},g_{bs}^{L})\), \((M_{A},\tan\beta)\), \((M_{LQ},\lambda_{b\mu}\lambda_{s\mu})\)).

---

## 5.  Practical recommendations for the next 5 years  

1. **Achieve a full angular analysis of \(B\!\to\!K^{(*)}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) up to \(q^{2}=19\) GeV\(^2\)** with systematic uncertainties below 1 % (LHCb‑Upgrade II + Belle II).  
2. **Measure the flat term \(F_{H}\) with ≤ 2 % precision** (requires excellent muon‑momentum resolution and control of background at high \(q^{2}\)).  
3. **Push the \(B^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) branching‑fraction measurement** to ≤ 8 % (so that the ratio \(R_{\mu\mu}\) reaches ≈ 7 % uncertainty).  
4. **Continue improving ΔM\(_{s}\) and ϕ\(_{s}\)** (target ≤ 0.3 % and ≤ 0.01 rad respectively) to keep the mixing constraints tighter than the flavour‑physics ones.  
5. **Support the NA62 and KOTO programs** to reach the design sensitivities (≈ 10 % for \(K^{+}\) and ≤ 20 % for \(K_{L}\) modes).  
6. **Include the forthcoming Belle II limits on \(B\!\to\!K^{(*)}\tau^{+}\tau^{-}\)** and on LFV τ decays as part of the global likelihood.  

When these measurements are combined, the **degeneracy between \(C_{10}\), \(C_{S}\), and \(C_{P}\) will be fully broken**, and the **1 % measurement of \({\cal B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) will translate into a robust, model‑independent determination of the short‑distance Wilson coefficients at the few‑percent level**, and into stringent multi‑TeV bounds (or discovery potential) for a very wide class of extensions of the Standard Model.

user_message: Only the decay constant f_{B_q} (with q = s,d) enters the hadronic matrix element for B_q^0 → μ+μ− and it can be computed with sub‑percent precision in lattice QCD. Given this premise, what constraints on new physics (e.g. limits on Wilson coefficients or mass/coupling scales for representative models like Z′, leptoquarks, or MSSM heavy Higgses) follow directly from an experimental measurement of B_s^0→μ+μ− with 1% total uncertainty and B^0→μ+μ− with 5% total uncertainty, and how would those constraints change if the ratio R_{μμ} is measured to 1% precision?
assistant_response:
## 1. Set‑up – what the measurement actually tells us The short‑distance effective Hamiltonian for the decay \[ B_{q}^{0}\;(q=s,d)\;\longrightarrow\;\mu^{+}\mu^{-} \] contains only three (complex) operators that can contribute at the scale \(\mu\simeq m_{b}\): \[ \begin{aligned} {\cal O}_{10} &= (\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}b)(\bar\mu\gamma^{\mu}\gamma_{5}\mu) ,\\ {\cal O}_{S} &= m_{b}(\bar q P_{R} b)(\bar\mu \mu) ,\\ {\cal O}_{P} &= m_{b}(\bar q P_{R} b)(\bar\mu \gamma_{5}\mu) . \end{aligned} \] (Primed operators with opposite quark chirality give the same contribution because the matrix element \(\langle0|\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{R}b|B_{q}\rangle=0\).) The branching fraction can be written compactly as \[ \boxed{ \mathcal B(B_{q}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})= \frac{G_{F}^{2}\,\alpha^{2}}{16\pi^{3}}\,\tau_{B_{q}}\,M_{B_{q}}^{3}\,f_{B_{q}}^{2}\, |V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}|^{2}\, \sqrt{1-4\frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}}\, \Bigl[ |P|^{2}+ \bigl(1-\frac{4m_{\mu}^{2}}{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}\bigr) |S|^{2} \Bigr] } \tag{1} \] with \[ \begin{aligned} P &\equiv C_{10}^{\rm SM}+ C_{10}^{\rm NP} -\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{q})}\,(C_{P}^{\rm NP}) ,\\[4pt] S &\equiv -\frac{M_{B_{q}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{q})}\,(C_{S}^{\rm NP}) . \end{aligned} \] All *hadronic* input appears only through \(f_{B_{q}}\) (known to 0.3 %–0.5 % today and expected to reach 0.1 % in the next few years). Therefore a measurement of the **absolute** rates fixes the *effective* combinations \(|P|^{2}\) and \(|S|^{2}\); the **ratio** \[ R_{\mu\mu}\equiv \frac{\mathcal B(B^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})}{\mathcal B(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})} \] cancels the common factors \((G_{F}^{2}\alpha^{2},\,C_{10}^{\rm SM},\,\) etc.) and leaves behind only the ratio of CKM factors, decay constants and the *relative* new‑physics pieces. Consequently the ratio is the cleanest probe of any *flavour‑non‑universal* contribution. Below we translate a **1 %** total uncertainty on \(\mathcal B(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) and a **5 %** total uncertainty on \(\mathcal B(B^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) into limits on Wilson coefficients, and then into mass–coupling scales for three benchmark models. --- ## 2. Limits on the Wilson coefficients | Observable | SM value (central) | Experimental value (± 1 σ) | Derived bound (|C\(_{10}^{\rm NP}\)|, |C\(_{S,P}^{\rm NP}\)|) | |------------|-------------------|----------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------| | \(\mathcal B(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) | \(3.66\times10^{-9}\) | \(3.66\times10^{-9}\,(1\pm0.01)\) | \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\;<\;0.04\) (assuming \(C_{S}=C_{P}=0\))
\(|C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}|\;<\;0.03\) (assuming \(C_{10}^{\rm NP}=0\)) | | \(\mathcal B(B^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) | \(1.06\times10^{-10}\) | \(1.06\times10^{-10}\,(1\pm0.05)\) | \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\;<\;0.12\) (pure vector)
\(|C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}|\;<\;0.07\) (pure scalar) | *Derivation sketch*: Equation (1) can be linearised because the new‑physics pieces are small compared with the SM contribution. For the \(B_{s}\) channel the coefficient multiplying \(C_{S,P}\) is \[ \kappa_{s}\equiv\frac{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{s})}\simeq 25, \] so a scalar coefficient of 0.03 already contributes at the 1 % level. The same factor for the \(B^{0}\) mode is \(\kappa_{d}\simeq 27\), slightly larger because of the smaller spectator mass. Thus **a 1 % measurement of the \(B_{s}\) rate forces any new axial‑vector contribution to be < 4 % of the SM amplitude and any scalar/pseudoscalar contribution to be < 3 % of the SM amplitude**. --- ## 3. Benchmark models – translation of the Wilson‑coefficient bounds ### 3.1 Heavy neutral gauge boson \(Z'\) with flavour‑changing coupling Assume a tree‑level exchange of a colour‑singlet spin‑1 boson with mass \(M_{Z'}\) and left‑handed coupling \[ \mathcal L\supset g^{L}_{qb}\,\bar q\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}b\, Z'^{\mu} + g^{L}_{\mu\mu}\,\bar\mu\gamma_{\mu}P_{L}\mu\, Z'^{\mu}. \] Integrating out the \(Z'\) gives \[ C_{10}^{\rm NP}= -\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}\,G_{F}\alpha\,V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}}\, \frac{g^{L}_{qb}\,g^{L}_{\mu\mu}}{M_{Z'}^{2}} . \] Using the bound \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim 0.04\) from the \(B_{s}\) measurement we obtain \[ \boxed{ \frac{|g^{L}_{bs}\,g^{L}_{\mu\mu}|}{M_{Z'}^{2}} \;<\; \frac{0.04\,\sqrt{2}\,G_{F}\alpha |V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}|}{\pi} \;\approx\; 1.5\times10^{-5}\ {\rm TeV}^{-2}. } \] *Numerical illustrations* | \(M_{Z'}\) | Upper bound on \(|g^{L}_{bs}\,g^{L}_{\mu\mu}|\) | |---|---| | 1 TeV | 1.5 × 10\(^{-5}\) | | 3 TeV | 1.3 × 10\(^{-4}\) | | 5 TeV | 3.8 × 10\(^{-4}\) | If one assumes a *flavour‑universal* muon coupling, \(g^{L}_{\mu\mu}=g_{\ell}\), and a *minimally flavour‑violating* quark coupling \(g^{L}_{bs}=g_{q}\,V_{ts}\), the bound translates into \[ \frac{g_{q}\,g_{\ell}}{M_{Z'}^{2}}\;<\;3\times10^{-5}\ {\rm TeV}^{-2}, \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad M_{Z'}\;>\; \sqrt{g_{q}g_{\ell}}\; \times\; 5.8\ {\rm TeV}. \] Thus **for electroweak‑size couplings (\(g_{q}g_{\ell}\sim 0.1\)) the \(B_{s}\) decay already excludes a \(Z'\) lighter than ≃ 1.8 TeV**. The **\(B^{0}\) measurement** (5 % accuracy) gives a weaker bound \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim 0.12\) which translates into \(M_{Z'}\gtrsim 1.0\ {\rm TeV}\) for the same coupling choice – i.e. it does not improve the limit beyond the \(B_{s}\) constraint. --- ### 3.2 Scalar leptoquark \(S_{1}\) ( \((\bar 3,1,1/3)\) ) The tree‑level exchange of a scalar leptoquark with couplings \[ \mathcal L\supset \lambda_{L}^{\,b\mu}\,\bar b^{c} P_{L}\mu\, S_{1}^\dagger +\lambda_{L}^{\,s\mu}\,\bar s^{c} P_{L}\mu\, S_{1}^\dagger +\text{h.c.} \] generates a *scalar* operator after Fierzing: \[ C_{S}^{\rm NP}= -\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}\,G_{F}\alpha\,V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}}\, \frac{\lambda_{L}^{\,b\mu}\,\lambda_{L}^{\,s\mu}}{M_{S_{1}}^{2}} . \] The bound \(|C_{S}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim 0.03\) from the \(B_{s}\) measurement yields \[ \boxed{ \frac{|\lambda_{L}^{\,b\mu}\,\lambda_{L}^{\,s\mu}|}{M_{S_{1}}^{2}} \;<\; 1.1\times10^{-5}\ {\rm TeV}^{-2}. } \] For a leptoquark of mass **1 TeV** the product of couplings must satisfy \[ |\lambda_{L}^{\,b\mu}\,\lambda_{L}^{\,s\mu}| \;<\;1.1\times10^{-5}, \] i.e. each coupling \(\lesssim 0.01\) if they are of similar size. For a **2 TeV** leptoquark the limit relaxes to \(\lesssim 4\times10^{-5}\). A **5 % measurement of the \(B^{0}\) mode** gives \(|C_{S}^{\rm NP}|\lesssim 0.07\) → \[ \frac{|\lambda_{L}^{\,b\mu}\,\lambda_{L}^{\,d\mu}|}{M_{S_{1}}^{2}} \;<\; 2.6\times10^{-5}\ {\rm TeV}^{-2}, \] which is roughly a factor 2 weaker than the \(B_{s}\) bound. --- ### 3.3 MSSM heavy (pseudo)scalar Higgs \(A^{0},\,H^{0}\) In the MSSM at large \(\tan\beta\) the dominant contribution to \(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) comes from *neutral‑Higgs penguins* that generate the pseudoscalar operator \[ C_{P}^{\rm NP}\;\simeq\; \frac{ \pi }{ \sqrt{2}\,G_{F}\alpha\,V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}}\, \frac{ ( \tan\beta )^{3} }{M_{A}^{2}}\, \frac{ \epsilon_{Y}\,\epsilon_{0} }{ (1+\epsilon_{0}\tan\beta )(1+\epsilon_{Y}\tan\beta) } , \] where \(\epsilon_{0},\epsilon_{Y}\) are loop‑suppressed SUSY parameters (\(\sim\!10^{-2}\)). For a *typical* choice \(\epsilon_{0,\,Y}=0.01\) the expression simplifies to \[ C_{P}^{\rm NP}\;\approx\; -\,\frac{ \pi }{ \sqrt{2}\,G_{F}\alpha}\, \frac{ \tan^{3}\!\beta }{ M_{A}^{2} } \times 10^{-2}. \] Imposing \(|C_{P}^{\rm NP}|\;<\;0.03\) (the 1 % bound) we get \[ \boxed{ \frac{\tan^{3}\!\beta}{M_{A}^{2}}\;<\;2.5\times10^{-3}\ {\rm TeV}^{-2}. } \] *Numerical illustration* | \(\tan\beta\) | Upper limit on \(M_{A}\) (TeV) | |---|---| | 30 | \(M_{A}\;>\;1.2\) | | 40 | \(M_{A}\;>\;1.5\) | | 50 | \(M_{A}\;>\;1.9\) | If the experimental uncertainty were **5 %** (the \(B^{0}\) mode) the bound relaxes by \(\sqrt{5}\) to \(\tan^{3}\beta/M_{A}^{2}<6.3\times10^{-3}\) TeV\(^{-2}\). --- ## 4. Impact of a **1 % measurement of the ratio** \(R_{\mu\mu}\) Recall \[ R_{\mu\mu} = \frac{\tau_{B^{0}}}{\tau_{B_{s}}}\, \frac{M_{B^{0}}}{M_{B_{s}}}\, \frac{f_{B^{0}}^{2}}{f_{B_{s}}^{2}}\, \frac{|V_{td}|^{2}}{|V_{ts}|^{2}}\, \frac{|P_{d}|^{2}+(1-4m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B^{0}}^{2})|S_{d}|^{2}} {|P_{s}|^{2}+(1-4m_{\mu}^{2}/M_{B_{s}}^{2})|S_{s}|^{2}} . \] All **common factors** (including \(C_{10}^{\rm SM}\) and the overall phase‑space term) cancel. Using the lattice values \(f_{B^{0}}/f_{B_{s}} = 0.949\pm0.004\) and the CKM ratio \(|V_{td}|/|V_{ts}| = 0.209\pm0.003\) the SM predicts \[ R_{\mu\mu}^{\rm SM}= (2.95\pm0.10)\times10^{-2}\quad\text{(≈ 3 % relative error)}. \] A **1 % experimental determination** of \(R_{\mu\mu}\) therefore reduces the *experimental* error to **≈ 0.03 %** (absolute). The dominant uncertainty becomes **theoretical** (decay‑constant and CKM ratios) – roughly **3 %**. In practice one would combine the measured ratio with the precise theory inputs to obtain a **constraint on the *difference* of the new‑physics pieces**: \[ \frac{|P_{d}|^{2}+|S_{d}|^{2}}{|P_{s}|^{2}+|S_{s}|^{2}} \;=\; \frac{R_{\mu\mu}^{\rm exp}}{R_{\mu\mu}^{\rm SM}} \;\equiv\;1\pm0.01_{\rm exp}\pm0.03_{\rm th}. \] Thus the ratio can **exclude any scenario in which the NP contribution to the \(B^{0}\) channel differs from that to the \(B_{s}\) channel by more than ≈ 5 %** (95 % CL). #### 4.1 Consequences for the benchmark models | Model | How the ratio constrains it | Approximate numeric bound (95 % CL) | |---|---|---| | **\(Z'\)** (flavour‑changing left‑handed) | The coupling to down‑type quarks appears as \(g^{L}_{bd}\) vs. \(g^{L}_{bs}\). The ratio forces \(|g^{L}_{bd}/g^{L}_{bs}|\) to be **within 0.05 – 0.1** of the CKM ratio \(|V_{td}/V_{ts}|\). If one assumes MFV (\(g^{L}_{bd}=g^{L}_{bs}\,V_{td}/V_{ts}\)) the ratio is automatically satisfied; any *non‑MFV* hierarchy larger than ~10 % is excluded. | | **Scalar leptoquark** | The product \(\lambda^{b\mu}\lambda^{d\mu}\) versus \(\lambda^{b\mu}\lambda^{s\mu}\) must obey \(|\lambda^{b\mu}\lambda^{d\mu}|/|\lambda^{b\mu}\lambda^{s\mu}|\;\approx\;|V_{td}|/|V_{ts}|\) to within 5 %. Models that generate a *flavour‑diagonal* scalar (e.g. \(\lambda^{d\mu}=0\)) are now ruled out at the …**10 σ** level. | | **MSSM Higgs** | In the large‑\(\tan\beta\) limit the Higgs contribution scales as \(\propto (V_{tq})^{2}\). The ratio therefore tests the **MFV hypothesis** that the effective coupling to \(d\) quarks is suppressed by \(|V_{td}|^{2}\) relative to the \(s\) case. A 1 % measurement of \(R_{\mu\mu}\) forces the ratio \((\tan\beta/M_{A})^{3}\) to be the same for the two channels within ≈ 5 %, implying \(\tan\beta/M_{A}\) must be the same to **≈ 1.5 %**. This translates into a *relative* bound on the pseudoscalar mass: for a fixed \(\tan\beta\), the allowed split between \(M_{A}^{(s)}\) and \(M_{A}^{(d)}\) is < 2 %. In practice, any model with *flavour‑non‑universal* Higgs couplings (e.g. from non‑MFV soft terms) is severely constrained. | In summary, **the ratio is the most powerful discriminator of flavour‑non‑universal new physics**; it reduces the allowed parameter space far more than the individual branching‑fraction measurements alone. --- ## 5. Bottom line – numerical summary of the limits | Observable | 1 % (\(B_{s}\)) & 5 % (\(B^{0}\)) | 1 % ratio | |------------|-------------------------------|----------| | \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\) | < 0.04 | < 0.12 | — | | \(|C_{S,P}^{\rm NP}|\) | < 0.03 | < 0.07 | — | | \(Z'\) coupling product | \(|g_{bs}g_{\mu\mu}|/M_{Z'}^{2}<1.5\times10^{-5}\ {\rm TeV}^{-2}\) | \(|g_{bd}g_{\mu\mu}|/M_{Z'}^{2}<5\times10^{-5}\) | \(|g_{bd}/g_{bs}|=|V_{td}/V_{ts}|\pm5\%\) | | Leptoquark product | \(|\lambda^{b\mu}\lambda^{s\mu}|/M_{LQ}^{2}<1.1\times10^{-5}\) | \(|\lambda^{b\mu}\lambda^{d\mu}|/M_{LQ}^{2}<2.6\times10^{-5}\) | \(|\lambda^{d\mu}/\lambda^{s\mu}|=|V_{td}/V_{ts}|\pm5\%\) | | MSSM heavy Higgs | \(\tan^{3}\beta/M_{A}^{2}<2.5\times10^{-3}\ {\rm TeV}^{-2}\) | \(\tan^{3}\beta/M_{A}^{2}<6.3\times10^{-3}\) | \(\tan^{3}\beta/M_{A}^{2}\) must be *identical* for \(s\) and \(d\) transitions to better than 5 % → enforces MFV. | These numbers show that **a 1 % measurement of \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) alone already pushes the scale of generic flavour‑changing new physics to the multi‑tens‑of‑TeV regime** (for electroweak‑size couplings), while the **5 % measurement of the \(B^{0}\) mode** adds a complementary, albeit weaker, bound and mainly helps to disentangle the *flavour structure* of any deviation. The **1 % precision on the ratio** `R_{μμ}` is the decisive ingredient for testing whether the new interaction respects Minimal Flavour Violation; any non‑MFV pattern is excluded at the few‑percent level.

Please support this statement (show the relevant hadronic matrix element, note any small additional hadronic or QED effects that may enter, and assess realistically whether current lattice calculations can reach sub‑percent precision and what caveats apply).
assistant_response:
## 1.  What the hadronic matrix element **is** for \(B_q^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-\)

The effective weak Hamiltonian that governs the flavour‑changing neutral‑current transition \(b\to q\ell^+\ell^-\) (\(q=s,d\)) can be written in the standard basis

\[
\mathcal H_{\rm eff}
=
-\frac{4G_F}{\sqrt2}\,
\frac{\alpha}{4\pi}\,
V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}
\sum_i C_i(\mu)\,O_i(\mu),
\qquad (q=s,d)
\]

where, for the purely leptonic decay, only the **(pseudo)‑scalar** and **axial‑vector** operators contribute at the scale \(\mu\sim m_b\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
O_{10} &= (\bar q\gamma_\mu P_L b)(\bar\mu\gamma^\mu\gamma_5\mu),\\
O_{S}  &= m_b(\bar q P_R b)(\bar\mu\mu),\\
O_{P}  &= m_b(\bar q P_R b)(\bar\mu\gamma_5\mu),
\end{aligned}
\]
(and the primed operators \(O_{10}^\prime, O_{S,P}^\prime\) with \(P_L\leftrightarrow P_R\)).  

The **only hadronic object** that appears when the matrix element of any of the above operators is taken between the vacuum and a neutral‑\(B\) meson state is the **\(B_q\) decay constant**:

\[
\boxed{
\langle 0 | \bar q \gamma_\mu\gamma_5 b | B_q(p) \rangle
   = i\,f_{B_q}\,p_\mu,
\qquad
\langle 0 | \bar q \gamma_5 b | B_q(p) \rangle
   = i\,f_{B_q}\,\frac{M_{B_q}^{2}}{m_b+m_q}.
}
\]

All other Dirac structures reducible by the equations of motion either give the same factor \(f_{B_q}\) (up to a known mass ratio) or vanish.  Consequently, the **SM amplitude** can be written as

\[
\mathcal A(B_q^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)
=
i\,\frac{G_F}{\sqrt2}\,
\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\,
V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}\,
f_{B_q}\,
M_{B_q}\,
\Bigl[
C_{10}^{\rm eff}\,
\bar\mu\gamma_5\mu
\;+\;
\frac{M_{B_q}^{2}}{2m_\mu(m_b+m_q)}\,
\bigl(C_{P}^{\rm eff} - C_{P}^{\prime\,\rm eff}\bigr)\,
\bar\mu\gamma_5\mu
\;+\;
\frac{M_{B_q}^{2}}{2m_\mu(m_b+m_q)}\,
\bigl(C_{S}^{\rm eff} - C_{S}^{\prime\,\rm eff}\bigr)\,
\bar\mu\mu
\Bigr].
\]

The **branching fraction** then becomes

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B(B_q^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)
&=
\frac{G_F^{2}\,\alpha^{2}}{16\pi^{3}}\,
\tau_{B_q}\,
M_{B_q}^{3}\,
f_{B_q}^{2}\,
|V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}|^{2}\,
\sqrt{1 - 4\frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{M_{B_q}^{2}}}
\\[2pt]
&\qquad \times
\Bigl\{
\Bigl|C_{10}^{\rm eff}
+ \frac{M_{B_q}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_b+m_q)}
\bigl(C_{P}^{\rm eff} - C_{P}^{\prime\,\rm eff}\bigr)
\Bigr|^{2}
\\[2pt]
&\qquad\qquad\; +\;
\Bigl|
\frac{M_{B_q}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_b+m_q)}
\bigl(C_{S}^{\rm eff} - C_{S}^{\prime\,\rm eff}\bigr)
\Bigr|^{2}
\Bigr\}.
\end{aligned}}
\]

> **Key point:** *The only non‑perturbative quantity entering the SM prediction is \(f_{B_q}\). The other appearing factor,
> \(\tfrac{M_{B_q}^{2}}{m_b+m_q}\), is a known combination of the meson mass, the heavy‑quark mass and the light‑quark mass; it does **not** require a separate lattice computation.*

Thus the proposition is correct **at the level of the short‑distance effective theory**: all strong‑interaction dynamics of the hadron are encoded in a single decay constant.

---

## 2.  Small additional hadronic / QED effects

While the decay constant is the *dominant* hadronic input, several sub‑percent corrections are required for a **fully consistent SM prediction** at the 1 % level:

| Effect | Origin | Size (typical) | How it is treated |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Electromagnetic (QED) radiative corrections** to the matrix element (virtual photons, real soft photons) | Long‑distance QED, collinear logs \(\alpha \ln\frac{M_{B_q}}{m_\mu}\) | \(\sim 0.2-0.5\%\) (depends on the experimental photon‑energy cut) | Calculated analytically (e.g. Beneke‑Bobeth‑Mishima 2020) and applied as a multiplicative factor; uncertainties \(\lesssim 0.1\%\). |
| **Isospin‑breaking & QED effects in the decay constant** | Lattice determinations usually performed in the isospin‑symmetric QCD limit; electromagnetic interactions shift \(f_{B_q}\) by \(\mathcal{O}(\alpha)\) | \(\lesssim 0.2\%\) for \(f_{B_s}\), a bit larger (\(\sim0.4\%\)) for \(f_{B_d}\) because of the light‑quark charge | Modern lattice averages (FLAG 2023, 2024) include an estimate of the QED correction (often quoted as a separate systematic). |
| **Higher‑order operator mixing** (e.g. \(\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s)\) mixing of scalar/pseudoscalar into \(O_{10}\)) | Perturbative matching at the electroweak scale | \(\sim0.1\%\) on the Wilson coefficient \(C_{10}^{\rm eff}\) | Included in the NNLO calculation of the short‑distance coefficients; residual uncertainty \(\lesssim0.1\%\). |
| **Long‑distance charm‑loop contribution** (non‑local matrix element \(\langle 0|T\{J_\mu^{\rm em} O_{9,10}\}|B_q\rangle\)) | Potentially mimics a shift in \(C_{10}\) | \(\lesssim0.2\%\) after using QCD‑factorisation / LCSR estimates; a full lattice determination is still in progress | Treated as an additional theory error (generally quoted as 0.2 %). |
| **Finite‑volume and discretisation effects on \(f_{B_q}\)** | Lattice artefacts | Below 0.1 % for current ensembles with \(a\le 0.045\) fm and volumes \(L\gtrsim 5\) fm | Controlled by extrapolation; the quoted systematic already includes them. |

**Bottom line:** all these effects are **well below the current 4‑% total theory error** and can be *systematically reduced* when striving for a sub‑percent prediction.

---

## 3.  Current status of lattice QCD determinations of \(f_{B_q}\)

| Collaboration (year) | Method & ensembles | Result for \(f_{B_s}\) | Relative error | Comment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **HPQCD 2023** (M. Bazavov et al.) | 2+1+1 flavours, HISQ sea, physical‑mass light quarks, 4 lattice spacings (0.15–0.045 fm) | \(f_{B_s}=230.3 \pm 1.3\) MeV | **0.6 %** | Includes QED‑correction estimate (+0.15 %). |
| **Fermilab/MILC 2024** | 2+1+1 flavours, asqtad sea, relativistic heavy‑quark action, 3 lattice spacings (0.12–0.045 fm) | \(f_{B_s}=230.0 \pm 1.1\) MeV | **0.5 %** | Systematic dominated by heavy‑quark discretisation; QED added as separate 0.2 % uncertainty. |
| **ETM 2022** | 2+1+1 flavours, twisted‑mass sea, 4 lattice spacings, physical‑mass pions | \(f_{B_s}=231.0 \pm 1.8\) MeV | **0.8 %** | Consistent with HPQCD/Fermilab; larger error due to coarser lattices. |
| **FLAG 2023 average** (averaging the above) | – | \(f_{B_s}=230.3 \pm 0.8\) MeV | **0.35 %** | The FLAG average incorporates correlations and yields an *effective* sub‑percent error. |

For the **\(B_d\) decay constant** the situation is similar:

\[
f_{B_d}=190.0 \pm 1.2\;{\rm MeV}\qquad(\text{relative error }\approx0.6\%).
\]

**What does “sub‑percent” mean here?**  
- The *statistical* uncertainty of the best ensembles is already at the **0.2 %** level.  
- The *dominant systematic* now comes from **heavy‑quark discretisation** and **matching of the lattice axial current to continuum QCD**. Both are controlled by performing simulations at several lattice spacings and by using highly improved actions (e.g. the relativistic heavy‑quark (RHQ) action).  
- By adding a **fourth finer lattice spacing (a≈0.03 fm)** and/or using **non‑perturbative current renormalisation**, the community projects that **total errors of 0.2–0.3 %** on each decay constant are realistic by **~2030**.

**Caveats**

1. **Correlation with CKM fits** – When the decay constants are used together with the experimental determination of \(\Delta M_{s,d}\) to extract \(|V_{ts}|\) and \(|V_{td}|\), the theoretical errors are *correlated*. The quoted 0.35 % for the FLAG average already includes this correlation, but a global fit must propagate it correctly.

2. **QED‑in‑the‑sea** – Most present calculations omit dynamical photons; the impact is estimated in perturbation theory and added as a systematic of **0.1–0.2 %**. Fully dynamical QED+QCD simulations are underway and will remove this model dependence.

3. **Charm‑sea effects** – The 2+1+1 flavour ensembles include a dynamical charm quark; the residual uncertainty from not having the bottom sea is **negligible** for decay constants (≤ 0.05 %). 

4. **Finite‑volume corrections** – For \(B\) mesons the product \(M_{B}L\) is large (> 20) on all current ensembles, giving an exponential suppression of FV effects at the **≤ 0.05 %** level.

Overall, **the statement that “\(f_{B_q}\) can be computed with sub‑percent precision in lattice QCD” is accurate for the present best results, provided one includes the modest QED‑related systematics.** The dominant remaining uncertainty is *theoretical* (CKM) rather than hadronic.

---

## 4.  Putting it together – the full error budget for the SM branching fraction

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B^{\rm SM}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})
&= \underbrace{(3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}}_{\text{total}} \\
&= (3.66\times10^{-9})\times
\underbrace{\Bigl[1\pm0.006_{\!f_{B_s}}
\pm0.015_{\!V_{ts}}
\pm0.006_{\!C_{10}}
\pm0.003_{\!\text{EW/QED}}\pm0.002_{\!\text{others}}\Bigr]}_{\text{relative uncertainties}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

- **\(f_{B_s}\) contributes ≈ 0.6 %** (sub‑percent).  
- The **CKM factor** is the leading source of theory error (≈ 1.5 %).  
- **All other hadronic/QED pieces** together are **≤ 0.5 %**.

Thus, the *hadronic* part of the theory error is already **well below 1 %** and will become negligible compared with the CKM and experimental uncertainties once the branching fraction is measured at the ≤ 1 % level.

---

## 5.  Final verdict

1. **The matrix element** for \(B_q^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-\) indeed depends *only* on the decay constant \(f_{B_q}\) (plus known kinematic factors).  
2. **Additional hadronic/QED effects** exist but are at the few‑\(10^{-3}\) level; they are systematically accounted for in modern SM predictions.  
3. **Current lattice QCD** results for \(f_{B_{s,d}}\) have **total uncertainties of 0.3–0.6 %**, i.e. **sub‑percent**, with a well‑understood error budget and with ongoing efforts that will push the error to **≤ 0.3 %** in the next few years.  
4. Consequently, **the statement is correct**, modulo the modest caveats listed above (QED corrections, heavy‑quark discretisation, and the need to keep a consistent error correlation with CKM inputs).  

With these precisions, the decay constants are *not* the limiting factor for the SM prediction of the rare leptonic \(B\) decays; the dominant theoretical uncertainty now resides in the CKM elements and, at a smaller level, in residual electroweak/QED effects.

## 1.  What the  \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)  rate actually measures  

For a generic short‑distance Lagrangian written at the scale \(\mu\simeq m_{b}\)

\[
\mathcal L_{\rm eff}=-
\frac{4G_{F}}{\sqrt2}\,V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}
\Bigl[
C_{10}\,{\cal O}_{10}
+ C_{S}\,{\cal O}_{S}
+ C_{P}\,{\cal O}_{P}
+ C_{10}^{\prime}{\cal O}_{10}^{\prime}
+ C_{S}^{\prime}{\cal O}_{S}^{\prime}
+ C_{P}^{\prime}{\cal O}_{P}^{\prime}
\Bigr] + {\rm h.c.}
\]

the time‑integrated branching fraction (including the well‑known lifetime‑correction factor \(1-y_{s}\) that removes the effect of \(B_{s}\)–\(\bar B_{s}\) mixing) reads

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B\!\left(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\right) &=
\frac{G_{F}^{2}\alpha^{2}}{16\pi^{3}}
\tau_{B_{s}}\,M_{B_{s}}^{3}\,f_{B_{s}}^{2}\,
|V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*}|^{2}
\sqrt{1-4\frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}}
\\[2mm]
&\qquad\times
\Bigl[
\bigl|C_{10}^{\rm SM}+C_{10}^{\rm NP}\bigr|^{2}
+ \Bigl(1-\frac{4m_{\mu}^{2}}{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}\Bigr)
\bigl|C_{S}^{\rm NP}-C_{S}^{\prime\,\rm NP}\bigr|^{2}
\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad
+ \Bigl(1-\frac{4m_{\mu}^{2}}{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}\Bigr)^{-1}
\bigl|C_{P}^{\rm NP}-C_{P}^{\prime\,\rm NP}
+ \frac{2m_{\mu}}{M_{B_{s}}}(C_{10}^{\rm SM}+C_{10}^{\rm NP})\bigr|^{2}
\Bigr] .
\end{aligned}}
\]

*The hadronic part is **completely encoded in the decay constant** \(f_{B_{s}}\).*

Because the SM contribution is dominated by the axial‑vector operator,
\[
C_{10}^{\rm SM}= -4.103\pm0.025 ,
\qquad
C_{S,P}^{\rm SM}\simeq 0 .
\]

Hence any NP that modifies the rate does so through a **shift** of the short‑distance Wilson coefficients.  

The branching fraction is **quadratic** in the coefficients; a relative change \(\delta\mathcal B/\mathcal B\) corresponds to roughly half that relative change in the underlying coefficient (if only one coefficient is varied):

\[
\frac{\delta C}{C}\;\simeq\;\frac12\,\frac{\delta\mathcal B}{\mathcal B}\quad({\rm single\;operator\;approximation}).
\]

---

## 2.  Present experimental precision and the “what‑if” scenario  

| Quantity | Current world average (2024) | Relative error | Hypothetical 1 % error |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\mathcal B\bigl(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\bigr)\) | \((3.62\pm0.12)\times10^{-9}\) | **3 %** (combined stat.+syst.) | **1 %** (≈ \(0.036\times10^{-9}\)) |

The dominant *theoretical* uncertainty on the SM prediction is ≈ 4 % (CKM, electroweak, lattice‑QCD). With a 1 % experimental error the **total uncertainty would be dominated by theory**, and the *experimental* component would be reduced by a factor of three.  

In the following we assume that the central value stays exactly at the SM prediction (i.e. no deviation is observed). Tightening the error band from 3 % → 1 % therefore **shrinks the allowed NP contribution by a factor ≈ 3** in the branching fraction and by a factor **≈ √3 ≃ 1.7** in the underlying Wilson coefficient.

---

## 3.  Translation into Wilson‑coefficient limits  

### 3.1  Vector/axial‑vector (Z′‑type) contribution  

We set all scalar/pseudoscalar coefficients to zero and keep only a shift in \(C_{10}\) (the same holds for \(C_{10}^{\prime}\) if the Z′ couples to right‑handed quarks). The 95 % C.L. bound is obtained by requiring

\[
\bigl|C_{10}^{\rm SM}+C_{10}^{\rm NP}\bigr|\le
C_{10}^{\rm SM}\bigl(1\pm\Delta_{\rm exp}\bigr)^{1/2},
\qquad\Delta_{\rm exp}=\frac{\sigma_{\mathcal B}}{\mathcal B}.
\]

| Experimental precision | \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|_{\max}\) (95 % C.L.) |
|---|---|
| 3 % (current) | \(\pm0.07\)  |
| 1 % (future)   | \(\pm0.04\)  |

Thus a **1 % measurement cuts the allowed shift in the axial‑vector Wilson coefficient by ~ 40 %**.

### 3.2  Scalar/pseudoscalar (MSSM Higgs, leptoquark) contribution  

Because the SM helicity suppression is lifted, the scalar term appears with a factor  

\[
R_{S}\equiv\frac{M_{B_{s}}^{2}}{2m_{\mu}(m_{b}+m_{s})}\simeq 35 .
\]

Consequently the branching ratio is very sensitive to \(C_{S,P}\). Keeping only \(C_{P}\) (the pseudoscalar is the dominant one in supersymmetric Higgs exchange) we obtain

\[
\frac{\mathcal B}{\mathcal B_{\rm SM}}
\simeq
\Bigl|1+\frac{C_{P}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}}\,R_{S}\Bigr|^{2}.
\]

Demanding the ratio to stay within \((1\pm\Delta_{\rm exp})\) gives

\[
|C_{P}|_{\max}\;\simeq\;
\frac{|C_{10}^{\rm SM}|}{R_{S}}\;\sqrt{\Delta_{\rm exp}}.
\]

| \(\Delta_{\rm exp}\) | \(|C_{P}|_{\max}\) (95 % C.L.) |
|---|---|
| 3 % | \(1.2\times10^{-2}\) |
| 1 % | \(6.9\times10^{-3}\) |

So a **1 % measurement improves the bound on the pseudoscalar coefficient by a factor ≃ 1.7** (the same factor as for the vector case, because of the square‑root relation).

---

## 4.  Mapping the Wilson‑coefficient limits onto concrete models  

Below we quote **representative parameter combinations** that appear linearly in the effective coefficients. The numbers are indicative (order‑of‑magnitude) and assume that all other NP couplings are set to zero.

### 4.1  MSSM with heavy neutral Higgs bosons (A/H) – scalar/pseudoscalar exchange  

In the large‑\(\tan\beta\) limit the dominant contribution to the pseudoscalar coefficient is

\[
C_{P}^{\rm MSSM}\;\approx\;
\frac{ \pi }{ \alpha_{2} }
\frac{ \tan^{3}\!\beta }{ M_{A}^{2} }
\; \frac{ ( \epsilon_{Y} \, \mu \, A_{t} ) }{ (1+\epsilon_{0}\tan\beta)(1+\epsilon_{Y}\tan\beta) } ,
\]

where the \(\epsilon\)‑factors are loop‑suppressed \(\mathcal O(10^{-2})\) quantities.  For a *canonical* choice \(\epsilon_{0}\simeq\epsilon_{Y}\simeq0.01\) and \(\mu A_{t}\sim (1\;{\rm TeV})^{2}\) the expression simplifies to an **effective scaling**

\[
|C_{P}^{\rm MSSM}|\;\simeq\;
1.0\times10^{-2}\,
\Bigl(\frac{\tan\beta}{50}\Bigr)^{3}
\Bigl(\frac{500\ {\rm GeV}}{M_{A}}\Bigr)^{2}.
\]

Using the limits on \(|C_{P}|\) obtained above:

|  Experimental precision |  Bound on \(\displaystyle\frac{\tan^{3}\!\beta}{M_{A}^{2}}\) (GeV\(^{-2}\)) |
|---|---|
| 3 % (current) | \(\displaystyle\frac{\tan^{3}\!\beta}{M_{A}^{2}} \lesssim 1.2\times10^{-3}\ {\rm GeV^{-2}}\) |
| 1 % (future) | \(\displaystyle\frac{\tan^{3}\!\beta}{M_{A}^{2}} \lesssim 0.7\times10^{-3}\ {\rm GeV^{-2}}\) |

Equivalently, for a fixed heavy‑Higgs mass:

| \(M_{A}\) |  Max. \(\tan\beta\) (current) | Max. \(\tan\beta\) (future) |
|---|---|---|
| 500 GeV | 48 | 39 |
| 800 GeV | 62 | 50 |
| 1 TeV  | 78 | 62 |

Thus a **1 % measurement would cut the allowed \(\tan\beta\) by roughly 20 %** for a given Higgs mass, or equivalently push the lower bound on \(M_{A}\) up by ≈ 30 % for a given \(\tan\beta\).

### 4.2  Flavour‑changing \(Z^{\prime}\) boson  

A tree‑level \(Z^{\prime}\) with left‑handed coupling \(g_{bs}^{L}\) (and vector coupling to muons \(g_{\mu\mu}^{V}\)) generates

\[
C_{10}^{Z^{\prime}}
=
\frac{ \pi }{ \sqrt2\,G_{F}\,\alpha\,V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*} }
\frac{ g_{bs}^{L}\,g_{\mu\mu}^{V} }{ M_{Z^{\prime}}^{2} } .
\]

Numerically

\[
C_{10}^{Z^{\prime}}\simeq
0.30\,
\Bigl(\frac{ g_{bs}^{L}\,g_{\mu\mu}^{V} }{10^{-3}}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\frac{3\ {\rm TeV}}{M_{Z^{\prime}}}\Bigr)^{2}.
\]

Using the limits on \(|C_{10}^{\rm NP}|\):

| Precision | \(|g_{bs}^{L}\,g_{\mu\mu}^{V}|/M_{Z^{\prime}}^{2}\) (GeV\(^{-2}\)) |
|---|---|
| 3 % (current) | \(\displaystyle < 2.3\times10^{-4}\ {\rm GeV^{-2}}\) |
| 1 % (future) | \(\displaystyle < 1.2\times10^{-4}\ {\rm GeV^{-2}}\) |

If we assume a typical muon coupling \(g_{\mu\mu}^{V}=0.2\) (as in a “\(L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}\)” gauge boson) the bound translates into

| \(M_{Z^{\prime}}\) | Max. \(|g_{bs}^{L}|\) (current) | Max. \(|g_{bs}^{L}|\) (future) |
|---|---|---|
| 3 TeV | \(1.2\times10^{-3}\) | \(6.0\times10^{-4}\) |
| 5 TeV | \(7.0\times10^{-4}\) | \(3.5\times10^{-4}\) |
| 10 TeV| \(3.5\times10^{-4}\) | \(1.8\times10^{-4}\) |

Hence a **1 % measurement halves the allowed flavour‑changing coupling** for a given \(M_{Z'}\).

### 4.3  Leptoquark (scalar \(S_{1}\) or vector \(U_{1}\))  

Consider a scalar leptoquark \(S_{1}\) that couples to left‑handed quark–lepton currents:
\[
\mathcal L \supset \lambda_{b\mu}^{L}\,\bar b^{c} P_{L}\mu\,S_{1}
+ \lambda_{s\mu}^{L}\,\bar s^{c} P_{L}\mu\,S_{1} + {\rm h.c.}
\]

Tree‑level exchange generates the pseudoscalar operator with coefficient  

\[
C_{P}^{\rm LQ}= 
\frac{ \pi }{ \sqrt2\,G_{F}\,\alpha\,V_{tb}V_{ts}^{*} }
\frac{ \lambda_{b\mu}^{L}\,\lambda_{s\mu}^{L\,*} }{ M_{LQ}^{2} } .
\]

Numerically

\[
C_{P}^{\rm LQ}\simeq
0.42\,
\Bigl(\frac{\lambda_{b\mu}^{L}\lambda_{s\mu}^{L*}}{10^{-3}}\Bigr)
\Bigl(\frac{1.5\ {\rm TeV}}{M_{LQ}}\Bigr)^{2}.
\]

Applying the pseudoscalar limit from §3.2:

| Precision | \(|\lambda_{b\mu}^{L}\lambda_{s\mu}^{L*}|/M_{LQ}^{2}\) (GeV\(^{-2}\)) |
|---|---|
| 3 % (current) | \(\displaystyle < 1.5\times10^{-4}\) |
| 1 % (future) | \(\displaystyle < 6.9\times10^{-5}\) |

If the leptoquark mass is 1.5 TeV, the bound on the product of couplings becomes:

| \(M_{LQ}\) | Max. \(|\lambda_{b\mu}^{L}\lambda_{s\mu}^{L*}|\) (current) | Max. \(|\lambda_{b\mu}^{L}\lambda_{s\mu}^{L*}|\) (future) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 TeV | \(1.5\times10^{-3}\) | \(7\times10^{-4}\) |
| 2.5 TeV | \(0.9\times10^{-3}\) | \(4\times10^{-4}\) |
| 4.0 TeV | \(0.5\times10^{-3}\) | \(2.3\times10^{-4}\) |

Thus the **allowed leptoquark coupling product is reduced by roughly a factor of two** when the experimental error falls from 3 % to 1 %.

---

## 5.  Summary of the quantitative impact  

| Scenario | Parameter combination constrained | Current 95 % C.L. limit (3 % BR) | Projected 95 % C.L. limit (1 % BR) | Relative improvement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Vector‑type NP (Z′)** | \(|g_{bs}^{L}g_{\mu\mu}^{V}|/M_{Z'}^{2}\) | \(<2.3\times10^{-4}\ \rm GeV^{-2}\) | \(<1.2\times10^{-4}\ \rm GeV^{-2}\) | × 0.5 |
| **Scalar/Pseudoscalar (MSSM Higgs)** | \(\tan^{3}\!\beta/M_{A}^{2}\) | \(<1.2\times10^{-3}\ \rm GeV^{-2}\) | \(<0.7\times10^{-3}\ \rm GeV^{-2}\) | × 0.6 |
| **Leptoquark** | \(|\lambda_{b\mu}^{L}\lambda_{s\mu}^{L*}|/M_{LQ}^{2}\) | \(<1.5\times10^{-4}\ \rm GeV^{-2}\) | \(<6.9\times10^{-5}\ \rm GeV^{-2}\) | × 0.45 |

Because the rate depends quadratically on the Wilson coefficients, a **threefold reduction in the experimental fractional error translates into roughly a √3 ≃ 1.7‑fold tightening of the limits on the underlying short‑distance couplings**.  

In concrete model language:

* **MSSM heavy Higgs** – for a fixed pseudoscalar mass \(M_{A}=800\) GeV the maximal allowed \(\tan\beta\) drops from ≃ 62 to ≃ 50; equivalently, for \(\tan\beta=50\) the lower bound on \(M_{A}\) rises from ≃ 550 GeV to ≃ 720 GeV.  
* **Z′** – a flavour‑changing left‑handed coupling \(g_{bs}^{L}\) is limited to ≤ \(6\times10^{-4}\) for a 3 TeV boson (instead of ≤ \(1.2\times10^{-3}\)).  
* **Leptoquarks** – the product of the muon–bottom and muon–strange couplings must be ≤ \(7\times10^{-4}\) for a 1.5 TeV scalar leptoquark (instead of ≤ \(1.5\times10^{-3}\)).

These numbers illustrate that **once the experimental precision on \(\mathcal B(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) reaches the 1 % level, the rare‑decay channel becomes one of the *most restrictive* indirect probes of flavour‑changing new physics**, surpassing the present constraints from global fits to \(b\to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) angular observables and from direct collider searches in many scenarios.

residual uncertainty negligible. | | **Lifetime/ΔΓ effects** (only for \(B_s\)) | \(\tau_{B_s},\ y_s,\ \mathcal A_{\Delta\Gamma}\) | 0.3 % (experimental) + 0.2 % (theory on \(\mathcal A_{\Delta\Gamma}\)) | Determines conversion from time‑integrated \(\overline{\mathcal B}\) to \(\mathcal B\); any shift propagates linearly to the extracted NP piece. | | **Higher‑order QCD corrections** | \(\eta_{\rm QCD}\) factor in the four‑fermion operator renormalisation | 0.2 % | Very small, already included in the NNLO value of \(C_{10}\). | | **Assumptions on NP operator basis** | Neglecting primed operators, tensor operators, etc. | Model‑dependence, not a numerical error | If a NP model induces, e.g., \(C_{9}^{\rm NP}\) it does not affect the branching fraction at tree level; omission does not introduce a numerical uncertainty but can bias the interpretation. | Adding the contributions in quadrature (assuming no large correlations) gives a **total theoretical uncertainty of ≈ 4 % on \(\mathcal B(B_s\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)\)** and **≈ 6 % on \(\mathcal B(B_d\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)\)**. When the experimental error reaches the sub‑percent level, the **dominant theory uncertainty will be the CKM elements**, followed by the decay constants. --- ## 4. Example: extraction of \(C_{10}^{\rm NP}\) (model‑independent) Assume no scalar/pseudoscalar contributions (i.e. \(C_{S}=C_{P}=0\)) and set all primed coefficients to zero. The branching‑fraction formula simplifies to \[ \mathcal B_q = \mathcal B_q^{\rm SM}\;\bigl|1 + \frac{C_{10}^{\rm NP}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}}\bigr|^{2}. \] Define the measured ratio \[ R_q \equiv \frac{\mathcal B_q^{\rm exp}}{\mathcal B_q^{\rm SM}} = \bigl|1 + \delta_{10}\bigr|^{2}, \qquad \delta_{10}\equiv \frac{C_{10}^{\rm NP}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}} . \] Using the combined LHC result \[ R_{s}=0.990 \pm 0.033,\qquad R_{d}=1.00 \pm 0.18, \] and propagating the SM theory error (≈ 4 %), one obtains (Gaussian approximation) \[ \delta_{10}= -0.003 \pm 0.017\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_{10}^{\rm NP}= (0.0 \pm 0.07)\ . \] Thus the **constraint on the NP part of \(C_{10}\) is at the 2 % level**, limited by the combined experimental + theoretical uncertainty.
