assistant_response:
## 1  Why the electron mode is hard and what we have to fight

| Challenge | Origin | Typical size (≈ LHC) |
|-----------|--------|----------------------|
| **Very low signal yield** – SM branching fraction \( \sim 10^{-13} \) | Loop + helicity suppression | < 1 event even with the full HL‑LHC statistics |
| **Bremsstrahlung in the detector material** | Electrons radiate photons in the VELO, tracker, and especially in the support structures before the magnet | Momentum resolution for a 5 GeV/c electron worsens from \(\sigma_p/p\sim0.5\%\) (muon) to \( \sim 2–3\% \); invariant‑mass tail extends down to \(\sim 4\) GeV/c\(^2\) |
| **Large combinatorial background** | Random pairs of tracks that survive electron‑ID cuts; also hadrons mis‑identified as electrons (π, K) | After tight PID, still \(\mathcal O(10^{5})\) candidates per fb\(^{-1}\) in the \(B\)‑mass window |
| **Peaking backgrounds from partially‑reconstructed decays** | e.g. \(B\to K^{(*)}e^+e^-\) where the hadron is missed, or \(B\to h^+h^-\) with both hadrons mis‑ID’d as electrons | Produce a narrow peak under the signal if the missing particle is soft (often < 200 MeV) |
| **Trigger bandwidth** | Low‑\(p_T\) electrons are abundant in minimum‑bias events but the trigger must keep the rate manageable | Electron‑trigger thresholds are typically 2–3 GeV (LHCb) or 10 GeV (ATLAS/CMS) – many signal electrons fall below these |

Because the expected signal is essentially zero in the SM, **the goal of every analysis is to push the background down to the level where a single observed candidate would already be statistically significant**. Below is a map of the concrete tools that the four experiments currently employ, followed by the upgrades that will make the biggest impact.

---

## 2  Current experimental strategies

### 2.1  Common analysis chain (used by LHCb, ATLAS, CMS)

| Step | What is done | LHCb implementation | ATLAS/CMS implementation |
|------|--------------|---------------------|--------------------------|
| **Online trigger (L0/HLT1)** | Require at least one high‑\(p_T\) electron (or e‑γ cluster) with loose ID, plus a displaced‑vertex signature (large impact parameter or secondary‑vertex fit). | LHCb L0: \(E_T(e) > 2.5\) GeV, HLT1: 2‑track secondary vertex with at least one electron ID. | Single‑electron trigger \(p_T > 10\) GeV + displaced‑track requirement in the HLT. |
| **Offline pre‑selection** | Tighten the impact‑parameter significance, flight‑distance significance, and vertex‑fit χ²; require the two tracks to form a good‑quality vertex and to point back to the primary vertex. | IP\(_\chi^2\) > 25, SV χ²/ndf < 5, pointing angle > 0.999. | Similar cuts on transverse impact parameter and 3‑D flight distance; use the “track‑jet” b‑tagger to enrich b‑hadron content. |
| **Electron identification (PID)** | Combine information from the RICH (LHCb), ECAL shower shape, HCAL veto, and track‑matching. | RICH likelihood \( \Delta \ln \mathcal L(e-\pi) > 5\), ECAL E/p within 0.9–1.1, HCAL energy < 0.1 E. | ATLAS/CMS use a multivariate electron ID (likelihood or BDT) that includes calorimeter shower shapes, transition‑radiation (ATLAS), inner‑tracker dE/dx, and track‑cluster matching. |
| **Bremsstrahlung recovery** | Search for photons in a narrow cone around the track, add them back to the electron momentum (“recovery”) | LHCb: photons reconstructed in ECAL and SPD are attached if ΔR < 0.05. | ATLAS/CMS: use “Gaussian‑Sum‑Filter” (GSF) tracking (CMS) or “dynamic clustering” (ATLAS) to associate bremsstrahlung clusters; improve mass resolution to ~30 MeV. |
| **Multivariate background suppression** | Train a Boosted Decision Tree (BDT) or Deep Neural Network on simulated signal vs. data sidebands. Input variables: decay‑time, isolation (track‑multiplicity in a cone), PID scores, kinematic variables (p\(_T\) of the B, pointing angle). | LHCb BDT uses 12 variables, optimized on 2015–2018 data, achieving a background rejection factor of ~10⁴ at 40 % signal efficiency. | CMS uses a Gradient‑Boosted classifier with 15 inputs; ATLAS uses a likelihood ratio built from similar observables. |
| **Mass window fit** | Perform an unbinned maximum‑likelihood fit to the invariant mass distribution. Signal shape is a Crystal‑Ball (core Gaussian + low‑mass tail for unrecovered bremsstrahlung). Background is modelled with an exponential (combinatorial) plus possible peaking components. | Signal resolution after recovery: σ_m ≈ 25 MeV (LHCb). Peaking background from \(B\to K e^+e^-\) is modelled with a dedicated MC template and constrained by control channels. | CMS mass resolution ≈ 30 MeV, ATLAS ≈ 35 MeV; peaking backgrounds constrained using control regions in data (e.g. by inverting a kaon‑veto). |
| **Normalization** | Use a high‑rate, topologically similar channel (e.g. \(B^+\to J/\psi(\mu\mu)K^+\) or \(B_s\to J/\psi(\mu\mu)\phi\)) to translate a yield limit into a branching‑fraction limit, canceling production‑cross‑section and luminosity uncertainties. | LHCb normalises to \(B^+\to J/\psi K^+\) (BR known to 3 %). | ATLAS/CMS normalise to \(B^0\to K^{*}\mu\mu\) for which the acceptance is similar. |
| **Cross‑checks & control samples** | Validate electron PID and bremsstrahlung recovery with \(J/\psi\to e^+e^-\) and \(\Upsilon\to e^+e^-\) samples; validate combinatorial background shape with high‑mass sidebands; validate peaking background with \(B\to K e^+e^-\) after removing the kaon. | LHCb uses a “tag‑and‑probe” method on \(J/\psi\) for PID efficiency; systematic uncertainties on the efficiency are at the 2 % level. | CMS uses Z→ee events to calibrate the ECAL energy scale and bremsstrahlung recovery efficiency. |

### 2.2  Belle II specific tactics (e⁺e⁻ environment)

| Feature | How Belle II exploits it |
|---------|--------------------------|
| **Clean initial state & full‑event reconstruction** | Use the “Full‑Event‑Interpretation” (FEI) algorithm to reconstruct the companion \(B\) (tag side) in hadronic or semileptonic modes. This gives a precise knowledge of the signal‑B momentum, allowing a missing‑mass constraint that sharpens the invariant‑mass resolution even with unrecovered bremsstrahlung. |
| **Beam‑energy constraint** | The beam‑energy‑substituted mass \(m_{\rm ES} = \sqrt{E_{\rm beam}^2 - |\vec p_B|^2}\) and the energy difference \(\Delta E\) are used in a 2‑D fit. | Improves background discrimination dramatically; combinatorial background falls exponentially in \(m_{\rm ES}\). |
| **Excellent electromagnetic calorimetry** | Belle II’s CsI(Tl) crystal ECAL has an energy resolution of \(\sigma_E/E \simeq 1.6\%/\sqrt{E(\text{GeV})}\), allowing a more complete bremsstrahlung recovery (photons down to 20 MeV are reconstructed). | Mass resolution after recovery ∼ 15 MeV, better than LHC experiments. |
| **Particle‑ID system (TOP, ARICH)** | Provides clean \(e/\pi\) separation down to a few hundred MeV, reducing hadron‑mis‑ID background to the \(10^{-5}\) level. |
| **Continuum background suppression** | Use event‑shape variables (thrust, Fox‑Wolfram moments) and a BDT to suppress \(e^+e^-\to q\bar q\) (q = u,d,s,c) that produce fake B candidates. | Reduces the combinatorial yield by a factor ∼ 50 while keeping > 60 % of signal. |
| **Normalization** | Use \(B^+\to J/\psi(\ell\ell)K^+\) or \(B^0\to D^-\pi^+\) with the same tagging method to cancel systematic uncertainties. | Systematics on the absolute efficiency are at the 3 % level. |

Current Belle II limits (2024, 190 fb\(^{-1}\)) are

\[
\mathcal B(B_s\to e^+e^-)< 2.5\times10^{-8},\qquad
\mathcal B(B_d\to e^+e^-)< 1.1\times10^{-8},
\]

still far above the LHC limits but with a very clean systematic environment.

---

## 3  Which detector upgrades will give the biggest gain?

| Upgrade | Experiment | What it improves for \(B\to e^+e^-\) | Expected impact on the limit (order‑of‑magnitude) |
|---------|-----------|--------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| **Vertex‑Locator (VELO) material reduction** | LHCb Upgrade II (2029‑2035) | Less bremsstrahlung before the first measurement point → lower low‑mass tail, better mass resolution (σ_m down from 25 MeV to ≈ 18 MeV). | Improves signal‑to‑background by ≈ 30 % (background under the signal peak shrinks). |
| **High‑granularity, low‑noise ECAL** | LHCb Upgrade II & CMS Phase‑2 (HL‑LHC) | Finer clustering → higher bremsstrahlung‑photon recovery efficiency (up to 90 % vs 70 %). | Increases effective signal efficiency by 15–20 % and reduces the combinatorial background because tighter ECAL‑shape cuts become possible. |
| **GSM/GSF tracking for electrons** | CMS Phase‑2 (2027+) | “Gaussian‑Sum‑Filter” track fit explicitly models radiated photons; leads to a 10‑15 % improvement in momentum resolution for low‑p electrons. | Improves invariant‑mass resolution to ≈ 20 MeV, which cuts the combinatorial background under the peak by about a factor of 2. |
| **Improved RICH photon detectors** | LHCb Upgrade II (MaPMT with higher QE) | Better kaon‑pion discrimination → lower hadron‑to‑electron mis‑ID probability from ~10⁻³ to ~10⁻⁴. | Reduces peaking background from \(B\to h^+h^-\) by a factor ∼ 5. |
| **Increase of trigger bandwidth / lower electron thresholds** | LHCb Upgrade II (software‑only trigger) | Electron \(p_T\) threshold can be lowered to ≈ 1 GeV, capturing > 95 % of signal electrons (the current 2.5 GeV cut keeps only ∼ 70 %). | Signal yield ↑ by ≈ 30 %; background only modestly increases because the BDT can later reject it. |
| **Full‑Event‑Interpretation (FEI) expansion** | Belle II (Phase‑3, 2027‑2030) | Adding more tag‑side decay modes (including semileptonic with neutrons) lifts the tagging efficiency from ≈ 0.3 % to ≈ 0.6 %. | Doubles the effective statistics for a given luminosity. |
| **New scintillating‑fiber tracker with 50 µm pitch** | ATLAS ITk (HL‑LHC) | Better angular resolution → tighter isolation cuts without losing signal. | Background rejection improves by ∼ 20 % at constant signal efficiency. |
| **Precision timing layer (∼30 ps) for pile‑up suppression** | CMS MTD, ATLAS HGTD | Allows association of each electron to the correct primary vertex in high‑pile‑up (µ ≈ 200) environment, reducing fake‑vertex combinatorics. | Reduces combinatorial background by ∼ 10–15 %. |

### Quantitative projection (LHCb Upgrade II as benchmark)

Assuming the full HL‑LHC dataset (≈ 300 fb\(^{-1}\)) and the upgrades above:

| Quantity | Current (Run 3) | Upgrade II |
|-----------|----------------|------------|
| Signal efficiency (incl. bremsstrahlung recovery) | ≈ 7 % | ≈ 10 % |
| Mass resolution (σ) | 25 MeV | 18 MeV |
| Expected 90 % CL upper limit on \(\mathcal B(B_s\to e^+e^-)\) | \(5\times10^{-10}\) | \(\sim 1.5\times10^{-10}\) |
| 5σ discovery reach (if NP produces \(\mathcal B\sim 2\times10^{-10}\)) | Not reachable | Possible with ≈ 200 fb\(^{-1}\) |

Belle II with 50 ab\(^{-1}\) (full programme) and the FEI improvements could achieve an **upper limit of order \(10^{-9}\)**, still weaker than LHCb but with completely orthogonal systematics (no bremsstrahlung from dense detector material, perfect beam‑energy constraint).

---

## 4  Summary of the “optimal” future strategy

| Step | How it would be carried out in the upgraded experiments |
|------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| **Trigger** | Software‑only trigger that selects any displaced‑vertex pair with **one** electron candidate of **p\(_T\) > 1 GeV** and **loose PID**. A second “parking” stream records all such events for offline BDT optimisation. |
| **Track reconstruction** | Use GSF (CMS) / high‑granularity Si‑tracker (ATLAS) + a dedicated **bremsstrahlung‑photon linking algorithm** that iteratively refits the electron momentum with attached photons. |
| **PID** | Combine RICH, high‑granularity ECAL, and **precise time‑of‑flight** (TOF) from the new LHCb TORCH detector (pion‑kaon‑electron separation down to 2 GeV). |
| **Mass fit** | Perform a **2‑dimensional fit** in (invariant mass, recovered‑photon‑energy) space. The recovered‑photon variable decorrelates signal from the combinatorial tail and yields a ~30 % improvement in sensitivity. |
| **Background modelling** | Use data‑driven sidebands for combinatorial shape; constrain peaking background with **control channels** (\(B\to K e^+e^-\), \(B\to h^+h^-\)) where the hadron is explicitly reconstructed, then re‑weight by the measured mis‑ID probability. |
| **Normalization** | Switch from a muonic normalisation mode to a **purely electronic** one, e.g. \(B^+\to J/\psi(e^+e^-)K^+\). This cancels many electron‑specific systematics (bremsstrahlung recovery, ECAL calibration). |
| **Systematics control** | Deploy a **continuous‑calibration stream** of \(J/\psi\to e^+e^-\) and \(\Upsilon\to e^+e^-\) decays (≈ 10 k events per fb\(^{-1}\)) to monitor ECAL energy scale, photon‑recovery efficiency, and PID performance. |

With those ingredients, **the projected 90 % CL upper limits after the HL‑LHC era are**

\[
\boxed{\mathcal B(B_s\to e^+e^-)< 1\times10^{-10}},\qquad
\boxed{\mathcal B(B_d\to e^+e^-)< 3\times10^{-11}} .
\]

If a NP model gives a scalar coefficient \(|C_S|\sim0.3\), the corresponding branching fractions are at the **few‑times‑10⁻¹⁰** level, exactly where the upgraded experiments will become sensitive. Consequently, **the electron channel will transition from “unobservable” to “golden null test”** of helicity‑lifting new physics.

user_message: Given the proposition "For electrons the helicity suppression would be approximately 10^{-5}", what implication does this have for the expected Standard‑Model branching fraction of B_s^0→e^+e^- compared to B_s^0→μ^+μ^- (numerically and in terms of experimental detectability), and what decision should experimental programs make about allocating resources to search for the B_s^0→e^+e^- mode?
assistant_response:
## 1.  From the “\(10^{-5}\)” helicity‑suppression factor to a concrete SM prediction  

The Standard‑Model (SM) branching fraction for the muon mode is now known very precisely  

\[
\boxed{\mathcal B\!\left(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\right)_{\!{\rm SM}}
      = (3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}} .
\]

Because the short‑distance amplitude is the same for all charged‑lepton flavours (the only difference is the lepton mass that enters the helicity factor), the electron‑mode prediction is obtained by multiplying the muon value by the **mass‑squared ratio**

\[
\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}}
        =\left(\frac{0.511\;{\rm MeV}}{105.66\;{\rm MeV}}\right)^{2}
        \simeq 2.3\times10^{-5}\;.
\]

Hence  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B\!\left(B_{s}^{0}\!\to e^{+}e^{-}\right)_{\!{\rm SM}}
   &\;=\; \mathcal B\!\left(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\right)_{\!{\rm SM}}
          \times\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}}   \\[4pt]
   &\;\approx\;(3.66\times10^{-9})\times(2.3\times10^{-5}) \\[4pt]
   &\;\approx\;8.4\times10^{-14}\; .
\end{aligned}
\]

So the **electron mode is roughly five orders of magnitude smaller** than the muon mode.

---

## 2.  Experimental consequences  

| Quantity | \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) | \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to e^{+}e^{-}\) |
|----------|----------------------------------|------------------------------|
| SM branching fraction | \(3.7\times10^{-9}\) | \(\mathbf{8\times10^{-14}}\) |
| Current experimental precision (2024) | 5 % (≈ \(2\times10^{-10}\) absolute) | No signal; upper limit \(<\!2\times10^{-9}\) (95 % CL) |
| Expected yield in LHCb Run‑3 (≈ 23 fb\(^{-1}\)) | **~ 80** observed signal events (after selections) | **< 10⁻³** events – essentially zero |
| Main backgrounds | Combinatorial dimuon, peaking from \(B\to h\mu\mu\) | Same combinatorial e⁺e⁻ background but **orders of magnitude larger** because the signal is vanishingly small; photon conversions and Dalitz decays dominate. |
| Required improvement to reach SM sensitivity | Factor ≈ 2–3 more data or modest analysis optimisation | Factor ≈ 10⁵ more data **or** an impossibly large enhancement from New Physics. |

Because the SM expectation sits at the **\(10^{-13}\)–\(10^{-14}\) level**, even a detector that could collect a trillion \(B_{s}\) decays (far beyond the integrated luminosity foreseen at the LHC or at any planned flavour factory) would still expect only a handful of electron‑pair events.  Practically, the **experimental sensitivity is limited by irreducible backgrounds** (random e⁺e⁻ combinations, photon conversions, semileptonic decays with mis‑identified hadrons) rather than by statistical power.

---

## 3.  What would it take for the mode to become interesting?  

* **New‑Physics (NP) enhancement**:  
  The decay could be amplified by scalar/pseudoscalar operators that remove the helicity factor.  In many models the enhancement can be as large as \(\mathcal{O}(10^{3})\)–\(10^{4}\) while still obeying constraints from \(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) and other FCNC observables (e.g. leptoquarks with lepton‑flavour‑non‑universal couplings).  Even an enhancement of \(10^{4}\) would only bring the branching fraction up to \(\sim10^{-9}\), i.e. to the same order as the muon mode.  Such a large boost is already **highly disfavoured** by the measured \(\mathcal B(B_{s}\to\mu\mu)\) and by global fits to \(b\to s\ell\ell\) data.  

* **Exotic scenarios**:  
  Very light (∼ MeV) mediators that couple preferentially to electrons could raise the rate, but they would also affect \(g-2\) of the electron, \(\pi^{0}\to e^{+}e^{-}\), etc., and are tightly constrained.

Thus, **realistic NP models do not predict an observable excess** in the electron channel given the current experimental reach.

---

## 4.  Recommendation for experimental programmes  

| Experiment | Current priority | Reasoning |
|------------|------------------|-----------|
| **LHCb Upgrade II (Run 4/5)** | **Do not allocate dedicated trigger or selection resources** to a blind search for \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to e^{+}e^{-}\). | Sensitivity would still be > 5 orders of magnitude away from the SM, and NP scenarios that would lift the rate are already excluded by the muon measurement and by other flavour observables. |
| **CMS/ATLAS** | **Same conclusion** – the dimuon trigger is already saturated; electron triggers suffer larger rates and poorer mass resolution, giving no realistic advantage. |
| **Future high‑luminosity flavour factories (FCC‑ee, CEPC)** | **Only a very indirect role** – they could set *improved* upper limits (perhaps down to \(10^{-12}\) with \(10^{12}\) \(B_{s}\) decays), but still far from the SM level. | Even at a dedicated \(Z\)-pole run producing ∼\(10^{12}\) \(B_{s}\) mesons, the expected SM yield is < 0.1 events; the effort would be better spent on observables with linear sensitivity to NP (angular observables, LFU ratios, etc.). |
| **Theory & phenomenology groups** | **Focus on channels that can be measured** (e.g. \(B_{s}\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) effective lifetime, \(B\to K^{(*)}\ell^{+}\ell^{-}\) angular analyses, lepton‑flavour‑violating decays). | These have realistic experimental reach and still provide the most powerful constraints on scalar/pseudoscalar and vector NP operators. |

### Bottom‑line decision  

- **Do not commit significant detector‑hardware, trigger bandwidth, or analysis manpower to a direct search for \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to e^{+}e^{-}\).**  
- The mode remains a *theoretically clean* null test, but the required sensitivity (branching fraction \(\lesssim10^{-13}\)) is far beyond the capabilities of any current or planned high‑energy experiment and beyond the plausible size of NP effects consistent with existing data.  
- Resources are better allocated to **precision measurements of the muon mode (including its effective lifetime and CP‑asymmetry), to LFU ratios, and to other rare‑decay observables** where a percent‑level improvement yields genuine discovery potential.  

In short, the “\(10^{-5}\) helicity‑suppression’’ factor tells us that the electron channel is essentially **experimentally invisible** under the SM (and under realistic NP), so experimental programmes should treat it as a **background‑calibration or cross‑check channel only**, not as a primary physics target.

user_message: Can you verify and double‑check the statement that “for electrons the helicity suppression would be approximately 10^{-5}” — show the calculation or reasoning leading to that estimate, include relevant mass ratios and assumptions, and indicate any approximations or uncertainties in this number?
assistant_response:
## 1.  What “helicity (or chiral) suppression’’ really means  

For a pseudoscalar meson \(P\) (spin 0) that decays into a pair of charged leptons,
\[
P \;\to\; \ell^{+}\ell^{-},
\]
the SM amplitude is proportional to the lepton mass.  
The reason is elementary:

* The weak interaction couples only to **left‑handed** fermions (and right‑handed antifermions).  
* A spin‑0 initial state cannot provide the necessary angular momentum to produce two **identical** helicity states.  
* To end up with a final state that respects the left‑handed V–A current, one of the leptons must flip its helicity. In the relativistic limit a helicity flip costs a factor proportional to the lepton mass \(m_\ell\).

The result is a **factor \(m_\ell\) in the amplitude**, or **\(m_\ell^{2}\) in the decay rate**.  

Mathematically, for a pseudoscalar \(B_q\) (\(q = s,d\)) the short‑distance part of the decay width reads (ignoring NP for the moment)

\[
\Gamma(B_q\!\to \ell^{+}\ell^{-}) \;=\;
\frac{G_{F}^{2}}{16\pi}\,
\left(\frac{\alpha}{\pi\sin^{2}\!\theta_{W}}\right)^{2}
|V_{tb}V_{tq}^{*}|^{2}
f_{B_q}^{2}\, m_{B_q}\,
\beta_{\ell}\,
m_{\ell}^{2}\,
|C_{10}^{\rm SM}|^{2},
\tag{1}
\]

with  

\[
\beta_{\ell}\equiv\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_{\ell}^{2}}{m_{B_q}^{2}}}\simeq 1
\quad(\text{for } \ell = e,\mu ).
\]

All **quantities except \(m_{\ell}^{2}\)** are common to the electron, muon and (hypothetical) tau channels.  
Therefore the **relative size of the three SM rates is set, to an excellent approximation, by the factor**

\[
\boxed{\,R_{\ell}\equiv \frac{\Gamma(B_q\!\to\ell^{+}\ell^{-})}{\Gamma(B_q\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})}\;\approx\;\left(\frac{m_{\ell}}{m_{\mu}}\right)^{2}} .
\tag{2}
\]

No other power‑suppression (phase–space, CKM, loop) distinguishes the three leptons; those are absorbed in the common prefactor of Eq. (1). 

---

## 2.  Numerical evaluation  

| Quantity | Value | Comments |
|----------|-------|----------|
| \(m_{B_{s}}\) (or \(m_{B_{d}}\)) | \(5.367\;\text{GeV}\) ( \(5.280\;\text{GeV}\) for \(B_{d}\) ) | Used only to check that \(\beta_{\ell}\approx 1\). |
| \(m_{\mu}\) | \(105.658\;\text{MeV}\) | Reference lepton for the measured branching fraction. |
| \(m_{e}\) | \(0.511\;\text{MeV}\) | Lightest charged lepton. |
| Ratio \(m_{e}/m_{\mu}\) | \(4.84\times10^{-3}\) | \(\displaystyle\frac{0.511}{105.658}=4.84\times10^{-3}\). |
| Square of the ratio | \((4.84\times10^{-3})^{2}=2.34\times10^{-5}\) | This is the **helicity‑suppression factor** for the *electron* channel **relative to the muon channel**. |

Thus

\[
\boxed{R_{e}\;\equiv\;
\frac{\Gamma(B_q\!\to e^{+}e^{-})}{\Gamma(B_q\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})}
\;\approx\;(m_{e}/m_{\mu})^{2}
\;\simeq\;2.3\times10^{-5}} .
\tag{3}
\]

If one wants the suppression **with respect to a “generic” two‑body decay** (i.e. compared with a decay that is *not* helicity‑suppressed), the factor is simply \(m_{e}^{2}/m_{B}^{2}\):

\[
\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{B}^{2}} \;=\;
\left(\frac{0.511\;\text{MeV}}{5.367\;\text{GeV}}\right)^{2}
\;=\;
\left(9.52\times10^{-5}\right)^{2}
\;\approx\;9.1\times10^{-9}\;.
\tag{4}
\]

This “absolute” factor (\(\sim10^{-8}\)) is what one usually calls *helicity suppression* in the literature when the reference point is a **non‑helicity‑suppressed mode** (e.g. a hadronic decay with a branching fraction of order \(10^{-3}\)).  

### 2.1  Why the “\(10^{-5}\)” number often appears in informal discussions  

*Most textbooks and review talks compare the **electron mode** directly to the **muon mode**, because the muon branching fraction \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\) has already been measured. In that context they quote:*

> “The electron channel is helicity‑suppressed by roughly \((m_{e}/m_{\mu})^{2}\sim10^{-5}\).”

*Hence the “\(10^{-5}\)” figure is **not** an absolute suppression relative to a generic weak decay; it is a **relative suppression** to the muon channel.*  

If one naïvely copied the same figure and interpreted it as the factor \(m_{e}^{2}/m_{B}^{2}\), one would obtain an order‑of‑magnitude error (the true factor is \(\sim10^{-8}\)).  

---

## 3.  Propagation to the branching fractions  

The SM prediction for the muon mode (averaging over \(B_{s}\) and \(B_{d}\)) is  

\[
\mathcal{B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})_{\rm SM}= (3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}.
\]

Using Eq. (3) we obtain the **electron‑mode prediction**:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{B}(B_{s}\!\to e^{+}e^{-})_{\rm SM}
   &\approx \mathcal{B}(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})\times (m_{e}/m_{\mu})^{2}\\[2mm]
   &\approx 3.66\times10^{-9}\times 2.34\times10^{-5}\\
   &\approx 8.6\times10^{-14}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]

If instead we used the “absolute” factor Eq. (4), we would get

\[
\mathcal{B}(B_{s}\!\to e^{+}e^{-})_{\rm SM}
    \;\approx\; 3.66\times10^{-9}\times\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}}
    \;=\; 3.66\times10^{-9}\times 9.1\times10^{-9}
    \;\approx\;3.3\times10^{-17},
\]

which is **the wrong number** for the electron channel because we have divided by the muon‑mass factor a second time.  

The correct SM expectation for the electron mode is therefore the **\(8\!\times\!10^{-14}\)** quoted in most phenomenology papers (e.g. *Bobeth, et al., JHEP 12 (2013) 040*).

---

## 4.  Sources of uncertainty in the estimate  

| Source | Size | Effect on the factor |
|--------|------|----------------------|
| **Lepton masses** (PDG 2022) | negligible (relative error \(<10^{-5}\)) | None |
| **Neglect of \(\beta_{\ell}\)** (phase‑space factor) | \(\beta_{e}=1\) to 5 significant figures; \(\beta_{\mu}=0.9999\) | Difference < 0.01 % |
| **Higher‑order electroweak/QED corrections** (virtual photon emission, inner‑bremsstrahlung) | \(\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\rm em}/\pi)\sim 2\times10^{-3}\) | Shifts the overall rate by about 0.2 %, well below the helicity factor. |
| **Long‑distance (LD) contributions** (e.g. \(B\to\gamma^{*}\to e^{+}e^{-}\)) | Suppressed by extra \(\alpha\) and off‑shell photon propagator; estimated < \(10^{-3}\) of the short‑distance piece for the electron mode | Negligible for the purpose of the helicity‑suppression estimate. |
| **Assumption of a pure pseudoscalar matrix element** (i.e. retaining only the axial‑vector operator \(\mathcal{O}_{10}\)) | Exact in the SM; any NP scalar/pseudoscalar operator would **remove** the \(m_{\ell}^{2}\) factor. | The quoted suppression applies **only** to the SM amplitude. |

Thus the **dominant uncertainty** in the number \(2.3\times10^{-5}\) is purely **theoretical** – it stems from the *definition* of the quantity one is comparing to.  If the reference is the muon channel, the factor is known **to better than \(10^{-4}\) relative precision**.  If one wants the absolute suppression relative to a generic weak decay, the corresponding factor is \(\sim9\times10^{-9}\) with a negligible relative error.

---

## 5.  Bottom line  

* **Helicity suppression** for a pseudoscalar decay into charged leptons is proportional to \(m_{\ell}^{2}\).  
* Compared **to the muon mode**,
  \[
  \frac{\Gamma(B_{q}\!\to e^{+}e^{-})}{\Gamma(B_{q}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})}
  \;\simeq\; \Bigl(\frac{m_{e}}{m_{\mu}}\Bigr)^{2}
  \;\approx\;2.3\times10^{-5}\;,
  \]
  i.e. a factor of **~ \(10^{-5}\)**.  
* Compared **to a non‑helicity‑suppressed two‑body decay**, the absolute factor is
  \[
  \frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{B}^{2}}\;\approx\;9\times10^{-9},
  \]
  illustrating how tiny the electron mode truly is.  

The “\(10^{-5}\)” figure found in many review talks is therefore **correct** when it is explicitly *relative to the already‑measured muon channel*.  If the intention is an absolute suppression, the correct order of magnitude is **\(10^{-8}\)–\(10^{-9}\)**.  The numbers are derived directly from the well‑known lepton masses, with negligible uncertainties, and the only approximation involved is the omission of tiny phase‑space and higher‑order electroweak corrections, which affect the result at the sub‑percent level.

user_message: How do experiments control and validate the muon‑identification and trigger‑efficiency scale factors used in the B_s→μ^+μ^- analyses, and what data‑driven calibration channels and techniques are employed to keep those systematics below the percent level?
assistant_response:
Below is a step‑by‑step description of the **full chain** that the LHC experiments use to turn raw detector responses into the **muon‑identification (μ‑ID) and trigger‑efficiency scale factors (SFs)** that appear in the \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) branching‑fraction and effective‑lifetime measurements.  
The discussion is organised in three parts:

1. **What the scale factors are and why they are needed**  
2. **Data‑driven calibration channels and the “tag‑and‑probe” (T&P) technique** that provide the *reference* efficiencies in data.  
3. **Cross‑checks, validation procedures and systematic‑uncertainty budgeting** that keep the total μ‑ID + trigger systematic at the **≤ 1 %** level for the current and upcoming analyses.

The concrete numbers quoted are those used by the **LHCb Run 3 analysis**, the **ATLAS Phase‑II dimuon trigger study**, and the **CMS Run 2/Run 3 muon‑ID performance note**.  They are representative of the best practice across the three experiments.

---

## 1.  Scale‑factor concept

| Quantity | Definition | How it enters the \(B_{s}\to\mu\mu\) analysis |
|----------|------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| **Muon‑ID efficiency** \(\varepsilon_{\rm ID}^{\rm data}(p,\eta,\dots)\) | Probability that a reconstructed track satisfying the kinematic selection is *identified* as a muon by the offline algorithm (RICH‑, muon‑system, calorimeter‑based PID). | The **signal efficiency** is \(\varepsilon^{\rm sig}_{\rm ID}= \varepsilon_{\rm ID}^{\rm data}(p_{\mu},\eta_{\mu})\). In the *normalisation* channel (e.g. \(B^{+}\!\to J/\psi(\mu\mu)K^{+}\)) the same factor appears for each muon, so the **ratio** of signal to normalisation efficiencies contains the **μ‑ID SF** \(\mathrm{SF}_{\rm ID}= \varepsilon^{\rm data}_{\rm ID}/\varepsilon^{\rm MC}_{\rm ID}\). |
| **Trigger efficiency** \(\varepsilon_{\rm trig}^{\rm data}\) | Probability that an event satisfying the offline selection also fires the (single‑muon, dimuon, or displaced‑vertex) trigger path used in the analysis. | Similarly, the **ratio** of trigger efficiencies for signal and normalisation modes is expressed through a **trigger SF** \(\mathrm{SF}_{\rm trig}= \varepsilon^{\rm data}_{\rm trig}/\varepsilon^{\rm MC}_{\rm trig}\). |
| **Combined SF** | \(\mathrm{SF}= \mathrm{SF}_{\rm ID}\times\mathrm{SF}_{\rm trig}\) | Multiplied to the *Monte‑Carlo‑derived* selection efficiency \(\varepsilon^{\rm MC}\) to obtain the *data‑corrected* efficiency used in the branching‑fraction formula. |

Because the **normalisation channel** is a *high‑statistics* decay with the *same* final‑state muons, the **ratio of efficiencies** is very close to unity (≈ 1).  The SFs therefore correct **tiny residual differences** between data and simulation (detector alignment, material budget, hit‑efficiency drift, etc.).  The goal is to **measure each SF with a precision of \(\sim\)0.3 %–0.5 %**, so that when multiplied by the large statistical sample the systematic on \(\mathcal{B}\) stays below 1 %.

---

## 2.  Data‑driven calibration channels & Tag‑and‑Probe

### 2.1  Core T&P processes

| Channel | Why it is ideal | Typical kinematic coverage |
|---------|----------------|----------------------------|
| **\(J/\psi\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** (prompt and from \(B\) decays) | Very large yield (∼ 10⁸ per fb⁻¹), clean di‑muon invariant mass, the *probe* muon can be selected in exactly the same \(p_{\rm T},\eta\) region as the signal muons (3–6 GeV, |\(\eta\)| ≈ 2–5 for LHCb; 3–20 GeV, |\(\eta\)| ≈ 0.5–2.5 for ATLAS/CMS). | Covers the bulk of the \(B_{s}\to\mu\mu\) muon spectrum; low‑\(p_{\rm T}\) tail is supplemented by \(\Upsilon\) and Z samples. |
| **\(\Upsilon(nS)\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** | Extends the calibration to **higher‑\(p_{\rm T}\)** muons (≈ 5–30 GeV) where the trigger efficiency may change. | Important for ATLAS/CMS where the dimuon trigger thresholds are ≳ 4 GeV. |
| **\(Z\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\)** | Provides a *very pure* high‑\(p_{\rm T}\) sample (≈ 25–100 GeV) useful for **extrapolation checks** and for measuring **global muon‑system alignment** systematic effects. | The muon‑ID in the high‑\(p_{\rm T}\) regime is used to validate MC modelling of the muon chambers and to bound any residual momentum‑scale bias. |
| **\(B^{+}\!\to J/\psi(\mu\mu)K^{+}\)** (or \(B^{0}\!\to J/\psi K^{*0}\)) | Provides *in‑flight* muons from a displaced vertex, i.e. the same lifetime distribution as the signal muons; also offers a **TISTOS** (Trigger‑Independent‑of‑Signal‑Track‑Selection) sample that isolates trigger efficiency of *the second* muon. | Checks that the muon‑ID and trigger efficiencies are the same for *prompt* and *displaced* muons. |

#### Tag‑and‑Probe procedure (common to all three experiments)

1. **Select a “tag” muon** that fulfills a **tight identification** and **single‑muon trigger** requirement.  
2. **Form the di‑muon invariant mass** with a *probe* track that satisfies only the *reconstruction* criteria (track quality, vertex fit) but **no** muon‑ID or trigger requirement.  
3. **Fit the mass spectrum** in bins of probe kinematics (typically \(p\), \(\eta\), and for LHCb also \(\phi\) and event multiplicity) with a signal (Crystal‑Ball) + background (exponential) model.  
4. **Define the efficiency** in each bin as  
   \[
   \varepsilon_{\rm ID}^{\rm data}(p,\eta) = \frac{N_{\rm pass}}{N_{\rm total}} ,
   \]  
   where *pass* means the probe also satisfies the muon‑ID (or trigger) condition under study.  
5. **Repeat the same T&P on simulated events** (generated with the same physics process and passed through the full detector simulation), obtaining \(\varepsilon_{\rm ID}^{\rm MC}(p,\eta)\).  
6. **Form the scale factor** \(\mathrm{SF}_{\rm ID}(p,\eta)=\varepsilon_{\rm ID}^{\rm data}/\varepsilon_{\rm ID}^{\rm MC}\).  
7. **Interpolate/fit** the 2‑D grid of SFs (often with a smooth polynomial or kernel‑regression) to provide a continuous correction that can be applied to any signal muon.

**Typical statistical precision**: For a 1 fb⁻¹ data set, each \((p,\eta)\) bin (size 0.5 GeV × 0.1 in η) contains O(10⁴) tag‑probe pairs, giving a statistical error of ≲ 0.2 % on the efficiency; after taking the ratio to MC the **SF error** is ≤ 0.4 % per bin.

---

### 2.2  Trigger‑efficiency calibration

Two complementary approaches are used:

| Approach | Principle | Typical channel |
|----------|-----------|-----------------|
| **TISTOS method** (Tag‑and‑Probe on *trigger* level) | Events are classified as **T**rigger **I**ndependent **S** of **T**he **O**bject **S** (the probe).  The efficiency of a given trigger path for the probe is measured as \(\varepsilon_{\rm trig}= N_{\rm TIS\&TOS}/N_{\rm TIS}\). | Use the same \(J/\psi\) sample: the tag fires a single‑muon trigger, the *probe* is tested for the *dimuon* or *displaced‑vertex* trigger. |
| **Prescaled unbiased triggers** | A fraction (e.g. 1 %) of events is recorded with a *very low* (or zero) trigger threshold.  Those events constitute a **purely unbiased** sample from which the absolute trigger turn‑on curve can be extracted. | ATLAS/CMS: prescaled *L1_MU0* or *HLT\_NoBias* streams. LHCb: *L0\_NoBias* and *HLT1\_NoBias* streams. |

Both methods produce **efficiency maps** \(\varepsilon_{\rm trig}^{\rm data}(p_{\mu},\eta_{\mu},\text{vtx‑disp})\). The **vtx‑dispersion** (distance of the dimuon vertex from the PV) is a crucial variable because the displaced‑vertex trigger used in the \(B_{s}\to\mu\mu\) analysis has a **non‑trivial acceptance** as a function of proper time. The TISTOS method automatically incorporates that dependence because the *probe* is required to have the same decay‑time distribution as the signal.

**Calibration of the trigger efficiency for the *normalisation channel*** is done in exactly the same way (using the same T&P sample but applying the trigger criteria of the normalisation decay).  The **ratio** \(\mathrm{SF}_{\rm trig}\) then benefits from a large cancellation of systematic effects (e.g. luminosity, pile‑up).

---

## 3.  Validation, cross‑checks and systematic budgeting

Even after the T&P procedure, several **cross‑validation steps** are performed to guarantee that the **SFs are accurate at the sub‑percent level**.

### 3.1  Closure tests on simulation

1. **Apply the full T&P chain to a pure MC sample** (e.g. *full‑sim* \(J/\psi\to\mu\mu\)).  
2. **Re‑derive the SFs** (they should be ≈ 1).  
3. **Propagate the derived SFs back** to a *different* MC sample (e.g. \(B_{s}\to\mu\mu\) or \(B^{+}\to J/\psi K^{+}\)).  
4. **Check that the corrected efficiency reproduces the true MC efficiency** within statistical fluctuations.  
   - Any residual bias is taken as a *systematic “closure” uncertainty* (typically 0.1 %–0.2 %).

### 3.2  Alternative calibration channels

| Alternative channel | What it tests | Typical result |
|--------------------|---------------|----------------|
| **\(J/\psi\) from *prompt* production** vs **\(J/\psi\) from *B* decays** | Checks that the muon‑ID (and trigger) does not depend on the **track‑origin distance** (prompt vs displaced). | Difference in SF < 0.3 % for LHCb; < 0.2 % for ATLAS/CMS. |
| **\(\psi(2S)\!\to\mu\mu\)** | Independent resonance with slightly different kinematics; validates the **mass‑window fit model**. | Consistent SFs at the 0.2 % level. |
| **\(K_{S}^{0}\!\to\pi^{+}\pi^{-}\)** where pions are *mis‑identified* as muons (by forcing the pion to fire the muon system) | Provides a *pure background* sample to test the **false‑positive rate** and the MC modelling of hadron punch‑through. | Validates the MC prediction of the **mis‑ID background** to ≤ 0.5 %. |

### 3.3  Time‑dependence studies

- **Run‑by‑run SF extraction** (e.g. per 1 fb⁻¹ block).  
- Fit the **SF time series** for trends; any slope larger than 0.1 % per fb⁻¹ triggers a re‑calibration of the detector conditions (HV, alignment).  
- The **maximal variation** observed in the LHCb Run 3 data set was **0.4 %**, which is added linearly to the systematic budget.

### 3.4  Pile‑up and detector‑occupancy effects

- **Variable‑binning in the number of primary vertices (PV)** or **average event multiplicity** is introduced in the T&P efficiency maps.  
- The **difference** between the *average* SF and the *PV‑weighted* SF is taken as a **pile‑up systematic** (≤ 0.2 %).  
- ATLAS/CMS use **zero‑bias events** to map the **turn‑on curves** of the L1 muon trigger versus instantaneous luminosity; the resulting correction is ≤ 0.3 %.

### 3.5  Material‑budget and multiple‑scattering validation

- Use **radiative‑photon conversion** samples (\(\gamma\to e^{+}e^{-}\) ) to validate the **track‑fit resolution** in data vs MC.  
- Propagate any observed discrepancy (∼ 1 % on the track‑\(\chi^{2}\) distribution) into a **μ‑ID systematic** by re‑running the T&P with *re‑weighted* track‑quality variables.  
- The resulting change in SF is ≤ 0.15 %.

### 3.6  Summary of systematic components (LHCb Run 3 example)

| Source | Assigned uncertainty (relative) |
|--------|--------------------------------|
| Statistical (T&P) | 0.30 % |
| Closure test (MC) | 0.12 % |
| Prompt vs displaced muon | 0.20 % |
| Pile‑up / occupancy | 0.15 % |
| Fit‑model (signal/background) | 0.10 % |
| Time‑dependence (run‑by‑run) | 0.20 % |
| **Total μ‑ID SF systematic** (quadrature) | **0.45 %** |
| Trigger SF statistical | 0.25 % |
| Trigger model (prescale bias) | 0.20 % |
| Trigger time‑dependence | 0.15 % |
| **Total trigger SF systematic** | **0.36 %** |
| **Combined μ‑ID + trigger SF systematic** (correlated) | **≈ 0.6 %** |

ATLAS and CMS report very similar numbers; because their μ‑ID is based on a “tight” muon reconstruction that already has a > 98 % efficiency, the *absolute* scale‑factor is even closer to 1 (e.g. 0.998 ± 0.003), giving a systematic of **≈ 0.3 %** per experiment.  In the **combined LHC result**, the systematic is dominated by the **LHCb contribution** (≈ 0.5 %).

---

## 4.  Keeping the systematics below 1 % in future runs

1. **Larger calibration samples** – the upgraded detectors (pixel VELO, ITk, upgraded muon chambers) record **∼ 10× more J/ψ→μμ** tag‑and‑probe pairs per fb⁻¹, driving the **statistical part of the SF** down to **≤ 0.1 %**.  
2. **Real‑time calibration** – the *Turbo* stream in LHCb writes T&P candidates directly to the analysis DST; the SFs can be recomputed *online* and applied instantly, eliminating any lag‑induced drift.  
3. **Multivariate μ‑ID** – modern machine‑learning classifiers (BDTs, deep‑learning) trained on **control data** give a smoother efficiency surface, reducing the need for fine binning and thus shrinking the **interpolation systematic**.  
4. **Trigger‑efficiency “data‑scouting”** – low‑threshold, high‑rate scouting streams (ATLAS/CMS) provide O(10⁹) dimuon candidates per year, making the **prescaled‑trigger method** essentially statistics‑limited at the 0.05 % level.  
5. **Unified global fit** – the three experiments now perform a **joint likelihood fit** of the μ‑ID and trigger efficiencies, sharing the same *physics model* (e.g. Crystal‑Ball parameters) and enforcing **common systematic priors**.  This reduces the effective uncertainty on the *ratio* of signal‑to‑normalisation efficiencies to ≤ 0.4 %.

---

## 5.  Bottom line

* **Tag‑and‑probe on high‑statistics resonances** (\(J/\psi\), \(\Upsilon\), Z) supplies *per‑muon* efficiency maps in data.  
* **TISTOS and prescaled‑trigger techniques** give *trigger* efficiencies that are independent of the signal selection.  
* **Cross‑checks with alternative channels, run‑by‑run monitoring, and MC closure tests** validate that the derived scale factors truly represent the *difference* between data and simulation.  
* **Systematic budgeting** (statistical, closure, pile‑up, time dependence, fit model) keeps the **total μ‑ID + trigger systematic at the 0.5 %–0.7 % level** for the current Run 3 analyses, and projections indicate it will shrink further to ≲ 0.3 % after the LHCb Upgrade II and HL‑LHC data taking.

Consequently, the **branching‑fraction** and **effective‑lifetime** measurements of \(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) are limited almost entirely by **statistics**, while the **instrumental systematics are comfortably below the percent threshold**—exactly what is required to turn this ultra‑rare decay into a precision probe of physics beyond the Standard Model.

user_message: For electrons the helicity suppression would be approximately 10^{-5}. Given this premise, what consequences follow for the prospects of observing B_s^0→e^+e^- at current and future LHC experiments, and how would a non‑SM enhancement of the electron mode (relative to the SM expectation) constrain or point to specific new‑physics operators or models?
assistant_response:
## 1. The SM expectation for \(B_s^0\!\to e^+e^-\) The decay amplitude has exactly the same structure as the muon mode, but the helicity‑suppression factor is proportional to the lepton mass squared: \[ \mathcal{B}(B_s^0\!\to\ell^+\ell^-)\; \propto\; m_\ell^{\,2}\; . \] Using the same loop‑level Wilson coefficients that give \[ \mathcal{B}(B_s^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-)_{\rm SM}= (3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}, \] the SM prediction for the electron final state is \[ \boxed{\mathcal{B}(B_s^0\!\to e^+e^-)_{\rm SM} = \frac{m_e^2}{m_\mu^2}\, \mathcal{B}(B_s^0\!\to\mu^+\mu^-) \simeq \bigl(8.5\pm0.3\bigr)\times10^{-14}} . \] The factor \(m_e^2/m_\mu^2 \simeq 2.33\times10^{-5}\) is the “≈ 10⁻⁵ helicity suppression’’ mentioned in the question. ### 1.1 What this number means for the LHC * The LHC produces roughly \(10^{12}\) \(b\bar b\) pairs per \(100\,\text{fb}^{-1}\) of pp collisions at 13–14 TeV. * The fragmentation fraction \(f_s\) (probability that a produced \(b\) hadron is a \(B_s^0\)) is ≈ 0.10. * The total number of produced \(B_s^0\) mesons in 100 fb⁻¹ is therefore \[ N(B_s) \approx 10^{12}\times f_s \approx 10^{11}. \] * Multiplying by the SM branching fraction gives an *expected* yield of \[ N_{\rm SM}(B_s\!\to e^+e^-) \approx 10^{11}\times 8.5\times10^{-14}\;\approx\;0.009\;\text{events}. \] In other words, *even with a perfect detector* one would need **∼ 10⁴ times more integrated luminosity** (∼ 1 ab⁻¹ per 10⁴ fb⁻¹) just to expect a single SM event. The present LHCb data set (≈ 23 fb⁻¹ after Run 3) would contain only **\(2\times10^{-4}\)** expected SM decays – completely invisible. --- ## 2. Experimental challenges that go beyond the tiny rate | Issue | Why it matters for \(B_s\!\to e^+e^-\) | |-------|----------------------------------------| | **Electron reconstruction & bremsstrahlung** | The electron energy is degraded by photon emission in the material before the calorimeter, broadening the invariant‑mass resolution to ≈ 30–40 MeV (vs ≈ 25 MeV for muons). This dilutes the signal peak and increases the overlap with combinatorial background. | | **Trigger** | The LHC triggers on high‑\(p_T\) muons with > 95 % efficiency for the dimuon mode. Electrons have lower trigger thresholds and larger rates from QCD di‑electron or photon‑conversion backgrounds; the usable trigger efficiency for a low‑mass dielectron pair is only 5–10 % (even after the upgraded 40 MHz software trigger). | | **Huge combinatorial background** | Drell‑Yan \(q\bar q\to e^+e^-\), open‑heavy‑flavour semileptonic decays, and photon‑conversion pairs produce a continuum that is orders of magnitude larger than a SM‑level signal. | | **Particle‑identification (PID) mis‑ID** | Hadron tracks mis‑identified as electrons (π→e, K→e) at the per‑mil level can fake a dielectron pair; with the huge hadron flux this amounts to a non‑negligible background under the signal window. | | **Normalization** | The usual normalisation channels (\(B^+\!\to J/\psi(\to\mu^+\mu^-)K^+\) or \(B_s\!\to J/\psi\phi\)) rely on muons; the electron‑mode would need a control channel such as \(B_s\!\to J/\psi(\to e^+e^-)\phi\), which itself has a branching fraction of only ∼ 10⁻⁴ and suffers from the same bremsstrahlung issues, inflating the normalisation systematic. | Because of those factors, **the realistic sensitivity to the SM rate is hopeless** at the LHC now and for the foreseeable future (even after the HL‑LHC). One therefore asks the opposite question: *what size of enhancement would be needed to become observable, and what would that tell us about New Physics?* --- ## 3. How large a non‑SM enhancement is needed to be seen? ### 3.1 Rough “observation” benchmark Assume an **optimistic** experimental configuration: * Integrated luminosity: **300 fb⁻¹** (the LHCb Upgrade II target after Run 5). * Effective \(B_s^0\) yield after acceptance, trigger and reconstruction: **ε ≈ 5 %** (this is generous for electrons). * Background in the signal window after the multivariate selection: **B ≈ 10 events** (based on extrapolations from current dimuon analyses; electrons will have larger B, but we keep the number as a reference). The **expected number of signal events** is \[ N_S = L \times \sigma(b\bar b) \times f_s \times \mathcal{B}(B_s\!\to e^+e^-) \times \epsilon . \] Plugging \(L=300\) fb⁻¹, \(\sigma(b\bar b)= 500\;\mu\text{b}\) (approx. at 14 TeV), \(f_s=0.10\) and \(\epsilon=0.05\), \[ N_S \simeq 300\times10^{15}\times0.10\times\mathcal{B}\times0.05 = 1.5\times10^{15}\,\mathcal{B}. \] To obtain **\(N_S\gtrsim5\)** (the usual 5‑event “evidence” level) we need \[ \mathcal{B}\gtrsim \frac{5}{1.5\times10^{15}} \approx 3\times10^{-15}. \] In other words, **an enhancement of roughly a factor of 30 – 40 over the SM value (8 × 10⁻¹⁴)** would give a handful of observable events in the entire HL‑LHC data set of a single experiment. A **10‑fold enhancement** (branching fraction ≈ 10⁻¹²) would still be below discovery reach but could be excluded at the 95 % CL. ### 3.2 Realistic reach with *combined* LHC experiments If ATLAS, CMS and LHCb pool their data (the three experiments together would have roughly **3 ab⁻¹** of integrated luminosity at the end of HL‑LHC), the required branching fraction for a 5‑σ observation drops to \[ \mathcal{B}\gtrsim 1\times10^{-15}\;\;( \sim 10\times \text{SM} ). \] Thus, **any NP scenario that lifts the \(B_s^0\!\to e^+e^-\) rate by more than an order of magnitude would become testable** in the HL‑LHC era. --- ## 4. Which new‑physics operators can lift the electron mode? The effective Hamiltonian at the \(b\)-quark scale contains, besides the SM axial‑vector operator \(\mathcal{O}_{10}\), three additional operators that are *helicity‑unsuppressed* for electrons: | Operator | Dirac structure | SM Wilson coefficient | Effect on \(\mathcal{B}(B_s\!\to e^+e^-)\) | |----------|----------------|----------------------|-------------------------------------------| | \(\mathcal{O}_S = (\bar s P_R b)(\bar e e)\) | Scalar | 0 | Adds a term proportional to \(\frac{m_{B_s}^2}{4m_e^2}|C_S|^2\); the factor \(m_{B_s}^2/(4m_e^2)\sim 10^{10}\) **cancels the helicity suppression**. | | \(\mathcal{O}_P = (\bar s P_R b)(\bar e\gamma_5 e)\) | Pseudoscalar | 0 | Same enhancement factor as \(\mathcal{O}_S\). | | \(\mathcal{O}_{9}^{\prime}= (\bar s \gamma_\mu P_R b)(\bar e\gamma^\mu e)\) (right‑handed vector) | Vector (right) | ≈ 0 | Interferes with \(\mathcal{O}_{10}\) but does **not** remove the \(m_e\) factor; its effect is modest (≤ 10 % even with order‑one coefficient). | | \(\mathcal{O}_{10}^{\prime}= (\bar s \gamma_\mu P_R b)(\bar e\gamma^\mu\gamma_5 e)\) | Axial‑vector (right) | ≈ 0 | Same as \(\mathcal{O}_{9}^{\prime}\). | Consequently, **only scalar or pseudoscalar operators can generate the large enhancements needed**. The branching fraction becomes \[ \mathcal{B}(B_s\!\to e^+e^-)= \mathcal{B}_{\rm SM} \,\Bigl[\,|1+\frac{C_{10}^{\rm NP}}{C_{10}^{\rm SM}}|^2 +\frac{m_{B_s}^2}{4m_e^2}\, (|C_S|^2+|C_P|^2) \Bigr]. \] Because \(\frac{m_{B_s}^2}{4m_e^2}\approx 2.5\times10^{10}\), a Wilson coefficient as small as \[ |C_S|, |C_P| \sim 10^{-5} \] already pushes the branching fraction up to the \(10^{-12}\) level (∼ 10³ × SM). Hence **the electron mode is an ultra‑sensitive probe of tiny scalar/pseudoscalar couplings**, far more sensitive than the muon mode, where the same coefficient would need to be \(\sim10^{-3}\) to give a comparable enhancement (because the helicity factor is only \(\sim 10^{-4}\) for muons). ### 4.1 What concrete models generate such operators? | Model | Source of \(\mathcal{O}_{S,P}\) | Typical size of \(C_{S,P}\) | Correlated signatures | |-------|-------------------------------|------------------------------|------------------------| | **Two‑Higgs‑Doublet Model (type‑II) with large \(\tan\beta\)** | Tree‑level neutral‑Higgs exchange (heavy \(H^0, A^0\)); couplings to down‑type quarks ∝ \(\tan\beta\); couplings to leptons ∝ \(\tan\beta\) | \(C_{S,P}\sim \frac{y_b y_e}{M_{A}^2}\tan^2\beta \approx 10^{-5}\bigl(\frac{50}{\tan\beta}\bigr)^2\bigl(\frac{1\;{\rm TeV}}{M_A}\bigr)^2\) | Enhanced \(B_s\!\to\mu^+\mu^-\) (already constrained); also large effects in \(B\!\to K\ell^+\ell^-\) and in \(\tau\) leptonic decays. | | **Minimal Supersymmetric SM (large \(\tan\beta\) regime)** | Higgs‑mediated “double‑penguin” diagram; also neutralino‑loop contributions to scalar operators | Similar scaling as 2HDM, but with additional \(\frac{\mu A_t}{M_{\tilde t}^2}\) factor; can give \(C_{S,P}\sim10^{-5}\) for \(\tan\beta\gtrsim30\) and moderate SUSY masses. | Correlated with \(B\!\to X_s\gamma\), \(B_s\) mixing, and \(g-2\) of the muon. | | **Leptoquark \(S_1\) (scalar, \(SU(2)_L\) singlet)** | Tree‑level exchange generates \( (\bar s P_R b)(\bar e P_L e)\) after Fierz rearrangement | \(C_S \approx \frac{y_{be}\,y_{se}^\ast}{2M_{LQ}^2}\). For \(y\sim0.1\) and \(M_{LQ}=1\) TeV, \(C_S\sim5\times10^{-6}\). | Same leptoquark also contributes to \(b\to s\nu\nu\) and to the charged‑current anomalies (\(R_{D^{(*)}}\)). | | **Z′ with vector‑like couplings to electrons and scalar mixing** | Generates \(\mathcal{O}_{S,P}\) only at one loop if Z′ mixes with a heavy scalar; typically very suppressed, but can be sizable if the scalar sector is extended (e.g., a light dark‑photon mixing with a CP‑odd Higgs). | Model‑dependent; can reach \(C_{S,P}\sim10^{-5}\) for \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) couplings and sub‑TeV mediators. | Accompanied by visible dilepton resonances, dark‑photon searches, and modifications of \(B\to K^{(*)}\ell\ell\). | | **Axion‑like particles (ALP) with flavor‑changing couplings** | Pseudoscalar ALP exchange yields an effective \(\mathcal{O}_P\). | For a light ALP (\(m_a\ll m_{B_s}\)), \(C_P\sim \frac{g_{b s a} g_{e e a}}{m_a^2}\). Even with \(g\sim10^{-5}\) and \(m_a\sim100\) MeV one obtains \(C_P\sim10^{-5}\). | Leads to a resonant peak in the \(e^+e^-\) invariant mass if the ALP is on‑shell; complementary searches in \(B\to K a\), \(a\to e^+e^-\). | **Key point:** *A measured branching fraction larger than the SM by a factor of ≳ 10 would immediately point to scalar/pseudoscalar operators with Wilson coefficients of order \(10^{-5}\), a regime that is essentially invisible in the muon mode because the muon helicity suppression is already weak.* --- ## 5. user_message: Could you show the same helicity‑suppression calculation using the B_d mass instead of the B_s mass, and give the resulting numerical electron‑to‑muon suppression factor and the estimated B_d→e+e− branching fraction?
assistant_response:
### 1.  Helicity‑suppression factor for a generic neutral‑\(B_q\) meson  

For a pseudoscalar meson \(B_q^0\;(q=s,d)\) the short‑distance decay amplitude of  
\(B_q^0\!\to \ell^+\ell^-\) contains the factor  

\[
\mathcal A\;\propto\; m_\ell \;,
\qquad
\Gamma\;\propto\; m_\ell^{\,2}\,,
\]

so that the **branching fraction** carries the dimensionless factor  

\[
\boxed{\,\frac{m_\ell^{2}}{m_{B_q}^{2}}\,}.
\]

All other ingredients (CKM elements, loop function \(Y(x_t)\), decay constant \(f_{B_q}\) …) are *the same* for the two lepton flavours; the only difference between the electron and the muon modes is this factor.

---

### 2.  Numerical values (PDG 2024)

| Quantity | Symbol | Value |
|----------|--------|-------|
| \(B_d^0\) mass | \(m_{B_d}\) | \(5.279\,\text{GeV}\) |
| Muon mass | \(m_{\mu}\) | \(0.105658\,\text{GeV}\) |
| Electron mass | \(m_{e}\) | \(0.000511\,\text{GeV}\) |

---

### 3.  Helicity‑suppression factors

#### 3.1 Muon mode  

\[
\frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{m_{B_d}^{2}}
  =\frac{(0.105658)^{2}}{(5.279)^{2}}
  =\frac{0.01117}{27.86}
  \approx 4.0\times10^{-4}.
\]

#### 3.2 Electron mode  

\[
\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{B_d}^{2}}
  =\frac{(0.000511)^{2}}{(5.279)^{2}}
  =\frac{2.61\times10^{-7}}{27.86}
  \approx 9.4\times10^{-9}.
\]

#### 3.3 Ratio (electron / muon)  

\[
\frac{m_{e}^{2}/m_{B_d}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}/m_{B_d}^{2}}
  =\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}}
  =\left(\frac{0.000511}{0.105658}\right)^{2}
  \approx 2.3\times10^{-5}.
\]

So **the electron mode is suppressed by a factor of roughly \(2\times10^{-5}\) (i.e. about \(10^{-5}\)) relative to the muon mode**, exactly the same numerical factor that appears for the \(B_s\) system because the meson mass cancels in the ratio.

---

### 4.  Estimated Standard‑Model branching fraction for \(B_d^0\!\to e^+e^-\)

The SM prediction for the muon channel (latest flavour‑averaged value) is  

\[
\mathcal B\!\left(B_d^0\!\to \mu^{+}\mu^{-}\right)_{\!{\rm SM}}
        = (1.06 \pm 0.09)\times10^{-10}.
\]

Multiplying by the electron‑to‑muon helicity factor:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B\!\left(B_d^0\!\to e^{+}e^{-}\right)_{\!{\rm SM}}
&\;=\;
\mathcal B\!\left(B_d^0\!\to \mu^{+}\mu^{-}\right)_{\!{\rm SM}}
\times\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}}\\[4pt]
&\;\approx\;
(1.06\times10^{-10})\times(2.3\times10^{-5})\\[4pt]
&\;\approx\;
2.4\times10^{-15}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\mathcal B\!\left(B_d^0\!\to e^{+}e^{-}\right)_{\!{\rm SM}}
\;\simeq\;2\times10^{-15}\; } 
\]

The theoretical uncertainty is dominated by the same sources that affect the muon channel (decay constant \(f_{B_d}\), CKM factor \(|V_{tb}V_{td}^\ast|\)), and is at the few‑percent level; the **overall error is negligible compared with the \(\sim10^{-15}\) central value**.

---

### 5.  Quick sanity check – comparison with the \(B_s\) case  

*For \(B_s\):*  

\[
\mathcal B(B_s\!\to\mu\mu)_{\!{\rm SM}}\!\approx3.66\times10^{-9},
\qquad
\mathcal B(B_s\!\to e e)_{\!{\rm SM}}
  \approx3.66\times10^{-9}\times2.3\times10^{-5}
  \approx 8\times10^{-14}.
\]

*For \(B_d\):*  

\[
\mathcal B(B_d\!\to\mu\mu)_{\!{\rm SM}}\!\approx1.06\times10^{-10},
\qquad
\mathcal B(B_d\!\to e e)_{\!{\rm SM}}
  \approx2.4\times10^{-15}.
\]

The **electron‑to‑muon suppression factor is the same** (≈ \(2\times10^{-5}\)) in both cases; the absolute numbers differ because the underlying CKM factor \(|V_{tb}V_{td}^\ast|\) is smaller than \(|V_{tb}V_{ts}^\ast|\) and because \(m_{B_d}<m_{B_s}\) by a modest amount.

---

### 6.  Bottom line  

* Using the \(B_d\) mass gives a helicity‑suppression factor of \(9.4\times10^{-9}\) for the electron mode, versus \(4.0\times10^{-4}\) for the muon mode.  
* The **ratio** of the two is **\(2.3\times10^{-5}\)** – i.e. the electron channel is suppressed by roughly **\(10^{-5}\)** relative to the muon channel.  
* The SM predicts  

\[
\boxed{\mathcal B(B_d^0\!\to e^{+}e^{-})\;\approx\;2\times10^{-15}},
\]

far below any current or near‑future experimental sensitivity, which is why experiments only quote limits (e.g. \(\mathcal B<2.8\times10^{-9}\) at 90 % CL from LHCb). The extreme helicity suppression, together with the already tiny CKM‑induced rate, makes \(B_d\to e^+e^-\) an essentially unobservable SM process.

Below is a **step‑by‑step, full‑precision calculation** that starts from the particle‑mass numbers recommended by the 2022 PDG and ends with the numerical values you asked for:

| Quantity | Symbol | PDG 2022 value (rounded to the shown digits) |
|----------|--------|----------------------------------------------|
| \(B_{s}^{0}\) mass | \(m_{B_{s}}\) | \(5.366\,77\;\text{GeV}\) |
| Muon mass | \(m_{\mu}\) | \(0.105\,658\,3745\;\text{GeV}\) |
| Electron mass | \(m_{e}\) | \(0.000\,510\,998\,9461\;\text{GeV}\) |
| Fine‑structure constant at the weak scale (used in the SM expression) – not needed for the ratio | \(\alpha\) | \(1/127.9\) |
| Fermi constant – not needed for the ratio | \(G_{F}\) | \(1.1663787\times10^{-5}\;\text{GeV}^{-2}\) |
| Lifetime \(\tau_{B_{s}}\) – not needed for the ratio | \(\tau_{B_{s}}\) | \(1.509\;\text{ps}\) |

---

## 1.  Helicity‑suppression factor for a generic lepton  \(\ell\)

For a pseudoscalar decay mediated by the axial‑vector operator \(\mathcal O_{10}\) the decay width contains the factor  

\[
\Gamma(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\ell^{+}\ell^{-})\;\propto\; m_{\ell}^{2}\,\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_{\ell}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}}}\; .
\]

Because \(m_{\ell}\ll m_{B_{s}}\) (even for the muon) the phase‑space square‑root is essentially **1**:

\[
\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_{\ell}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}}}=1-\mathcal O\!\left(\frac{m_{\ell}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}}\right)
\approx 0.9999\;\;( \text{muon})\;,\;0.99999999\;(\text{electron}) .
\]

Thus the **helicity‑suppression factor** is practically just  

\[
\boxed{ \frac{m_{\ell}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}} } .
\]

---

## 2.  Numerical evaluation of the ratio  \(m_{e}^{2}/m_{\mu}^{2}\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
m_{e}^{2} & = (0.000\,510\,998\,9461\;\text{GeV})^{2}
          = 2.610\,180\,08\times10^{-7}\;\text{GeV}^{2},\\[4pt]
m_{\mu}^{2} & = (0.105\,658\,3745\;\text{GeV})^{2}
            = 1.116\,744\,74\times10^{-2}\;\text{GeV}^{2},\\[4pt]
\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}} & =
\frac{2.610\,180\,08\times10^{-7}}{1.116\,744\,74\times10^{-2}}
= 2.337\,354\,4\times10^{-5}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{\,\displaystyle\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}} = 2.34\times10^{-5}\,}
\]

Rounded to **one significant figure** this is indeed **\( \sim 10^{-5}\)**, confirming the statement you wanted to check.

---

## 3.  Helicity‑suppression factor for the two specific leptons

Using \(m_{B_{s}} = 5.366\,77\;\text{GeV}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}}
&= \frac{1.116\,744\,74\times10^{-2}}{(5.366\,77)^{2}}\\
&= \frac{1.116\,744\,74\times10^{-2}}{28.801\,0}\\
&= 3.877\,89\times10^{-4},\\[6pt]
\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}}
&= \frac{2.610\,180\,08\times10^{-7}}{28.801\,0}\\
&= 9.063\,03\times10^{-9}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Notice that  

\[
\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}}\;=\;
\frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}}\times\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}}
\;=\;
(3.8779\times10^{-4})\times(2.3373\times10^{-5})
\approx 9.06\times10^{-9},
\]

which is a useful cross‑check.

---

## 4.  From the known \(B_{s}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\) branching fraction to the electron mode

The SM prediction (including all short‑ and long‑distance pieces, NNLO QCD, NLO EW, lattice‑QCD decay constant, etc.) is

\[
\boxed{\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})_{\rm SM}
      = (3.66\pm0.14)\times10^{-9}} .
\]

Because **the short‑distance Wilson coefficients are the same** for \(\mu\) and \(e\) (the SM has no scalar/pseudoscalar contributions), the *only* difference between the two modes is the helicity factor.  Therefore

\[
\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to e^{+}e^{-})_{\rm SM}
=
\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to\mu^{+}\mu^{-})_{\rm SM}\times
\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}}.
\]

Insert the numbers:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to e^{+}e^{-})_{\rm SM}
&= (3.66\times10^{-9})\times(2.3373544\times10^{-5})\\[4pt]
&= 8.55\times10^{-14}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If we propagate the ±0.14 × 10⁻⁹ uncertainty on the muon branching fraction (≈ 3.8 %), the absolute error on the electron mode is  

\[
\delta\mathcal{B}(B_{s}\!\to e^{+}e^{-})\approx
0.038\times 8.55\times10^{-14}
\simeq 3.3\times10^{-15},
\]

so we can quote

\[
\boxed{\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to e^{+}e^{-})_{\rm SM}
      = (8.5\pm0.3)\times10^{-14}} .
\]

---

## 5.  Summary of the numerical chain

1. **Lepton‑mass squares** (exact PDG values)  

   \[
   m_{e}^{2}=2.610\,180\times10^{-7}\;\text{GeV}^{2},\qquad
   m_{\mu}^{2}=1.116\,7447\times10^{-2}\;\text{GeV}^{2}.
   \]

2. **Ratio of the squares**  

   \[
   \displaystyle\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{\mu}^{2}} = 2.34\times10^{-5}.
   \]

3. **Helicity factor for the \(B_{s}\) meson**  

   \[
   \frac{m_{e}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}} = 9.06\times10^{-9},\qquad
   \frac{m_{\mu}^{2}}{m_{B_{s}}^{2}} = 3.88\times10^{-4}.
   \]

4. **Predictive step**  

   \[
   \boxed{\mathcal{B}(B_{s}^{0}\!\to e^{+}e^{-})\;\approx\;
          (3.66\times10^{-9})\times(2.34\times10^{-5})
          \;=\;8.5\times10^{-14}} .
   \]

Thus the **electron mode is roughly \(2.3\times10^{-5}\) (i.e. ≈ 10⁻⁵) times more suppressed than the muon mode**, and its Standard‑Model branching fraction is of order **\(10^{-13}\)–\(10^{-14}\)**—far below any current or near‑future experimental reach.

assistant_response:
# Benchmark Suite for Comparing a Lightweight Primal‑Dual (PD) Scheme vs. an OCO‑Projected Gradient (OCO‑PG) Implementation **Target platform** – micro‑grid controller (e.g., Cortex‑A53 or similar) with ≤ 1 ms decision budget, 256 KB flash, 64 KB RAM. **Goal** – prove that the chosen algorithm satisfies **real‑time safety**, **computational**, and **accuracy** requirements before field deployment. --- ## 1. Test Matrix Overview | **Test #** | **Name** | **What it measures** | **Key Metrics** | **Pass‑Fail Criterion** | |------------|----------|----------------------|----------------|--------------------------| | 1 | **Synthetic Stress‑Load** | Worst‑case computational load & numerical stability | • Wall‑clock time per decision (µs) < budget
• Max CPU utilisation %
• Number of Newton iterations (OCO‑PG)
• Dual‑vector overflow / NaN events (PD) | PD: ≤ 30 µs, no overflow.
OCO‑PG: ≤ 700 µs, ≤ 5 Newton iters, final residual ‖Az‑S‖₂ ≤ 10⁻⁶. | | 2 | **Real‑World Trace Replay** | End‑to‑end latency & throughput on realistic demand streams | • End‑to‑end latency (t_total) < 1 ms
• Acceptance ratio (AR) vs. offline optimum
• Cumulative revenue loss (ΔRev) | PD: AR ≥ 95 % of offline optimum, ΔRev ≤ 5 % ; OCO‑PG: same, plus projection feasibility 100 %. | | 3 | **Voltage‑Safety Monte‑Carlo** | Probability of violating voltage limits under forecast errors | • Violation probability (P_viol) < 10⁻⁴
• Empirical CDF of voltage error | Both: P_viol ≤ 10⁻⁴. PD may be allowed a tiny safety‑margin slack (see §4). | | 4 | **Power‑Flow Consistency Check** | Accuracy of the **apparent‑power** model (norm) after each decision | • Norm error ε_S = max_t|‖A x_t‖₂ – S| / S < 10⁻⁵ (OCO‑PG)
• Dual‑price bound violation (ε_dual) < 10⁻⁴ (PD) | PD: ε_dual ≤ 10⁻⁴. OCO‑PG: ε_S ≤ 10⁻⁵. | | 5 | **Robustness to Parameter Drift** | Sensitivity to slowly changing line impedances or sensor bias | • Performance degradation slope (ΔAR / Δparameter) < 0.5 % per 5 % drift
• Auto‑re‑tune frequency needed | Both: Must stay within bounds for at least 24 h without retune. | | 6 | **Memory‑Footprint & Determinism** | Resource usage and worst‑case execution time (WCET) analysis | • Static RAM usage (KB) < 40 KB
• Flash size (KB) < 200 KB
• WCET ≤ 95 % of 1 ms budget | PD: ≤ 10 KB RAM, ≤ 30 KB flash.
OCO‑PG: ≤ 30 KB RAM, ≤ 60 KB flash. | | 7 | **Fail‑Safe Fallback Test** | Behaviour when the algorithm cannot finish in time or encounters numerical failure | • Time to switch to safe‑curtail mode (µs)
• Safe‑curtail loss (ΔRev_safe) | Both must trigger safe‑curtail ≤ 5 µs after detection and keep ΔRev_safe ≤ 2 % of total revenue. | | 8 | **Power‑Cycle & Warm‑Start Test** | Effect of controller power‑on/off cycles on convergence | • Number of warm‑start iterations to reach steady state (< 3)
• Steady‑state latency after warm‑start | PD: 1 warm‑start iteration; OCO‑PG: ≤ 2 iterations. | | 9 | **Integration Latency Test** | End‑to‑end pipeline latency including communication (CAN/Modbus) | • Total loop time (sensor → decision → actuation) < 2 ms | Both must be ≤ 2 ms. | |10| **Energy‑Cost Trade‑off Sensitivity**| Impact of the algorithm’s step‑size / η on revenue vs. safety slack | • Pareto curve (ΔRev vs. P_viol) – should dominate baseline | PD/ OCO‑PG curves must lie **above** the baseline (linear‑only) curve for the same safety slack. | --- ## 2. Detailed Description of Each Test ### Test 1 – Synthetic Stress‑Load * **Input:** Randomly generated request vectors `d_t ∈ ℝⁿ` (n = 30–60 variables) drawn from a heavy‑tailed distribution (Pareto α = 1.5) to create occasional huge apparent‑power spikes. * **Procedure:** Run the controller for 10⁶ decisions, record per‑iteration CPU cycles, peak memory, and for OCO‑PG the number of interior‑point Newton steps taken to converge. * **Why:** Guarantees that the algorithm can survive worst‑case computational bursts that may appear during sudden DER activation. ### Test 2 – Real‑World Trace Replay * **Dataset:** At least 3 months of high‑resolution (1 s) DER request logs from a comparable micro‑grid (solar PV output, storage charge/discharge bids, load curtailment requests). Include at least 5 % of events that push the apparent‑power limit. * **Procedure:** Replay the timestamps **exactly** as they occurred, feeding each request to the algorithm. Compare the cumulative revenue to an offline optimal solution computed by a mixed‑integer SOCP solver (Gurobi/CPLEX) on the same 3‑day windows. * **Metric calculation:** - Acceptance Ratio (AR) = #accepted / #total. - ΔRev = (Revenue_opt – Revenue_algo) / Revenue_opt. ### Test 3 – Voltage‑Safety Monte‑Carlo * **Model:** Use the linearized DistFlow model `V = V₀ – R·P – X·Q` plus a second‑order term to emulate AC non‑linearity. * **Monte‑Carlo:** For each time step, perturb the forecasted real/reactive powers with zero‑mean Gaussian noise (σ = 5 % of nominal). Run the algorithm, then run a full AC power‑flow to check the true voltage. Record any violation of `[V_min, V_max]`. * **Goal:** Show that the algorithm’s safety margin (e.g., `V_min+δ, V_max−δ`) is sufficient to keep violations below the target probability. ### Test 4 – Power‑Flow Consistency Check * **PD:** After each decision, compute the dual slack `s = S – λᵀ A x`. ## Hybrid “Fast‑Primal‑Dual + Periodic Exact Projection” Controller The idea is to **use the ultra‑light primal‑dual (PD) update on every incoming request** (Δt ≈ 1–10 ms) and **intermittently enforce exact feasibility** by solving a single SOCP projection on the current allocation vector **x**. The projection acts as a **safety‑net** that pulls the state back into the true second‑order‑cone (SOC) feasible set \[ \mathcal{F}\;=\;\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;|\;\|A x\|_{2}\le S\}, \] or, when several independent cones are present, \[ \mathcal{F}\;=\;\bigcap_{c=1}^{C}\{x\;|\;\|A_c x\|_{2}\le S_c\}. \] Below is a complete design recipe that tells you **when** to trigger the projection, **how** to set the triggering parameters, and **what** performance you can expect on a typical low‑power grid controller (ARM‑Cortex‑A53 / M4, 256 KB flash, 64 KB RAM, 1 ms decision budget). --- ### 1. High‑frequency primal‑dual loop | Step (executed every request *t*) | Cost | |-----------------------------------|------| | Compute reduced cost `ρ_t = p_t – λ^\top A d_t` (scalar) | O(n) | | Accept if `ρ_t ≥ 0` and `‖A d_t‖₂ ≤ S – λ^\top A d_t` | O(n) | | If accepted:
 `x ← x + d_t`
 `λ ← λ + η·(A d_t /‖A d_t‖₂)` | O(n) | | If rejected: do nothing | – | *All operations are plain vector arithmetic; on a 2 GHz Cortex‑A53 the whole loop finishes in **≈ 15 µs** for n = 30 (typical feeder).* --- ### 2. When to launch the exact SOCP projection Two complementary triggers are used; the projection is launched **as soon as either condition becomes true**. | Trigger | Definition | Rationale | Typical parameter range | |--------|------------|-----------|--------------------------| | **(a) Dual‑norm threshold** | `‖λ‖₂ ≥ ρ_thr` | The dual vector grows roughly proportional to the “used” portion of the SOC ball. When it gets large the PD update starts to lose accuracy (the linear‑approximation of the cone surface is poor). | ρ_thr ∈ [0.6 S, 0.8 S] (scaled by ‖A‖₂ if A is not identity). | | **(b) Primal residual threshold** | `r_t = ‖A x‖₂ – S ≥ ε_thr` (positive slack violation) | Directly measures how far the current primal point has drifted **outside** the feasible SOC because of rounding or cumulative error. | ε_thr ≈ 0.03 S … 0.05 S (i.e., 3–5 % of the apparent‑power limit). | | **(c) Periodic timer** | Every **K** decisions (e.g., K = 100–500) *or* every **T_sec** (e.g., T = 0.5 s) | Guarantees a projection even if the two thresholds are never crossed (e.g., when the system stays well inside the cone). | K chosen such that the total CPU for the projection fits the budget (see §3). | **Why both (a) and (b)?** - (a) monitors the *dual* side – useful when the PD algorithm accepts many small requests that increment λ slowly but eventually saturate the cone. - (b) monitors the *primal* side – catches the situation where λ has been deliberately capped (for stability) and the state drifts outward. --- ### 3. Choosing *K* and the thresholds #### 3.1 Computational budget calculation Assume the controller must finish **all work** (PD + possible projection) within a **100 ms control window** (typical for distribution automation). | Component | Execution time (typical) | |-----------|---------------------------| | PD update per request | 15 µs | | Requests per window (Δt = 10 ms) | 10 | | Total PD time per window | 150 µs | | SOCP projection (dense A, n = 30) | 300 µs (5–10 Newton iterations) | | **Maximum number of projections** per window | \((100 ms – 150 µs) / 300 µs ≈ 330\) | Thus we can afford **several hundred projections** per second on this hardware. In practice we keep the projection **much rarer** (to preserve head‑room for communications, measurement processing, etc.). A safe rule is: \[ \boxed{K \in [100,\, 400]\;\;\text{requests} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \text{projection every } 1\!-\!4\text{ s}}. \] If the system is **highly volatile** (large ramping DERs), shrink K to **100** (≈ 1 s). If the load profile is smooth, you can raise K to **500** (≈ 5 s) and rely more on the dual‑norm threshold. #### 3.2 Threshold scaling Let `σ_max = ‖A‖₂` (largest singular value) and `σ_min = λ_min(AᵀA)^{1/2}` (smallest). Set \[ \boxed{\rho_{\text{thr}} = \alpha_{\lambda}\; \frac{S}{\sigma_{\max}},\qquad \epsilon_{\text{thr}} = \alpha_{r}\; S}, \] with typical **α‑values**: | Parameter | Recommended α range | Effect | |-----------|--------------------|--------| | α_λ (dual‑norm) | 0.6 – 0.8 | Larger α → fewer projections, higher risk of drift. | | α_r (primal residual) | 0.03 – 0.05 | Larger α = more tolerance before correction; choose the lower end if voltage safety is critical. | **Why divide by σ_max for λ?** The dual vector lives in the *dual cone* and its natural scale is `S/σ_max`. Using this scaling makes the threshold **dimensionally homogeneous** across different network topologies. --- ### 4. Projection step (what the controller actually solves) At a trigger moment we solve \[ \min_{z}\;\|z-x\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\|A z\|_{2}\le S . \] Because the objective is Euclidean, the **optimal projection** has a closed‑form expression when `A` is diagonal (or can be diagonalised offline). If `A = U Σ V^{\top}` is known, we can pre‑compute `U, Σ, V`. Then 1. Compute `y = V^{\top} x` (O(n²) once, store `V`). 2. Solve the scalar problem \[ \min_{w}\;\|w-y\|_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\|\Sigma w\|_{2}\le S . \] This reduces to a **single‑parameter shrinkage**: find a scalar `τ ≥ 0` such that \[ w_i = \frac{y_i}{1+τ \sigma_i^{2}},\qquad \sum_i \frac{\sigma_i^{2} y_i^{2}}{(1+τ \sigma_i^{2})^{2}} = S^{2}. \] Solve for `τ` via a short Newton or bisection (≤ 5 iterations). 3. Recover `z = V w`. When the controller cannot hold `V` (memory limit) we fall back to the **dual‑cone Newton** method: \[ \begin{aligned} \text{Find } \mu \ge 0 \text{ s.t. } &\|A(x - \mu A^{\top}v)\|_{2}=S,\\ v = \frac{A x}{\|A x\|_{2}} . \end{aligned} \] Only a **scalar root‑finding** is needed; each evaluation requires one matrix‑vector multiply (`A v`). This is the fastest way to obtain an exact projection on a tiny MCU (≈ 200 µs for n = 30). --- ### 5. Full algorithm pseudo‑code ```c // ---------- PARAMETERS ---------- const double eta = 0.8 / kappa(A); // PD step size const double rho_thr = 0.7 * S / sigma_max; const double eps_thr = 0.04 * S; const int K = 200; // periodic trigger // ---------- STATE ---------- Vector x = zeros(n); // current allocation Vector lambda = zeros(m); // dual for each cone (m = #cones) int counter = 0; // ---------- MAIN LOOP (called for every new demand) ---------- void onRequest(Demand d, double price) { // 1. reduced cost double rc = price - dot(lambda, A*d); // O(n) // 2. feasibility test double normAd = norm2(A*d); if (rc >= 0 && normAd <= S - dot(lambda, A*d)) { // accept x += d; // O(n) lambda += eta * (A*d) / normAd; // O(n) } // else reject (do nothing) // 3. increment counter & test triggers counter++; bool trigger = false; if (norm2(lambda) >= rho_thr) trigger = true; if (norm2(A*x) - S >= eps_thr) trigger = true; if (counter >= K) trigger = true; // 4. safety correction if needed if (trigger) { x = project_onto_SOC(x, A, S); // SOCP projection (≈200‑600 µs) // reset dual to a consistent value: lambda = (S / norm2(A*x)) * (A*x); // point on dual cone counter = 0; // restart periodic timer } } ``` - `project_onto_SOC` can be the **dual‑cone Newton** routine (scalar root‑find) or the **pre‑diagonalised shrinkage** routine if memory permits. - After the projection the dual vector is **re‑initialized** to the *closest* dual feasible point (`λ = (S/‖A x‖) A x`). This eliminates any drift that could have accumulated while the PD updates were running. --- ### 6. Expected performance | Metric | Predictive model | |--------|------------------| | **Throughput loss vs. pure PD** | On average **≤ 1 %** extra rejections because the projection only *tightens* the feasible set; the dual is re‑aligned afterwards, so the PD loop resumes its original acceptance rate. | | **Safety violation probability** | With the combined thresholds the probability that `‖A x‖₂ > S` for more than one time step is **< 10⁻⁴** in realistic Monte‑Carlo simulations (load forecast error σ ≈ 5 %). | | **CPU utilisation** (Cortex‑A53, 1 ms slot) | PD loop ≈ 15 µs per request. One projection every 200 requests ≈ 300 µs → total < 1 % of the 1 ms budget. | | **Memory footprint** | PD data: 2 × n ≈ 240 bytes. Projection routine (dual‑cone Newton) needs only a few temporaries → < 2 KB total. | | **Robustness to poor conditioning** | The dual‑norm threshold automatically forces a projection before λ grows to the point where numerical errors dominate. Empirically κ(A) up to 30 still yields stable operation with ρ_thr = 0.7 S/σ_max. | --- ### 7. Practical tuning checklist 1. **Offline compute** `σ_max = ‖A‖₂` and `κ(A)`. 2. **Pick η** = `0.8 / κ(A)` (theoretical optimum ≤ 1/κ). 3. **Set** `ρ_thr = 0.7·S/σ_max`. If after a few days you see the dual norm hitting the ceiling too early, raise α_λ to 0.8. 4. **Run a short pilot** (≈ 30 min) and log `r_t = ‖A x‖−S`. If `r_t` routinely exceeds **0.03 S**, lower α_r to 0.025. 5. **Adjust K** so that the projection frequency never exceeds **5 %** of the total CPU budget (measure actual projection time on the target MCU). 6. **Validate** by running a full AC power‑flow check on a subset of the logged states; the projection must keep the true voltages inside the regulatory band (e.g., 0.95‑1.05 p.u.). --- ## 8. Bottom line – when to use the hybrid scheme | Scenario | Hybrid PD + Periodic Projection | Reason | |----------|--------------------------------|--------| | **High‑speed inverter droop (≤ 10 ms per request), limited RAM** | **Yes** – primal‑dual handles the bulk of the work, projection runs rarely (K ≈ 200) and costs < 1 % CPU. | | **Medium‑speed (≈ 0.5 s) market‑clearing, safety‑critical voltage limits** | **Yes** – periodic projection guarantees exact SOC feasibility; thresholds can be relaxed because timing is generous. | | **Very large network (n > 200) with dense A** | **Possibly not** – each projection becomes expensive (O(n · log 1/ε)). Consider a **decomposed** version: run PD locally per zone and only project *zone‑aggregates* centrally. | | **Platform without floating‑point unit** | **No** – the projection needs at least 32‑bit float; stay with pure PD and add a very conservative safety margin (lower S by 10 %). | | **Research prototype where code size is irrelevant** | **Yes**, the hybrid gives the best of both worlds and lets you explore the trade‑off curve experimentally. | In short, **the hybrid controller is the recommended practical compromise**: keep the cheap, deterministic primal‑dual updates running at the full arrival rate, and **guard the system with an exact SOC projection** triggered either by a **dual‑norm cue**, a **primal slack cue**, or a **periodic timer**. By choosing - `K` in the **100‑400** range, - `ρ_thr ≈ 0.6–0.8 · S/σ_max`, - `ε_thr ≈ 0.03–0.05 · S`, you obtain **near‑optimal throughput**, **hard safety guarantees**, and **CPU usage well within the limits of a modest grid‑edge controller**.
