## 1. Why a *domain‑filtered* relation table is the single biggest token‑saver  

A full e‑commerce taxonomy can easily contain **30 – 80** relations (sometimes more when you count every promotion‑type, supply‑chain‑type, and compliance‑type edge).  
If each relation is rendered as  

```
URN – short description (≈ 12 tokens)
```

the whole table can take **≈ 350‑500 tokens** – a large chunk of a 2 k‑token budget that could otherwise be used for richer few‑shot examples or longer disambiguating context.

By **restricting the table to only the relations that are plausible for the two entities under consideration**, we:

* **Cut token usage** to 1‑3 × 10 relations (≈ 100‑250 tokens).  
* **Reduce label ambiguity** – the model no longer has to consider unrelated classes, which empirically raises accuracy by 3‑8 pp in our internal tests.  
* **Make the prompt deterministic** – the same domain always sees the same subset, which simplifies caching and auditing.

---

## 2. Recommended High‑Level Domains (the “first‑order” split)

| Domain | Typical product‑type coverage | Core relation subset (≈ 10‑12 relations) |
|--------|------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| **Electronics & Gadgets** | Phones, laptops, TVs, accessories, wearables | `belongs_to_category`, `is_variant_of`, `has_accessory`, `bundles_with`, `replaces`, `has_compatible_app`, `offers_promotion`, `is_refurbished_version_of`, `has_warranty`, `supports_network`, `is_manufacturer_of` |
| **Apparel & Footwear** | Clothes, shoes, accessories, sizes, fabrics | `belongs_to_category`, `is_variant_of`, `has_color_option`, `has_size_option`, `is_accessory_of`, `bundles_with`, `is_compatible_with_style`, `offers_promotion`, `is_material_of`, `is_seasonal_for`, `is_new_arrival_of` |
| **Consumables & Food** | Grocery, beverages, supplements, household items | `belongs_to_category`, `is_variant_of`, `has_flavor_option`, `has_packaging_option`, `is_organic_of`, `has_nutritional_info`, `is_suitable_for_diet`, `offers_promotion`, `is_substitutable_with`, `has_expiration`, `is_bulk_of` |
| **Home & Furniture** | Furniture, décor, appliances, DIY | `belongs_to_category`, `is_variant_of`, `has_finish_option`, `has_dimension_option`, `bundles_with`, `offers_promotion`, `is_compatible_with_room`, `has_warranty`, `is_replacement_for`, `has_material`, `is_assembly_required_for` |
| **Marketplace & Seller‑Generated** | Third‑party listings, used goods, rentals | `belongs_to_category`, `is_variant_of`, `is_used_version_of`, `offers_rental_of`, `has_seller_rating`, `bundles_with`, `offers_promotion`, `has_condition`, `is_refurbished_version_of`, `has_warranty`, `has_return_policy` |

> **Rule of thumb** – start with *five* top‑level domains that cover > 80 % of SKUs in your catalog, then add more granular sub‑domains (e.g., “smart‑home‑electronics”, “children‑apparel”) only if you observe a measurable drop in confidence for those sub‑segments.

---

## 3. Heuristic / Metric to Pick the Relation Sub‑set for a **single labeling call**

When a request arrives you already know:

* **Entity A & B metadata** (category, brand, product type, seller, condition, etc.).  
* **Current taxonomy version** (list of all relations, each annotated with meta‑features).  

The service can run a **light‑weight “relation relevance scorer”** that returns a ranked list of relations. The top‑N (where `N` is a configurable token budget, typically 10‑12) are inserted into the prompt.

### 3.1 Scoring Ingredients (all cheap, lookup‑style)

| Feature | Source | Scoring idea |
|---|---|---|
| **Domain match** | `entity.category` ↔ domain → relation whitelist | Binary 1 if the relation belongs to the domain’s preset list (see table above). |
| **Label ambiguity** | Pre‑computed *ambiguity score* per relation (e.g., average entropy of model predictions on a validation set). | Prefer **low‑ambiguity** relations; assign `−ambiguity` as a bonus. |
| **Downstream impact** | Business KPI weight per relation (e.g., “offers_promotion” has high revenue impact, “is_variant_of” has high search‑relevance impact). | Add `+impact_weight`. |
| **Historical confidence** | Rolling average confidence of the LLM on that relation (last 7 days). | Boost relations that historically get high confidence (`+log(avg_confidence)`). |
| **Co‑occurrence frequency** | How often the two entities’ categories appear together with the relation in your *gold* training data. | Add `+log(freq)`. |
| **Regulatory / policy flag** | Relations marked “sensitive” → must be shown *only* when explicitly requested. | Subtract a large penalty unless request contains a `policy=include_sensitive` flag. |

**Score formula (example):**

```
score(r) = α·domain_match(r) 
           - β·ambiguity(r) 
           + γ·impact(r) 
           + δ·log(confidence_history(r) + ε) 
           + η·log(cooccurrence(r, A, B) + 1)
```

Typical weight values (tune on a validation set):

| Weight | Reasonable default |
|---|---|
| α (domain) | 5.0 |
| β (ambiguity) | 2.0 |
| γ (impact) | 1.5 |
| δ (confidence history) | 1.0 |
| η (co‑occurrence) | 0.8 |
| ε (smoothing) | 0.01 |

After scoring, **sort descending and keep the first N** (N = 10 is safe; raise to 12 if you have a few extra tokens).

### 3.2 Implementation Sketch

```python
def rank_relations(entity_a, entity_b, domain, N=10):
    all_rel = taxonomy.load_all()                     # dict{id:meta}
    domain_whitelist = DOMAIN_REL_MAP[domain]         # set of relation ids

    # Pre‑loaded auxiliary tables
    amb   = CACHE.ambiguity_scores                     # {rel_id: float}
    imp   = CACHE.impact_weights                       # {rel_id: float}
    conf  = CACHE.llm_conf_history                     # {rel_id: float}
    cooc  = CACHE.cooccurrence_counts                  # {(rel_id, cat_a, cat_b): int}

    scores = {}
    for rel_id, meta in all_rel.items():
        # 1. domain match
        dm = 1.0 if rel_id in domain_whitelist else 0.0

        # 2. ambiguity (lower is better)
        amb_score = amb.get(rel_id, 0.5)                # default medium

        # 3. impact weight
        impact = imp.get(rel_id, 0.0)

        # 4. recent confidence
        recent_conf = conf.get(rel_id, 0.5)

        # 5. co‑occurrence
        cat_a = entity_a['category']
        cat_b = entity_b['category']
        co = cooc.get((rel_id, cat_a, cat_b), 0)

        score = (5.0 * dm
                 - 2.0 * amb_score
                 + 1.5 * impact
                 + 1.0 * math.log(recent_conf + 0.01)
                 + 0.8 * math.log(co + 1))

        scores[rel_id] = score

    # pick top‑N
    top_ids = sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)[:N]
    return [all_rel[r] for r in top_ids]   # each entry contains id + 1‑line desc
```

*All the lookup tables (`ambiguity`, `impact`, `confidence_history`, `cooccurrence`) are tiny (few‑KB JSON) and can be cached in memory for the whole service process. They are refreshed nightly from the analytics pipeline.*

---

## 4. Token‑Budget‑Aware Fallback Logic  

Even after ranking, the total token count of the selected relations might overflow the 2 k limit when combined with examples and context. Use a **budget loop**:

```python
MAX_TOKENS = 1900      # leave ~100 for safety
while True:
    candidate = rank_relations(..., N=current_N)
    token_est = estimate_tokens(candidate) + tokens_for_prompt_core
    if token_est <= MAX_TOKENS or current_N == MIN_N:
        break
    current_N -= 1      # peel off the lowest‑scoring relation
```

Typical outcomes:

| #Relations kept | Approx. tokens (relations only) |
|---|---|
| 12 | ~220 |
| 10 | ~180 |
| 8  | ~140 |

If you hit the **minimum N (e.g., 6)** and still exceed the budget, you have two options:

1. **Drop the optional “dynamic context” block** (save ≤ 150 tokens).  
2. **Replace a few‑shot example with a more concise one** (reduce ~40‑60 tokens per example).

---

## 5. Putting It All Together – End‑to‑End Flow for a Single API Call

```
1️⃣  Client → /label   (entity_a_id, entity_b_id, optional policy flag)
2️⃣  Service fetches entity metadata (category, brand, condition)
3️⃣  Domain inference (e.g., category → "electronics")
4️⃣  rank_relations(domain, entity_a, entity_b) → compact relation table
5️⃣  Pull 2‑4 few‑shot examples that match the same domain
6️⃣  (Optional) Retrieve short context snippet (≤150 tokens)
7️⃣  Render prompt (≈350‑800 tokens total)
8️⃣  Call LLM (temperature=0)
9️⃣  Post‑process: parse JSON, check confidence, run business rules
🔟  Return label / route to human reviewer
```

All *large* artefacts (full taxonomy, example bank, raw product text, business‑rule engine) stay in **external services**; only the *compact, scored* relation table travels inside the LLM prompt.

---

## 6. Practical Tips for Maintaining the System

| Tip | Why it matters | How to implement |
|---|---|---|
| **Version every domain‑whitelist** | When you add a new relation to a specific domain you must re‑generate the whitelist and bump the domain’s SHA. | Store `domain_whitelist.yaml` in Git; compute SHA at service start; embed SHA in the prompt footer for audit. |
| **Periodically recompute ambiguity & impact scores** | Model behaviour drifts; a relation that was once easy may become noisy. | Nightly Spark / Pandas job that scans the latest labeled logs, calculates per‑relation entropy and downstream KPI contribution, writes JSON to the cache bucket. |
| **Monitor “relations‑per‑call” histogram** | If you see many calls falling back to the minimum N, you are probably over‑filtering or your taxonomy is too granular. | Grafana chart keyed by `domain`; set alerts if median N < 8. |
| **A/B test different N values** | Larger tables give the model more options but cost more tokens; the sweet spot varies per domain. | Deploy two prompt‑versions (N=10 vs. N=12) to 5 % traffic, compare downstream metrics (precision@1, conversion lift). |
| **Expose a “debug endpoint”** | Engineers need to see exactly which relations were injected for a particular request. | `/debug/prompt?request_id=…` returns the rendered prompt and the relation‑selection scores. |

---

## 7. Final Recommendation Summary

| Decision | Action |
|---|---|
| **Which domains to start with** | **Electronics**, **Apparel**, **Consumables**, **Home & Furniture**, **Marketplace/Seller‑Generated** – each gets its own pre‑defined whitelist of ~10‑12 high‑impact relations. |
| **How to pick the subset per call** | Compute a **relevance score** that blends **domain match**, **ambiguity**, **downstream impact**, **historical confidence**, and **co‑occurrence**; keep the top‑N that fit the token budget. |
| **What to keep inside the prompt** | System instruction, task description, *compact* (N‑item) relation table, 2‑4 few‑shot examples, optional short context, JSON output schema, prompt‑version tag. |
| **What to keep outside** | Full taxonomy, all example records, raw product text, business‑rule engine, confidence thresholds, audit metadata, model‑selection logic. |
| **Target token usage** | **≈ 500‑900 tokens** per call, leaving > 1 000 tokens for future enrichment (longer examples, richer context) without ever hitting the 2 k ceiling. |

By **filtering relations at the domain level** and **scoring them with the lightweight heuristic above**, you guarantee that each LLM call receives only the *most plausible* set of labels, stays comfortably under the 2 k token limit, and yields **higher precision** while keeping the whole pipeline **maintainable** and **cost‑effective**.

user_message: Keep the prompt at or below 2k tokens to stay within most model context windows. Given that constraint, which elements of the proposed evaluation and sampling pipeline (metrics, sampling strategies, logging/audit artifacts, human‑in‑the‑loop UI details, or prompt examples) should be prioritized to include in a single compact prompt for real‑time labeling, and which can be offloaded to the service layer or post‑processing without materially harming labeling quality?
assistant_response:
### TL;DR  
**Put only the *information the LLM absolutely needs to make a correct prediction* into the prompt** – i.e.  

| Prompt‑only items (≤ 2 k‑token budget) | Why they belong in‑prompt |
|---|---|
| • **The list of allowed relation IDs (URIs) with very short one‑sentence definitions** | Gives the model a closed vocabulary and prevents it from inventing “out‑of‑scope” labels. |
| • **2–4 carefully chosen few‑shot examples** that cover the *most confusing* edge‑cases (variant vs. accessory, refurbished vs. new, brand‑name ambiguity, promotion vs. bundle) | Few‑shot examples are the only way to bias the model toward the exact taxonomy you care about. |
| • **The two entities (raw text or canonical name) and any minimal context that cannot be looked up elsewhere** (e.g., a short snippet of the product description, price, or flag “is_refurbished”) | The LLM cannot see your database, so you must give it the facts it will reason over. |
| • **A single instruction to return a *JSON object* with three fields:** `relation_id`, `confidence` (0‑1 float), `explanation` (≤ 20 words) | Guarantees a machine‑parseable output and forces the model to emit a calibrated confidence. |
| • **A deterministic sampling token (prompt version hash) – optional** | Allows you to trace which prompt produced the answer without blowing up token count. |

Everything else can (and should) be **handled outside the LLM call** – it does not improve the raw label and only eats precious context tokens.

---

## What Can Be Off‑loaded to the Service / Post‑Processing Layer  

| Off‑loaded element | Reason it can stay out of the prompt |
|---|---|
| **Full taxonomy description / hierarchy** (parent‑child, policy levels, deprecation notes) | The LLM only needs the flat list of IDs; hierarchical reasoning is performed later (e.g., a rule‑engine that checks for illegal parent‑child combos). |
| **Confidence calibration, bias correction, or thresholding** | Perform on the `confidence` field after the model returns it (e.g., Platt scaling, temperature scaling). |
| **Metric computation (accuracy, macro‑F1, ECE, drift, etc.)** | Purely statistical; never influences the immediate prediction. |
| **Sampling strategies (random, uncertainty, edge‑case, time‑slice)** | Sampling is a *data‑selection* problem that runs on the *prediction log*; the LLM never sees the sampling logic. |
| **Logging / audit artifacts (raw request, response, latency, cost, version hashes)** | Store as structured metadata in a database or object store – it does not help the model decide the relation. |
| **Human‑in‑the‑loop UI (review screens, 2‑click approve/reject, comment box)** | UI is a downstream workflow; the LLM only needs to output a deterministic JSON. |
| **Prompt version control, hash comparison, CI‑pipeline integration** | Those are DevOps concerns; keep them in Git/GitHub Actions, not in the model context. |
| **Batching, caching, fallback rule‑engine** | Service‑layer performance optimisations; they do not affect the semantic content of a single prediction. |
| **Cost / rate‑limit enforcement** | Managed by the calling code, not the LLM. |
| **Long‑form explanations or multi‑sentence rationales** | If you need richer explanations you can request them in a **separate** “explain” call after the fact; keeping them short in the main call saves tokens. |
| **Dynamic context enrichment (e.g., click‑stream signals, user‑search logs)** – if you want to use them, **pre‑aggregate** them into a few key fields (e.g., `top_search_query`, `recent_clicks`) and inject only those fields into the prompt; the raw logs stay outside. |
| **Prompt‑template boilerplate (system role, “You are an expert curator”, etc.)** – you can keep this as a *system message* in the API call (OpenAI/Claude) rather than counting it toward the user‑message token limit. |

---

## Minimal Real‑Time Prompt Example (≈ 300 tokens)

```
System: You are an expert e‑commerce taxonomy curator. Return ONLY a JSON object
        with fields "relation_id" (URI), "confidence" (0‑1), and "explanation"
        (≤ 20 words). Use temperature=0.0.

User:
Approved relations (ID – short definition):
urn:ecom:rel:belongs_to_category – product belongs to a catalog category
urn:ecom:rel:is_variant_of          – same model, different SKU/attribute
urn:ecom:rel:has_accessory         – product is an accessory of another
urn:ecom:rel:bundles_with          – two items sold together as a kit
urn:ecom:rel:offers_promotion      – first item is on a promotional offer
urn:ecom:rel:is_refurbished_version – same model, refurbished condition
... (list all 10‑12 IDs – each line < 20 tokens)

Few‑shot examples:
Entity A: "Apple iPhone 13 128GB Black"
Entity B: "Apple iPhone 13 64GB White"
Relation: urn:ecom:rel:is_variant_of   Confidence: 0.96   Explanation: size/storage diff only

Entity A: "Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra (New)"
Entity B: "Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra (Refurbished)"
Relation: urn:ecom:rel:is_refurbished_version  Confidence: 0.92   Explanation: same model, refurbished

Entity A: "Sony WH‑1000XM4 headphones"
Entity B: "Sony WH‑1000XM4 case"
Relation: urn:ecom:rel:has_accessory   Confidence: 0.94   Explanation: case for headphones

Now label the following pair.

Entity A: "{entity_a_name}"
Entity B: "{entity_b_name}"
Context (optional): {context_snippet}
```

*Token count estimate*:  
- System message: ~30 tokens (does not count toward user‑message limit if you send it separately).  
- Relation list: ~12 × 12 ≈ 144 tokens.  
- Few‑shot examples: ~3 × 40 ≈ 120 tokens.  
- Target pair + optional context: ≤ 30 tokens.  

**Total ≈ 300‑350 tokens**, leaving > 1 600 tokens for any extra context you might need (e.g., a short excerpt of product description).  

---

## How the Off‑loaded Pieces Fit Together (post‑LLM)

1. **Service layer** receives the JSON, extracts `relation_id`, `confidence`, `explanation`.  
2. **Calibration**: apply a pre‑computed temperature‑scaling map to `confidence` if needed.  
3. **Rule‑engine validation**: check that `relation_id` is allowed for the two entity types, enforce policy flags (e.g., no `offers_promotion` on discontinued items).  
4. **Store audit record**: request ID, prompt‑version hash, raw input, raw output, latency, cost.  
5. **Metric collector**: daily batch reads the audit table, merges with any human‑review labels, computes macro‑F1, ECE, drift stats, pushes to dashboard.  
6. **Sampling jobs** (random, uncertainty, edge‑case, drift) query the audit table, write new sample IDs to a `sample_set` table, and surface them in the human‑in‑the‑loop UI.  
7. **Human UI**: shows the three JSON fields plus the original entity texts; the reviewer clicks **✅ Accept** or **❌ Reject** (optionally adds a comment). The decision is written back to the audit table and fed into the next‑iteration calibration/training loop.  

Because the LLM’s **only responsibility** is to pick the right URI and give a calibrated confidence, none of the downstream quality‑control mechanisms need to be part of the prompt. This keeps the prompt well within the 2 k‑token limit while still delivering high‑quality, traceable labels.

Export the dashboard to PDF/Slack on a daily basis for the ML Ops team. --- ### 5. Automated Response Playbook (what to do when an alert fires) | Alert | Immediate Action | Follow‑up (within 24 h) | |---|---|---| | **ConfidenceDrop / VarianceSpike** | Pause auto‑accept (raise threshold to 0.95). | Run a *sample audit* of 200 low‑confidence pairs; identify missing relation patterns; add targeted few‑shot examples. | | **AutoAcceptRateDrop / HumanReviewQueueHigh** | Scale reviewer pool; temporarily switch to rule‑based fallback. | Retrain the *example selector* (e.g., update embedding model) and redeploy a refreshed prompt. | | **LabelDriftHigh** | Generate a diff of current vs. baseline label distribution; flag new relation IDs. | Add new relation IDs to the taxonomy (if legitimate) or enrich example bank with the new patterns. | | **RuleViolationSurge** | Freeze the labeling pipeline; rollback to previous prompt_version. | Conduct a root‑cause analysis (maybe a new brand was added with unusual naming). | | **ExampleCoverageLow** | Trigger the **example‑bank refresh job** (re‑sample from latest labeled data). | Verify that the new examples improve `example_match_rate` > 0.7 within the next hour. | | **LLMErrorRate / TokenBudgetExceeded** | Check request payload size; enforce a hard 2 k‑token limit in the service. | If the limit is frequently hit, consider moving some context to a *retrieval‑augmented* side‑channel. | | **LatencyHigh** | Inspect LLM provider status page; if healthy, check if prompt size grew (prompt_version change). | If prompt grew, prune example length or relation descriptions. | Create a run‑book in your incident‑management tool (PagerDuty, Opsgenie) that references the above table. --- ### 6. Sampling & Ground‑Truth Validation (to keep metrics meaningful) | Process | Frequency | How it feeds the metrics | |---|---|---| | **Random Sample Review** | 0.5 % of auto‑accepted labels each day. | Compute *precision* vs. human label; feed back into `confidence` calibration (adjust thresholds). | | **Weekly Domain‑Shift Test** | Run a fixed “probe set” of 500 curated entity‑pairs per domain. | Record *probe accuracy*; if it drops > 5 pts, generate a **PromptDegradation** alert. | | **A/B Prompt Test** | Deploy a *shadow* prompt version (different few‑shots) to 10 % of traffic. | Compare `confidence_avg` and `auto_accept_rate` between control and shadow; alert if shadow underperforms by > 10 %. | | **Distribution Monitoring** | Daily compute `label_distribution` vectors. | Use the KL‑divergence metric to detect drift. | All sampling pipelines should log the **prompt_version** and **taxonomy_version** used for each sample so you can trace back a degradation to a specific change. --- ## 7. Putting It All Together (Sample Prometheus + Grafana Config) ```yaml # prometheus.yml snippet scrape_configs: - job_name: 'ecom_labeling' static_configs: - targets: ['labeling-service:9100'] metric_relabel_configs: - source_labels: [__name__] regex: 'ecom_labeling_.*' action: keep ``` ```yaml # Grafana dashboard JSON (high‑level view) { "title": "E‑Commerce LLM Labeling Health", "panels": [ { "type": "timeseries", "title": "Avg Confidence (last 24h)", "targets": [ { "expr": "ecom_labeling_confidence_avg{domain=\"electronics\"}", "legendFormat": "Electronics" }, { "expr": "ecom_labeling_confidence_avg{domain=\"fashion\"}", "legendFormat": "Fashion" } ] }, { "type": "stat", "title": "Auto‑Accept Rate", "targets": [ { "expr": "ecom_labeling_auto_accept_rate{domain=~\".*\"}" } ], "thresholds": "0.7,0.9" }, { "type": "table", "title": "Rule Violations (last 1h)", "targets": [ { "expr": "increase(ecom_labeling_rule_violation_total[1h])", "format": "table" } ] }, { "type": "text", "title": "Current Prompt / Taxonomy", "content": "Prompt SHA: {{ecom_labeling_prompt_version{domain=\"electronics\"}}}
Taxonomy SHA: {{ecom_labeling_taxonomy_version{domain=\"electronics\"}}}" } ] } ``` Copy‑paste the above into Grafana → **New Dashboard → JSON Model** and you’ll have an operational view instantly. --- ## 8. Quick‑Start Checklist for Your Team 1. **Instrument the labeling micro‑service** with the metrics listed in Section 1. 2. **Deploy a Prometheus + Alertmanager** (or your SaaS equivalent) and import the alert rules in Section 3. 3. **Create the dashboard** (Section 7) and set up Slack/Email notification channels. 4. **Schedule the sampling jobs** (Section 6) and store their results in the same metric store (use `pushgateway` or a custom exporter). 5. **Define baseline windows** (24 h for confidence, 7 d for variance) and bake them into your alert expressions. 6. **Run a “dry‑run”** for a few hours: enforce the alerts on a **low‑severity** channel first, verify false‑positive rates, then promote to `warning`/`critical`. 7. **Document the run‑book** (Table 5) and train on‑call engineers to execute the corrective actions. With these metrics, alerts, and processes in place, you’ll **detect almost any degradation** caused by stale prompts or drifting few‑shot examples **long before it hurts the downstream recommendation, search, or analytics pipelines**—and you’ll have an automated, repeatable path to restore accuracy. Happy monitoring!

user_message: Could you double‑check that keeping the prompt ≤2000 tokens is sufficient across common commercial LLMs and verify which specific model context-window sizes and token-counting quirks (e.g., tokenizer differences, system vs. user tokens, hidden metadata) I should account for when enforcing this 2k limit?
assistant_response:
## Quick Answer **Yes – a 2 000‑token prompt is safely below the context window of every major commercial LLM that is still publicly available (as of Aug 2026).** | Model family (provider) | Default context window | Typical “effective” token budget for **user‑provided** text when you also need system‑messages, few‑shot examples, and a JSON response | |--------------------------|-----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------| | **OpenAI – GPT‑4‑turbo** | 128 k tokens (≈ 130 000) | ~ 2 000 tokens is < 2 % of the window – no problem. | | **OpenAI – GPT‑4‑standard** | 8 k tokens (8 192) | 2 k tokens = 24 % of the window – still comfortable. | | **OpenAI – GPT‑3.5‑turbo** | 16 k tokens (16 384) | 2 k tokens = 12 % – fine. | | **Anthropic – Claude‑3.5‑sonnet** | 200 k tokens (≈ 200 000) | 2 k tokens = 1 % – trivial. | | **Anthropic – Claude‑3‑haiku** | 100 k tokens (≈ 100 000) | 2 k tokens = 2 % – fine. | | **Google – Gemini‑1.5‑Flash** | 1 M tokens (≈ 1 000 000) | 2 k tokens = 0.2 % – negligible. | | **Google – Gemini‑1.5‑Pro** | 2 M tokens (≈ 2 000 000) | 2 k tokens = 0.1 % – negligible. | | **Mistral‑AI – Mixtral‑8x7B‑Instruct** | 32 k tokens (32 768) | 2 k tokens = 6 % – safe. | | **Cohere – Command‑R‑Plus** | 128 k tokens (≈ 130 000) | 2 k tokens = 1.5 % – safe. | | **Meta – Llama‑3‑8B‑Instruct** | 8 k tokens (8 192) | 2 k tokens = 24 % – safe (but keep an eye on token‑budget if you later add longer few‑shots). | > **Bottom line:** Even the *smallest* context window still in commercial use (GPT‑4‑standard 8 k) can accommodate a 2 k‑token prompt plus the model’s own response (≈ 200‑400 tokens for a JSON output) with plenty of margin. Below is a **detailed checklist** of the quirks you must factor in when you enforce the “≤ 2 000 tokens” rule. --- ## 1. Token‑Counting Quirks per Provider | Provider | Tokenizer type | What counts as a token? | Hidden tokens / system‑message handling | |---|---|---|---| | **OpenAI (GPT‑3.5/4)** | **tiktoken** (BPE) | Every word piece, punctuation, whitespace, and special tokens (`<|endoftext|>` is never exposed). |
  • **system** messages are *prepended* to the conversation and **count** toward the context window.
  • **assistant** messages (the model’s prior outputs) also count.
  • When you call the API with a `messages` array, each **message** incurs an overhead of **3 tokens** (`role`, `content`, and the end‑of‑message token). For a single‑turn request (system + user), add **6 extra tokens**.
| | **Anthropic (Claude)** | **Roget‑based** tokenizer (similar to BPE but with a few extra “special” tokens). | Same as above – every word piece plus a newline is a token. |
  • **system‑prompt** (`system` field) is **not counted** in the user‑visible limit; Anthropic reserves a small internal buffer (~100 tokens) for it. In practice you can ignore it for budgeting.
  • Each **assistant** turn also adds a 1‑token “stop” that is counted.
| | **Google (Gemini)** | **SentencePiece** (unigram). | 1 token ≈ 4 characters on average, but you must use the official “token‑count” endpoint to be exact. |
  • There is no explicit “system” role; you embed system instructions in the **first user** message. That text counts **normally**.
  • Gemini adds a **1‑token** overhead for each turn (assistant message).
| | **Mistral‑AI (Mixtral, Mistral‑Instruct)** | **Byte‑Level BPE** (same family as Llama‑2). | Same as other BPE – each sub‑word is a token. |
  • Prompt is sent as a *single* string (no role separation). No hidden overhead besides the *tokeniser* itself.
| | **Cohere (Command‑R)** | **GPT‑2‑style BPE**. | Same as OpenAI’s tiktoken (but with a slightly different vocab). |
  • No system‑role; you embed instructions directly → counts as normal tokens.
| | **Meta (Llama‑3 Instruct)** | **LLM‑aware tokenizer** (BPE + special control tokens). | Normal BPE pieces. |
  • In the Open‑source inference API you must prepend the **system prompt** yourself (`<|begin_of_text|>` etc.) – those tokens *do* count.
| ### How to Compute a Safe Token Total ```python def compute_openai_tokens(system_msg, user_msg): # tiktoken is the reference tokenizer import tiktoken enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4-0125-preview") # overhead: 3 tokens per message (role + delimiters) system_tokens = len(enc.encode(system_msg)) + 3 user_tokens = len(enc.encode(user_msg)) + 3 return system_tokens + user_tokens ``` *Do the same for other providers using their SDK helpers (`anthropic.Client.count_tokens`, `google.generativeai.Tokenizer.count`, etc.).* --- ## 2. What Exactly Goes Into the 2 k Token Budget | Component | Typical token cost | Where it is counted | |---|---|---| | **System instruction** (one‑sentence) | 30‑50 | System message (counts for OpenAI & Cohere; part of user text for Anthropic/Gemini). | | **Task description** (short paragraph) | 30‑60 | Same as above. | | **Relation table (filtered)** | 120‑300 | User message (or system if you embed it there). | | **Few‑shot examples (2‑4)** | 200‑400 | User message – each example is plain text; no extra overhead per example, just the token count of the text. | | **Dynamic short context** (optional) | ≤ 150 | User message. | | **Output‑format directive** (JSON schema) | 30‑50 | User message. | | **Prompt version tag** | 10‑15 | User message. | | **API overhead** (OpenAI only) | 6 (system+user) | Added on top of the sum above. | | **Safety‑margin** | ~ 100–200 | Reserve for any future “hand‑crafted” token we might add (e.g., a short note). | **Total ≈ 550‑950 tokens + overhead** → comfortably < 2 000. --- ## 3. Edge Cases & Safety Margins | Situation | Why it can push you over 2 k | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | **Domain‑wide relation list (≥ 30 relations)** | Each relation line adds ~10‑15 tokens (ID + description). 30 × 15 ≈ 450 tokens. | Pre‑filter to *only the relations that appear in the current domain* (e.g., electronics = 12 relations). | | **Very long few‑shot examples** (full product titles + long explanations) | 4 examples × 120 tokens ≈ 480 tokens. | Keep examples concise (strip to title + short brand information). | | **Including full product description as “Context”** (≈ 500 tokens) | Adds ~500 tokens directly. | Use a **retriever** to shrink to ≤ 150 tokens; keep the rest in a separate “document store”. | | **Embedding policy‑metadata (e.g., GDPR flags) inside the prompt** | Extra lines can add 100‑200 tokens. | Store policy flags in a *service‑side* lookup; only add a single flag token (e.g., `policy:public`). | | **Multiple turns (conversation style)** | Each turn adds overhead and cumulative tokens. | For batch labeling keep it to a **single turn** (system + user → assistant). If you need multi‑turn (e.g., clarification), handle it in the *service*, not by expanding the user prompt. | **Recommendation:** Reserve **≈ 300 tokens** as a safety buffer (2 000 – 1 700) and programmatically assert: ```python MAX_PROMPT_TOKENS = 2000 assert token_count <= MAX_PROMPT_TOKENS - 300, "Prompt too large!" ``` --- ## 4. Provider‑Specific “Hidden” Tokens | Provider | Hidden token source | Approx. size | |---|---|---| | **OpenAI** | 3 tokens per message (role marker, `\n` separator, end‑of‑message). For a 2‑message request → **6 tokens**. | +6 | | **Anthropic** | System prompt is stored separately; not counted toward the 200 k limit. | 0 | | **Google Gemini** | Adds a **single token** (`<|assistant|>`) after each assistant turn. | +1 per turn | | **Cohere** | No hidden overhead beyond the raw text. | 0 | | **Mistral / Llama** | If you use the Open‑AI‑compatible API wrapper (`v1/chat/completions`), you will incur the same 3‑token‑per‑message overhead. | +3 per message | | **Meta** (open‑source inference) | You must prepend `<|begin_of_text|>` and `<|assistant|>` manually; those count as normal tokens (≈ 2 tokens). | +2 | When building a **generic prompt‑builder** that can target multiple vendors, factor in a *provider‑specific offset*: ```python OVERHEAD = { "openai": 6, "anthropic": 0, "google": 1, "cohere": 0, "mistral": 6, # if you use chat format "llama": 6, } total = token_count_user + OVERHEAD[provider] ``` --- ## 5. Practical Token‑Counting Workflow for Production 1. **At service start** load the appropriate tokenizer for each model you may call (tiktoken, transformers’ `AutoTokenizer`, Anthropic’s `client.count_tokens`, Google’s `generativeai.Tokenizer`). 2. **When a request arrives**: - Build the *raw* prompt string (system + user). - Call `tokenizer.encode(prompt_string)` to get `n_user_tokens`. - Add the provider‑specific overhead (see table above). - **Assert** `n_total ≤ 2000`. If it exceeds, automatically: - ↓ Reduce the number of few‑shot examples (fallback to 2 instead of 4). - ↓ Trim the relation list (keep top‑N by domain usage). - ↓ Shorten the optional context (e.g., truncate to 100 tokens). 3. **Log** the final token count, the overhead breakdown, and the selected model version for audit. --- ## 6. Example: Token Accounting for an OpenAI GPT‑4‑turbo Call Suppose we have: - System message (45 tokens) - User message consisting of: * Relation table (180 tokens) * 3 few‑shot examples (260 tokens) * Entities + short context (120 tokens) * Output schema + version tag (40 tokens) **Raw token sum** = 45 + 180 + 260 + 120 + 40 = **645** **OpenAI overhead** = 6 (3 per message) **Total** = **651** tokens → Well under 2 000. Even if we double the examples (add another 86‑token example) we still sit at ~ 735 tokens. --- ## 7. Checklist for Engineers | ✔️ Item | How to verify | |---|---| | **Model‑specific context window** | Keep a config file (e.g., `model_limits.yaml`) with `max_context_tokens` per model. | | **Tokenizer correct for version** | Pin the tokenizer library version together with the model API version (e.g., `tiktoken==0.7.0`). | | **System‑vs‑user token split** | Write a small unit test that builds a 2‑message request and asserts `len(enc.encode(system)) + len(enc.encode(user)) + 6 == total`. | | **Safety buffer** | Enforce `MAX_PROMPT_TOKENS = 2000 - 300`. | | **Dynamic trimming logic** | Implement a fallback pipeline that removes the longest few‑shot example first, then shrinks the relation table, then truncates context. | | **Monitoring** | Export `prompt_token_count` and `model_name` to Prometheus; set an alert if > 1 800 tokens for any request. | | **Cross‑provider compatibility** | Run the same prompt through all tokenizers in CI and verify the count stays ≤ 2 k for each. | --- ### Bottom Line Recap * A **2 000‑token prompt** comfortably fits inside **all** current commercial LLM context windows, even the smallest (8 k) ones. * The only “hidden” tokens you need to add are **provider‑specific message overheads** (usually ≤ 6 tokens). * Keep the prompt itself minimal (system + task description + filtered relation list + 2‑4 concise few‑shots + optional short context + JSON schema). * Store everything else (full taxonomy, large example bank, raw product descriptions, business‑rule engine) in external services and inject only the *filtered* pieces you actually need for a given call. Following the token‑budget checklist above guarantees you stay under the 2 k limit while preserving maximum labeling accuracy and keeping the pipeline maintainable across any of the major commercial LLMs.

user_message: What tooling and UI features should a human review interface include to make rapid audits of LLM‑generated relation labels efficient and reliable for product catalog teams?
assistant_response:
Below is a **complete design blueprint** for the “Human Review Console” that product‑catalog teams will use every day to audit LLM‑generated relation labels.  
It is written as a **layered checklist** (tooling → UI → workflow → integration) so you can copy‑paste the relevant pieces into a product spec, an engineering ticket, or a design brief.

---

## 1️⃣ HIGH‑LEVEL REQUIREMENTS (Why the console exists)

| Goal | Success Indicator |
|------|-------------------|
| **Speed** – reviewers should be able to **accept / reject** a prediction in ≤ 3 seconds. | < 2 s mean decision time measured on a 200‑sample pilot. |
| **Reliability** – the UI must prevent accidental mis‑clicks, capture the reason for a change, and store an immutable audit trail. | 0 % “ghost‑accepts” after a post‑mortem audit. |
| **Context** – reviewers need the *entity texts*, *structured attributes*, *raw source documents* (feed, supplier sheet, review snippets) **and the LLM’s explanation**. | 95 % of “reject” decisions are justified without leaving the screen. |
| **Scalability** – the same UI must handle a few dozen items per day (manual audit) **and** thousands per day (crowd‑sourced QA, semi‑automated batch review). | No performance degradation up to 10 k rows per session. |
| **Traceability** – every action (accept, reject, edit, comment) is linked to a **versioned prompt**, **taxonomy SHA**, **LLM model + temperature**, and **timestamp**. | Full audit log export meets SOX / GDPR requirements. |
| **Feedback Loop** – the outcome of the review must flow back automatically to the **prompt‑generation / model‑fine‑tuning pipeline**. | One‑click “Send to Retrain” button creates a training example in the data‑store. |

---

## 2️⃣ TOOLING STACK (What to build on)

| Layer | Recommended Tech (production‑grade) | Why it fits an e‑commerce KG |
|-------|--------------------------------------|------------------------------|
| **Front‑end** | React (with TypeScript) + Material‑UI (MUI) or Ant Design + Redux Toolkit for state | Component library gives clean tables, chips, dialogs; TypeScript prevents typo‑driven bugs. |
| **Data Grid** | TanStack Table (formerly React‑Table) or AG‑Grid Enterprise (free tier for core features) | Virtualized rendering → smooth scrolling even with 10 k rows; column pinning, custom cell renderers. |
| **Back‑end API** | FastAPI (Python) + Pydantic models + Uvicorn + PostgreSQL + Redis cache | FastAPI integrates nicely with the same Python ecosystem you already use for the LLM service; async I/O keeps latency low. |
| **Audit Store** | Append‑only PostgreSQL table + WAL‑based snapshots **or** immutable object store (AWS S3 + Glue catalog) + version‑ed JSON‑Lines files | Guarantees tamper‑evidence; can be replayed for compliance. |
| **Authentication / Authorization** | OIDC (Keycloak, Auth0) → RBAC roles (Reviewer, Senior Reviewer, Admin) | Fine‑grained permissions (e.g., only senior reviewers can change taxonomy mappings). |
| **Search & Filtering** | Elasticsearch or Typesense (lightweight) for full‑text search over entity titles, SKUs, supplier notes | Enables “find all predictions that contain ‘refurbished’”. |
| **Real‑time Collaboration** (optional) | WebSockets (FastAPI‑WebSocket) + Yjs (CRDT) for concurrent editing | Useful for pair‑review sessions or hand‑offs. |
| **Observability** | Grafana + Loki for UI logs, Prometheus for API latencies | Detect UI slowdowns or error spikes. |
| **CI / Deployment** | Docker + Kubernetes (or simple ECS/Fargate) + Helm chart | Guarantees reproducible environments; can roll‑back UI version together with prompt version. |

*All components are **cloud‑agnostic** (GCP, AWS, Azure) – you just point the DB and storage endpoints.*

---

## 3️⃣ UI COMPONENTS & Interaction Design

Below is a **screen‑by‑screen** description.  
Think of the interface as a **single‑page application (SPA)** with a persistent top‑nav bar, a left‑hand **filter pane**, and a central **data‑grid**. The UI should be responsive (desktop first, mobile optional).

### 3.1 Top Navigation / Global Controls

| Element | Function | Details |
|---|---|---|
| **Project selector** (dropdown) | Switch between catalog projects (e.g., “Electronics”, “Home & Garden”). | Propagates `catalog_id` to API requests. |
| **Prompt version badge** | Shows the SHA of the prompt used for the currently loaded batch. | Click to open a modal with the full prompt text and example list. |
| **Taxonomy version badge** | Same as above, but for the relation taxonomy. |
| **Batch controls** | *Start new batch*, *Resume paused batch*, *Export current batch*. | Batch ID is a UUID stored on the server; you can restart later. |
| **Search bar** | Global free‑text search across entity titles, SKUs, raw source text. | Powered by Elasticsearch; auto‑complete suggestions. |
| **User indicator** | Shows logged‑in user, role, and “logout”. | Used for audit stamps. |

### 3.2 Left Sidebar – Filters & Sampling Modes

| Filter | UI Widget | Typical values |
|--------|-----------|----------------|
| **Confidence range** | Dual‑thumb slider (0–1) | Default = `[0.0, 1.0]`; preset “high” (`≥0.9`), “mid” (`0.4‑0.6`), “low” (`<0.4`). |
| **Relation type** | Multi‑select chips (taxonomy list) | Allows focusing on a specific relation (e.g., `is_variant_of`). |
| **Prediction status** | Radio group: *All*, *Accepted*, *Rejected*, *Edited*, *Unreviewed*. | Helps reviewers finish a batch. |
| **Source channel** | Checkbox list (Supplier feed, Web crawl, User review, Internal catalog). | Useful for detecting channel‑specific drift. |
| **Date / ingestion window** | Calendar picker (single day or range). | Spot recent promotions, flash sales. |
| **Custom query** | Text area for Elasticsearch DSL (advanced). | Power users can craft precise queries. |
| **Sampling mode selector** | Tabs: *Random*, *Mid‑confidence*, *Edge‑case*, *Time‑slice*. | Triggers the back‑end to generate a fresh sample set. |
| **Batch size** | Numeric spinner (10‑10 000). | Set at the start of a review session. |

All filters are **debounced** (300 ms) to avoid hammering the API.

### 3.3 Central Data Grid – Row Layout

| Column | Content | UI / Interaction |
|--------|---------|------------------|
| **Checkbox** | Select multiple rows for bulk actions. | Sticky first column. |
| **Entity A** | Product title, SKU, thumbnail (if available). | Hover → tooltip with full attribute table (price, brand, stock status). |
| **Entity B** | Same as A. | Same interactions. |
| **Predicted Relation** | Chip with relation ID + readable label. | Color‑coded per relation (e.g., green for `belongs_to_category`, orange for `offers_promotion`). |
| **Confidence** | Progress bar (0‑100 %). | Click to see the numeric value and distribution histogram (modal). |
| **LLM Explanation** | Small text snippet (max 2 lines). | Expand → full explanation + raw LLM output (JSON). |
| **Context / Source Snippet** | Truncated source (≤ 120 chars). | Tooltip shows the full raw source (e.g., supplier description). |
| **Review Action** | **Three inline buttons**: <kbd>✔ Accept</kbd> | <kbd>✖ Reject</kbd> | <kbd>✎ Edit</kbd>. | Buttons stay sticky on scroll; keyboard shortcuts (`A`, `R`, `E`). |
| **Reviewer Comment** | Inline text field (appears after Reject/Edit). | Auto‑saves on blur; mandatory for Reject/Edit. |
| **Timestamp / Reviewer** | Auto‑filled after action. | Read‑only. |
| **History icon** | Small clock icon → opens a modal with full audit trail for that pair. | Shows every version (previous prompt, previous label, edits). |

**Virtualization** – Use TanStack Table’s `useVirtualizer` so rendering stays sub‑50 ms even with 10 k rows.

### 3.4 Row‑Level Actions (What happens under the hood)

| Action | Backend call | Side‑effects |
|--------|--------------|--------------|
| **Accept** | `POST /audit/{row_id}` with payload `{status: "accept", reviewer: user, confidence: <as‑shown>}` | Writes immutable audit record; updates `prediction_status` to *Accepted*. |
| **Reject** | Same endpoint, `{status:"reject", comment: "...", reviewer: user}` | Writes audit; optionally triggers “re‑label” job (see §5). |
| **Edit** | `POST /audit/{row_id}` with `{status:"edit", new_relation_id, new_confidence?, comment}` | Creates a **corrected label** that becomes the **ground‑truth** for downstream fine‑tuning. |
| **Bulk Accept/Reject** | `POST /batch_audit` with list of row IDs + common action. | Faster for high‑confidence batches. |
| **Export** | `GET /export?filter=…` → CSV/JSONL download. | Used for external QA or compliance snapshots. |
| **Send to Retrain** | `POST /retrain_queue` with selected rows. | Places rows in a training‑data registry; tags them with the current prompt SHA. |
| **Undo** (within 5 min) | `POST /undo/{audit_id}` | Reverts the audit record (creates a new “undo” entry). |

All API calls are **idempotent** (use row‑ID + action hash) so that accidental reloads do not duplicate records.

### 3.5 Modals / Overlays

| Modal | Trigger | Content |
|-------|---------|---------|
| **Prompt Viewer** | Click on Prompt badge. | Full prompt text, list of few‑shot examples, temperature, model name, hash, creation date. |
| **Taxonomy Viewer** | Click on Taxonomy badge. | Tree view of relations, descriptions, deprecation notes. |
| **Full Explanation** | Click on explanation column or the progress bar. | Shows: LLM raw JSON, token usage, temperature, token count, source context. |
| **History** | Click clock icon on a row. | Timeline: initial prediction → edits → re‑labels → final status. |
| **Bulk Action Summary** | After selecting rows and clicking “Bulk Accept”. | Confirmation dialog with count, estimated time, and a “download selected as CSV before applying” checkbox. |
| **Feedback / Bug Report** | Persistent floating button (✉). | Small form that auto‑attaches the current row’s data for the engineering team. |

---

## 4️⃣ WORKFLOW & USER STORIES

### 4.1 Typical Day‑to‑Day Review (Fast Path)

1. **Open console**, select **“Mid‑confidence”** mode, set confidence range `0.45‑0.55`, filter to `Relation = is_variant_of`, batch size **500**.  
2. System generates a **batch ID** (`b‑20260828‑001`) and loads the first screen (10 k rows max, paginated).  
3. Reviewer scans rows, **presses `A`** to accept most obvious matches (confidence > 0.48, clear product titles).  
4. For ambiguous rows, **presses `E`** → Edit dialog opens, selects the correct relation from a dropdown, adds optional comment.  
5. After 12 min, the reviewer hits **“Submit Batch”** → backend returns a **summary** (Accepted = 378, Edited = 32, Rejected = 90).  
6. System automatically **pushes the 32 edited rows** to the **Fine‑Tune Queue** (they become gold training examples).  
7. Reviewer clicks **“Export → CSV”** to hand the 90 rejected rows to a senior SME for a deeper dive.

### 4.2 Edge‑Case Review (Deep Dive)

1. Activate **“Edge‑case”** tab, filter to `source = Supplier feed` and `brand = "Apple"` (to catch brand‑name collisions).  
2. Use the **search bar** to look for “refurbished”.  
3. For each flagged row, open **History** modal to see if the same pair was previously labelled differently (detects inconsistency).  
4. Use **Bulk Reject** to mark all those that are clearly mis‑labelled, then add a **global comment** (“Supplier feed mixes fruit/brand”).  
5. Click **“Create ticket in Jira”** (integrated button) that pre‑populates a ticket with the filtered view link and comment.

### 4.3 Quality‑Assurance Audit (Monthly)

1. Run a **random stratified sample** of 5 000 rows from the last month.  
2. Export the **review log** to a data‑science notebook.  
3. Compute **macro‑F1, ECE, Brier** (using the functions from the previous answer).  
4. If any metric is out of band, **open a “Model‑Degradation” incident** (integrated with ServiceNow).  
5. The incident template automatically contains the **prompt version**, **taxonomy SHA**, **sample CSV**, and a **link to the console view** for reproducing the problem.

assistant_response:
## TL;DR  
**Yes – keep the prompt (including the few‑shot examples, schema tables, and any optional context) ≤ 2 000 tokens if you want to stay safely inside the context window of the *majority* of production LLM APIs today.**  

*Why it works*: most “chat‑completion” models (OpenAI GPT‑3.5‑Turbo, GPT‑4‑Turbo, Claude 2, Gemini 1.5‑Flash, Llama‑2‑Chat‑13B) expose a **8 k‑token context window** (sometimes 16 k, 32 k, or 100 k for the newest tier). The model’s response also consumes tokens, so the **prompt + max‑output‑tokens** must be ≤ window size. Leaving a 2 k‑token safety margin guarantees:

* you can ask for a reasonably long JSON answer (≈ 200–300 tokens) plus system messages without exhausting the window,  
* you avoid “context‑length‑exceeded” errors that would otherwise crash a batch job, and  
* you keep cost predictable (most providers charge per 1 k tokens for *both* prompt and output).

Below is a **complete reference** that:

1. **Confirms the 2 k‑token rule** with data from the major APIs (Oct 2024‑Nov 2024 snapshot).  
2. Lists **caveats** (different models, streaming, tokenizers, multilingual text, and hidden system‑message tokens).  
3. Shows **how to measure token usage** programmatically for each vendor.  
4. Gives **practical sizing guidelines** (template design, chunking, “rolling‑window” tricks) for when you *do* need more than 2 k tokens of prompt.  

Feel free to copy the code snippets into your data‑pipeline or CI checks.

---

## 1️⃣ CONFIRMING THE “≤ 2 k TOKENS” RULE

| Provider / Model | Published Context Window (tokens) | Typical “safe margin” used in production | Evidence source |
|------------------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------------|-----------------|
| **OpenAI** – `gpt-3.5-turbo` (default) | 4 096 | 2 000‑prompt + 1 000‑output | OpenAI docs (2024‑11) |
| **OpenAI** – `gpt-4-turbo` | 128 k (beta) – *but default quota for most accounts = 8 k* | 2 k‑prompt + 2 k‑output (conservative) | OpenAI release notes, community benchmarks |
| **Anthropic** – `claude-2.1` | 100 k (beta) – production default 100 k | 2 k‑prompt + 5 k‑output (most users use 2 k) | Anthropic API docs, “max_tokens” field |
| **Google Gemini** – `gemini-1.5-flash` | 1 048 576 (≈ 1 M) *but billed per 1 k* | No strict safety margin needed for small tasks; however many teams still cap at 2 k for latency reasons. | Gemini technical overview |
| **Meta Llama 2‑Chat** (hosted via Azure) | 8 k (standard) / 32 k (preview) | 2 k‑prompt + 2 k‑output | Azure OpenAI pricing sheet |
| **Mistral‑Large** (hosted on HuggingFace Inference) | 8 k | 2 k‑prompt + 2 k‑output | HF Inference docs |
| **Cohere** – `command-r-plus` | 128 k | 2 k‑prompt + 5 k‑output (most pipelines still use 2 k) | Cohere API reference |

**Take‑away**: **All of the “standard‑tier” models that most enterprises use have a **minimum guaranteed window of 4 k to 8 k tokens**. A 2 k‑token prompt leaves a comfortable cushion for the model’s reply and any system‑message overhead, making it a safe universal rule of thumb.

---

## 2️⃣ CAVEATS & EDGE CASES

| Situation | Why 2 k may be insufficient or overly conservative | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Models with larger windows (16 k, 32 k, 128 k)** | You could afford longer prompts, but cost per token still applies. Over‑loading the prompt can increase latency. | Use the larger window **only when you truly need it** (e.g., feeding an entire product catalog segment). Keep a *configurable* max‑prompt‑size per model. |
| **Streaming / incremental generation** | Some APIs (OpenAI, Claude) let you stream tokens back; the *total* tokens still count against the window, but you can stop early. | Set `max_output_tokens` low (e.g., 250) and stop streaming once you have a valid JSON. |
| **Multilingual text** | Tokenizers (tiktoken, Claude’s tokenizer, Gemini’s BPE) treat non‑ASCII characters as **more tokens per character**. A 2 k‑character Chinese paragraph could be ~3 k tokens. | Run a *pre‑flight token count* on the raw prompt; if token count > 2 k, truncate or translate to English where possible. |
| **System messages / role‑messages** | In chat‑style APIs you must also count **system** and **assistant** messages. A typical “You are an expert…” system prompt can be 50‑200 tokens. | Add those tokens to the 2 k budget (i.e., compute total = system + user + examples). |
| **Dynamic context tables (e.g., taxonomy of 200 relations)** | Each relation entry (“ID – label – description”) can be 10‑15 tokens; 200 entries ≈ 2 500 tokens, already over the limit. | **Compress** the table: use IDs only, store longer descriptions in a side‑lookup service, or send only the *subset* relevant to the current domain. |
| **Prompt engineering tricks (chain‑of‑thought, tool‑use)** | Adding chain‑of‑thought exemplars can double the prompt size. | Keep chain‑of‑thought examples **short** (one‑sentence reasoning) and limit to 2‑3 per class. |
| **Batching many pairs in one request** | You may be tempted to send 20 pairs in a single prompt to reduce API calls. That quickly blows up token count. | **Batch size ≈ 5–10 pairs** when using few‑shot; otherwise, stick to one pair per call for reliability. |
| **Token‑count rounding / hidden whitespaces** | Some tokenizers count leading/trailing spaces as separate tokens. | Normalise whitespace (`' '.join(text.split())`) before counting. |

---

## 3️⃣ HOW TO MEASURE TOKEN USAGE (Code Snippets)

### 3.1 OpenAI (tiktoken)

```python
import tiktoken

def count_openai_tokens(prompt: str, model: str = "gpt-3.5-turbo"):
    enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model(model)
    return len(enc.encode(prompt))

# Example
prompt = "You are an e‑commerce taxonomy expert.\n\n" + ...  # your full prompt
print(count_openai_tokens(prompt, "gpt-4-turbo"))   # returns integer token count
```

*Note*: `tiktoken` also offers `model_to_encoding` for older models.

### 3.2 Anthropic (Claude)

Anthropic ships a small Python helper:

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic
from anthropic import Tokenizer  # pip install anthropic[extra]

def count_anthropic_tokens(prompt: str):
    tokenizer = Tokenizer()
    return tokenizer.encode(prompt).num_tokens

print(count_anthropic_tokens(prompt))
```

If you’re using the HTTP API directly, you can also ask for token usage in the response (`"completion_usage": {"input_tokens": ..., "output_tokens": ...}`) after the call.

### 3.3 Google Gemini

```python
from google.generativeai import GenerativeModel, configure
import google.generativeai as genai

def count_gemini_tokens(text: str, model_name="gemini-1.5-flash"):
    # Gemini does not expose a public tokenizer; use the unofficial library:
    from genai_tokenizer import Tokenizer  # pip install genai-tokenizer
    tokenizer = Tokenizer(model_name)
    return tokenizer.count_tokens(text)

print(count_gemini_tokens(prompt))
```

(If you want a guaranteed count, you can call the API with `"safety_settings": [{"category":"HARM_CATEGORY_DANGEROUS","threshold":"BLOCK_NONE"}]` and set `"max_output_tokens":0`; the response returns `"usageMetadata":{"promptTokenCount":…}` without generating text.)

### 3.4 Cohere

```python
import cohere
client = cohere.Client('YOUR_API_KEY')

def count_cohere_tokens(text):
    # Cohere returns token count on a dummy generate call
    resp = client.generate(
        model='command-r-plus',
        prompt=text,
        max_tokens=1,          # minimal generation
        temperature=0.0,
        stream=False,
        return_likelihoods='NONE',
        truncate='NONE'
    )
    return resp.meta.tokens.input_tokens

print(count_cohere_tokens(prompt))
```

### 3.5 General wrapper

You can abstract all of the above:

```python
def token_count(prompt: str, provider: str, model: str):
    if provider == "openai":
        return count_openai_tokens(prompt, model)
    elif provider == "anthropic":
        return count_anthropic_tokens(prompt)
    elif provider == "gemini":
        return count_gemini_tokens(prompt, model)
    elif provider == "cohere":
        return count_cohere_tokens(prompt)
    else:
        raise ValueError("Unsupported provider")
```

Use this function in a **pre‑flight check** before sending the request.

---

## 4️⃣ PRACTICAL GUIDELINES FOR SIZING PROMPTS

### 4.1 The “2 k‑Token Budget” Formula

```
max_window = provider_window(provider, model)          # e.g. 8192
safety_margin = 2000                                  # our rule of thumb
max_output   = 500   # leave room for JSON + explanation
max_prompt   = max_window - safety_margin - max_output
```

| Provider | `max_window` (default) | `max_prompt` (using 2 k safety) |
|---|---|---|
| OpenAI `gpt‑3.5‑turbo` | 4 096 | 1 596 |
| OpenAI `gpt‑4‑turbo` (8 k) | 8 192 | 5 692 |
| Anthropic `claude‑2.1` | 100 k | 98 k (effectively unlimited) |
| Gemini `flash` | 1 048 576 | 1 046 576 (practically unlimited) |
| Llama‑2‑Chat‑13B (Azure) | 8 192 | 5 692 |

**Implementation tip** – expose `max_prompt` as a **configurable constant** per model in your service’s config file.

### 4.2 Prompt‑Design Checklist (keep you under the limit)

| Component | Typical token cost | How to trim |
|---|---|---|
| System message (“You are an expert …”) | 40‑120 | Keep to 1‑2 sentences; move long policy text to a DOC URL and mention the URL only. |
| Relation taxonomy table (ID‑label‑desc) | 10 tokens per entry (≈ 200 tokens for 20 relations) | Store only **ID + short label** in the prompt; keep full description in a side‑lookup that the LLM can request via a “tool”. |
| Few‑shot examples | 30‑80 tokens each (depends on entity text length) | Limit to **2‑3** examples per class; use *placeholder* tokens like `<PRODUCT_A>` and replace them at runtime with the actual names (makes token count deterministic). |
| Optional context (e.g., recent clicks, review snippets) | 5‑15 tokens per snippet | **Summarise** (e.g., “Top‑3 user intents: …”) or truncate to the first 100 characters. |
| Entity text (product title, description) | 1‑2 tokens per word; Chinese ~1.5 tokens/char | **Truncate** to the first 12‑15 words; add an ellipsis “…”. |
| Expected output format (JSON schema) | 30‑70 | Keep minimal – just the key names (`relation_id`, `confidence`, `explanation`). |
| **Total** | ≤ 2 000 | Verify with the token‑count function. |

### 4.3 When You *Need* More Than 2 k Tokens

| Technique | When to use | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Chunked taxonomy lookup** | > 30 relations or long descriptions | Send only the *subset* of relations that are *relevant* to the current domain (e.g., only electronics‑specific relations). Determine relevance via a quick rule‑based filter (`entity_a.category`). |
| **External tool / function calling** (OpenAI `function` calling, Claude `tools`) | You need the full description but want to keep the prompt short | Include a short “tool request” in the prompt (`call get_relation_desc(id)`) and let the model invoke the helper; the LLM only sees the ID. |
| **Rolling context window** | You have a long list of entity pairs that share a common background (e.g., same brand) | Send the background once (≤ 500 tokens) and then stream each pair in separate calls with `system` message referencing the previous `assistant` message via “memory”. |
| **Hybrid retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG)** | Need to feed a giant product catalogue (10 k+ items) | Store the catalogue in a vector store; the prompt contains only the *retrieved* nearest neighbours (usually ≤ 10) and a short “retrieved‑summary” token budget. |
| **Model‑switching** | Prompt > 2 k unavoidable (e.g., legal clause extraction) | Use a **larger‑window model** (Claude‑2.1 100 k, Gemini‑1.5‑Flash 1 M) for those rare heavy‑weight calls. Keep a fallback to the cheaper 4 k model for the majority. |

**Safety net**: before dispatching a large prompt, always run the token‑count check and, if it exceeds `max_prompt`, automatically **fallback** to the next‑larger model or **reject** with a clear log message.

*Add this wrapper to every labeling micro‑service; unit‑test it with a few edge‑case strings (long Chinese text, many emojis, etc.) to confirm the token count matches reality.*

## 6️⃣ QUICK‑Reference Cheat‑Sheet

| Model (2024) | Default context window | Recommended max prompt (2 k margin) | Typical max output you can still ask for |
|--------------|------------------------|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `gpt‑3.5‑turbo` | 4 k | 1 600 tokens | 400–500 tokens |
| `gpt‑4‑turbo` (8 k) | 8 k | 5 600 tokens | 800–1 000 tokens |
| `claude‑2.1` | 100 k | 98 k | 2 k (most apps never need more) |
| `gemini‑1.5‑flash` | 1 M | ~1 M (no practical limit) | 2 k‑5 k |
| `llama‑2‑chat‑13b` (Azure) | 8 k | 5 600 tokens | 800 tokens |
| `command‑r‑plus` | 128 k | 126 k | 2 k |
| **Rule of thumb** | ≥ 4 k → keep prompt ≤ 2 k | ≥ 8 k → keep prompt ≤ 5 k if you need longer answers | Adjust upward proportionally if you have a larger window and you *know* you’ll need more context. |

---

## 7️⃣ FINAL Checklist for Your Team

1. **Define `SAFETY_MARGIN = 2000` tokens** globally (override per model if you have a larger‑window plan).  
2. **Implement a pre‑flight token counter** (`token_count`) for every request.  
3. **Log `prompt_tokens` and `output_tokens`** for every call; alert if `prompt_tokens` > `max_prompt`.  
4. **Keep system messages ≤ 150 tokens** and move any long policy text to a side‑resource.  
5. **Compress tables** (IDs only) and use *function calling* for long descriptions.  
6. **When exceeding the budget**:  
   * try truncating the *entity* text first,  
   * then drop low‑importance few‑shot examples,  
   * finally fall back to a larger‑window model (if you have one).  
7. **Unit‑test** with the longest realistic real‑world prompt you expect (e.g., a refurbished product plus a 100‑word user review). Verify the token counter matches the API’s reported usage.  
8. **Document** the token budget in the API spec (OpenAPI `x-token-limit` extension) so downstream engineers know the limits.

---

### Bottom Line

- **Yes** – *≤ 2 k tokens* is a solid, provider‑agnostic safety threshold for the majority of production LLM APIs today.  
- **Measure** with the vendor‑specific tokenizer (or a reliable third‑party library).  
- **Plan** for the occasional need for larger contexts by using chunking, external tools, or higher‑window models.  
- **Automate** the check and monitoring; that’s what will keep your e‑commerce KG‑labeling pipeline accurate, cost‑effective, and failure‑free as the catalog evolves.

# Automated Few‑Shot Prompt Construction Pipeline  
**Goal:** For every (entity‑A, entity‑B) pair that must be labeled, build a **≤ 2 000‑token** prompt that contains  

* a short, *stable* system instruction,  
* a **compact, highly relevant few‑shot example set**,  
* **contextual signals** (e.g., recent clicks, supplier notes, taxonomy hints),  

and then call the LLM. The pipeline must be **fully automated**, **low‑latency**, **cost‑aware**, and **observable**.

---

## 1. High‑Level Architecture Diagram

```
+---------------------------+      +-------------------+      +-------------------+
|   Entity‑Pair Producer    | -->  |   Prompt Builder  | -->  |   LLM Service API |
+---------------------------+      +-------------------+      +-------------------+
          |                                 |                         |
          |  (entity ids, raw text)          |  (prompt text)          |  (JSON label)
          v                                 v                         v
+-------------------+          +--------------------+        +---------------------+
|   Context Store   | <------> | Example Selector   | <------|  Prompt Cache (Redis)|
+-------------------+          +--------------------+        +---------------------+
          ^                                 ^                         |
          |                                 |                         |
+-------------------+          +--------------------+                |
|   Taxonomy /      | <------> | Summarizer Engine  | <----------------+
|   Policy Service  |          +--------------------+   (prompt hash →  |
+-------------------+                                             stored prompt)
```

*All components run as independent micro‑services (Docker/K8s) and communicate via gRPC/HTTP+JSON. The flow is:*

1. **Entity‑Pair Producer** (e.g., a change‑data‑capture stream from the catalog DB) emits a pair `({id_A},{id_B})`.  
2. **Prompt Builder** pulls:
   * the **system instruction** (static, < 50 tokens),  
   * a **hand‑picked few‑shot set** (dynamic, ≤ 1 200 tokens),  
   * **contextual signals** (dynamic, ≤ 600 tokens),  
   * concatenates them, checks token count, caches the final prompt, then forwards it to the LLM.  

If the cached version already exists for the *same* (entity‑pair, taxonomy version, context version) it is reused, saving time and tokens.

---

## 2. Component Details

### 2.1. Taxonomy / Policy Service (Static Config)

* **Inputs:** versioned taxonomy JSON/YAML (`relations.yaml`).  
* **Outputs:**  
  * **System instruction** (≤ 50 tokens).  
  * **Relation table** formatted for the prompt (e.g., a markdown table).  
* **Versioning:** stored in Git; a SHA (`taxonomy_sha`) is included in every prompt hash.

### 2.2. Context Store (Dynamic Signals)

| Source | Typical size | Token budget | Pre‑processing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product title / short description | ≤ 30 tokens | 0 – 50 | raw text, no change |
| Brand / category hierarchy | ≤ 10 tokens | 0 – 20 | normalized IDs |
| Recent click‑stream (last 3 events) | 3 × ≈ 30 tokens | ≤ 90 | truncate to most recent |
| Supplier feed notes (max 2 lines) | ≤ 40 tokens | ≤ 50 | sentence‑case |
| Promotion / discount flag | 1 token | 1 | boolean literal |
| *Optional* user‑review snippet (1‑sentence) | ≤ 30 tokens | ≤ 40 | strip PII |

*All fields are **token‑counted** on ingestion (using the same tokenizer as the target LLM). If total > 600 tokens, the **Summarizer Engine** is invoked (see §2.4).*

### 2.3. Example Selector (Few‑Shot Retrieval)

**Goal:**  Choose the *most informative* ≤ N examples (N ≈ 10–12) that together stay under the *few‑shot budget* (≈ 1 200 tokens).  

#### 2.3.1. Indexing  

* Store every **labeled training triple** (`entity_A`, `entity_B`, `relation_id`) in a **dense vector store** (e.g., FAISS, Qdrant) using a **dual‑embedding** strategy:  

  1. **Entity embedding** – 384‑dim sentence‑transformer (`all-MiniLM-L6‑v2`) on concatenated titles.  
  2. **Relation‑aware embedding** – concatenate the relation ID token (`<REL:belongs_to_category>`) to the entity text before encoding, so that examples of the same relation cluster together.  

* Also store a **metadata bucket**: `relation_id`, `source_quality` (human‑curated vs. auto‑generated), **timestamp** (for freshness).

#### 2.3.2. Retrieval Logic (per request)

```python
def select_few_shot(pair, taxonomy_sha, max_few_shot_tokens=1200):
    # 1️⃣ Encode the query pair
    q_vec = embed(pair.title_A + " " + pair.title_B)

    # 2️⃣ Retrieve top‑K (K=50) candidates
    candidates = vector_store.search(q_vec, k=50)

    # 3️⃣ Rank candidates by a composite score:
    #    score = α * similarity + β * freshness + γ * source_quality
    #    (α≈0.6, β≈0.2, γ≈0.2)
    ranked = sorted(candidates,
                    key=lambda c: (0.6*c.similarity +
                                   0.2*recency_score(c.ts) +
                                   0.2*c.quality))

    # 4️⃣ Greedy pack until token budget exhausted
    selected = []
    used = 0
    for cand in ranked:
        ex_text = format_example(cand)   # ~70‑100 tokens per example
        ex_tok = token_len(ex_text)
        if used + ex_tok > max_few_shot_tokens:
            break
        selected.append(ex_text)
        used += ex_tok
    return selected
```

*Why a greedy pack?*  
- Guarantees **deterministic token usage** (no post‑hoc trimming).  
- Simple to parallelize; we rarely need optimal packing because each example is roughly the same size.

#### 2.3.3. Diversity Guard (optional)

If the top‑K candidates belong to a single relation, enforce **relation diversity** by forcing inclusion of the *next most similar* example from an *under‑represented* relation (up to a max of 3 distinct relations). This improves **generalisation** when the query is ambiguous.

### 2.4. Summarizer Engine (Context Compression)

When the raw contextual signals exceed **≈ 600 tokens**, we run a *lightweight* summarizer (e.g., `gpt‑3.5‑turbo` with temperature 0) that:

* **Extracts** the most salient sentences (using a relevance score vs. the entity pair).  
* **Reduces** each field to a **single sentence** or bullet.  

Implementation:

```python
def compress_context(raw_context, target_tokens=600):
    prompt = f"""You are a concise e‑commerce summarizer.
Given the following fields, keep only the information that helps decide the relation between
Entity A and Entity B. Return a JSON with the same keys, each value shortened to at most 2 sentences.

{json.dumps(raw_context, indent=2)}
"""
    response = llm_chat(prompt, max_output_tokens=target_tokens)
    return json.loads(response)
```

*The summarizer is cached per `(entity_A_id, entity_B_id, taxonomy_sha)` to avoid recomputation.*

### 2.5. Prompt Builder (Token‑Budget Enforcer)

1. **Assemble static parts**  
   - System instruction (≈ 40 tokens).  
   - Relation table (≈ 200 tokens; static, shared across all requests).  

2. **Insert selected few‑shot examples** (≈ 1 200 tokens max).  

3. **Insert compressed contextual signals** (≈ 600 tokens max).  

4. **Add the current query** (entity titles + optional raw snippet) – usually ≤ 80 tokens.  

5. **Compute total token count** using the target model’s encoder (`tiktoken` for OpenAI, `anthropic‑tokenizer`, etc.).  

6. **If total > 2 000**, fall back in this order:  

   a. **Trim few‑shot examples** (remove the lowest‑scoring example).  
   b. **Re‑compress context** with a stricter target (‑20 % tokens).  
   c. **If still > 2 000**, abort and log a “prompt‑overflow” event; route the pair to a **rule‑based fallback**.

7. **Generate a deterministic hash** of the final prompt (`sha256(prompt_text)[:10]`).  

8. **Store in Prompt Cache** (`Redis` with TTL = 48 h). Subsequent identical pairs hit the cache instantly (≈ 1 ms).

### 2.6. LLM Service API Wrapper

* Handles **retry logic**, **circuit‑breaker**, **rate‑limit throttling**.  
* Enforces **temperature=0** (deterministic) for production labeling.  
* Returns **structured JSON** (relation_id, confidence, explanation).  
* Emits **metadata** (`prompt_hash`, `prompt_token_count`, `output_token_count`, `latency_ms`) to the **Monitoring Service**.

### 2.7. Monitoring & Metrics

| Metric | Description | Alert Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| `prompt_token_count` | Tokens used in the constructed prompt. | > 1 900 (warning) |
| `few_shot_example_count` | Number of examples injected. | < 5 (info) – may indicate overly aggressive trimming. |
| `context_compression_ratio` | `raw_context_tokens / compressed_tokens`. | > 3 (info) |
| `cache_hit_rate` | % of requests served from Prompt Cache. | < 70 % (investigate cache TTL or key design). |
| `llm_latency_ms` | Round‑trip time to the LLM. | > 800 ms (warning) |
| `cost_per_1k_tokens` | Running total of token usage * model price. | > budgeted amount (daily/weekly). |
| `label_accuracy_estimate` | Aggregate of `confidence` scores after human audit. | < 0.85 (trigger re‑tuning). |
| `prompt_overflow_rate` | % of requests that needed fallback trimming. | > 5 % (review selection criteria). |

All metrics are pushed to **Prometheus**, visualized in **Grafana**, and archived in **BigQuery** for long‑term analysis.

---

## 3. End‑to‑End Request Flow (Pseudo‑Code)

```python
def label_relation(pair):
    # 0️⃣ early cache lookup
    cache_key = f"{pair.id_A}:{pair.id_B}:{taxonomy_sha}"
    cached = redis.get(cache_key)
    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)

    # 1️⃣ fetch static system instruction & relation table
    system_instr = taxonomy_service.get_system_instruction()
    rel_table   = taxonomy_service.get_relation_table()

    # 2️⃣ retrieve raw contextual signals
    raw_ctx = context_store.get_signals(pair.id_A, pair.id_B)

    # 3️⃣ select few‑shot examples
    few_shot = example_selector.select_few_shot(pair)

    # 4️⃣ compress context if needed
    if token_len(raw_ctx) > 600:
        ctx = summarizer_engine.compress_context(raw_ctx, target_tokens=600)
    else:
        ctx = raw_ctx

    # 5️⃣ build prompt (token‑budget enforced)
    prompt = prompt_builder.build(
                system_instr=system_instr,
                relation_table=rel_table,
                few_shot_examples=few_shot,
                context=ctx,
                query_pair=pair,
                max_tokens=2000)

    # 6️⃣ store prompt in cache (hash based)
    prompt_hash = sha256(prompt.encode()).hexdigest()[:10]
    redis.setex(f"prompt:{prompt_hash}", 48*3600, prompt)

    # 7️⃣ call LLM
    response = llm_wrapper.chat(prompt, max_output_tokens=400)

    # 8️⃣ log metadata
    monitoring.emit({
        "prompt_hash": prompt_hash,
        "prompt_tokens": token_len(prompt),
        "output_tokens": response.output_token_count,
        "latency_ms": response.latency_ms,
        "cache_hit": False,
    })

    # 9️⃣ cache final label (so next identical pair skips all steps)
    redis.setex(cache_key, 48*3600, json.dumps(response.json))

    return response.json
```

---

## 4. What to Do When the 2 k‑Token Limit Is Tight

| Situation | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| **Too many candidate examples** (e.g., 20‑plus highly similar) | Increase the **similarity threshold** when retrieving candidates, or limit retrieval to top‑K = 30 before greedy packing. |
| **Context fields keep blowing up** (e.g., a product description of 1 500 tokens) | **Pre‑summarize** all long free‑text fields at ingestion time (store a 2‑sentence abstract) and only fetch the abstract for real‑time labeling. |
| **Unexpected spikes in token usage** | Deploy an **asynchronous token‑budget auditor** that runs nightly on the request logs, flags any > 1 950‑token prompts, and surfaces them to the data‑engineer on‑call. |
| **Model upgrade expands max context** (e.g., moving from GPT‑3.5‑turbo to GPT‑4‑turbo) | Keep the **2 k rule** for *production* for latency & cost reasons; create a **parallel “high‑budget” pipeline** for offline bulk jobs that can safely use 5–8 k tokens. |

---

## 5. Tools & Libraries (as of Aug 2026)

| Layer | Recommended open‑source / cloud component |
|---|---|
| **Vector store** | **Qdrant** (cloud‑managed) or **FAISS** + `ivf‑pq` for high‑throughput. |
| **Embedding model** | `sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2` (fast, 384‑dim) or `e5‑base` for higher quality. |
| **Tokenizer** | `tiktoken` (OpenAI), `anthropic‑tokenizer`, `google‑generativeai` (for Gemini). |
| **Cache** | **Redis** (cluster mode) with TTL; can also use **AWS ElastiCache**. |
| **LLM API wrapper** | **OpenAI’s python SDK**, **Anthropic’s python client**, **Google Generative AI SDK** – all support `max_output_tokens` and `temperature`. |
| **Summarizer** | Tiny instruction‑tuned model `llama‑3‑8B‑Instruct` hosted on your own GPU cluster (≈ 0.2 USD/1 k tokens vs. 0.03 USD for a full‑size model). |
| **Monitoring** | **Prometheus** + **Grafana**, **OpenTelemetry** instrumentation for latency & token metrics. |
| **Orchestration** | **Kubernetes** + **Argo Workflows** for batch re‑run jobs; **Knative** for on‑demand HTTP services. |
| **CI/CD** | GitHub Actions that run a **prompt token‑size test** on every PR (`python -c "assert token_len(prompt) <= 2000"`). |

---

## 6. Checklist for a New Deployment

| ✅ | Item |
|---|---|
| **Prompt size limit** – enforce ≤ 2 000 tokens in CI and at runtime. |
| **Few‑shot example budget** – ≤ 1 200 tokens (≈ 12 examples). |
| **Context budget** – ≤ 600 tokens after compression. |
| **Cache hit‑rate** ≥ 80 % after 1 h of traffic. |
| **Latency SLA** ≤ 300 ms (cold start) + LLM latency ≤ 800 ms. |
| **Cost tracking** – token usage logged per day, alerts on > 5 % rise. |
| **Accuracy audit** – weekly sample of 500 auto‑labels, compute human‑review agreement; retrain selector if agreement < 0.90. |
| **Versioned artefacts** – taxonomy SHA, prompt SHA, selector model version stored in DB alongside each KG triple. |
| **Fallback path** – rule‑engine for any request that exceeds token budget after all trimming steps. |

---

### TL;DR Pipeline Summary

1. **Ingest** entity pair → fetch **static taxonomy** (system instruction + relation table).  
2. **Retrieve** a *dense similarity* set of labeled triples; **rank** by similarity + freshness + quality.  
3. **Greedy‑pack** the top‑ranked examples until the **few‑shot budget** (≈ 1 200 tokens) is reached.  
4. **Gather** dynamic contextual signals; **compress** if > 600 tokens (light summarizer).  
5. **Assemble** prompt, **verify** token count ≤ 2 000, **hash** and **cache** it.  
6. **Call** the LLM, **store** the label, **log** metrics.  
7. **Monitor** token usage, cache hit‑rate, latency, confidence‑based accuracy; loop back to adjust retrieval thresholds or summarization aggressiveness.

Following this design you will **maximise labeling accuracy** (by presenting the model with the most relevant, high‑quality examples and up‑to‑date context) **while guaranteeing that every request stays comfortably under the 2 k‑token limit**, keeping latency low, cost predictable, and the whole system maintainable. Happy prompting!

## User‑Facing Receipt – What a Non‑Technical Person Needs at a Glance | **Section** | **What to Show** | **Why it Helps Understanding** | **How to Phrase It (Plain Language)** | |-------------|------------------|--------------------------------|----------------------------------------| | **1. Header & Reference** | • Title (e.g., *“Benefits Eligibility Decision”*)
• Unique receipt number (e.g., **#2026‑08‑28‑00123**)

What You Changed** | • Exact data you added or edited (e.g., name, date of birth, relationship)
• A tiny icon or check‑mark confirming the entry was accepted | Makes the user confident that the system recorded the right information. | “You added a dependent: **Emma Rivera**, born 03/12/2018, relationship = Child.” | | **5. New Situation (After Your Change)** | • Updated eligibility status
• Updated score or a visual “you passed the threshold” indicator | Shows the immediate result of the user’s action. | “After adding Emma, you are now **Eligible** (score = 0.78 > 0.70).” | | **6. Why the Change Matters** | • One‑sentence explanation linking the data change to the outcome (e.g., “Adding a qualifying child raised your score by 0.33, moving you above the eligibility threshold.”) | Turns a raw number into an understandable cause‑effect story. | “Your eligibility is based on a score. Adding a qualified child increased your score enough to meet the program’s cut‑off.” | | **7. Human Review (If Applicable)** | • Whether a case‑worker will still look at the case
• Name, photo (optional), role, and expected review time | Reinforces that a person still has final authority, which is comforting for socially sensitive decisions. | “Your case will be reviewed by **Maria G., Senior Benefits Officer**.
